# Legion on Kubernetes

This runbook covers the worker image, the session store, the Kubernetes runtime, the operator-launched controller, and the one thing in it a role does for itself:
running a workload in the cluster from a role ([Running a workload in the cluster from a role](#running-a-workload-in-the-cluster-from-a-role)).

This file uses semantic line breaks: one sentence per line, and a long sentence may break after a clause.
A blank line separates list items.
Add a new item next to the item it belongs with, never at the end of a list unless it belongs there, so two pull requests that add items or change different sentences do not conflict.
`bun scripts/semantic-line-breaks.ts docs/kubernetes.md` checks the layout, and `--write` fixes it.

The Go coordinator (`packages/daemon`, LEGION-208) runs each process as an Agent Sandbox;
its live proof is `scripts/e2e/stage4b-sandbox-tree.sh` on the production cluster.
The TypeScript daemon no longer runs on Kubernetes:
it refuses `runtime: kubernetes` at config load and names the Go daemon (LEGION-286), and its sources were deleted on 2026-10-03.
Its runtime's section below is kept for reference until someone removes it (LEGION-223).

## Worker image

Every Legion agent process under `runtime: kubernetes` — architect, planner, implementer, tester, reviewer, merger
— runs from one image, `ghcr.io/cybermonklabs/legion-worker` (public), on Oh My Pi or, for a phase worker `worker_backends` puts on `claude`, on Claude Code.
It carries:

- the pinned OMP fork build the daemon's default `omp_invocation` names
  — the linux-x64 archive of the release the single pin source `.omp-pin` names, fetched at build time from that release's download address and checked against the Dockerfile's `ARG OMP_SHA256` (a bump of `.omp-pin` moves that digest in the same commit), and laid out as a tmux host's `mise x github:cybermonklabs/oh-my-pi@<version>` lays it out;
  installed at `/opt/omp/bin/omp` (`LEGION_OMP_PATH`);

- `legion` (`packages/daemon`), compiled from the same commit at `go.work`'s Go version, static, at `/opt/legion/bin/legion` — the `legion` on `PATH` and the image's `ENTRYPOINT` — with the `agent-secrets` client beside it at `/opt/legion/bin/agent-secrets`.
  It links the commit it was built from: `docker run --rm ghcr.io/cybermonklabs/legion-worker@sha256:… version` prints `legion (devel) commit <sha>`.
  It embeds Legion's role prompts (`packages/daemon/internal/prompts/roles`:
  phase workers compose `core/<role>.md`, `mechanics/headless.md`, and the per-role residue;
  merger composes headless plus its residue; root architect, controller, and sub-architect prompts remain single-file).
  The daemon snapshots its own into its state directory before a pane can read them and inlines that snapshot into each pod it runs, and `legion probe-image`, given no `--role-references`, resolves the task agents and skills named by the prompts the image's own `legion` embeds (`packages/daemon/cmd/legion/probe_image.go`);

- `@sjawhar/pi-envoy` and `@sjawhar/pi-legion` packed from that commit's `packages/pi-envoy` and `packages/pi-legion` (the exact `bun pm pack` steps `release.yaml`'s `pi_envoy_build` and `pi_legion_build` jobs run), unpacked at `/opt/legion/pi-envoy` and `/opt/legion/pi-legion`, the two roots a pod names as Oh My Pi's explicit extensions
  — a role relaunched onto a newer plugin contract in a kept pod loads the generation directory's copies instead, installed from npm at `$XDG_STATE_HOME/legion-plugins/g<generation>/node_modules/@sjawhar/{pi-envoy,pi-legion}` ("Contract discipline" below)
  — the Envoy plugin first, with extension discovery on.
  Neither is linked into the OMP profile: a plugin both installed and named by `--extension` loads twice, and the image probe refuses an image whose Envoy plugin does.
  A human debugging inside a pod with a bare `omp` has the CodeGraph tool and the repository's extensions but no Legion or Envoy tools unless it passes `--extension /opt/legion/pi-envoy --extension /opt/legion/pi-legion`;

- the pin of Claude Code (`@anthropic-ai/claude-code`) and nothing else of it:
  the committed `package.json` and `package-lock.json` of `packages/daemon/docker/claude-code`, which pin one exact version and carry the npm `sha512` integrity of every tarball, at `/opt/legion/claude-code`.
  The image carries no Claude Code: its licence reserves every right and grants no redistribution, and `ghcr.io/cybermonklabs/legion-worker` is public.
  A pod whose role runs on the `claude` backend installs the pinned release at every launch instead, in its generation's start script (`claudeCodeBlock`, `packages/daemon/internal/runtime/sandbox/plugins.go`):
  it copies the pin into `<role state home>/legion-claude-code/g<generation>` on the issue pod's disk, dropping every earlier generation's install there, runs `npm ci --ignore-scripts --omit=dev` from it under a bounded `flock` on the issue's npm cache
  — `npm ci` holds each tarball to the lockfile's integrity — and then holds the installed binary's `--version` to the pin.
  The binary the agent command names is that generation's `node_modules/@anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64/claude`, a self-contained ELF (with scripts off, the npm package's own `bin` stub stays a stub).
  A fetch that fails or does not verify prints a `legion claude-code: …` line and fails that launch loudly, before anything execs, and the daemon charges it as a launch failure;
  there is no Claude Code in the image to fall back to.
  And `@sjawhar/claude-envoy` from the same commit at `/opt/legion/claude-envoy` — the plugin root a phase worker on the `claude` backend loads:
  its `dist/envoy-channel.js` is that worker's one MCP server, holding the `legion` tool, its claim, the Envoy tools and the phase reminder's hook endpoint, and its `legion/` is the generated Legion plugin (the skills, the task agents and the reminder's hooks) Claude Code loads as a second `--plugin-dir`.
  claude-envoy ships as a build of that commit's source, which the image's `plugin` stage makes (`scripts/build.ts --out` on the Bun `.bun-version` pins), not as the tree's `dist/` and `legion/`, which lag the source until main's rebuild commits them, nor as a pack:
  no workflow releases that package, so the image is where a Kubernetes deployment gets it.
  The pin and the plugin are in every image, whatever a deployment's `worker_backends` names
  — one image serves both harnesses — and every probe of the image checks both (`legion probe-image`'s Claude lane, below, and its `claude-code` row);
  no build and no probe fetches Claude Code;

- `@bopstack/pi-codegraph`, installed at `/opt/omp-plugins` from the committed lockfile at `packages/daemon/docker/omp-plugins` (its `package.json` is the pin;
  the build resolves nothing from npm), the one plugin linked into the OMP profile `legion` (`OMP_PROFILE=legion`;
  plugins resolve to `/home/legion/.omp/profiles/legion/plugins/node_modules`), backed by the CodeGraph CLI (`@colbymchenry/codegraph`, installed at `/opt/codegraph` from the committed lockfile at `packages/daemon/docker/codegraph`) at `/opt/codegraph/bin` (`PATH`)
  — the `codegraph` tool a tester queries for `affected` tests and a reviewer for `impact`/`callers` blast radius (`packages/daemon/internal/prompts/roles/core/tester.md`, `core/reviewer.md`).
  A pod's agent has that tool because its launch loads profile plugins (dispatch://LEGION-629), which the capability report's `codegraph` row says ([The deployment's capability report](#the-deployments-capability-report));

- OMP's native module, extracted at build into `/home/legion/.omp/natives/<version>-<digest prefix>/` (the version and the first 12 hexadecimal digits of the embedded addons' digest):
  from 18.11.0 OMP writes only the variant the CPU selects (AVX2 or not), so this is the build runner's variant, and a pod whose node selects the same one extracts nothing, while a node that selects the other has each role write that one (124 MiB) into its own home overlay, on the pod's `role-homes` volume, at its first OMP run;

- pinned Bun, `jj` (Sami's fork, the version the dogfood daemon runs) and `gh` at `/usr/local/bin`, and `git` at `/usr/bin/git` from the `debian:trixie-slim` base
  — jj's git backend requires git >= 2.42 (bookworm's 2.39.5 made every `jj git clone` in the init container fail), so the build also proves the image's jj accepts its git with a network-free `jj git clone` of a scratch bare repository before the probes run, and its last step refuses a git anywhere but `/usr/bin/git`;

- the leak guard in front of those two, which is what makes a pod's own writes pass Legion's check before a byte reaches a remote:
  `/opt/legion/bin/git` and `/opt/legion/bin/jj`, root-owned wrappers that lead every pod's `PATH`, and `/opt/legion/githooks/pre-push`, root's hook in a root-owned directory no role can write (`packages/daemon/docker/git`, `docker/jj` and `docker/githooks/pre-push`).
  The git wrapper changes two commands, a commit and a push, and runs every other one unchanged.
  A commit goes to `legion git --real /usr/bin/git`, which adds the commit's `Omp-Session` and `Legion-Role` trailers and then runs the real git.
  It adds each line only when its value is valid, and only when git alone would accept the commit's message and the two lines change nothing else.
  It adds none when the caller asks git for an isolated configuration, as hermetic tests do: `GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM` set to a value git reads as true, or `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null`.
  The two lines record which session and which role made the commit, and they guard nothing.
  A push runs with `-c core.hooksPath=/opt/legion/githooks` immediately before the subcommand, after the caller's own global options, and with the push's own `--no-verify` taken out:
  git itself computes the update lines and hands them to that hook, which runs `legion leak-check pre-push`, and `jj git push` makes its push by shelling out to the `git` its `PATH` names, so this one wrapper catches a role's own push and jj's.
  git takes the last `-c` of a name, so that placement outranks a caller's own `-c core.hooksPath` and the runtime's `core.hooksPath=/dev/null` pin alike, and the pin still holds for every other command.
  The jj wrapper gives jj that wrapper as `git.executable-path` on every command line, and once more as the line's last layer after a push, which outranks every configuration file and a `[[--scope]]` for one command alike.
  It reads a command as jj does, aliases and `ui.default-command` expanded, runs the expansion it read, and before a `jj git push` or a `jj gerrit upload` checks that the git jj would run is that wrapper, by `PATH` and by jj's own `git.executable-path`, refusing in the shared check's own setup-error words where it is not, or where it cannot read the command.
  Then it hands a `jj git push` to `legion jj --real /usr/local/bin/jj`, which runs the push step and then the real jj with the line it read, but for a revision argument whose meaning the rewrite changed, which then names the commits it named before the step, as the step left them, and with `--ignore-working-copy` where the step took its one snapshot of the working copy, so the push takes no second one (`docs/deployment.md`, "What a pane's `gh`, `git` and `jj` are").
  The step gives each commit the push sends the author of the role its first `Legion-Role` trailer names, from `LEGION_ROLE_IDENTITIES` (contract entry `20261125161436`, below), and prints one `legion jj:` line for each commit it rewrote.
  It sets no author on an immutable commit, one a remote bookmark holds, one only a git tag names or one whose role has no identity, nor, but for an empty author, where it prints that it could not.
  The build's last step asserts that each wrapper is first on `PATH` with the real binary behind it and that the hook is root's and executable;

- the rules engine that hook and those wrappers run:
  `legion leak-check` is the shell door to `packages/daemon/internal/leakguard`, and the engine the rules run through, gitleaks, is linked into the `legion` binary as a library, so no pod can meet an absent engine.
  The binary embeds no rule file:
  the private-name rules a pod runs are the deployment's own, which the daemon hands each launch ([The deployment's private-name rules](#the-deployments-private-name-rules)).
  So a pod can meet a rule file that is missing or that the guard cannot use, and the guard then refuses the write as a setup failure.
  The rules read a push's added paths and diff as git writes them and scan each one as it arrives, and a refusal shows at most 40 lines and counts the rest, so the pass holds one line, the record in hand, and one commit's author, committer and message, whatever the number and size of the push's files; what grows with the push is the list of its commit ids, and with one long line that line's size, held whole a few times over (a 73 MB line took 416 MiB), since a split line could hide a match that crosses the split.

- the shared public leak check those wrappers and that hook run, which is not in the image:
  it is published by tag from a repository the deployment names, and the image carries the pin alone (`ARG LEAK_CHECK_TAG`, exported as `ENV LEGION_LEAK_CHECK_TAG`), so moving the pin is an image build, and a deployment that names a manifest digest (below) moves its `manifest_sha256` in the same change.
  The deployment names the check with one operator setting of two values, set together or not at all: the repository it is published from (`owner/name`) and the check's manifest digest at that tag (64 lowercase hex digits).
  The manifest digest covers every file the check runs from, in this order: `public-leak-check.sh` (the launcher every write runs), `public_leak_check.py` (the program it execs), `README.md`, and `must-pass-lines.txt` (which the check's self-test reads); these are the files the check's own install procedure installs into a home and records a sha256 of each of.
  It is the sha256 of the four lines `sha256sum` prints of them, so `(cd leak-check && sha256sum public-leak-check.sh public_leak_check.py README.md must-pass-lines.txt) | sha256sum` prints it (`leakguard.Manifest`).
  A launcher script edited beside an unchanged program is therefore another check.
  The two values are `LEGION_LEAK_CHECK_REPOSITORY` and `LEGION_LEAK_CHECK_MANIFEST_SHA256` in the daemon's environment, or the `leak_check` block of `legion.yaml`, whose `repository` and `manifest_sha256` override the two variables one by one:

  ```yaml
  leak_check:
    repository: example-org/deployment
    manifest_sha256: <the manifest digest of the pinned tag's leak-check directory>
  ```

  The loader refuses one value without the other, naming the one that is set and the two places the missing one may come from, a repository that is no `owner/name`, and a digest that is not 64 lowercase hex digits.
  A daemon before the setting refuses the `leak_check` key and ignores the two variables, so a deployment sets the variables first and the release that reads them follows.
  At boot the daemon logs which check it runs: `daemon: the deployment leak check is configured: …`, with the setting's `repository` and `manifest_sha256` as fields of the line.

- the shared check's way into a pod, which takes the setting above:
  the pod's launcher names its pin in its hello, and the daemon reads the check at that tag from the named repository with a read-only token of its own, which its implement App mints as a read lease on that repository's owner (`leakCheckToken`, `internal/daemon/kubernetes.go`).
  The daemon reads each tag once and keeps that served tarball and its manifest digest in memory (`leakguard.Source`).
  It pushes the check's directory to the launcher before it sends any start (`serveLeakCheck`, `internal/runtime/sandbox/launcher.go`).
  The launcher installs it once per launcher process, before any role starts:
  it unpacks the check into a staging directory, records the tag there, runs the check once with `--help` to see that it names its own shapes, and renames the result over `/legion/scratch/leak-check/` (`checkInstall`, `internal/launcher/leakcheck.go`).
  Every role is told that copy as `PUBLIC_LEAK_CHECK`, and the manifest digest as `LEGION_LEAK_CHECKER_MANIFEST_SHA256` (`mainEnvironment`, `internal/runtime/sandbox/manifest.go`, which names the install's own constant).
  The digest a role is told is the one its pod was built under, which the pod's template records (`legion.dev/leak-checker-manifest-sha256`): a pod kept after the deployment moved its worker image's pin and its `manifest_sha256` together holds the install of the old pin, so a role started in it before its update round is told the old digest and starts, and can push its work and answer that round (`keptPod.checker`, `launch.leakChecker`).
  A recorded digest other than the setting's is drift, so an update round opens over such a pod and replaces it once its workers have pushed (`leakCheckDrift`): a corrected digest, or a moved repository, reaches every pod.
  A pod that records none was built under no setting or by a daemon before the record.
  If its reconnected launcher holds no install, the daemon computes the manifest of the tarball it will push to that exact session, records and tells that served digest before the first slice, then starts the role only after that session installs it.
  A served digest other than the setting is drift, so the kept pod starts safely under its own pin and its update round replaces it.
  If its launcher holds an install from before, the role is told none and that install runs unhashed, as every check did before the setting, until the pod is next replaced.
  The role's name for the digest is not the daemon's, so a configuration a role loads, `legion config check` among them, never reads one half of the daemon's setting without the other.
  A `legion gh` call that writes nothing is read by the check alone only where the check's `public_leak_check.py` hashes to the sha256 this release's read rule was proven against, which the release compiles in (`ghReadsProvenCheck`, `cmd/legion/gh_reads.go`); under any other check it gets the whole guard, and the digest a role is told plays no part in it.
  Each role's `legion worker-shim` only reads the install, and starts no agent when the install is absent, records another tag, its tag file is refused, or it has a manifest digest other than the one the role is told (`leakguard.Installed`, read by `spawnOnce`, `internal/shim/shim.go`): so a pin moved without the deployment's `manifest_sha256` starts no role.
  Under the digest, the guard of every write holds the check it finds to it as well: a check whose manifest digest is anything else, or that misses a file of it, refuses the call, a `legion gh` read included, with `LEAK CHECK SETUP ERROR: <the write>: the shared public leak check found is not the one the deployment names`, naming the digest told and the digest found (`Guard.sharedCheck`, `internal/leakguard/check.go`).
  Where the environment names no check, the shim names the install for everything it starts.
  The pod holds no credential for that repository and reads nothing of Dispatch.

- a deployment that names no check, which runs none:
  the daemon logs once at boot that the deployment leak check is not configured, naming the two variables; it pushes no check to any launcher, whatever pin its hello names; its roles are told neither `PUBLIC_LEAK_CHECK` nor the checker, so each shim reads no install and starts its agent; and a write with no check named anywhere is not refused for the check's absence, the guard's visibility read and the deployment's private-name rules still running over it where the deployment names a rule file ([The deployment's private-name rules](#the-deployments-private-name-rules)).
  A deployment that names neither a check nor a rule file has every write cleared with nothing read.

- the check's launches, rollbacks and tmux panes:
  a launcher whose process installed its pin says so in its hello and is pushed nothing, and a launcher of an older image names no tag and is pushed nothing.
  A new launcher process installs over what the directory held, so the controller's persistent volume never keeps an old check.
  The tag file is read without following a link or waiting on a fifo, and one that is no regular file or is past 256 bytes is read as no install of the pin (`installedTag`).
  A start whose check could not be installed is never sent, and is charged as a launch failure.
  The claim then carries the refusal's sentence as `leakCheckCause`, which begins `the shared public leak check could not be installed:` and says what failed.
  The daemon and the image pins move together, and a rollback of one is a rollback of the other:
  an older daemon pushes nothing and tells no digest, so a new image's shim starts the role, and every write it makes is refused for the check its environment names and its pod does not hold.
  A tag of that repository need not be protected for a role to run under the check the deployment named: a tag force-moved to other bytes has another manifest digest, which every shim and guard told the deployment's refuses; the daemon serves its earlier copy of the tag until it restarts.
  A tmux pane installs nothing, because no pin is set there and such a machine carries the check through the check's own installer.
  The daemon resolves that machine's check once per launch and tells the pane where it is, and the manifest digest as `LEGION_LEAK_CHECKER_MANIFEST_SHA256` where the deployment names one (`docs/deployment.md`, "What a pane's `gh`, `git` and `jj` are");

- the leak guard's answers to a role: a refused write is a command that wrote nothing and one of three lines on standard error:
  `LEAK CHECK: refusing <the write>: <the check that refused it>` is a name in the write.
  A private-name refusal shows each match with its record, the rule's description and its line, within the bounds of [The deployment's private-name rules](#the-deployments-private-name-rules).
  It shows the text because the agent that would make the write wrote it.
  `<the write>: GitHub answers 404 for <repo>, …` is a wrong name or a credential that cannot see it.
  `LEAK CHECK SETUP ERROR: <the write>: <what could not be made to run>` is a broken pod and not a name in the write at all.
  `legion leak-check` exits 0 for a write the guard cleared, 3 for one it refused and 2 for either of the other two — the shared check's own statuses — and 128 plus the signal when a SIGINT, SIGTERM or SIGHUP reaches it before it reports the guard's answer, whatever that answer was, and git stops the push on any of them but the first.
  `scripts/e2e/leak-guard-image-job.sh` drives all of this on a published digest, as one Job of this section's own shape ([Running a workload in the cluster from a role](#running-a-workload-in-the-cluster-from-a-role));

- `mise` at `/usr/local/bin/mise`, the binary the Dockerfile's `tools` stage checks against `ARG MISE_SHA256` (the build itself resolves no pin with it):
  two scripts a role runs, `scripts/e2e/lib/install-plugin-profile.sh` and the skill-scenario rig (`packages/pi-legion/scripts/skill-scenarios/rig.sh`), resolve the Oh My Pi pin with `mise where` and `mise x`.
  The image seeds no mise store, so the rig's first run in a fresh pod downloads the pin from GitHub into the role's own `MISE_DATA_DIR`, and mise reads `MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN` when it is set;

- `socat` from Debian trixie's archive, at `/usr/bin/socat`:
  a byte pipe that carries a connection over `kubectl exec` to a port the pod listens on at `127.0.0.1`, such as a dev server an agent runs (`kubectl -n legion exec -i <pod> -c roles -- socat - TCP:127.0.0.1:<port>`).
  `kubectl port-forward` reaches no listener in the pod under gVisor:
  the kubelet dials the pod's host-side network namespace, while the pod's sockets live in gVisor's own network stack.
  socat is one such pipe; `python3` or bash's `/dev/tcp` over the same `kubectl exec` works too.
  A listener bound to `0.0.0.0` is also reachable on the pod IP from inside the cluster, unless the deployment's NetworkPolicy denies that ingress;

- `unzip` from Debian trixie's archive, at `/usr/bin/unzip`:
  `model-gateway/apply_test.sh` of example-org/deployment calls it, and no package runner in the image reaches it.
  A role cannot install it in its pod either:
  the pod's `/usr/local/bin` and `/opt` are read-only, and `apt-get` cannot take dpkg's lock;

- `busybox` from Debian trixie's archive, `/usr/bin/busybox` alone:
  the `broker/` tests of example-org/deployment run their scripts under `busybox sh`, and without it they fail with "busybox is not on PATH".
  The package installs no applet links, so `wget` and `sh` stay GNU wget and dash, and a role runs an applet as `busybox <applet>`.
  Its `wget` and `ssl_client` applets check no TLS certificate, so no applet may become the image's `wget`: a role's `wget` would then fetch over https with no certificate check;

- `tmux` from Debian trixie's archive, at `/usr/bin/tmux`:
  the skill-scenario rig's panes need it, and without it in the image a role builds one from source after every pod replacement;

- WebKit's host libraries:
  the 56 Debian packages Playwright 1.64.1, the version `packages/dispatch` locks, names for WebKit on Debian 13, so a role runs the Dispatch browser suite's WebKit projects as the runtime user, which cannot run Playwright's `install-deps`.
  The image carries the libraries and not the browser, which `bun run e2e:install` downloads.
  The build launches that Playwright's WebKit once ([The image is probed before it publishes](#the-image-is-probed-before-it-publishes)), so a Playwright bump whose WebKit needs a library the image lacks fails the `worker-image` job;

- a generic toolchain for the repositories the workers work, specific to none of them:
  `uv` and `uvx`; `node`, `npm`, `npx` and `corepack` from Node 24 LTS, with `pnpm`, `pnpx`, `yarn` and `yarnpkg` linked to corepack's shims (the links `corepack enable` would write, which uid 1000 cannot);
  the Go toolchain at `go.work`'s version — `go` and `gofmt`, the tree at `/opt/go` (its `GOROOT`, which `go` finds by resolving the `/usr/local/bin/go` symlink;
  the image sets no `GOROOT`), with the warm module cache of the two modules `go.work` binds, which the second paragraph after this list places;
  the AWS CLI v2's `aws`;
  the Google Cloud SDK 594.0.0's `gcloud` and `bq`, the SDK at `/opt/google-cloud-sdk` with `gsutil` left inside it and off `PATH`;
  azure-cli 2.93.0's `az`, a virtual environment at `/opt/azure-cli` on a CPython 3.13 that uv installs beside it, so the tree runs in any image that copies it whole;
  mikefarah's `yq` 4, the YAML processor, fetched rather than installed from apt because Debian's `yq` is a different program (kislyuk's Python wrapper over `jq`, 3.4.3 in trixie);
  and `kubectl` 1.35, the minor version of the API server of the production cluster the workers run on, which Kubernetes' version skew policy requires within one minor of kubectl (a deployment whose cluster runs another minor layers its own `kubectl` on the image:
  [Per-deployment toolchains layer on top](#per-deployment-toolchains-layer-on-top)) — all at `/usr/local/bin`, which is on the image's `PATH` and every pod's.
  Each is a pinned release whose linux/amd64 download the build checks against a pinned SHA-256 before unpacking or installing it (the `ARG`s at the top of `worker.Dockerfile`;
  `kubectl`'s is the SHA-256 Kubernetes publishes beside the binary, taken once the binary's Sigstore signature verifies).
  The Google Cloud SDK's pin is the SHA-256 of its versioned archive as it was downloaded on 2026-11-18, since Google publishes none for a versioned archive.
  azure-cli installs from wheels alone, each held to the hash its lock, `packages/daemon/docker/azure-cli/requirements.txt`, names, and uv checks the CPython it runs on against the SHA-256 uv carries for that release.
  The image carries the client and no credential for it: what a worker reaches with `kubectl` is whatever Kubernetes identity the operator's pod gives it.
  A corepack shim runs the version a project's `packageManager` names, or else the default that corepack ships (the image sets `COREPACK_DEFAULT_TO_LATEST=0`, so never npm's newest release), fetched on first use into the user's corepack cache.
  Node, Go, the AWS CLI, the Google Cloud SDK and azure-cli keep their trees at `/opt/node`, `/opt/go`, `/opt/aws-cli`, `/opt/google-cloud-sdk` and `/opt/azure-cli`, outside `HOME`, so no volume a pod mounts under `HOME` shadows any of it;

- what the capability check (`packages/daemon/internal/capabilities`, which `legion probe-image` runs
  — [the probe subsection](#the-image-is-probed-before-it-publishes)) requires of the image, each outside `HOME` for the same reason:
  the language servers Oh My Pi's LSP tools start when a working directory carries their root markers
  — `gopls` (built static in the Dockerfile's `gopls` stage, at `/usr/local/bin/gopls`), `typescript-language-server` and `pyright-langserver`, the latter two installed under `/opt/language-servers/node_modules` by `npm ci --ignore-scripts` from `packages/daemon/docker/language-servers`'s own `package.json` and `package-lock.json` (the pins live in that `package.json`), with their launchers (and TypeScript's `tsc` and `tsserver`, and the `pyright` CLI) linked at `/usr/local/bin`.
  TypeScript stays on this repository's own major, since `typescript-language-server` runs `tsserver`, which TypeScript 7 no longer ships;
  the server resolves the TypeScript installed beside it unless the repository's own `node_modules` holds one, which it prefers.
  From Debian trixie's archive, at `/usr/bin`:

  - `python3` (the interpreter Oh My Pi's Python eval runs
    — `omp setup python --check` answers `available: true` on it) with Debian's PyYAML, `python3-yaml`, so `python3 -c "import yaml"` answers in a pod (the third paragraph after this list names the gates that need it)

  - `curl`, `wget`, `jq`

  - `flock` (from `util-linux`: the install Legion renders for an installing launch serialises on the issue's shared bun install cache with `/usr/bin/flock`, so a `roles` container whose image lacks it fails every installing launch;
    the apt line names the package even though Debian's `priority:required` set already brings it into the base, so the day a base drops it the build fails instead of every launch in the fleet)

  - `ssh-keygen` (from `openssh-client`, which also brings `ssh`, `scp` and `sftp`:
    they reach no host that `curl`, `wget`, `git`, `python3` and `socat` on the same apt line could not already reach, and what a pod may reach is Legion's decision, the withheld `network` capability row
    — dispatch://LEGION-5, the pod is the boundary, except a workload a role starts where its deployment's cluster admits it and the Service fronting it ([Running a workload in the cluster from a role](#running-a-workload-in-the-cluster-from-a-role))
    — a declaration the capability report renders, not a network control this repository ships;
    the package's setuid `/usr/lib/openssh/ssh-keysign` and setgid `/usr/bin/ssh-agent` lose those bits in the `runtime-base` stage, and the build's final step refuses an image where any file under `/usr/lib/openssh` or `/usr/bin/ssh-agent` carries one)

  - `psql` (from `postgresql-client`: the Dispatch browser suite, which a reader-facing Dispatch change must pass before it merges, is the pair `bun run e2e` and `bun run e2e:clock`, the second running the three wall-clock projects that are out of the first's selection, and both reach `psql` through `packages/dispatch/e2e/psql.ts` — `packages/dispatch/e2e/seed.ts` calls it for every spec's database reset
    — and the local stack `bun run dispatch:local` (`packages/dispatch/e2e/local-instance.ts`) refuses to start without `go`, `psql`, `flock`, `openssl` and `python3` on `PATH`, and without `docker` too unless a `DATABASE_URL` is given;
    the image carries `go`, `flock`, `openssl` and `python3`, a `DATABASE_URL` stands in for `docker`, and `psql` was the one a role had no way to supply, so a role on a digest without it cannot run the suite its own change owes
    — Debian's `psql` is a Perl wrapper around the versioned client, and it resolves because `perl-base` is in the image)

  - `redis-cli` (from `redis-tools`: no repository of the project speaks Redis today, and it is carried anyway, at about a megabyte, because a second image roll costs more than a megabyte)

  - `sqlite3` (a repository's own SQLite fixture or database has no other way to open from a shell, and Oh My Pi's own profile databases under `~/.omp/profiles/legion` are SQLite as well;
    a role's session is not one of them — it is `results.jsonl`, `state.json` and `title` under `XDG_STATE_HOME`, and the session store these pods otherwise use is Postgres)

  - `nc` (from `netcat-openbsd`, for the reachability check a role would otherwise write as an inline Python loop:
    the package ships `/usr/bin/nc.openbsd` and the `nc` name comes from the alternatives system rather than being a file of the package, so every gate asks for `nc` and never `nc.openbsd`)

  - `dig` (from `bind9-dnsutils`, the package trixie's virtual `dnsutils` resolves to:
    how a role whose connection to a service name fails tells "the name does not resolve" from "the packets are dropped")

  - `gcc` (with `libc6-dev`, the libc headers and startup files it links with:
    the C compiler Go's cgo builds with, and Go refuses `-race` without cgo, so they are what lets a role run the race detector;
    the paragraph after the list of what the image carries says how cgo's default is kept)

  - `chromium` for the browser tools, installed without its Recommends (no setuid sandbox: Oh My Pi launches it with `--no-sandbox --disable-setuid-sandbox`).
    Oh My Pi picks its browser from `PUPPETEER_EXECUTABLE_PATH` first, else the first Chrome or Chromium it finds on `PATH`, and downloads Chrome for Testing into its cache only with none of those
    — so the image's `chromium` is the one every worker gets, with nothing downloaded, and the probe runs that same resolution.
    The image sets no `PUPPETEER_EXECUTABLE_PATH`:
    a variable the image's `ENV` sets is one `runtime.kubernetes.pod.env` is refused, and an operator's pod env naming another browser is what the probe checks (it runs that executable), not something to refuse.

  `jq` and `ssh-keygen` are real binaries so a worker's subprocesses
  — `bun test`, a script, a subagent's shell — find them, where the harness's `jq` builtin reaches only the bash tool.
  A subprocess's `jq` is therefore the image's `/usr/bin/jq`, trixie's, while the bash tool's own `jq` stays the harness's builtin, a different engine (jaq), so an expression is checked with the engine the script will run (`docs/solutions/legion/worker-pane-shell-gotchas.md`, "The bash tool's `jq` is jaq").
  `uv` still installs each project's own Python, from its `.python-version` or `requires-python`, the first time the project runs (`uv sync`, `uv run`):
  in a Sandbox pod that is on the issue's volume ([Anatomy of a Sandbox pod](#anatomy-of-a-sandbox-pod));
  elsewhere it is uv's default, `~/.local/share/uv/python`.
  The image's `python3` is for Oh My Pi's own eval, not a project's interpreter.

`gcc` on `PATH` would turn cgo on by default (stock Go does whenever it finds a C compiler), so the image keeps it off and a role opts in per command, `CGO_ENABLED=1 go test -race …`, with no `CC`, zig or linker override.
Two places hold the default.
The image's `ENV CGO_ENABLED=0` reaches every process that inherits the image's environment:
the bash tool, subagents, `go test`'s test binaries, a `go/build` reader such as `go/types`' source importer (which reads only the process environment), and a toolchain Go switches to for `GOTOOLCHAIN` or a `go.mod` `toolchain` line.
A `CGO_ENABLED=0` line the build appends to `/opt/go/go.env`, the file Go reads for a distributor's defaults, holds where that environment is scrubbed:
Oh My Pi's Python eval kernel, which starts from an allowlisted environment without `CGO_ENABLED`, and a test that runs `go` under an environment it builds.
The build's toolchain step reads `go env CGO_ENABLED` with the variable removed from the environment and fails unless it is `0`, so the build fails if the `go.env` line is ever lost.
`go env -w CGO_ENABLED=1` does not override the image's `ENV`, because Go ranks the process environment above its `go env -w` file;
and `runtime.kubernetes.pod.env` refuses `CGO_ENABLED`, as it refuses every variable the image's `ENV` sets.
Two cases get Go's own default, cgo on: a scrubbed environment that also switches toolchain (the switched toolchain's `go.env` lacks the line), and a `go/build` reader under a scrubbed environment (it never reads `go.env`).
With `gcc` present both work: the switched toolchain's builds succeed, linked dynamically, and the reader's cgo processing runs.
A deployment still pinning an older image digest has no `gcc` and needs zig as `CC` (`docs/solutions/testing/the-race-detector-runs-in-a-worker-pod-with-zig-as-the-c-compiler-and-a-library-callback-from-an-earlier-test-writes-your-log-sink-INFRA-182.md`).

The image also carries the Go module cache of the two modules `go.work` binds, so a role's first Go build in this repository reads no package registry.
The build fills it in the Dockerfile's `go-modules` stage, which copies `go.work`, `go.work.sum` and each module's `go.mod` and `go.sum`, runs `go mod download` and copies no source, so a commit never rebuilds it.
The runtime stage copies the download cache alone
— the module zips, `.mod` and `.info` files and their hashes, 380 MiB over 419 module zips
— to `/home/legion/go/pkg/mod/cache/download`, as the runtime user, its files 0644 in 0755 directories, so a role can add a module the cache does not hold.
The extracted module trees are left out:
`go` extracts what a build needs from the zips, and the whole module cache
— those trees and this download cache together — is 2.2 GiB, which buys nothing in every pull.
A pod tells every role `GOMODCACHE=/legion/go/mod` on the issue's volume (`roleEnvironment`, `manifest.go`), which is empty on a new volume and goes with that volume ([The disk dies with its pod](#the-disk-dies-with-its-pod), [A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)), so the image's copy reaches a role as a proxy rather than as its `GOMODCACHE`:
the build rewrites `/opt/go/go.env`'s `GOPROXY` line to `file:///home/legion/go/pkg/mod/cache/download|https://proxy.golang.org|direct`, and the `|` makes a go command fall through to the public proxy after any error, so a module the cache does not hold still resolves.
The `go-modules` stage deletes every `@v/list` and `@latest` file from the cache before the runtime stage copies it, and the final stage's toolchain step fails the build if one is there.
Such a file would name the versions of this image and no other, and a file proxy answers a list request from it with no error, so `go get X@latest`, `go get -u`, `go list -m -u all` and `go list -m -versions` would stop at this image's pins in every repository a role opens.
Without those files the file proxy answers a version query with a 404, and the query falls through to `proxy.golang.org`, while the `.info`, `.mod` and `.zip` of a pinned version still come from the cache.
`go.env` is the place for it rather than the final stage's `ENV`, for the reason the cgo paragraph above gives in reverse:
a variable the image's `ENV` sets is one `runtime.kubernetes.pod.env` may not set, while a `go.env` default leaves `GOPROXY` to an operator, a role, or one command, each of which outranks it through the process environment.
The `go-modules` stage also deletes the cache's `sumdb` directory, the checksum-database tiles and lookups `go mod download` fetches for the `go.mod` sums `go.work.sum` lacks: they differ with the hour they are read, so with them each build's copy of the cache was new bytes and a new layer.
A pod's go reads the cache only through the file proxy, which has never served the checksum database (a go asks for it at `<proxy>/sumdb/<name>/supported`); a go whose own `GOMODCACHE` is the image's fetches from `sum.golang.org` the checksums it lacks, as it does for any module the cache does not hold.

The image's `python3` carries Debian's PyYAML, `python3-yaml`, because six of this repository's own gates read a workflow or `.github/ci-images.yaml` with `import yaml`:
`.github/scripts/check-action-pins.sh`, `check-bun-version.sh`, `check-ci-images.sh`, `check-image-trigger-paths.sh`, `check-release-credentials.sh`, and `check-ci-filters.sh` through `ci_filter_coverage.py`.
A role runs those gates on its own change, so an image without PyYAML fails every one of them.
Debian's package is the route rather than `pip`, because the image installs system packages in one `apt` step and trixie marks its `python3` externally managed (PEP 668).

`gcloud`, `bq` and `az` trust Debian's root bundle, `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt`, so, as the image's other clients do, they refuse a chain that ends at the distrusted emSign or AAA root.
As the SDK ships, `gcloud` and `bq` trust the CA files it bundles, which hold the compromised emSign and AAA roots.
So the build sets the SDK's installation property `core/custom_ca_certs_file` to Debian's bundle, and turns off the SDK's update check and its usage reporting.
A role's own gcloud configuration, or `CLOUDSDK_CORE_CUSTOM_CA_CERTS_FILE`, overrides that property, as a role's `AWS_CA_BUNDLE` overrides the image's.
`/usr/local/bin/az` is a link to a wrapper, `packages/daemon/docker/azure-cli/az`, which sets `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` to Debian's bundle and `AZURE_CORE_COLLECT_TELEMETRY=no`, each only when it is unset or empty.
The wrapper sets them rather than the image's `ENV`, because Oh My Pi's Python tool starts its kernel with an allowlisted environment, which an `ENV` default would not reach ([Per-deployment toolchains layer on top](#per-deployment-toolchains-layer-on-top)).
azure-cli 2.93.0 has no setting that stops its version check:
`az` reads `https://azcliprod.blob.core.windows.net/cli` at the first command in a configuration directory, at the first command after its own version changes, and at every `az version` and `az --version` (the wrapper's comment cites the source).

It runs as user `legion` (uid 1000, declared numerically so `runAsNonRoot` can verify it from the image alone) with `HOME=/home/legion`, which must be writable (OMP writes logs and `models.db` under `~/.omp/profiles/legion`;
every session is a row in the session database).
The image sets `USER=legion` too, so a process that reads `USER` finds the runtime user's name there (the skill-scenario rig's scripts run under `set -u`).
Like every variable the image's `ENV` sets, `runtime.kubernetes.pod.env` may not set `USER`: `legion start`, `legion config check` and the daemon's boot refuse it, whatever digest the deployment pins (`ImageEnv`, `packages/daemon/internal/runtime/sandbox/operatorpod.go`).
Mount writable volumes below the profile directory, never at `/home/legion` itself:
everything the image-time probe proved lives under `HOME` — the CodeGraph plugin's link and the lock at `~/.omp/profiles/legion/plugins`, the natives at `~/.omp/natives`, the warm Go module cache at `~/go/pkg/mod/cache/download` — and a volume at `HOME` (an `emptyDir`, or a `HOME` volume under `readOnlyRootFilesystem`) shadows all of it silently.
It is `linux/amd64` only: the OMP fork release has no linux/arm64 build.
One commit ⇒ one image, with one exception:
a fresh pod still loads the image's own copies of `@sjawhar/pi-envoy` and `@sjawhar/pi-legion`, from the commit, never from an npm release, but a role relaunched onto a newer plugin contract in a kept pod loads the release's published pair, installed from npm under the generation directory ("Contract discipline" below)
— what the image does take from npm is pinned:
the CodeGraph CLI, the CodeGraph plugin, TypeScript and the two npm language servers all by the committed lockfiles under `packages/daemon/docker/` (`codegraph`, `omp-plugins`, `language-servers`).

### The tools a role's own work needs

The image carries the five clients above
— `psql`, `redis-cli`, `sqlite3`, `nc` and `dig` — the PostgreSQL 18 server with `pgvector` and `/usr/local/bin/legion-testpg` ("A test database in the pod" below, where the roles container's launcher starts it), `unzip`, `yq`, `gcloud`, `bq`, `az`, `mise`, `tmux`, `busybox` and WebKit's host libraries (the list above), and for everything the image does not carry the one documented step is the pinned form of the three package runners it already has:
`uvx`, `bunx` and `go run`, plus `uv run --with` where what a role needs is a library rather than a command.
The two answer different halves of the question.
The image answers the tools a role may not arrange for itself
— `apt` cannot write a system prefix in an unprivileged container, unpacking a package by hand works for some tools and not for others, and a client a role unpacks onto its own `PATH` is the withheld `operator-setup` capability
— while the runners answer the tools no image can anticipate.

What decided it is the container, not the cost.
Measured on 2026-10-25 in a role container of a deployment, in the issue pod of six role containers that the one-container pod replaced:
the role is an unprivileged user, `/usr/local/bin` and `/opt` are read-only, `/home` is read-only while `$HOME` (`/home/legion`) under it is writable, and `apt-get` cannot take dpkg's lock even to download.

```text
$ id
uid=1000(legion) gid=1000(legion) groups=1000(legion)
$ apt-get install -d -y postgresql-client
E: Could not open lock file /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend - open (13: Permission denied)
E: Unable to acquire the dpkg frontend lock (/var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend), are you root?
```

So `apt` cannot write a system prefix in an unprivileged container.
Unpacking a package's files by hand is a separate question
— it works for some tools and not for others (the extraction item below)
— and what rules it out is not the unpacking but the test the role's own skill states, in `skills/legion-worker/references/withheld-capability.md`, "What the withheld capability is, and what it is not":
an extraction under that writable `$HOME` is outside the sanctioned form whatever a role scopes it to, and so is a client left where the role's later commands and its subagents resolve it, which is the withheld `operator-setup` capability (`packages/daemon/internal/capabilities/capabilities.go`).
A test harness's own prefix on the issue's disk, reached by an absolute path or through a `PATH` its own script exports around its own commands, passes that test and is the role's own business
— which is how the Dispatch browser suite's rootless Postgres with pgvector is stood up in a pod today.
So a role wanting a client of its own on its `PATH` has the image, a pinned runner, or `uv run --with` for a library.
The five priced options and their verdicts:

Each item below names an option and its measurement, then the verdict on it.

- the image carries the five clients — 20 Debian packages and 5.9 MiB of downloads (6,216,928 bytes), from `apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends --print-uris bind9-dnsutils netcat-openbsd postgresql-client redis-tools sqlite3` against this image's own installed package set, so it is the true increment.
  In the unit a cold launch pays — compressed image size, each read from that image's own manifest in the registry, and each image's `org.opencontainers.image.revision` read from its config blob
  — this branch's head, `ghcr.io/cybermonklabs/legion-worker:sha-afa29128061f` (revision `afa29128061fc10dd6c6aa3755ba051b98b84e02`), is 24 layers and 1026.9 MiB (1,076,764,060 bytes) against the 24 layers and 1019.0 MiB (1,068,477,764 bytes) of the base it forks from, `:sha-92dbeea3d391` (revision `92dbeea3d3911b5fb08e279fb201634a84ffe72e`):
  8,286,296 bytes, 7.9 MiB on an image of a gigabyte, of which the runtime stage's Debian layer is 8,285,191 bytes (327,156,512 → 335,441,703), the other 23 layers carrying 1,105 bytes between them and none of them differing by more than 3,164 bytes

  **chosen**

- a per-issue install onto the issue's disk
  — the issue's disk is 49 GiB, and every cache already sits on it (`XDG_CACHE_HOME`, `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `XDG_STATE_HOME`, `TMPDIR`, `GOCACHE`, `GOMODCACHE`, `BUN_INSTALL_CACHE_DIR`, `UV_CACHE_DIR` and `UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR`, the nine `skills/legion-worker/references/withheld-capability.md` lists), so disk is not what rules it out

  **rejected for a compiled client on a role's `PATH`**:
  `apt` refuses above, and leaving one unpacked where a role's later commands resolve it is the withheld `operator-setup` capability (decision dispatch://LEGION-200), the extraction item below.
  Still right for a language's own package set — which is the runner item — and for a test harness's own prefix, which only its own commands resolve through

- a runner the image already provides, pinned and failing closed
  — `uvx ruff@0.14.0 --version` takes 1.7 s with the uv cache empty and 0.15 s warm;
  `bunx --package @biomejs/biome@2.6.3 biome --version` 0.3 s with bun's cache warm;
  `go run github.com/nats-io/natscli/nats@v0.1.5 --version` 7.2 s with the module cache warm, 103 s on a cold one

  **chosen, as documentation rather than new code**: the image already carries all three

- extracting Debian packages onto the issue's disk
  — 30 packages, 11 MiB of downloads, 105 MiB extracted;
  `redis-cli`, `sqlite3` and `dig` ran from the prefix with `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` set and `psql` did not, Debian's `/usr/bin/psql` being a Perl wrapper that loads `PgCommon.pm` through Perl's own search path, which no extraction prefix is on

  **rejected as the way to get these five clients onto a role's `PATH`**:
  that is the withheld `operator-setup` capability (`packages/daemon/internal/capabilities/capabilities.go`, decision dispatch://LEGION-200) under the test in `skills/legion-worker/references/withheld-capability.md`, "What the withheld capability is, and what it is not", and it is fragile for exactly the client this change exists for.
  The same unpacking inside a test harness's own environment passes that test and is a different verdict — and it would not have got a role `psql` either way

- `runtime.kubernetes.setup`, the operator-set command run before each role's agent starts — it runs on every start of every role, six times per issue

  **rejected**: it buys nothing the image does not, since it is still an unprivileged container

The forms a role types, the rule that a pin names a coordinate as well as a version, and the line between a sanctioned pinned run and the withheld `operator-setup` capability are a role's own documentation rather than an operator's, and they live in one place:
`skills/legion-worker/references/tools.md`.
The worker image ships that skill, so a role reads it where it works, and a tool no runner reaches is the image change that reference spells out, with the grep that finds its sites.

### A test database in the pod

A role whose change owes a Postgres test has one in its own pod.
The image carries the PostgreSQL 18 server with `pgvector` beside the `psql` above
— 18 is CI's version and Cloud SQL's — and `/usr/local/bin/legion-testpg`, whose `ensure` runs `initdb` if the data directory is empty, starts the server on loopback port 5433, and creates the DSN's login role and the database the DSN names, owned by that role.

A deployment turns it on with `runtime.kubernetes.test_postgres: true`, a key of its own beside `pod` rather than inside it.
Then:

- The **roles container's launcher**, PID 1 of the one `roles` container, runs `legion-testpg
  ensure` once at container start, before any role's agent, and every 15 seconds after, so a postmaster that exits is restarted and a start that died with the server up but its role, `vector` or database unmade is finished by the next tick:
  what `ensure` tests is the DSN, not the port.
  It is not `runtime.kubernetes.setup`: that command runs inside a role's own PID namespace, so the server would be a child of that role's generation and would die with it, and the next role would find a stale data directory and no postmaster.

- The **daemon** puts `LEGION_TEST_PG_DSN` in the start command of every role of such an issue pod, and refuses the name in `runtime.kubernetes.pod.env`, so no deployment line can point a role at another server.
  The value it sends is `postgres://legion_test@127.0.0.1:5433/postgres?sslmode=disable`, the one database every image's server serves, and the pod's launcher replaces it with the DSN that launcher serves, or takes the variable out when it serves none.
  The deployment pins the daemon and the worker image apart, so the process that serves the database is the one that names it: a role is told the database its own pod's server holds, whichever of the two builds is older.

- The **data directory** is `/var/run/legion/roles/testpg` (`LEGION_TESTPG_DIR`), a disk `emptyDir` the daemon mounts there and covers inside every role namespace, so no role can write or corrupt the cluster while its tests use it, and it dies with the pod
  — every issue starts on an empty cluster.
  That `emptyDir` carries no `sizeLimit`, as the role homes volume beside it does not:
  what bounds it is the pod's own ephemeral-storage limit, and a runaway test that fills the node's disk through it is evicted with all six roles.
  The WAL settings below bound the server's steady state, not a test writing rows.

- The **server's log** is `server.log` in that directory.
  The launcher names the file to the script (`LEGION_TESTPG_LOG`) and creates it before the first `ensure`, and every role reads it at `/var/run/legion/testpg.log`, the path `LEGION_TEST_PG_LOG` names:
  role-init binds that one file there read-only, over an empty root-owned file the image makes.
  It binds the file and not its directory because gVisor does not lock a read-only bind.
  Measured in an issue pod on 2026-11-17, a role's own `unshare -Urm` remounted a read-only bind read-write, which Linux refuses; the cover over the roles directory held (its unmount answered `EINVAL`).
  A role with a writable view of the directory could replace `server.log` with a link, and the next `pg_ctl start` or `ensure` would write the server's output through it, into `postgresql.auto.conf` for one.
  A role that remounts its view of the bound file read-write the same way can write the file, truncate it or `chmod` it, since the file is the launcher's and a role's agent maps to the launcher's user;
  it can neither replace the file with a link or another file nor remove it, since the file is a mount point: measured in an issue pod on 2026-11-18, after that remount a rename over it, an unlink of it and a link over it each answered `EBUSY`.
  Nothing that reads the cluster's configuration reads the log.
  A `chmod 000` would make the next start's writes to the log fail, and with them the start, so `legion-testpg` puts the log back as a regular file of its own, mode 0600, at the head of every start, and the image's build proves a restart over a `chmod 000` log.
  role-init opens the log without following a link and binds it only when it is a regular file, so nothing planted at the log's path reaches a role.
  The script and the server only ever append to the file or truncate it in place, so every role's bind keeps pointing at the file the server writes.
  The daemon's image probe (`legion probe-image --role-namespaces`) makes the same read-only bind of a file, so a runtime that refuses it fails the boot probe rather than every role's start.
  The server logs every connection with `log_connections=all`: the backend the postmaster forks for a connect writes a `connection received` line with the client's port, then the authentication, the authorization, and the setup time with the fork's share of it.
  With `log_disconnections` it logs each session's end.
  That costs about 350 bytes a connection (measured over 4,241 connections, about half of them refused at `max_connections`), for the pod's life, and the launcher's own `ensure` every 15 seconds is one more connection each time, whose five lines measured 653 bytes, about 3.7 MB a day:
  the pod's ephemeral-storage limit bounds the log, as it bounds the data directory.
  So a connect that failed with lines of its own failed in the server, and the log names why;
  a fork the postmaster could not make logs `could not fork new process for connection` instead, with no `connection received` line;
  and a connect with neither line never reached the postmaster.
  The listen queue Postgres asks for is twice `max_connections` (`legion-testpg`'s comment gives the number), below the 1,024 gVisor allows (`net.core.somaxconn`), and gVisor's network stack drops a burst past it while the postmaster is still forking, with no line at all.
  Measured on 2026-11-17 against a server whose queue was 40, a burst of 2,500 connects ended some in EOF, which libpq reports as `server closed the connection unexpectedly`, and left the rest waiting until the client's own timeout, while the postmaster stayed up and served the next connect at once;
  under that burst a fork took 20 ms at the median and 109 ms at the 95th percentile.
  No server setting widens the queue past the runtime's 1,024, so a suite that opens more connections than that at once has to open them in smaller steps or retry them.

- The DSN's user is `legion_test`, created `LOGIN CREATEDB CREATEROLE NOSUPERUSER` after the start;
  `initdb`'s superuser is the container's own OS user (`legion`).
  A test gets `create
  database`, `drop database` and `create role` and not the cluster superuser, because a superuser can `COPY … TO PROGRAM` and so run commands as the server's process.
  `CREATEROLE` is there because a suite that makes a role and then connects as it
  — CI's Postgres lets it, since every login there is a test login — would otherwise fail in the pod alone.
  So that the role it makes can log in, `pg_hba.conf` trusts every role on loopback, and the line before that rejects the cluster's superuser over TCP:
  a test that creates a role and connects as it works in the pod as it does in CI, and no login over the DSN's port
  — the superuser's own name included — reaches the superuser, so the trust the created roles need cannot be turned into `COPY … TO PROGRAM`.
  The role is also granted `pg_signal_backend`, which `drop database … with (force)` needs to end the backends still attached to the database it drops
  — an autovacuum worker among them — and which reaches nothing else: it signals a backend and gives no read, no command and no database the role is not already in.
  A plain `drop database` makes the server end that autovacuum worker itself and needs no such right:
  the clause is there to end a connection a test left open, which is why the helpers write it.
  Without the grant `packages/daemon/internal/workflow`'s tests fail in the pod alone, at a different three each run, with `permission denied to terminate process` (SQLSTATE 42501), and pass in CI, whose login is a superuser.
  It is granted `pg_monitor` too — `pg_read_all_settings`, `pg_read_all_stats` and `pg_stat_scan_tables`.
  Every role connects as the same login, so each already sees its siblings' backends in full in `pg_stat_activity`;
  what the grant adds is the detail of backends under other roles of the cluster, the superuser's connections from `ensure`'s steps and the login roles a suite creates and connects as, of background processes such as autovacuum, and the settings only a superuser reads.
  It reads no file, since it does not hold `pg_read_server_files`, and runs no program.

- `ensure` is idempotent and cheap when the server is up:
  it returns after one connection through the DSN itself (`psql … select 1`, with a connect timeout), and otherwise initialises and starts under `flock -o`.
  The `-o` closes the lock's descriptor in the child, without which the server inherits it and every later `ensure` waits on a lock the server holds for the pod's life.
  That connection is a connection: a suite that has taken every slot the server allows (the script's `max_connections`, which `packages/envoy/internal/dispatch/testlimits/testlimits_test.go` holds to `testlimits.ServerConnections` plus Postgres's default superuser reserve) makes each tick's `ensure` fail and log, and spend a slot trying, until the suite gives them back.

- Each run of the script is bounded at 60 s.
  The first `ensure` runs before the launcher serves any role, and the daemon gives a pod 120 s to boot by default, so an `ensure` that hangs costs that pod a log line and not its boot.

- A postmaster the node kills comes back within a tick, but **not with what was in it**:
  this cluster runs `fsync=off` and `synchronous_commit=off`, so a `kill -9` can lose the last commits
  — in the run that found this, a role created just before the kill was gone after recovery, and a later run of the same kill kept it.
  The DSN's own role is among what can be lost, and `start()` creates it again, so the server heals itself; a test's rows do not.
  Nothing here is a database to keep anything in.

- The daemon's **image probe proves it under the runtime a pod runs on**:
  for a deployment that sets the key, the probe Sandbox's `legion probe-image` carries `--test-postgres <its own
  volume>`, which runs `legion-testpg check` and `ensure`, makes and drops a database through the DSN every role is told, and stops the server.
  So a gVisor the server cannot start under refuses the daemon's boot probe (`legion probe-boot`, "Probing a configuration before the daemon boots on it") rather than every pod's first Postgres test.
  The image build runs the same sequence in its own toolchain self-check, under the builder's runtime.

- `legion-testpg ensure` refuses a DSN that carries a password or names a host that is not loopback, so a wrong deployment line logs a refusal instead of starting a server.
  It does not stop a test from using such a DSN; the skill rule does (`skills/legion-worker/references/tools.md`, "The database your tests use").

- `template1` carries the `vector` extension, so every database made from it has pgvector, and the Dispatch browser suite runs on a database a role makes for it there (`createdb`, then `DATABASE_URL`).

- The image's own build runs `legion-testpg check` and a real `initdb`, start, `create database` and extension read as the runtime user, so a build whose server package or script stops working fails there rather than at every pod's start.

- **Upgrading.**
  This release refuses one operator mount the release before it took: a `runtime.kubernetes.pod.volume_mounts[].mount_path` at `/var/run/legion/testpg.log` (or `/run/legion/testpg.log`, the same path through the image's link), where role-init now binds the server's log.
  The loader refuses it in every deployment, whether or not it sets `runtime.kubernetes.test_postgres`:
  `runtime.kubernetes.pod.volume_mounts[<i>].mount_path /var/run/legion/testpg.log overlaps /var/run/legion/testpg.log, which Legion mounts in every pod: a mount may be neither at, under, nor above one of Legion's` (`CheckPod`, `packages/daemon/internal/runtime/sandbox/operatorpod.go`).
  A daemon of this release does not start on a file it refuses, so run this release's `legion config check` on the file before the rollout (`legion start --check-config` on a release from before that command), and move such a mount elsewhere.
  A pod on a worker image of an earlier release reads no log and tells no role `LEGION_TEST_PG_LOG`, whatever release the daemon runs: the launcher, role-init and the file the log is bound over all come from the image.

### Image size and pull time

A node that has never run the image pulls it whole before the pod's init containers start, so the image's compressed size is a cold launch's first cost.
Before the capability tools above, `ghcr.io/cybermonklabs/legion-worker:1.18.1` was 12 layers and 369 MiB compressed (386,510,448 bytes).
With them it is 22 layers and 1007 MiB compressed (1,056,280,622 bytes, the `sha-ff33c8c9fb1b` build of the pull request that added them):
the Debian layer grows from about 30 MiB to 307 MiB, almost all of it Chromium and the library closure it depends on;
the Go toolchain is 64 MiB and `gopls` 20 MiB; Node's tree with the two npm language servers is 66 MiB.
The warm Go module cache is a layer of its own, 380 MiB over 419 module zips with their `.mod`, `.info` and hash files
— the download cache alone, not the whole 2.2 GiB module cache, whose other half is the extracted trees
— measured on disk from `go mod download` over `go.work`'s two modules in a worker pod on 2026-10-29 rather than from a built image:
the zips are compressed already, so the layer should land near that figure, and the image's first build is what measures it.
The five client tools ([The tools a role's own work needs](#the-tools-a-roles-own-work-needs)) cost 7.9 MiB
— not a slice of that 22-layer figure, but a difference measured like for like between a later pair of builds, this branch's head and the base it forks from:
the head `ghcr.io/cybermonklabs/legion-worker:sha-afa29128061f` (revision `afa29128061fc10dd6c6aa3755ba051b98b84e02`) is 24 layers and 1026.9 MiB (1,076,764,060 bytes) where the base it forks from, `:sha-92dbeea3d391` (revision `92dbeea3d3911b5fb08e279fb201634a84ffe72e`), is 24 layers and 1019.0 MiB (1,068,477,764 bytes)
— 8,286,296 bytes, of which the runtime stage's Debian layer is 8,285,191 bytes (327,156,512 → 335,441,703);
the other 23 layers carry the remaining 1,105 bytes between them, no single one of them differing by more than 3,164 bytes in either direction.
Each size is read from that image's own manifest in the registry and each revision from its config blob;
a layer rebuilt from the same content still compresses to a slightly different size, so read the figure as 7.9 MiB rather than as its last digits.
dispatch://INFRA-3257 makes the image larger again, each size read from the image's manifest in the registry on 2026-11-18:
`ghcr.io/cybermonklabs/legion-worker@sha256:25d2edfc2a8c1bb7c3cb83689456f8e2892d91a7fcd544f9cf6719528395c5fe`, the `sha-c665b75abc16` build of that issue's pull request, is 39 layers and 2,332,350,242 bytes compressed, where legion-v20.25.1's `sha256:fd41039d01eda098e66f0475b359ac298732c1f256e2e029f1be469a382cacbd` is 35 layers and 1,865,031,383 bytes
— 467,318,859 bytes more, +25%.
Among what the pull request adds are the Google Cloud SDK, azure-cli and WebKit's host libraries (the image's contents above); no figure for any one of them is recorded here.
On EKS, how long a node takes to pull that is not recorded here: the stage 4a launch below is where it is measured.
The pull must fit the launch's wait for the role's launcher before any init container runs:
`worker_boot_timeout_seconds` (`packages/daemon/internal/config/config.go`;
120 s by default), which the wait extends only once an init container is running (`awaitRoleLauncher`, `packages/daemon/internal/runtime/sandbox/relaunch.go`;
"Liveness rules" below); a launch whose launcher has not connected by then fails and is counted.
On GKE Autopilot (measured 2026-10-16), an issue or controller pod usually waits for a node of its own ([Anatomy of a Sandbox pod](#anatomy-of-a-sandbox-pod)) and pulls the image cold there:
2m23s and 3m33s from creation to the first init container in the two launches measured (1m19s and 2m25s of that waiting for the node, 56s and 58s pulling), and one cold pull of a new digest on an existing node took 2m14s by itself
— so a GKE deployment needs a larger `worker_boot_timeout_seconds` (for example 300) to keep that provisioning-plus-pull time from being counted as a launch failure.
The image probe's own wait is derived from the same key:
each attempt's budget is `slow_command_timeout_seconds` (300 s by default), or, when `worker_boot_timeout_seconds` plus a 60 s margin is larger, that instead (`ProbeBudget`, `packages/daemon/internal/daemon/kubernetes.go`)
— so the capacity stop below (under "The image is probed before it publishes") always has room, within one attempt, to see a probe pod's Unschedulable age pass the boot timeout.
From Sandbox creation through the probe container starting, the daemon allows a separate 300 s startup phase: the documented 213 s cold start fits that bound.
Once it observes the probe container running, it starts the command phase for the attempt budget and gives `probe-image` a relative command budget 60 s shorter, leaving the command's deadline to report before the daemon collects its exit and log.
Pod scheduling and image pull consume the startup phase, so the worst-case boot wait is the 300 s startup bound plus the attempt budget.
The image probe pod reserves 500m CPU, a value set while `legion probe-image` also ran a TLS check of the image's clients, the longest part of its run, which it no longer makes.
Every timing measured for that value came from a probe that ran that check: the slowest of eleven runs at 500m took 147 s, 93 s inside the 240 s command budget of the defaults, and the slowest of sixteen at 1 CPU 104 s (2026-11-20, each in a CPU-quota scope on a development host).
No run without that check has been measured, so the value is kept until the command's other checks are audited, and a measurement of the probe as it then runs sizes it (`probeReservation`, `packages/daemon/internal/daemon/kubernetes.go`).
A check stopped by the probe's aggregate deadline (`--probe-budget`) has no verdict: the launch probes (`daemon.ProbeImage`, recorded as `launch probes: …`), a capability row checked after it (`unanswered`), a role's overlay read that returned after it, and the reads of `omp --version` and `omp --help` for the OK line's two marks that failed after it (recorded as `omp-version: …` and `omp-session-id: …`).
A failure seen before the deadline still fails, and a failure decides over a check with no verdict.
Where nothing failed and something has no verdict, `legion probe-image` prints `legion probe-image: worker probe has no verdict: <check>: <detail>; …` and exits 75, `EX_TEMPFAIL` (`bootprobe.NoVerdictExit`); every failure still exits 1.
The boot log names a derived bound when it applies, and so does `legion config check`.
Oh My Pi's boot after it fits the registration deadline, `worker_boot_timeout_seconds × worker_boot_registration_deadline_intervals` (360 s by default).
The stage 4a harness's `image-probe` and `root-ready` checks (`scripts/e2e/README.md`) are where a launch of the published image on the production cluster is measured.

### The image is probed before it publishes

The daemon refuses to serve unless its OMP exposes `pi.agents` and actually loads `pi-legion` with `pi-envoy` beside it, the two at one plugin interface version and without the pre-split package (`packages/daemon/internal/daemon/bootgate.go`).
The image build's final step runs `legion version`, requiring the commit the workflow built, and the plugin's `dispatch` shim (`/opt/legion/pi-envoy/bin/dispatch --help`, which needs its bundled `dist/dispatch.js` and the image's Bun), then `legion probe-image`:
the same two probes, run by the daemon's own code, plus two only the image runs
— the session-storage probe, which prints `session-storage=probed` on the OK line ([The image guard](#the-image-guard)), and the Claude lane, on `--claude-root /opt/legion/claude-envoy` and `--claude-code-pin /opt/legion/claude-code` (the image's own paths, which the flags default to, so the daemon's probe Sandbox below checks them too):
that root's built channel server (`dist/envoy-channel.js`) and generated Legion plugin (`legion/.claude-plugin/plugin.json`), each a regular file, and the daemon API contract the root's own manifest declares, which the image's build of it wrote;
and Claude Code's pin, which must name one exact version and lock that release and its `linux-x64` package, the one whose binary a pod's install runs, at that version with the `sha512` integrity `npm ci` holds each tarball to.
The lane reads the pin and fetches nothing:
installing from it would make the publish and every boot probe depend on the npm registry and could not promise a pod's later fetch anyway, so the image proves it is self-consistent and the fetch is proved where it happens, by each Claude launch's start script and by `scripts/e2e/claude-backend-sandbox.sh` (`verifyClaude`, `packages/daemon/internal/daemon/bootgate.go`).
Each of the lane's refusals names a build of the image from this daemon's commit.
The two probes the daemon shares hold the Legion plugin to the daemon's own contract number ([Contract discipline](#contract-discipline)), the Envoy plugin's interface to the one the Legion plugin speaks, and resolve every task agent and skill Legion's prompts name (`task(agent="…")`, `skill://…`) by name through the same launch (the agents and skills each plugin ships are listed below), so a build whose OMP or plugins are broken fails instead of publishing.

The Legion plugin ships these in `agents/`:

- `oracle`

- `deep-worker`

- `thermonuclear-deep-review`

- `thermonuclear-code-quality`

- the architect's `design-outsider`

- the planner's `plan-gap-analyst` and `plan-reviewer`

- the architect's `goal-red-team`

It ships this with Legion's other skills in its `dist/skills`:

- `simplify-settled-diff`

The Envoy plugin ships these skills in its `dist/skills`:

- `agent-secrets`

- `approval-review`

- `asd-ste100`

- `dispatch`

- `dispatch-first`

- `dispatch-writing-specs`

- `envoy`

- `outside-message`

- `plain-words`

- the reviewer's pair, `thermonuclear-code-quality` and `thermonuclear-deep-review`, which both
  harnesses install

The build has none of the operator's model configuration, so it leaves those agents' models unresolved (`--skip-agent-models`).
It then checks every image-site row of the capability table (`packages/daemon/internal/capabilities`) against the image, as a worker's Oh My Pi would find each
— `omp setup python --check`, the `chromium` on `PATH` (or the browser a `PUPPETEER_EXECUTABLE_PATH` in the pod's env names) run with `--version`, the three language servers on `PATH`, the CodeGraph CLI with its plugin enabled in the profile's lock, the tools listed below on `PATH` with `go version` running, and the `claude-code` row's claude-envoy root and Claude Code pin, as the Claude lane held them, with the `npm` that installs from the pin and the `node` that checks the installed version on `PATH`.
The tools on `PATH` are these:

- `go`

- `gcc`

- `curl`

- `wget`

- `python3`

- `node`

- `bun`

- `uv`

- `kubectl`

- `jq`

- `ssh-keygen`

- `flock`

- `psql`

- `redis-cli`

- `sqlite3`

- `nc`

- `dig`

It then prints the table, one `probe-image: capability <name>: <status> (<detail>)` line per row, before the OK line:
`probe-image: OK (/opt/omp/bin/omp) session-storage=probed extensions=discovered agent-models=skipped capabilities=checked model-fallback=on omp-version=omp/18.18.6 omp-session-id=<state> daemon-api-version=<N>` (`model-fallback=on` is Oh My Pi's own default for `retry.modelFallback`:
the build runs under no operator overlay, where a probe pod reads the operator's value;
the mark reads `unread` when the probe could not read `retry.modelFallback` under the pod's Oh My Pi settings
— the probe pod's log says why — and the daemon's report shows the row open).
`omp-version` is the first non-blank line that the image's `omp --version` prints, with each run of whitespace in it written as `_`.
`omp-session-id` says whether `omp --help` lists the `--session-id` flag: `taken`, `absent`, or `unread` when the read of the help failed before the probe's deadline (the probe pod's log says why); `omp-version` reads `unread` the same way.
A read of either that fails after the deadline gives no mark: it has no verdict, as above, so the probe prints no OK line and exits 75.
An image row the image carries prints `present` with its evidence (`codegraph`'s:
the CLI on PATH and the plugin enabled in the profile's lock, which a pod's launch loads with extension discovery on).
A live row prints `reported` (``a claimed session reports it while it runs, so the probe cannot check it; `legion state` renders it: <summary>``:
the probe proves nothing of it; [The deployment's capability report](#the-deployments-capability-report) says what each session measures), a deployment row `reported` too, naming what the daemon measures that row from (`the daemon reports it from <source>: <summary>`, where `<source>` is the row's own, such as `the deployment's configuration` for `resource-limits` and `each repository cache's last health read` for `repository-cache-room`), a withheld row `withheld` with its decision, and an image row the image lacks `missing` with why.
A build whose image lacks a capability fails, the probe naming every missing one.
The daemon's Agent Sandbox runtime runs the same command in a probe Sandbox, `legion-probe-<project>-<digest12>`, with its own contract, under the operator's pod, at every boot, and requires `agent-models=resolved`:
each agent's model resolves, with a working key, as the task tool resolves a subagent's (`packages/daemon/internal/runtime/sandbox/probe.go`).
Before those probes the probe Sandbox's command adds `--role-namespaces /var/run/legion/role-probe`, a disk `emptyDir` (`role-probe`) the probe pod mounts there as an issue pod mounts `role-homes`:
the probe first runs one role generation through `legion launcher role-init` as an issue pod's launcher runs every role, over a layout of its own in that directory and with its own `legion version` as the shim, and exits 1 with `legion probe-image: role namespaces: <why>` when the runtime or node refuses what that generation makes (`launcher.CheckRoleNamespaces`):
user, mount, PID and IPC namespaces of its own;
its gh, private and state directories bound at the fixed paths, and a test database's log file bound read-only at its own fixed path, as every role of a pod that serves the pod's test database gets it;
an overlay whose lower layer is an empty home directory on the probe's own `emptyDir`;
its own `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`, memory filesystems at `/run/lock` and `/dev/shm`, a devpts at `/dev/pts` and an mqueue at `/dev/mqueue`;
the covers and its own `/proc`; and `legion version` started as uid 1000 in a nested user namespace, which must exit 0.
So such a cluster fails the daemon's boot rather than every role's start.
The probe does not test the overlay over the image's own `/home/legion`, whose lower layer is on the container's root filesystem, the home's volumes bound back on top of it, or the copy of the role's own config home:
those run first when a role starts in an issue pod.
The image build's own run passes no `--role-namespaces`, since a build's container may not make the namespaces.
The runtime requires `capabilities=checked` too:
an image whose `legion` predates the capability check prints no such mark and is refused naming that (`Succeeded without checking the capability list (its legion CLI predates the
check): build the image from this daemon's commit`), a line that carries `capabilities=browser-skipped` (a probe run with `--skip-browser`, which the daemon's probe never passes) is refused naming that mark, and a probe pod that exits 1 on a missing capability is refused with its log tail, which names it (`capability <name> is missing: <detail>` under the table's `missing` row;
