the stage 4a harness's `image-probe-capability-negative` check drives that with an operator pod env `PUPPETEER_EXECUTABLE_PATH=/nonexistent/chromium`).
With `runtime.kubernetes.agent_secrets.exchange_audience` set, the runtime also requires `omp-session-id=taken`, because it starts each new Oh My Pi role with `--session-id <id>`.
So it refuses every line that does not say `omp-session-id=taken`: one that says `absent` or `unread`, and one that carries no such mark.
The refusal names the flag and the setting, and it names the Oh My Pi version where the line carries one.
The first cybermonklabs/oh-my-pi release that takes the flag is `v18.18.6-sami.20261117-074351`.
The version does not show this, because every release of the fork's 18.18.6 line prints `omp/18.18.6`.
The check needs a daemon of this release or later.
Such a daemon refuses an image whose `legion` is older than this release before this check, because that `legion` confirms another daemon API contract.
This check refuses an image whose `legion` has this daemon's API contract but prints no `omp-session-id` mark.
The Oh My Pi that this release's `.omp-pin` names takes the flag, so with the setting the runtime refuses only a worker image built on an older pin.
Without the setting, the runtime does not judge the two marks.
It logs both on the line of every passed probe, `sandbox runtime: the worker image passed its probe`.
A probe pod whose container exits 75 (`bootprobe.NoVerdictExit`) is a transient attempt, not a refusal: the daemon logs `boot probe failed transiently; waiting to run it again` with the detail `pod <name> exited 75 with no verdict: …`, and runs a new probe pod after the retry's wait, 10 s doubling, within the six attempts.
After the sixth such attempt the boot exits with `the worker image probe never completed within its retry budget (6 attempts): pod <name> exited 75 with no verdict: …`, which names each step with no verdict.
Any other exit of the probe container, exit 1 included, is the image's refusal.
A daemon of an earlier release reads exit 75 as a refusal, as it reads exit 1, and the `legion` of an earlier worker image exits 1 where this one exits 75, so a slow first run is waited out only where both the daemon and the worker image carry this release.
An image the kubelet cannot use refuses the boot at once, from the probe pod's status: a container waiting `InvalidImageName` or `ErrImageNeverPull`.
A pull the registry refused because it does not have the image refuses it once the kubelet has met that answer on two pulls:
a container waiting `ErrImagePull` or `ImagePullBackOff` whose whole message, after the back-off's `Back-off pulling image "<ref>":
ErrImagePull: ` when it carries one, is containerd's answer that the registry had no manifest for the reference, naming that one reference throughout (`rpc error: code = NotFound desc = failed to
pull and unpack image "<ref>": failed to resolve reference "<ref>": <ref>: not found` on a local pull, or `… failed to resolve image: <ref>: not found` through containerd's transfer service, the default pull from containerd 2.1), with the pod's `Failed` events (`Failed to pull image "<ref>":
<that answer>`) counting two pulls or more.
One answer is no proof: containerd 2 resolves a digest as a manifest and then as a blob, and reports the blob request's 404
— which a registry such as GHCR answers for a manifest it holds — over a manifest request the network cut.
The kubelet pulls again about ten seconds after the first failure, and the daemon reads the events at most every 15 s, so the refusal comes within about half a minute of the first pull (on kubelet 1.32 and later, whose `ImagePullBackOff` message carries the failed pull's error;
an older kubelet's carries none, so the refusal waits for a read that finds the container waiting `ErrImagePull`, later but within the attempt): `worker image sha256:<digest>
failed its probe: the registry does not have image <image>: …`, quoting the kubelet.
Every other failed pull — credentials the registry refused (`pull access denied`, `401`, `403`;
Docker Hub answers a repository it does not have this way), a registry the node cannot reach (`i/o timeout`, `connection refused`, `connection reset by
peer`), a rate limit (`429`, `toomanyrequests`), a server error, containerd's other not-found answers (`no resolve hosts`, a manifest past its size limit, a manifest or layer the registry named and then did not serve), and a manifest-404 met on one pull
— may pass on a later attempt, and stays under the six-attempt budget.
One exception follows from containerd 2 reporting a 404 over a failed request:
on a node whose containerd tries a mirror before the registry (`hosts.toml`), a mirror without the image is refused as a missing image while the registry behind it stays unreachable or keeps refusing the node's credentials.
A volume of the operator's pod block (`runtime.kubernetes.pod.volumes`) that a `volume_mounts` entry mounts, naming a ConfigMap or Secret that does not exist in the daemon's namespace, or asking a key it lacks, leaves the probe pod `Pending` with the kubelet's `FailedMount` (`configmap "<name>" not found` or `configmaps "<name>" not
found`, `secret "<name>" not found` or `secrets "<name>" not found`, `configmap references
non-existent config key: <key>`, `references non-existent secret key: <key>`;
the kubelet attempts no volume that no container mounts, so an unmounted one produces no event and no refusal);
the daemon reads the pod's events once the pod is scheduled, at most every 15 s (`mountRecheck`), and refuses on the first such event, with no retry, naming the probe pod, the volume, the object the pod block gives it from and the kubelet's message — `the probe pod <name>
cannot mount volume "<volume>", which runtime.kubernetes.pod.volumes gives it from ConfigMap "<name>":
<kubelet message>` (or `Secret "<name>"`, `PersistentVolumeClaim "<name>"`, `NFS export
<server>:<path>`; a `projected` volume lists each ConfigMap and Secret source joined with `and`;
a volume the block does not name reads `the probe pod <name> cannot mount volume
"<volume>", which runtime.kubernetes.pod.volumes does not name: <kubelet message>`;
a share's own refusals, a claim the scheduler cannot find, a mount the node ran and that failed, and gVisor's failed start over a share it cannot read, are under [Network shares](#network-shares))
— within one event read (15 s plus the wait loop's 500 ms tick) of the kubelet's first `FailedMount`, minutes into the boot rather than after the six attempts of the retry budget (about 71 minutes at the production budget), so a daemon under its Deployment's startup probe refuses, exits and is restarted with its usual back-off, each restart's probe refusing the same way in the log, until the object exists.
A container waiting `CreateContainerConfigError` whose message names such an object (one its environment reads:
`couldn't find key <key> in ConfigMap <ns>/<name>` or `… in Secret <ns>/<name>`, or the not-found forms above) is refused the same way from the pod's status: `the probe pod <name>
cannot configure its container probe (waiting: CreateContainerConfigError), a ConfigMap or Secret it
reads being missing: <kubelet message>`.
The `FailedMount` forms the kubelet retries itself and heals (`failed to sync configmap cache: timed out waiting for the condition` and the secret form, `object
"<ns>"/"<name>" not registered`, `Unable to attach or mount volumes … timed out waiting for the
condition`) stay under the six-attempt budget, and the providers Secret, which every pod mounts, keeps its own earlier rule and wording (`cannot mount the providers Secret …`);
the stage 4a harness's `image-probe-missing-volume-negative` check drives the refusal with a volume `operator-missing` from a ConfigMap `<operator ConfigMap>-missing` that does not exist, mounted at `/etc/legion-operator-missing`.
The runtime keeps the line's `model-fallback` mark for the deployment's capability report ([The deployment's capability report](#the-deployments-capability-report)).
To run it yourself: `docker run --rm ghcr.io/cybermonklabs/legion-worker@sha256:… probe-image --plugin-root /opt/legion/pi-legion --envoy-plugin-root /opt/legion/pi-envoy --skip-agent-models` (both roots are required:
the Legion and Envoy plugin roots a Sandbox pod loads the plugins from, so the probe loads them the same way;
`--claude-root` and `--claude-code-pin` default to the image's own `/opt/legion/claude-envoy` and `/opt/legion/claude-code`;
without `--skip-agent-models` it also resolves each agent's model, which needs the operator's model roles).
`--skip-browser` leaves the browser row unchecked, for the build of an image meant for a deployment that turns Oh My Pi's browser off (`browser.enabled: false`) and so carries no Chromium:
that row reads `unchecked`, and the OK line carries `capabilities=browser-skipped` in place of `capabilities=checked`.
The daemon's probe never passes the flag and refuses that line, so such an image runs only where no probe runs, under `runtime: tmux`.
Oh My Pi downloads Chrome for Testing on first use when it finds no browser, so the deployment's own overlay must turn the browser off.
A step of its own, before that final one, runs every toolchain command listed above as `legion`, from the image `PATH` — the language servers (`gopls version`, `typescript-language-server --version`, `tsc --version`, and `pyright --version` for `pyright-langserver`, which takes no `--version`), `go
version` with `go env GOROOT` required to be `/opt/go`, `gcc --version` (Go's cgo, and so its race detector, needs it), `go env CGO_ENABLED` with `CGO_ENABLED` removed from the environment required to be `0` (so the build fails if `/opt/go/go.env`'s `CGO_ENABLED=0` line, the default a scrubbed environment depends on, is ever lost), `go env GOPROXY` read the same way and required to be the `file:///home/legion/go/pkg/mod/cache/download|https://proxy.golang.org|direct` that same `go.env` carries, with the cache it names held to the runtime user, to a writable download directory and to carrying no `@v/list` and no `@latest` file, `gofmt`, `kubectl version --client`, `yq --version`, `gcloud --version`, `bq version`, `az version`, and trixie's commands included
— the corepack shims fetching their shipped default pnpm and yarn into a scratch directory the step removes.
`gcloud`, `bq` and `az` keep their configuration in that scratch directory too (`CLOUDSDK_CONFIG`, `AZURE_CONFIG_DIR`), so nothing of theirs lands in the runtime user's home.
The step then reads the SDK's two installation properties back through `gcloud config get-value`, from a configuration directory that sets neither, and requires Debian's root bundle for `core/custom_ca_certs_file` and `true` for `component_manager/disable_update_check`.
Trixie's commands are these:

- `python3` with `python3 -c "import yaml"` for its PyYAML

- `curl`

- `wget`

- `jq --version`

- `flock --version`

- `psql --version`

- `redis-cli --version`

- `sqlite3 --version`

- `nc -h`

- `dig -v`

- `unzip -v`

- `chromium --version`

- `socat -V`

- `tmux -V`

- `busybox --help`, its first line alone

`ssh-keygen` takes no `--version`, so the step generates a throwaway ed25519 key in that scratch directory and fingerprints it with `ssh-keygen -l`.
Two of the five clients are odd the same way:
`nc` takes no `--version` either, so the step runs `nc -h`, which prints its usage and exits 0, under the `nc` name the alternatives system installs and never `nc.openbsd`;
and `dig -v` prints its version on stdout, measured in a pod of the image (`dig -v
2>/dev/null` prints `DiG 9.20.30-1~deb13u1-Debian`, `dig -v 2>&1 >/dev/null` prints nothing).
`busybox` takes no `--version`: its `--help` exits 0 and names the version on its first line, so the step prints that line alone.
The step checks `yq` with `--version` rather than `-v`, which is mikefarah's verbose flag:
`-v` emits `level=DEBUG` lines and reads stdin rather than printing a version.
It reruns only when the toolchain or an earlier layer changes, so a commit that only rebuilds `legion` needs no package registry.
A WebKit check runs in a build stage of its own, `webkit-check`, as `legion`, on the same base as the image.
It downloads the WebKit build of the Playwright `packages/dispatch` locks, about 90 MB from Playwright's CDN, into a scratch directory it removes, and launches it once, headless, through Playwright's own host validation (`packages/daemon/docker/webkit-launch.mjs`).
So a pull request that moves `packages/dispatch` to a Playwright whose WebKit needs a library the image lacks fails the `worker-image` job.
Playwright checks that download against no hash, so nothing it writes may reach the image:
only the launch's one line, `webkit: Playwright <version> launched WebKit <version>`, crosses, as a marker file the runtime stage binds, prints and checks right after the toolchain step and the Claude Code pin.
That bind is what makes BuildKit build the stage at all.
The stage reads Node from the toolchain stage's `/opt/node` and `playwright-core` from the plugin-deps stage by bind mount, and BuildKit reads a bind mount's source by content, so it reruns only when the base or its packages, the Node pin, the locked Playwright or `webkit-launch.mjs` changes, never for a change to the plugins, the skills, the toolchain step or `legion`.
To check a published image's toolchain end to end, a project Python install included:

```sh
docker run --rm --entrypoint sh ghcr.io/cybermonklabs/legion-worker@sha256:… -c '
  uv --version &&
  node --version &&
  npm --version &&
  aws --version &&
  kubectl version --client &&
  yq --version &&
  gcloud --version &&
  bq version &&
  az version &&
  mise --version &&
  go version &&
  go env GOPROXY &&
  gcc --version &&
  gopls version &&
  python3 --version &&
  python3 -c "import yaml" &&
  jq --version &&
  flock --version &&
  psql --version &&
  redis-cli --version &&
  sqlite3 --version &&
  nc -h &&
  dig -v &&
  unzip -v &&
  tmux -V &&
  busybox --help >/dev/null &&
  ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -f /tmp/k &&
  chromium --version &&
  uv python install 3.13 &&
  uv run --python 3.13 python -c "print(1)"'
```

### Pin by digest, never by tag

`legion.yaml` `runtime.kubernetes.image` accepts only `ghcr.io/cybermonklabs/legion-worker@sha256:…`.
A tag is mutable; the daemon must know exactly what it probed, so a tag reference is refused at startup with `runtime.kubernetes.image must be pinned by digest (@sha256:…)` (`packages/daemon/internal/config/kubernetes.go`).

Where the digest is published:

- the job summary of every run that builds the image:
  `release.yaml`'s run on `main`, `ci.yaml`'s run on a pull request (its `worker-image` job), or a dispatched `Worker Image` run (Actions → the run → Summary);

- the body of the `legion-v<version>` GitHub release, under "Worker image", when `release.yaml` released `legion` in the same run (`gh release view legion-v<version> --json body -q .body`);

- `docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/cybermonklabs/legion-worker:<tag>` for a `sha-` or `<legion version>` worker-image tag.

Worker-image tags: `sha-<12 hex of the built commit>` on every run that builds (on a pull request that is the PR head, never the ephemeral merge commit);
`<legion version>` only on `main` when the `publish` job released that version in the same run, added after it by `release.yaml`'s `worker_image_release` job on the digest that run's `worker_image` pushed.
Runs from any other ref publish the `sha-` worker-image tag only and never touch a release.
The package also currently holds `sha256-<image digest hex>` OCI referrer indexes from earlier proof runs;
each holds an attestation, not a worker image, so inspecting one does not print a worker-image digest.

A tag does not say which run published it:
a pull request run publishes the `sha-` tag of its head too, when two runs build one commit the tag names whichever pushed last, and a pull request can edit the workflow, whose token can push, to point a `sha-` tag at any digest already in the package.
The digest's GitHub artifact attestation does say.
Every run except a pull request's ends with the workflow's `attest` job, which attests the pushed digest with `actions/attest-build-provenance` and stores the attestation with GitHub;
in `release.yaml` that is a second call of the workflow after the `publish` job, which on `main` attests only when both plugins the image links are on npm.
Its Sigstore certificate carries what the run's OIDC token says, which no workflow edit can change:
its identity is the workflow file at the ref it was read from, and its source ref and source digest are the ref and commit the run started on.
To accept a digest only when a run on `main` built it from commit `<C>`, the commit its `sha-` tag names:

```bash
gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/cybermonklabs/legion-worker@sha256:… --repo cybermonklabs/legion \
  --cert-identity https://github.com/cybermonklabs/legion/.github/workflows/worker-image.yaml@refs/heads/main \
  --source-ref refs/heads/main --source-digest <C, all 40 hex digits> \
  --deny-self-hosted-runners
```

This human-facing command states the whole acceptance policy.
The Legion release follower adds `--format json` when it parses the verified certificate fields; that changes output only, not what the command accepts:

- `--cert-identity` matches the identity exactly.
  `--signer-workflow` matches it only as a prefix, so it would also accept a workflow whose path merely starts with `worker-image.yaml`.

- `--source-ref` refuses a run started on another branch that calls `cybermonklabs/legion/.github/workflows/worker-image.yaml@main`:
  that run's identity names `refs/heads/main`, and its source ref names the other branch.

- `--source-digest` refuses an image a run on `main` built from another commit, such as an older `main` image a pull request run pointed `sha-<C>` at.

- `--deny-self-hosted-runners` refuses an otherwise matching attestation from a self-hosted runner.

A pull request run attests nothing.
A pull request that edits the workflow to attest anyway gets `refs/pull/<n>/merge` in both the identity and the source ref, and a run dispatched from another branch gets `refs/heads/<branch>` in both, so the first two policy flags each refuse them.

The attestation is separate from the image's own BuildKit provenance, which the build keeps off (`provenance: false`).

### How it is built — and the iteration rule

`.github/workflows/worker-image.yaml` builds on the GitHub-hosted runner with `docker/setup-buildx-action` and `docker/build-push-action` (the pair `release-envoy-listener.yaml` uses).
Its layer cache is the GitHub Actions cache under the image's own scope (`cache-from: type=gha,scope=worker-image`).
Only a build on `main` writes it, only the final image's layers (`cache-to: type=gha,mode=min,scope=worker-image,ignore-error=true`);
a pull request's build reads what main wrote and writes none, because a newer head can cancel that build in the middle of a cache export, and because GitHub never lets a `main` run restore a branch's entries, so no pull request can put a layer into the attested release build.
The image is pushed with the workflow's own `GITHUB_TOKEN`: no third-party builder, no project variable, no extra credential.
It runs (1) from `release.yaml` on every `main` run (its push paths include every file the image builds from):
a build-only call beside the `publish` job, linking the plugin pair `legion_build` decided, then an attest-only call after `publish`;
(2) from the `worker-image` job of `ci.yaml` on every head of a pull request, on any base, whose diff its `worker_image` filter matches
— building the PR head and publishing `sha-` only (a stacked pull request publishes a `sha-` tag too, which a pin never accepts)
— and (3) by `gh workflow run worker-image.yaml --ref <ref>`.
Trigger (2) does not build every head.
A draft's head builds no image and publishes no `sha-` tag (ci.yaml's `changes` skips a draft).
Marking the pull request ready builds that head.
A pull request's builds share one concurrency group, so a newer push to the pull request cancels the build of an older head, waiting or running, and that older head gets no image.
Closing the pull request cancels its build too: `.github/workflows/tests-closed.yaml` joins ci.yaml's concurrency group and cancels its run.
No `main`, `release.yaml` or `workflow_dispatch` run is ever cancelled this way.
A reopen within about a minute of the close can race that closed run: `.github/workflows/tests-closed.yaml` says what happens and what to do.
The files the image builds from are every context source `worker.Dockerfile` copies:
the root manifest, lockfile, patches and each root workspace's `package.json` (the frozen install);
the packages it copies whole — the Dockerfile (`packages/daemon/docker/**`), the two plugins and what they bundle (`packages/pi-envoy/**`, `packages/pi-legion/**`, `packages/pi-shared/**`, `packages/envoy-client/**`, `packages/contracts/**`), the skills (`skills/**`) and the prepack that stages them (`scripts/pi-plugin-prepack.sh`);
the OMP pin (`.omp-pin`); the whole Go module the image compiles `legion` from (`packages/daemon/**`) and its build inputs;
the context's `.dockerignore`; and the workflows (`worker-image.yaml`, and `ci.yaml`, which calls it on a pull request).
What a pod executes is part of the image's behaviour
— the command a Sandbox pod runs, the launch probes `legion probe-image` runs in the image's final step and in the Go daemon's probe Sandbox, and every package they import
— so a change to any of it builds the image it is proven on, and a change that breaks the image fails on its own pull request rather than merging and publishing nothing.
The Go build inputs are `go.work`, `go.work.sum`, and `packages/envoy` (copied whole for the `agent-secrets` binary the image also builds):
the image compiles the Go `legion` at `go.work`'s Go version, so a change that moves it past the build stage's Go fails on its own pull request rather than in the next image build.
`.github/scripts/check-image-trigger-paths.sh` (the lint job of `ci.yaml`) parses the Dockerfile and fails when trigger (1) or (2) misses a file it reads, so these lists cannot drift from it.
It also fails when trigger (2)'s `worker_image` filter matches a file the build does not read (one the `.dockerignore` drops, or one no `COPY` names), since a pull request touching only that file would build an image for nothing;
the filter's `!` patterns drop those, under its step's `some-with-excludes`.
Trigger (2) selects by the pull request's whole diff:
on `pull_request`, the `changes` job of `ci.yaml` reads the pull request's file list, so a later commit that touches none of those paths (a docs fix, say) still gets the build and the PR head never loses it.
A filter on the pushed commits alone would leave such a head unguarded.
The `worker-image` job of `ci.yaml` grants the called workflow its `packages`/`contents` permissions, which apply to same-repo pull requests (this repository takes no fork PRs, whose token would be read-only).
The `attest` job's `id-token` and `attestations` scopes reach a pull request run only if it drops that job's `if:`, and its attestation then names `refs/pull/<n>/merge`, which the verify command above refuses.

**The image is built only by this workflow, on the GitHub-hosted runner.**
Never build it on a workstation — no `docker build`, `docker buildx`, or `docker compose build`:
an unrelated buildx job took the devbox host to load 646 on 2026-09-12 and the Legion daemon with it (the CI runner is not a workstation).
Iterate by pushing the PR branch (trigger 2;
a draft builds only once it is marked ready, and a push cancels the previous head's build) or, once merged, dispatching (trigger 3);
check the Dockerfile and workflow statically (`hadolint`, and actionlint with the command in `.github/ci-notes/README.md`, which runs the actionlint, the shellcheck and the severity that CI runs) and run `bun test` for the TypeScript.
Pulling and running the published image locally is fine.
A failed build is retried with `gh run rerun <run-id> --failed` or by pushing the branch again.
In a `release.yaml` run, `--failed` keeps the build jobs' recorded outputs, and a failed `publish` reruns whole, each step safe to repeat:
npm reuses a published version, the tag step accepts its own tag, the push to `main` pushes nothing once `main` holds that version, and the release step reuses a published release.
A whole-run rerun of `release.yaml`, or a `workflow_dispatch` of it while main's tip still carries a `legion-v` tag, re-executes `legion_build`, which reads that tag and decides the same version (`release-push.sh version` releases again a tag that names the run's commit;
the job holds only `contents: read` and no secret, so its rerun writes nothing), and `publish` releases that tag again, each step safe to repeat:
the image is rebuilt, `worker_image_release` moves the `<legion version>` tag to the rebuild's digest, and the release body's "Worker image" names that digest.
`release-envoy-listener.yaml` needs no re-run when its `release_publish` finds, at "Confirm the version", that another run took the tag first:
it publishes nothing and, when its commit still needs a release and no later run on main still running holds it, starts a new run on main itself by `workflow_dispatch`, which decides the version again and re-stamps the binaries.
That dispatched run is a concurrency group of its own, so no newer push to main replaces it while it waits; of the pushes waiting in the workflow's own per-ref group only the newest builds, and it holds the replaced commit's change.

The build has no prerequisites outside this repository.
After the first push there is one human action:
if the `legion-worker` GHCR package came out private, an anonymous `docker pull` fails until its visibility is set to public
— a package-settings action on GitHub with no API.

### Per-deployment toolchains layer on top

The base image carries Legion's own tools and the generic toolchain listed above, and nothing in it is specific to one repository, so a Go, Python or Node repository runs on the published image as it is.
A deployment whose repositories need more than that (a system library, another language, a different Node or Go line) builds its own image in **its** repo:

```dockerfile
FROM ghcr.io/cybermonklabs/legion-worker@sha256:…
# deployment toolchain here
```

and pins `runtime.kubernetes.image` to *that* image's digest.
The runtime sets every container's `PATH` itself (the image's `PATH` with its own directories in front), so an `ENV PATH` in the derived image never reaches a pod:
put the added commands in `/usr/local/bin` or `/usr/bin`, and outside `HOME`, where a pod's volumes would shadow them.
Oh My Pi's Python tool also starts its kernel with an allowlisted environment (`PATH`, `HOME`, `USER`, `TMPDIR`, the `LC_`, `XDG_` and `PI_` prefixes and a few more), so any other `ENV` of the derived image (a toolchain home such as `ELAN_HOME`, a cache directory) is missing there and in everything it spawns, while the bash tool keeps it:
when a command needs such a variable, install it as a wrapper in `/usr/local/bin` that sets the variable when it is unset.
What the deployment adds churns on its own schedule, not Legion's release schedule, and the deployment's repo owns its reproducibility.

From dispatch://INFRA-3257 on, the base image carries the Google Cloud SDK's `gcloud` and `bq` and azure-cli's `az`, so a deployment layer that installed them for its repositories no longer needs to.
A layer that still installs them collides with the base's:
an SDK unpacked at `/opt/google-cloud-sdk` writes over the base's tree, and a `gcloud`, `bq` or `az` linked into `/usr/local/bin` meets the base's link of that name, where `ln -s` without `-f` fails the build and a forced link or a copy replaces the base's program.
A stock SDK trusts the CA files it ships, which hold the compromised emSign and AAA roots: measured on 2026-11-18, gcloud 589.0.0 and bq 2.1.40 accepted the emSign chain ([Worker image](#worker-image)), so the layer's program would trust what the base's refuses.
Drop such a step.
A deployment that needs its own copy of the SDK first removes the base's tree (`rm -rf /opt/google-cloud-sdk`), then installs its copy at that path with `core/custom_ca_certs_file` set to Debian's bundle, as `packages/daemon/docker/worker.Dockerfile` does, so the base's links in `/usr/local/bin` run that copy.
An `az` of its own takes the base's place the same way: remove `/opt/azure-cli` first, then install the copy there behind a wrapper at `/opt/azure-cli/bin/az` that sets `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` to that bundle, as the base's wrapper does.

### Entrypoint

The image's `ENTRYPOINT` is `["legion"]`, so `docker run --rm <image> version` and `docker run --rm <image> probe-image --plugin-root /opt/legion/pi-legion --envoy-plugin-root /opt/legion/pi-envoy --skip-agent-models` work.
A pod never relies on it — the Kubernetes runtime sets every container's `command` explicitly (see [Anatomy of a Sandbox pod](#anatomy-of-a-sandbox-pod) below).
To run anything else in the image, override it: `docker run --rm --entrypoint sh <image> -c '…'`.

## Session store

A Legion agent's conversation — its OMP session — is by default a JSONL file under `HOME`, so a pod that loses its disk loses the conversation.
The OMP fork the daemon pins (`OMP_FORK_PIN`) can store the session in a SQL database instead, selected by two environment variables the pod (or a tmux pane) carries.
Under the Kubernetes runtime the daemon sets them for you when `legion.yaml` says `runtime.kubernetes.session_store: postgres` or `cloudsql-iam`, its two database stores ([Selecting the store](#selecting-the-store) below); the tmux runtime has no such setting.

### The two variables

| Variable                   | Settings equivalent (`config.yml`) | Value                                                                        |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `OMP_SESSION_STORAGE`      | `session.storage`                  | `sql`; unset (or `file`) is today's JSONL tree                               |
| `OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN_FILE` | `session.sql.dsnFile`              | absolute path of a `0600` file whose trimmed contents are one `postgres://…` URL |

The environment wins over the setting, the same way `OMP_AUTH_BROKER_URL` wins over `auth.broker.url`.
The connection string is delivered as a file, never as an environment value or an argument
— the same rule as `DISPATCH_TOKEN_FILE` and every other `*_FILE` variable the daemon writes.
The dialect follows the URL scheme; Legion delivers Postgres.

### What Oh My Pi creates

On the first start with `sql`, Oh My Pi's own `SqlSessionStorage` runs `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS
omp_session_files` (columns `path TEXT PRIMARY KEY`, `content TEXT NOT NULL`, `mtime_ms BIGINT NOT NULL`, `title TEXT`, `title_source TEXT`, `title_updated_at TEXT`) and warms its index from every row.
From the pinned build on, it also makes `omp_session_leases` (one row per session a live process holds: `session_id`, `holder`, `host`, `pid`, `acquired_at`, `heartbeat_at`) and its index `omp_session_leases_holder` where they are missing, as whichever login starts it; a login that owns no table needs `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` on that table, and its owner makes it first so that no agent login owns it (`docs/session.md` of the pinned tag gives the statements).
It also makes the blob table `omp_session_files_blobs` (one row per image a session names and cannot draw again: `sha256`, `content`, `byte_len`, `mime_type`, `created_ms`) and the reference table `omp_session_files_refs` (`path`, `sha256`) with its index `omp_session_files_rhash` on `sha256` the same way, and it refuses to start unless the reference table has an index on `sha256` and its login holds `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` on both tables.
Legion manages no schema and no migration: the tables are Oh My Pi's.
One row is one session; `path` is the same string the session would have had as a file, `content` is the JSONL transcript.

### Resume

`omp --resume=<row path>` — the value is exactly the session path the extension reports to the daemon at `/worker/started` as `ompSessionFile`, and in Postgres it is the row's `path` key:
`<sessions root>/<encoded cwd>/<timestamp>_<session id>.jsonl`.
The second child keeps that `ompSessionFile` field and carries the row path in it unchanged — no rename, no wire or contract change.
The key embeds the home-relative sessions root, so the resuming pod must carry the same two `OMP_SESSION_*` variables and the same `HOME` (and `OMP_PROFILE`) as the pod that wrote it, and the same `OMP_CONFIG_ROOT` or none: from the pinned build on, that variable replaces the home-relative root.
Nothing else about the resume's path changes: the daemon already relaunches a dead worker with `--resume=<recorded session file>`.

From the pinned build on, the session store holds a lease per session, and a resume of a session another live process still holds waits up to 35 seconds for it and then moves the process onto a new session id, which the daemon never recorded.
So every launch that resumes a recorded Oh My Pi session carries `OMP_SESSION_EXCLUSIVE=1`, in the generation's start command alone (a tmux pane carries it as one of its `-e` pairs), and a fresh launch or a Claude Code role carries nothing of it.
Under it that resume exits non-zero after the wait and moves nothing, and a lease lost or a session another writer replaced ends the process rather than moving it.
A process that ends on SIGTERM or SIGINT gives its lease back before it exits, so a resume after an ordinary stop waits for no lease: measured on 2026-11-19 on `18.18.6-sami.20261119-162325` in an issue pod, an exclusive resume launched right after its holder ended on SIGTERM finished a one-turn run 4.0 and 4.8 seconds after its launch in two runs, and an RPC resume answered `get_state` 7.0 seconds after its launch in one, where the holder's own first start had taken 3.9 seconds.
A resume after the process that held the session was killed (the memory guard, an out-of-memory kill, a stop grace that ran out) waits, up to 30 seconds after the dead process's last heartbeat, before the agent starts: measured the same way, an exclusive resume launched right after such a kill finished a one-turn run 24.1 and 25.6 seconds after its launch, and an RPC resume answered `get_state` 28.7 seconds after its launch, well inside the registration deadline (`worker_boot_timeout_seconds` × `worker_boot_registration_deadline_intervals`, 360 seconds by default).
The runtime sets the variable after the operator's: neither `runtime.kubernetes.pod.env` nor `runtime.tmux.pane_env` may name it, and neither runtime's `provider_keys` may name it either.

### Refusals

Every refusal is exit 1 with the message on stderr, and none falls back to file storage:

| condition                                                         | behaviour                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| both variables unset, settings at their defaults                  | JSONL files exactly as before; nothing is logged                                                                                                                                       |
| `OMP_SESSION_STORAGE=sql`, no file named by the variable or the setting | refuses, naming both `OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN_FILE` and `session.sql.dsnFile`                                                                                                        |
| the named file is missing or unreadable                           | `OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN_FILE names <path>, which could not be read: <reason>` (or `session.sql.dsnFile names …` when the setting supplied it)                                            |
| the named file is blank after trimming                            | `… names <path>, which is empty`                                                                                                                                                       |
| the file's contents are not a connection URL the driver accepts (for example the libpq keyword form `host=… user=… password=…`) | `… names <path>, but its contents are not a connection URL the database driver accepts` — the driver's parse error is not printed, since it embeds the whole string; never the contents |
| the database is unreachable or refuses the connection             | `… names <path>, but the session database could not be opened: <driver error> (<code>)` — for a closed port `Connection closed (ERR_POSTGRES_CONNECTION_CLOSED)`; the driver's error, never the connection string |
| any other `OMP_SESSION_STORAGE` value                             | `OMP_SESSION_STORAGE is "<value>"; expected "file" or "sql"`                                                                                                                           |
| the running Oh My Pi build predates the setting                   | the variables are ignored and the session stays on files — caught before it can happen: the session-storage launch probe (`verifySessionStorageSetting`, `boot-probes.ts`) runs inside the worker image through `legion probe-image` (see [The image is probed before it publishes](#the-image-is-probed-before-it-publishes)), fails on such a build so the image never publishes, and on a passing image prints `session-storage=probed` on the command's OK line, which a `legion probe-image` of this release prints only once that probe has passed, under every store ([The image guard](#the-image-guard)) — the daemon never probes a host OMP for it |

### What stays on the pod's disk

Only the transcript moves, and only the transcript survives the pod.
Tool artifacts, image blobs and `models.db` stay under the agent directory on local disk (`~/.omp/profiles/legion/agent/…`), and handoffs are records on each Dispatch issue.
A pod that dies loses those local files — the conversation it does not.
OMP's logs are under the role's state home (`/legion/scratch/state/<role>/omp/profiles/legion/logs`, [Anatomy of a Sandbox pod](#anatomy-of-a-sandbox-pod)), which is on the pod's own disk, the one directory of the issue's scratch named for the role (every role of the issue can still write it):
those logs, Chromium's `browser-profiles`, the plugin generation a stale-plugin relaunch installs and the workspace's CodeGraph index (`.codegraph/` in the workspace, 185 MB for this repository, built by a role's shim after its Oh My Pi starts) all live as long as the pod and no longer ([The disk dies with its pod](#the-disk-dies-with-its-pod)), except on a kept volume, where they live as long as the issue's Sandbox ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)).
Read a role's log from its pod's container while its pod is there; the pod that replaces it starts with none of it, unless the volume is kept.

### The extension under SQL storage

The Legion plugin (`@sjawhar/pi-legion`) recognises a `task` subagent inside a Legion worker without looking for the parent's transcript on disk:
its claim session records which session it bootstrapped on the interface the two plugins share, and a later session start in the same process with a different transcript path is a subagent (the check in `packages/pi-shared/src/subagent-session.ts`, which both plugins run).
Nothing in either plugin reads the two variables, and neither needs any other change for SQL storage.

### Selecting the store

Three keys in `legion.yaml`, all inside the `runtime.kubernetes` mapping:
`session_store` chooses the kind, and each kind carries the one key that opens its store.
The store is required, and must be one that keeps sessions in a database:

```yaml
runtime:
  kubernetes:
    session_store: postgres          # or cloudsql-iam; pvc and an omitted key are both refused
    session_dsn_secret: SESSION_DSN  # the providers-Secret key that holds the connection URL
```

```yaml
runtime:
  kubernetes:
    session_store: cloudsql-iam    # every pod signs in to Cloud SQL over IAM, and no URL is held anywhere
    session_database:              # the database each pod signs in to: instance, name and user are required
      instance: example-project:us-central1:example-instance  # the connection name, project:region:instance
      name: legion_sessions                                   # the database in that instance
      user: legion-sessions@example-project.iam               # the IAM login a pod signs in as
      # optional: the Google service account that each pod's proxy impersonates and signs in as.
      # With it, user must be that account's IAM login: its email without .gserviceaccount.com.
      impersonate_service_account: legion-sessions@example-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com
      # optional: the audience of a token that only each pod's launcher reads, which impersonates that account.
      # It is a workload identity provider's full resource name, and it needs impersonate_service_account.
      writer_audience: //iam.googleapis.com/projects/<number>/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/<pool>/providers/<provider>
```

`postgres` and `cloudsql-iam` both keep every pod agent's conversation, each role's and a daemon-launched controller's, in Oh My Pi's table;
what differs is how a pod reaches that database and what it must hold to do so (`Store` and `Database`, `internal/ompsessions/store.go`), which for the second of them is [What `cloudsql-iam` puts in a pod](#what-cloudsql-iam-puts-in-a-pod), below.
`pvc`, which kept each conversation a file in the `sessions` directory of the issue's disk, is refused, and so is an omitted `session_store`, which settles to it:
the loader gives both the same line and its reason (`readSessionStore`, `internal/config/kubernetes.go`):

```
runtime.kubernetes.session_store must name a store that keeps sessions in a database, and is
required (INFRA-80): an issue pod's disk is the pod's own ephemeral volume, deleted with the pod,
so a session kept as a file on it ('pvc', also what an omitted session_store means) dies with it,
the next launch's resume fails on the missing file (internal/launcher's sessionWritten), and three
such failures retire the claim
```

There is no silent default, because a default would be a deployment that boots and then loses every conversation at the first pod replacement.
A kept volume ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)) does not change this rule: a reset and each suspension of the issue delete that volume, and the issue's sessions must outlive both.
**So the deployment names its store and that store's key before this release boots**, and the database is reachable from the pods:
an upgrade that applies the image first has a daemon that refuses its own configuration at load ([Cutting over to the pod-owned disk](#cutting-over-to-the-pod-owned-disk)).
The session database's server must be PostgreSQL 16.4, 15.8, 14.13, 13.16 or 12.20 or later in its major, or any 17 or later (the August 2024 minor releases added `restrict_nonsystem_relation_kind`, which every transaction Legion runs on that database sets), or every session read and write fails with `unrecognized configuration parameter`.

Each kind names its own key and refuses the other's, an inert key being refused and never ignored:
`runtime.kubernetes.session_dsn_secret is not used when runtime.kubernetes.session_store is
cloudsql-iam; remove it`, and `runtime.kubernetes.session_database is not used when
runtime.kubernetes.session_store is postgres; remove it`.
`postgres` without its key is refused (`runtime.kubernetes.session_dsn_secret is required with runtime.kubernetes.session_store postgres:
the key of the providers Secret that holds the session database's postgres:// URL`), and so is a value that is no Secret data key (`[-._a-zA-Z0-9]+`), naming it.
`instance`, `name` and `user` are required, since no pod reaches the database without them;
`instance` must be a connection name the Cloud SQL connector uses whole
— `project:region:instance`, or `domain:project:region:instance` for a legacy domain-scoped project, with no whitespace anywhere, which its own parser (`instance.ParseConnName`) accepts and reads back as exactly that string, so a longer string it would take only part of is refused too (`ValidInstance`, `internal/ompsessions/store.go`, which the pod's proxy holds to as well);
and a member the mapping does not model is refused by name (`readSessionStore` and `readSessionDatabase`, `internal/config/kubernetes.go`).

`impersonate_service_account` is optional.
The loader refuses a value of it that is not a Google service account's email:
`runtime.kubernetes.session_database.impersonate_service_account "<value>" must be a Google service account's email, such as <name>@<project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com`.
When the member is set, the loader also refuses a `user` that is not that account's IAM login:
`runtime.kubernetes.session_database.user "<user>" must be "<login>": Cloud SQL's IAM login for the service account impersonate_service_account names is its email without .gserviceaccount.com`.
Both checks use `ompsessions.ServiceAccountLogin` (`internal/ompsessions/store.go`), and the pod's proxy holds to the same rule.

**What a pod signs in as, and what a deployment grants for it.**
Every Legion pod runs as the Kubernetes ServiceAccount that `runtime.kubernetes.pod.service_account` names (`ServiceAccountName`, `manifest.go`).
Under Workload Identity Federation for GKE, the pod's cloud identity is the principal of that ServiceAccount, a federated principal with no email address.
Cloud SQL takes only a user, a service account or a group as an IAM database login, so that principal cannot have a login.

`impersonate_service_account` names a Google service account for the pods to sign in as.
Each pod's proxy impersonates that account for both of the connector's token sources, and signs in as it (`connectorOptions`, `internal/sessionproxy`).
It impersonates the account with the pod's own credentials, or, where `writer_audience` is set, with a token that only the launcher reads (below).
Both sources must be the account's, because Google says that "the IAM account that you use to start the connector must be the same account that authenticates to the database" ([Log in using IAM database authentication](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/iam-logins)).
A deployment that sets the member makes these four things true in Google Cloud:

- The principal of the pods' Kubernetes ServiceAccount holds a role on the account, and that role holds `iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken`.
  `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` holds it.

- The account holds `roles/cloudsql.instanceUser` and `roles/cloudsql.client`.

- The account has an IAM database login on the instance, and the name of that login is `user`.

- The IAM Service Account Credentials API (`iamcredentials.googleapis.com`) is enabled in the cluster's project.
  GKE's Workload Identity prerequisites say to enable it ([Authenticate to Google Cloud APIs from GKE workloads](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/workload-identity)).
  A workload's `GenerateAccessToken` calls count against the quota of that project, unless the Kubernetes ServiceAccount names another quota project ([Use quota from a different project with Workload Identity Federation for GKE](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/workload-identity#quota-project)).

Use an account that has no other purpose.
Every process that has the pods' cloud identity can impersonate the account with any scope: every role in every pod of the deployment, and a `kubectl exec` shell in such a pod.
So each of them can do all that the account's roles let it do in Google Cloud, not only sign in to the session database.
Give the account the two Cloud SQL roles above and no other role.

Set the member in the same change that turns `cloudsql-iam` on.
A pod keeps the session flags it was created with for its whole life.
A role launched again into an issue pod whose update round is still open keeps that pod's flags.
So until the round replaces the pod, the role signs in as those flags say.
The controller's pod has no update round, so the next launch into it replaces it when its flags differ from the configured ones.

A refused impersonation, such as a missing grant or a disabled API, fails the proof dial.
The generation's start error then names the instance and carries Google's refusal, as any refused start does ([What `cloudsql-iam` puts in a pod](#what-cloudsql-iam-puts-in-a-pod)).

A daemon before this release refuses `impersonate_service_account` as an unknown key.
The worker image moves with the daemon at this release's daemon API contract.
So a rollback takes back the file, the daemon and the image together.

**A token that only the launcher reads.**
`writer_audience` is optional, and it needs `impersonate_service_account`.
Its value is the full resource name of a workload identity provider: `//iam.googleapis.com/projects/<number>/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/<pool>/providers/<provider>`.
With it, each pod carries a projected ServiceAccount token of that audience, and only the pod's launcher reads it.
Each pod's proxy exchanges that token at Google's Security Token Service and impersonates the account with the federated token, in place of the pod's own credentials.
The proxy's socket then admits only the launcher and the generation's Oh My Pi process ([What `cloudsql-iam` puts in a pod](#what-cloudsql-iam-puts-in-a-pod)).

The loader holds the value to `ompsessions.ValidWriterAudience` (`internal/ompsessions/store.go`), and the launcher and the proxy hold to the same rule.
The project is its number in decimal digits, never its id.
The pool and the provider are each 4 to 32 characters of `a-z`, `0-9` and `-`, and neither starts with `gcp-`, which Google keeps for itself.
`legion config check` and the daemon's boot load refuse the same files with the same words (`readSessionDatabase` and `checkWriterAudienceAgainstRoleTokens`, `internal/config/kubernetes.go`):

- the member without `impersonate_service_account`:
  `runtime.kubernetes.session_database.writer_audience needs runtime.kubernetes.session_database.impersonate_service_account: the writer token signs in to Cloud SQL only by impersonating that service account`

- a value of another form:
  `runtime.kubernetes.session_database.writer_audience "<value>" must be a workload identity provider's full resource name, //iam.googleapis.com/projects/<project number>/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/<pool id>/providers/<provider id>, each id 4 to 32 characters of a-z, 0-9 and - that does not start with gcp-`

- a blank value:
  `runtime.kubernetes.session_database.writer_audience must not be empty`

- the member under `postgres`, where `session_database` as a whole is refused:
  `runtime.kubernetes.session_database is not used when runtime.kubernetes.session_store is postgres; remove it`

- a value that is also the audience of a token every role of a pod reads: `agent_secrets.audience`, `agent_secrets.exchange_audience`, or the `audience` of a projected `service_account_token` source of a `pod.volumes` entry:
  `runtime.kubernetes.session_database.writer_audience must differ from runtime.kubernetes.agent_secrets.audience (both <value>): the broker's tokens are mounted where every role of a pod reads them, and the writer token is the launcher's alone`, and likewise `runtime.kubernetes.agent_secrets.exchange_audience`.
  For a pod volume, the refusal names the source, such as `runtime.kubernetes.pod.volumes[0].projected.sources[0].service_account_token.audience`, and says `every pod carries the operator's pod volumes, and a volume_mounts entry shows one to every role of the pod`.
  The loader refuses such a volume whether or not a `volume_mounts` entry names it.
  All these tokens have the pod's ServiceAccount as their subject.
  Every role of a pod that enrolls with the broker reads the broker's two tokens (`podTokenMounts`, `manifest.go`), and every role reads a pod volume that a `volume_mounts` entry mounts.
  With equal values, a role's process could exchange such a token as the writer token and sign in as the account.

- a value whose `https:` form, `https://iam.googleapis.com/projects/<number>/…`, is the audience of such a token:
  `runtime.kubernetes.session_database.writer_audience must differ from runtime.kubernetes.agent_secrets.audience (https://iam.googleapis.com/…), which a provider whose allowed audiences are empty takes as the same audience, its full resource name with the https: prefix: the broker's tokens are mounted where every role of a pod reads them, and the writer token is the launcher's alone`, and likewise for the other keys above.
  A provider whose allowed audiences list is empty takes a token whose audience is its full resource name with or without the `https:` prefix (`gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc`, `--allowed-audiences`), so such a token is a writer token too.

A deployment that sets the member makes these four things true:

- A workload identity pool has one OIDC provider that trusts the cluster's issuer.
  Its allowed audiences list names the member's value alone, so the provider takes no token of the `https:` form either.
  Left empty, the list also admits that form, which the loader refuses on every token a role reads, but not on a token the loader does not know of.
  Its attribute condition admits the Kubernetes ServiceAccounts that the pods run as.

- The account grants `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` to the principal, in that pool, of each Kubernetes ServiceAccount the project's pods run as, the controller's pod included:
  `principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/<number>/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/<pool>/subject/system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service account>`.
  `<namespace>` is `runtime.kubernetes.namespace`, and `<service account>` is each such ServiceAccount.
  At this release every pod, the controller's included, runs as the one that `runtime.kubernetes.pod.service_account` names (`ServiceAccountName`, `manifest.go`), so that is one principal.
  This grant takes the place of the account's grant to the pod's own principal, the first item of the list under "What a pod signs in as, and what a deployment grants for it" above.

- The Security Token Service API (`sts.googleapis.com`) and the IAM Service Account Credentials API (`iamcredentials.googleapis.com`) are enabled.

- Where the cluster has an admission policy on projected tokens, a rule of that policy admits the member's audience in the daemon's Sandbox pods.
  The pods ask for each such token for 3600 seconds (`workloadIdentityTokenSeconds`, `manifest.go`).

Turn `writer_audience` on in this order:

1. Make the four things above true: the pool and its provider, the account's grant to the pool's principal, the two APIs, and the admission rule where the cluster has one.
   A pod whose exchange or impersonation Google refuses fails its proof dial, and the generation's start error names the instance and carries Google's refusal.

2. Set `writer_audience`, and restart the daemon on the file.
   A pod keeps the session flags it was created with, and a writer audience added is a moved session store.
   So each pod takes the writer token when it is replaced: an issue pod by its update round, and the controller's pod at the next launch into it.

3. When every pod shows the writer setting, remove the account's grant to the pod's own principal.
   A pod shows it when its launcher container's command carries `--session-writer-audience`, and its proxy's start line ends `with the launcher's writer token`.
   Until that grant is gone, the pod's own credentials still impersonate the account, and every process that holds them can sign in as it.

A pod created under the member keeps `--session-writer-audience` in its launcher's command for its whole life, and its launcher refuses every Oh My Pi start that names no `agentExecutable` (`newSessionPeer`, `internal/launcher/sessionpeer.go`).
A daemon before the release that adds `writer_audience` sends no `agentExecutable`, and it refuses the member by name, as a key it does not know.
So turn `writer_audience` off on this release first, and roll back below it only after that, in this order:

1. On the release that carries the member, restore the account's grant to the pod's own principal, remove `writer_audience` from `legion.yaml`, and restart the daemon on the file.
   The grant comes first, because a pod created without the member impersonates the account with the pod's own credentials, and Google refuses them without the grant.
   Keep the writer pool, its provider and the account's grant to the pool's principal until step 2 is done: until its replacement, a pod that carries the fifth flag still exchanges the writer token, and each new generation in it proves a dial with that token.
   This release reads the fifth flag of every pod (`sessionProxyFlagsIn`, `internal/runtime/sandbox/addresses.go`), so each pod that carries it holds a moved session store.
   An issue pod is replaced by its update round, whose workers can still answer it, since this release names `agentExecutable` in every Oh My Pi start.
   The controller's pod is replaced at the next launch into it, whatever that launch installs (`movedInPod` in `addresses.go`, and `replace` in `internal/runtime/sandbox/relaunch.go`).

2. When no pod's launcher command carries `--session-writer-audience`, roll back the daemon and the worker image together, with the file that no longer names the member.
   This prints nothing then:
   `kubectl -n <namespace> get pods -l legion.dev/project=<project> -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].command}{"\n"}{end}' | grep -- --session-writer-audience`.
   `<namespace>` is `runtime.kubernetes.namespace`, and `<project>` is `legion.yaml`'s `project` lowercased with every non-alphanumeric removed (`claim.ProjectToken`), the value of every pod's `legion.dev/project` label: `ACME` reads `acme`.

A rollback that skips step 1 stops the controller and holds the issues whose pods carry the member.
A daemon before this release reads no fifth flag, so it sees no moved session store.
Where that daemon knows a plugin pair, every relaunch of an Oh My Pi claim recorded at this release's contract installs that pair (`stalePluginInstall`, `internal/daemon/specs.go`), and a launch that installs keeps its pod, whatever its image.
Each Oh My Pi start into such a pod is refused, and each refusal is charged as a launch failure, so the claim fails after `launch_failure_limit` refusals (3 by default), seconds apart.
A Claude Code start into such a pod is admitted: the launcher matches no agent's executable for a Claude Code generation, which its start environment names (`newSessionPeer`).

- The controller's claim fails, and the daemon's retry of it is again a launch that installs into the same pod.
  The controller stays down until its Sandbox is deleted (`kubectl -n <namespace> delete sandbox <name>`), and the next launch then makes a new one.

- An issue role's claim on Oh My Pi fails the same way, and a failed claim of the role that works the issue's phase holds the issue.
  The pod's update round asks no failed claim, and the replacement of the pod restarts none.
  So each such claim needs a retry once its pod is replaced: `legion claims retry --operator-token-file <file> --claim <token>`, or `--failed` in place of `--claim` for every failed claim.

`postgres` holds the whole connection URL, password and all, in one providers-Secret key.
The daemon never holds the connection string:
put it in the providers Secret (`legion-<project>-providers`) under the key `session_dsn_secret` names, as one `postgres://…` URL.
Every issue pod, the controller's pod and the image probe mount that key read-only at `/var/run/legion/providers/OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN`, whatever the key is called, so a Secret without it refuses boot at the image probe, naming the Secret and its keys (`internal/runtime/sandbox/manifest.go`, `providers`).

With the store settled, every generation a launcher starts gets two variables in its start command (`mainEnvironment`):
`OMP_SESSION_STORAGE=sql` and `OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN_FILE=/var/run/legion/providers/OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN`.
The pod baseline (`internal/podsafety`) keeps them, where it would otherwise set `OMP_SESSION_STORAGE=file`, and the worker shim, seeing the pointer in its environment, never exports the URL file into Oh My Pi's environment.
Neither variable may be the operator's (`pod.env`) or a provider key's, and neither may `OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN`, the name the URL file is mounted under (`CheckPod`).
Oh My Pi creates and migrates its own tables, `omp_session_files` and `omp_session_files_parts`, and from the pinned build on `omp_session_leases`, `omp_session_files_blobs` and `omp_session_files_refs` with their indexes, in the `public` schema when it starts; Legion manages no schema.
So the deployment's login needs to create tables there:
since Postgres 15, `CREATE` on the database is not enough, and the create is refused with `permission denied for schema public`.
Grant `USAGE, CREATE ON SCHEMA public` to the login (measured on Postgres 16.15:
`CONNECT, CREATE ON DATABASE` alone is refused, the schema grant creates the table), or make the login the schema's owner.

**One login, every conversation: what that costs.**
Under `postgres` every Legion pod's launcher container (an issue pod's `roles`, the controller's `controller`) mounts the providers Secret with the session database's URL among its keys, for every role of the pod, and the agent is told where that file is (`OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN_FILE`, above), so every agent in the deployment holds the login the whole table sits behind.
Oh My Pi's two tables are keyed by the session's recorded path and carry no tenant, project or issue column, so rights over the table are rights over every conversation in it:
the controller's, and every role's of every issue of every tree.
An agent that obeys text it was handed can therefore read another issue's transcript and rewrite it
— and these agents read issue bodies, pull request comments and fetched pages by design, so text written to be obeyed reaches them as a matter of course.
A rewritten row is not an inert file: it is what that role's next resume replays into its own agent, so the write lands in another agent's head.
The party reachable this way is any other issue, role or tree **of this deployment**, never one outside it:
the database holds this deployment's sessions, and no pod of it mounts another's.

Under `cloudsql-iam` there is no such credential to hold:
what the agent reads carries a login and no password at all (`Endpoint.AgentURL`, `internal/ompsessions/store.go`), and what it names is a unix socket in the generation's own directory on the role's own memory-backed private volume, which the pod's one `roles` container mounts under that role's directory alone and which no other role's namespace is shown (`legion launcher role-init`).
Any process of the role's own generation can still dial that socket, as any process in a pod can read the URL file under `postgres`:
this store removes the password, not that trade, and the rights the login has in the database are still every conversation's.
With `writer_audience`, the socket admits only the launcher and the generation's Oh My Pi process, and closes every other connection ([What `cloudsql-iam` puts in a pod](#what-cloudsql-iam-puts-in-a-pod)).
That limits which process connects, not what a connection reaches: the login's rights still cover every conversation, and code that runs inside Oh My Pi uses Oh My Pi's own connection ([Anatomy of a Sandbox pod](#anatomy-of-a-sandbox-pod), "the session transcripts").

Under `pvc` a session was a file on a disk only its own issue's pod could mount, so no issue could reach another's at all, and this release widens that boundary rather than keeping it.
That is the trade LEGION-654's spec accepts for sessions that outlive their pods, and it is a trade to weigh before the rollout rather than after:
a deployment that cannot accept one agent reaching another's transcript has no setting in this release that stops it.
Where it is closed properly is `dispatch://INFRA-228` — a credential per issue, or a row-level policy the database itself enforces
— and nothing in this release anticipates that work.

The login is not narrowed here, and narrowing it would buy nothing.
A login restricted to `omp_session_files` and `omp_session_files_parts` still reads and writes every row of both, which is the whole of the exposure above;
isolation has to be per issue — a credential of its own, or a policy the rows are checked against — and no table-level grant is that.
The project also declined the same narrowing on this same store on `dispatch://INFRA-244`, so deciding the other way here would put two contradictory postures on one credential in one deployment.
What this release does ask of the login is unchanged:
give it no rights beyond the database of those two tables, and treat its URL as a credential every agent holds.

A resume is held to the table, and to nothing on a disk.
A role's launcher looks the recorded session up in the table before it starts the child (`internal/launcher`, `resumable`, `sessionWritten`)
— under `postgres` through the same URL file the child will read, and under `cloudsql-iam` through its own pgx client over the socket its proxy has just bound and proven, which is that generation's own (`Endpoint.ClientURL`)
— and refuses the start when the table holds no such session (`resume session <path>: the session table holds no such session`):
a launch failure, never a fresh agent, and three of them retire the claim.
A database it cannot reach is asked again with a backoff (half a second, doubling to four seconds) for up to 30 seconds
— under `postgres` the URL file read afresh each time, since that file is a projection something else may replace — and only then refuses the start.
Neither `workspace-init` looks for a session file, and neither is told to expect one: there is no disk on which a session could be waiting.
A launch that creates the issue's pod provisions its workspace from the issue's pushed branch and continues its own session from the table;
a role launched into the pod already running provisions nothing and continues its session in the workspace the roles before it left.
Which launch is which, and what goes with a pod, is stated once in [The disk dies with its pod](#the-disk-dies-with-its-pod), and for a kept volume in [A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod).
A child issue re-admitted as a root of its own keeps its roles' sessions the same way (`Machine.Retree`):
they are rows, and no disk is carried into the new tree.

An agent whose workspace is newer than its session is told so before its next turn.
Provisioning records when it created a workspace, in the workspace's own `.jj/legion-created`, which jj never snapshots (`workspace.RecordCreated`).
At every resume the role's launcher compares that record with when the session was last written:
the row's `mtime_ms`, which Oh My Pi moves on every write and `legion sessions import` sets to the copied file's.
A workspace created after that write starts the generation with `LEGION_WORKSPACE_RECREATED=true`;
every other generation gets `false`, whatever the container's environment says, and so does a resume into a workspace with no record (one provisioned before the record was kept).
A record that is empty or not one RFC 3339 instant, which an init container killed mid-write can leave, decides only that notice:
the launcher logs it, takes the workspace as not recreated, and resumes.
At session start a Legion session's plugin reads the variable and saves one message to the session, ahead of the next turn whatever starts it (a task, an Envoy event):
`Your workspace was recreated since your last turn: it holds what was pushed
to legion/<KEY> (the repository's default branch if nothing was), and anything you had not pushed
is gone. …` (`packages/pi-legion/src/workspace-recreated.ts`, a steer that starts no turn), with an id of its own process in the message's `details`.
A prompt, the daemon's next task or a person's direct message that pi-envoy delivers as a user turn, first recovers a failed last turn, and Oh My Pi recovers an empty `length` stop by moving the branch back to that turn's parent, which takes the saved message off the branch with it.
The plugin's `before_agent_start`, which runs after that recovery on either path, sends the message again when the branch no longer holds this process's copy, a notice an earlier recreation saved not counting, and the turn saves it after the prompt.
The recovery leaves the first copy in the process's live context, so that process's requests keep its first copy alone, and an earlier recreation's notice stays where the history put it.
An Envoy card, a custom message sent to start a turn, goes through neither the recovery nor `before_agent_start`, so its branch keeps the saved message.
Measured on Oh My Pi `18.8.3-sami.20261009-045702`, with resumed sessions whose last turn was an ordinary reply, an empty `length` stop, or an empty `length` stop in a session already told at an earlier recreation (file storage for all three, and SQL storage for the first two):
the notice is in the stored session before the task arrives, the task's first model request carries this process's copy once, just after the history and before the task, and after the task the stored branch holds it, so a process lost in that turn resumes with the notice already there.
With the plugin before the re-send, the `length` case's stored branch had lost it; with the plugin before the id, so did the case of a second recreation.
A `task` subagent is never told.

A role on Claude Code keeps its conversation differently.
Its conversation is Claude Code's own transcript, under the role's `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` (`<role state home>/claude`), which Oh My Pi never reads.
Its generation is told `OMP_SESSION_STORAGE` and `OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN_FILE` as every role of its pod is (`sessionDSNFile`, `mainEnvironment`): Claude Code ignores both.
Under `postgres` the pointer is what keeps the shim from exporting the mounted URL, password and all, into Claude Code's environment, and under `cloudsql-iam` it names the password-less URL file the pod's launcher writes for every generation of the role it starts.
A relaunch continues the transcript with `--resume <session id>`, the id read from the recorded path.

**Where a Claude Code session lives across pods.**
The transcript and the phase reminder's record are files on the pod's disk, which dies with the pod ([The disk dies with its pod](#the-disk-dies-with-its-pod)), or, on a kept volume, with the issue's Sandbox ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)).
So the pod's launcher keeps both in Oh My Pi's session table while the generation runs (`internal/launcher`, `claude.go`), in its manager of that role in the `roles` container:
the role's state home is on the issue's disk, which the container and the role's own namespaces see at the same path, so the launcher reads and restores the files where Claude Code writes them.
Each Claude launch's start command carries `LEGION_CLAUDE_SESSION_ID`, the session its agent command starts or resumes, and nothing else carries it: no Oh My Pi role and no tmux pane.
Each file is a row of `omp_session_files`, keyed by its absolute path and written as Oh My Pi writes its own:
the transcript, `<CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR>/projects/<dir>/<id>.jsonl`, and the record, `<CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR>/legion-phase-stall-<id>.json`.
Every row has a `byte_len` and a `mtime_ms`, the file's mtime when it was saved, so the rows never stop an Oh My Pi process from loading its index.
The launcher holds one connection to the session database for the generation, through the generation's proxy socket under `cloudsql-iam`.
It saves a file that grew at most every 2 s, the transcript only up to its last newline.
Each save is one transaction that appends the new bytes as a part, and only over what that launcher saved last.
When another writer has moved the row, the launcher stops saving that file and logs it.
It never overwrites the row.
A save the database refuses is logged and tried again at the next save, and the agent runs on.

A resume looks the transcript's row up first, so the recreated-workspace notice below is decided from its last save.
Then the launcher writes each row to its path, but only where the file is missing or holds part of the row:
a longer file, which a relaunch into the same pod leaves, is not shortened.
The launcher reads a file there only as a regular file, and no further than one byte past its row, which is all that decision needs;
it opens a file it saves, and writes the marker below, the same way.
So a link, a fifo or anything else that is no regular file at one of those paths is refused at once in words naming it:
a resume over it fails, and a save is tried again at the next save.
Then Claude Code starts.
On a fresh session the launcher writes `<transcript>.legion-saved` beside the transcript once its first save has committed, and the claim boot of claude-envoy waits for that file as well as the transcript before it registers the session.
A transcript the daemon has recorded is then always in the table: otherwise the next pod's resume would be refused, and three refusals retire the claim.
After Claude Code exits, the launcher makes one last save before the generation's proxy closes.
Its deadline is the stop's grace less the proxy's 1 s drain.
This save is best effort: at the 9 s floor of `worker_stop_timeout_seconds`, a worker that spends its whole 5 s agent grace can leave it no time.
A hard kill (a node lost, a SIGKILL) makes no last save.
The table then holds what the last committed save left: the transcript up to a newline, without at most the lines of its last 2 s.
The daemon sends an interrupted task again, behind a sentence that names what the relaunch ended (the turn, its tool calls and each kind of background work the process last reported) and says that the subagents and background jobs of that turn are gone, so the worker checks what that turn did and does the rest again.
A Claude Code worker reports only at its Stop hook, so its newest report is older than the turn cut off: the sentence adds that the daemon has no report of what that turn started, and a process that left no activity report at all is told that every subagent and background job it started is gone.

The recreated-workspace notice reaches a Claude Code role too:
its own MCP server (`packages/claude-envoy`) reads `LEGION_WORKSPACE_RECREATED` at start and writes the same text into the session over the bridge's inbox, once per launch, recorded beside the phase reminder's state so a restarted server does not repeat it.

The variables are a generation's, but the store a pod was created under is the pod's:
the providers volume's session item under `postgres`, and under `cloudsql-iam` the session-proxy flags the pod's launcher container carries: three, a fourth when `impersonate_service_account` is set, and a fifth when `writer_audience` is set (`sessionStoreInPod`).
A pod that holds another session store than a pod created now would holds a move (`movedSessionStore`, `internal/runtime/sandbox/addresses.go`)
— one created before this release, under a deployment whose sessions were still files, one created under the other kind or another key, or, under `cloudsql-iam`, a changed instance, database or login, a service account named, dropped or changed, or a writer audience named, dropped or changed
— and the pod is replaced: an issue pod by its update round, and the controller's pod at the next launch into it ([The disk dies with its pod](#the-disk-dies-with-its-pod)).
Under `postgres` the image probe's container is told `OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN_FILE` too, so `legion probe-image`, which reads the providers directory as the shim does, never exports the URL into Oh My Pi's environment;
under `cloudsql-iam` the probe's pod mounts no session key and is told no pointer at all (`sessionDSNPointer`, `manifest.go`).

A resumed session also restores the model it last used, and the Oh My Pi `.omp-pin` names refuses, in `--mode rpc`, to resume one whose model the profile no longer has (`Could not restore model <provider>/<model>`, exit 1).
So a change to the pods' model route (`runtime.kubernetes.pod`, `provider_keys`) that drops a model fails the launch of every agent resuming a session on it until the route offers that model again.
Keep the route unchanged across the copy below in particular: there every session outlives the volume it was written on.

### What `cloudsql-iam` puts in a pod

No session key, anywhere.
No issue pod, no controller pod and no image-probe pod mounts one (`sessionSecretKey`, `internal/runtime/sandbox/manifest.go`, which answers for `postgres` alone), the daemon holds no connection string, and no URL of the database itself sits in a Secret, a volume, an argv, an environment value or a log: the one URL a role is given names the local socket its launcher binds, in a file on the role's own memory-backed private volume (below).
What the pod's `legion launcher` is told instead is where the database is
— `--session-instance <project:region:instance>`, `--session-database <name>` and `--session-user <login>`, in that order, the three values of `session_database` (`sessionProxyFlags` over `sessionProxyFlagNames`, `manifest.go`), once for every role it serves.
When `impersonate_service_account` is set, a fourth flag follows the three: `--session-impersonate-service-account <email>` (`sessionProxyAccountFlag`, `manifest.go`).
A launcher told the fourth without all of the three refuses the database as named in part before it connects, and names each missing flag (`validateSessionDatabase`, `internal/launcher/launcher.go`).
When `writer_audience` is set, a fifth flag follows the fourth: `--session-writer-audience <audience>` (`sessionWriterAudienceFlag`, `manifest.go`).
A launcher refuses the fifth before it connects, and says why: without the fourth, in another form than `ompsessions.ValidWriterAudience` takes, and in the single-role form, whose agent runs in the container's own namespaces, where the token would be in its view (`validateSessionDatabase`).
There is no address among them: the launcher binds each generation's socket in that generation's own directory, under the role's own private directory, which it already knows from `--roles-dir` (`--private-dir` in the controller's pod).

With `writer_audience`, the pod also carries the session writer token (`sessionWriterVolumes`, `manifest.go`).
It is one projected ServiceAccount token volume, `session-writer-token`, of the member's audience, for 3600 seconds, with mode 0440, where the token is the file `token`.
The kubelet writes a fresh token before the old one expires, and the proxy reads the file again at each exchange.
