Only the launcher's container mounts it, read-only, at `/var/run/legion/roles/session-writer` (`SessionWriterDir`, `names.go`, and `podTokenMounts`, `manifest.go`).
That container is the `roles` container of an issue pod, or the controller's container, which then runs the roles-dir form ([Daemon-launched controller](#daemon-launched-controller)).
No init container mounts it, and the image probe's pod carries none.
No role reads the token, because the directory is under `/var/run/legion/roles`, which role-init covers with an empty filesystem in each role's namespaces (`prepareRoleNamespace`, `internal/launcher/roleinit_linux.go`).
The launcher gives the path, `<roles-dir>/session-writer/token`, to its proxy alone, and writes it into no generation's environment and no file (`startSession`).
The volume name is Legion's in every deployment, with or without the member, so the loader refuses an operator's volume named `session-writer-token` (`CheckPod`).

Every generation of that role then gets its own connection, in this order (`manager.start`, `packages/daemon/internal/launcher/launcher.go`):

1. The launcher makes the generation's own directory, `/var/run/legion/private/g<generation>` as the role's namespace sees it, on the role's own memory-backed private volume, owner-only, and writes the connection URL into it as `OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN`, mode `0600`, created exclusively and without following a link
   — the way it writes that generation's boot token (`writeFiles`, then `startSession`).
   The URL names the socket at the path the role's own namespaces show it, which role-init binds back under `/var/run/legion/private`;
   the launcher, outside those namespaces, binds it at the role's directory of the roles directory.

2. It binds a unix socket beside that file, `.s.PGSQL.5432`, which is libpq's own name for a Postgres server on port 5432 (`ompsessions.SocketName`), and proves the credential path with one upstream connection before its start returns (`sessionproxy.Start`, `packages/daemon/internal/sessionproxy`).
   The socket is bound before anything is dialed, so a start that loses the address to something else costs no credential work.

3. Only then, when the start carries a resume, it looks the recorded session up in the table through that socket.

4. Only then does it start the worker shim, and so Oh My Pi, whose `OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN_FILE` names the file written in step 1 (`sessionDSNFile`, `manifest.go`).

A failure in any of the first three refuses the generation.
The start answers with the error, which names what failed:
clearing the private directory names it, or the entry it could not remove;
making the generation's directory or writing one of its files (a credential, the connection URL) names the generation and the file;
the proxy's start names the generation and the instance; the resume lookup names the recorded session file.
No child is started; the proxy, if it had started, is closed and the generation's directory removed, so nothing is left bound and nothing is left on disk (`endSession`).
An agent never runs against a proxy that cannot reach the database, because the proof dial happens before the proxy's start returns.
That dial is bounded at half the launcher's `--stop-grace` (5 s at the default `worker_stop_timeout_seconds` of 10), so an instance that never answers
— an unreachable private address, a handshake that stalls
— is refused, as `no answer within <bound>`, while the daemon still waits for the start's answer:
the daemon waits on a start until the launcher's connection deadline plus that same grace, so at least the whole grace remains however late the launcher connected (`proofTimeout`, `launcher.go`).
The launcher reads one command at a time, so the bound also keeps it free to read the stop the daemon sends after a start it gave up on.

The connection belongs to the generation, not to the pod.
The proxy keeps serving through the child's stop grace however the stop arrives
— the daemon's stop or the container's own SIGTERM
— so the session writes the agent makes while it shuts down are served:
the context the launcher starts the proxy with bounds only its start, and once started the proxy ends only when it is closed (`sessionproxy.Start`).
It is closed once the child, and in the pod the generation's leftover processes (`cleanExitedGeneration`), have exited, and before the generation's directory goes, so the launcher exits with nothing bound, nothing is left listening over a socket that has been removed, and between generations nothing is bound and no connection file exists (`manager.wait`).
The next generation binds a socket and writes a file of its own.

How long the proxy outlives the moment the generation is told to end, in a pod, where the launcher is PID 1 of its role's PID namespace (`signalGeneration`, `process.go`):

- **A stop** — the daemon's stop, with its grace, or the container's SIGTERM, with `--stop-grace` (`worker_stop_timeout_seconds`, which is also the pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`): at most that one grace.
  The stop's SIGTERM and, at the grace, its SIGKILL reach every process in the namespace, the child and whatever it left behind alike, so the leftovers' cleanup ends inside the same grace, and no process is left to hold a connection open.

- **A child that exits on its own** and leaves processes behind:
  in the controller's pod, where the launcher is not namespaced, the leftovers get up to `--stop-grace` more, SIGTERM then SIGKILL (`cleanExitedGeneration`, `internal/launcher/process.go`), with the proxy still serving them, so at most one grace after the child's exit.
  In an issue pod the role's own init is what signals them: SIGTERM over the role's namespace, then `roleNamespaceDrain`, two seconds, for them to go before the SIGKILL that ends the namespace (`runRoleShim`, `internal/launcher/roleinit_linux.go`), so at most two seconds after the child's exit.
  The role's output then says how that wait ended, with its span by role-init's own clock: `role-init: the role's namespace emptied <span> after its SIGTERM` when the processes left, or `role-init: the role's processes still ran <span> after its SIGTERM, the drain's bound of 2s: killing them` when the bound came first, which is where a git or a jj the role left can leave its lock in the issue's clone.

When the proxy is closed, it lets connections still open finish for up to one second (`sessionDrain`, `launcher.go`;
`Config.Drain`, `sessionproxy.go`), then closes both ends of those left.
In a pod that drain costs nothing, since every process that could hold a connection is gone by then;
it bounds the case where the launcher is not PID 1, where signals reach only the child's process group and a holder outside it could otherwise keep the stop, the next generation and the launcher's exit waiting.

That URL carries a login and no password, because the credential is the pod's own cloud identity or, with `impersonate_service_account`, the service account that identity impersonates:
the Cloud SQL Go connector puts it in the instance's ephemeral-certificate exchange (automatic IAM database authentication, `cloudsqlconn.WithIAMAuthN`), never in the Postgres startup packet, and mints one as it dials, per connection, from a certificate cache it keeps refreshed (`newConnectorDialer` and `serve`, `internal/sessionproxy`).
That is why the proxy reads no Postgres protocol at all:
it accepts a connection, dials the instance over its private IP, and copies bytes both ways
— which is what Google's own `cloud-sql-proxy` does over the same connector.
Google runs that connector as a container beside the application;
a Legion pod admits no further container, since `runtime.kubernetes.pod` takes only env, volumes, mounts and a service account, so the same library runs inside the pod's own first process, the launcher itself.

With `impersonate_service_account`, the connector also takes two token sources, and each of them impersonates that service account with the pod's own credentials (`cloudsqlconn.WithIAMAuthNTokenSources`, `connectorOptions`, `internal/sessionproxy`).
The source for the Cloud SQL Admin API has the `sqlservice.admin` and `cloud-platform` scopes.
The source for the database login has the `sqlservice.login` scope alone.
Each source refreshes its one-hour token for as long as the proxy serves.
The proxy's start line then names the account: `sessionproxy: serving <instance> on <socket> as <account>`.

With `writer_audience`, both sources impersonate the account with a federated token, never with the pod's own credentials (`connectorOptions`).
One federated source exchanges the writer token at Google's Security Token Service, `https://sts.googleapis.com/v1/token` (`STSTokenURL`, `internal/sessionproxy/sessionproxy.go`), where the pod-local metadata endpoint exchanges too.
The exchange names the member's value as its audience, a JWT as its subject token type and the `cloud-platform` scope.
The proxy gives both sources one IAM Service Account Credentials client, which puts the federated token on each `generateAccessToken` call.
The federated token is exchanged again five minutes before it expires (`writerTokenEarlyRefresh`), and each exchange and each `generateAccessToken` call has a bound of 30 seconds (`writerCallTimeout`).
So the proxy reads no credential of the pod: it looks up no Application Default Credentials and asks no metadata server.
Its start line says which credential signs in: `sessionproxy: serving <instance> on <socket> as <account> with the launcher's writer token`.

The two readers of that socket spell it differently, so `ompsessions.Endpoint` composes both (`internal/ompsessions/store.go`):

| reader | spelling | why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| the agent's Oh My Pi, through `OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN_FILE` | `AgentURL`: `postgres://<login>@localhost/<database>?path=<the socket>&sslmode=disable` | Oh My Pi hands the text to Bun's SQL client, which takes a unix socket as the URL's `path` parameter and ignores the host |
| the launcher's own resume lookup | `ClientURL`: `postgres:///<database>?host=<the socket's directory>&sslmode=disable&user=<login>` | pgx takes libpq's `host` as the socket's *directory* and appends `.s.PGSQL.5432` itself |

An IAM login holds an `@`, so both spellings are built with `net/url`, which percent-encodes it, and the socket path, wherever it lands.
Neither carries a password.
The file is the agent's to read through its pointer and nothing else's to export:
it is in the generation's private directory, not in the providers mount the worker shim exports from.

**Who may use the socket under `writer_audience`.**
With the member, the proxy reads the process at the other end of each connection it accepts, as the kernel recorded it at connect (`SO_PEERCRED`, `readPeer`, `peer_linux.go`).
It reads it before it dials anything for the connection (`admitted`, `sessionproxy.go`).
The generation's check admits two processes (`sessionPeer`, `internal/launcher/sessionpeer.go`):

- The launcher's own process, because the resume lookups (`resumable`, and `sessionByID` for a start that names its session by its id alone) and a Claude Code keeper (`claudeKeeper`) connect from it.

- The generation's Oh My Pi process.
  The check finds it in the process table (`memoryguard.Scan`), never from the process that connects.
  It reads the generation's role-init, then the role's shim, then the oldest direct child of the shim whose `/proc/<pid>/exe` is the agent's executable.
  The shim is the oldest direct child of the role-init that runs the launcher's own executable as `worker-shim` (`roleShim`, `internal/launcher/memoryguard.go`), the rule the memory guard uses too.
  The first connection that finds the Oh My Pi process pins its pid and its start time.
  Every later connection must come from that pid, with that start time, so a process that takes the pid after Oh My Pi ends is refused.

A Claude Code generation has no agent that connects, so its check admits the launcher alone.
The proxy closes every other connection before any dial, writes nothing back, and logs one line, which the container's log shows behind the role's prefix:
`sessionproxy: refused a connection to <instance> from pid <pid> (<command>): <reason>`.
`<command>` is the process's `/proc/<pid>/comm`, quoted because the process chooses it, or `?` when it cannot be read.
A connection whose peer cannot be read is closed in the same way, with the line `sessionproxy: refused a connection to <instance> from a process whose pid could not be read: <error>`.
A process table that cannot be read, a missing role-init, shim or agent, and a peer that is not the pinned process each refuse the connection, and `<reason>` says which.
A refused connection costs no dial and no credential work, and its line holds no token.

No other process of the role passes the check:

- A command that Oh My Pi runs is a descendant of Oh My Pi, so it is never a direct child of the shim.
  No process of the shim makes itself a subreaper, so an orphan goes to role-init, the init of the role's PID namespace.

- An orphan that runs `legion worker-shim` is younger than the real shim, and the check takes the oldest.

- The shim's other direct children (the secrets renewer, the working copy's adoption, the CodeGraph warm-up) run other executables.
  Oh My Pi's own helpers are its children, not the shim's.

The start command names the agent's executable as `agentExecutable` (`shimwire.LauncherStart.AgentExecutable`).
The daemon fills it for every Oh My Pi launch with the first word of the agent's own argv, `/opt/omp/bin/omp` in the image, and leaves it out of a Claude Code launch (`launcherCommand`, `internal/runtime/sandbox/launcher.go`).
The argv after `--` cannot say it, because a deployment's `setup` wraps the agent in `/bin/sh -c <script> legion-start`.
While that wrapper runs, the shim's child runs `/bin/sh`, so nothing is pinned until the wrapper's `exec`.
Under the member, the launcher refuses an Oh My Pi start whose `agentExecutable` is empty or not an absolute path (`newSessionPeer`).
It resolves the path's links once, because `/proc/<pid>/exe` names the file the links lead to.

The launcher also refuses a generation under the member unless `/proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope` reads an integer of 1 or more (`requireTraceScope`, `sessionpeer.go`).
The check admits Oh My Pi and none of its descendants.
That holds only while no descendant can act as Oh My Pi: take its admitted connection (`pidfd_getfd`), read or write its memory (`/proc/<pid>/mem`, `process_vm_writev`), or trace it.
Each of these needs ptrace attach access, and at a scope of 1 or more Yama refuses that access to a descendant.
A scope of 0, a file that cannot be read and text that is not an integer each refuse the start, and the start's error names the file and what it read:
`generation <n>: the session writer token needs /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope to read 1 or more, and it reads "0": a process of the role could then trace the agent and use its connection to the session database`.
A gVisor issue pod read 1 when this was measured, on 2026-11-19.
Nobody has measured the kernel of a microVM pod, so such a pod starts a generation under the member only where its own kernel reads 1 or more.

What the operator supplies is the three required values of `session_database`, the pods' cloud identity and the login's rights in the database.
The pods' cloud identity is the identity of the ServiceAccount that `runtime.kubernetes.pod.service_account` names.
Without `impersonate_service_account`, the connector signs in as that identity.
With it, the connector signs in as the service account, and the operator also supplies that fourth value and the four things [Selecting the store](#selecting-the-store) lists.
With `writer_audience`, the operator also supplies that fifth value and the four things that [Selecting the store](#selecting-the-store) lists for it.
The login's rights are the ones `postgres` needs too: Oh My Pi creates and migrates `omp_session_files`, `omp_session_files_parts` and, from the pinned build on, `omp_session_leases`, `omp_session_files_blobs` and `omp_session_files_refs` in the `public` schema when it starts, so the login needs `USAGE, CREATE ON SCHEMA public` beside the database, or it must own the schema.
`legion sessions import` is unchanged and keeps `--dsn-file`: it is the operator's own command, run with no launcher and no proxy, so the operator supplies a connection URL the machine it runs on can reach.
A tree volume is a PersistentVolumeClaim, so the copy itself runs where that claim can be mounted: in a pod of the worker image, under gVisor, with the volume mounted read-only at `/legion`, as the recipe under [Copying file sessions before turning it on](#copying-file-sessions-before-turning-it-on) lower on this page says.

### Starting fresh when a session is lost or wedged

A provider's content filter asks nothing of the operator.
Any of the four providers' filters (Anthropic's, OpenAI's, Google's and Amazon Bedrock's) moves the session to the next model of the deployment's own `retry.fallbackChains`, in the same session, and the plugin brings it back to the role's own model an hour later.
The refusal that lands after the model has already sent text is one of them: Oh My Pi does not walk its chain for that one, because the turn cannot be replayed, so the plugin walks it (`packages/pi-legion/src/model-fallback.ts`).
Each further refusal of the same model doubles that wait, to at most eight hours, and a clean turn on the model puts it back to one hour.
The two waits are a pane's and a pod's environment, `LEGION_REFUSAL_COOLDOWN_MS` (3600000, one hour) and `LEGION_REFUSAL_COOLDOWN_MAX_MS` (28800000, eight hours):
the daemon passes each to the worker it launches while its own environment holds it, and to its own controller, which the same fallback serves; a role told neither runs on those two numbers (`refusalCooldownVariables`, `internal/daemon/specs.go`).
The plugin writes each arming into the session's own transcript, so a worker the daemon relaunches on that session waits out the time that was left rather than coming back early.
The return undoes the fallback's own move and nothing after it: a session that no longer runs the model the fallback put it on, because a person's `/model` moved it or a relaunch started it on another model meanwhile, stays on the model it runs.

Every deployment sets `retry.fallbackRevertPolicy: never` beside its `retry.fallbackChains`, wherever it keeps them (the operator's `overlay.yml`, or a `role_config_files` overlay of its own).
Without it Oh My Pi returns the session to a model it suppressed itself, for a rate limit or for an error it could not classify, as soon as that suppression ends, and its floor for one it cannot time is five minutes, well inside the plugin's hour.
For a refusal the setting changes nothing, and the reason differs by path.
A refusal that lands before the model has sent any text is one Oh My Pi walks the chain for itself, and it pins the fallback it walks to, which the revert leaves alone however it is set; that pin ends at the plugin's timed return, a `setModel`, which clears it and puts the session back on the role's own model.
A refusal that lands after the text Oh My Pi leaves where it is, so the revert has no fallback of its own to move: there the plugin's own `setModel` walks the chain, and the same timed return brings the session back.
`scripts/e2e/refusal-fallback-omp.sh` measures the difference on a ten-minute cooldown: with the setting, no request at all reaches the refused model between the fifth minute and the tenth, and the first request after the tenth goes to that model again.
The same proof has two rate-limited panes, each with `retry-after: 60`.
For a 429 retried by the transport, the host sees only the timeout at its ten-minute first-event budget and suppresses the strong model for its five-minute floor.
For a 429 with `x-should-retry: false`, the host sees the 429 and suppresses the strong model for sixty seconds.
Both returns wait for that suppression, not the plugin's refusal cooldown, and the proof bounds the transcript's model switch to one request's cadence after suppression.
The final-429 pane requests every ten seconds, so ignoring suppression is visible before sixty seconds.

Two commands replace what a provider keeps refusing, and the compaction is the first of them, because a new session loses what the old one held — what the worker learned of its issue, and what it had not pushed or written down yet:

```sh
legion claims compact --claim <token> --operator-token-file <file>
```

It has the claim's Oh My Pi session write a summary of itself and then sends the claim whatever task it owes again, however much of the provider-error ladder's wait was left: the claim keeps its session, its workspace and everything it knows of its issue, and what goes is the length of the transcript the provider is asked to read.
The summary is text, because the daemon asks with instructions of its own: Oh My Pi runs its image-based snapcompact method only for a compaction that carries none, and a worker resumed on those images would need a vision model to read its own past (`compactInstructions`, `packages/daemon/internal/api/compact.go`).
The answer says whether the session was compacted and, when it was not, why — Oh My Pi's own words for a compaction it refused or skipped, `Already compacted` or `Nothing to compact (session too small)`, and the daemon's for a wait that ran out or a transport that failed — and whatever task the claim owed has gone again either way.
The command carries no deadline of its own, as no `legion claims` command does, and the daemon bounds that model call over the whole transcript at ten minutes (`runtime.CompactTimeout`).
While it runs the claim reads `working`, the daemon's one word for a busy agent, so the ladder's re-send and any newer task wait for its end, a second compaction is refused in its own words, and a fresh session is refused `CLAIM_IN_A_TURN`, since a claim whose session is being compacted is read before its process and the compaction in flight owns what becomes of its agent.

A session the compaction left refused is the fresh session's, and so is a claim stored working that no process stands behind, which the compaction refuses by name:

```sh
legion claims retry --claim <token> --operator-token-file <file> --fresh-session
```

It reaches a claim whose agent is registered, ready or idle, one that is suspended, failed or retired, and one stored working that no process stands behind, with no suspension held over it — one idle between the ladder's sends, a suspended one, one an operator stopped (`legion claims stop` retires the claim it stops), a failed one, a dead architect its project's controller has no other way back from, and an architect, a root's or a child's, as much as a phase worker (`freshSession`, `packages/daemon/internal/api/freshsession.go`).
It suspends the claim where the request arrives — a live agent and the claim no process stands behind alike — forgets the session that claim recorded, and starts it again.
A phase worker comes back with the task of the phase its issue stands in now, and an architect with its catch-up: a root's architect with its whole tree's, and a child's own architect with its issue's and every issue's under it.
A claim no process stands behind comes back with the task its dead turn held, which its suspension takes back and its start sends again.
A forget or a start the machine refuses after this request stopped the claim is answered 200, with that refusal and the state it left the claim in named in `phaseNotRestarted` and printed under the claim's own line, because the request changed the claim: a suspended claim is started by asking for a fresh session again, and a claim the refused step left in another state, such as `launching` with its launch tried again at the probe interval, is read in `legion claims list` before anything more is asked of it.
No `forget-session` comes before it, and no recovery here needs an edit of the daemon's store.

Both read the claim's process at the runtime, at the moment of the request, rather than the daemon's memory of an older report, which a daemon restart forgets, so what that read found is what answers a claim the daemon records as working.
That read records what it finds as the sweep's own report of the process would, so a read that finds the process running and clears a death charge writes the claim as the daemon holds it, in the same write that report makes; a refusal it answers stops, suspends, forgets, takes back and starts nothing.
Both refuse such a claim `CLAIM_IN_A_TURN` where the read finds the process running, since compacting or suspending a claim in a turn would cut that turn off and that turn may be the one that ends the run of refusals.
A claim whose session is being compacted takes that code too: it is answered before any process is read, because the compaction in flight owns what becomes of its agent.
A claim whose process the runtime would not answer for is refused `CLAIM_UNSETTLED`, and the refusal says the read was not answered: an unread process may be a running one, and it may be a dead one, so the claim is left exactly as the request found it, with nothing suspended, nothing forgotten and nothing started.
A claim stored working that records no process to read takes that code too, and its refusal says no process is recorded.
So does a claim that moved under the request where the daemon finds it no longer working or its process gone once more: the fresh session reads its process again when the machine refuses its suspension and otherwise answers what that second read finds, and the compaction gives that code where the machine refused it as working and the claim is no longer stored working; either says the claim moved and changes nothing of it.
Both refuse a claim between states, queued or with a launch in flight, and a claim left working under a relaunch the daemon's wake pacing parked, which has a launch in flight as much as those two (`CLAIM_UNSETTLED`).
Both refuse a claim a suspension is held over as well, in whatever state the hold found it, since what such a claim waits for is that hold's end rather than anything either recovery would do.
Where the read finds no process behind a claim stored working the two part: the fresh session reaches that claim, and the compaction refuses it `CLAIM_NOT_RUNNING`, naming `fresh_session` (`legion claims retry --fresh-session`) as what starts it again, because it has no agent to ask and no session to compact.
The project's own controller claim is the one exception: the fresh session refuses it in every state but failed or retired under `cyber_policy`, and the daemon's controller keeper does nothing for a controller stored working, so the compaction names the operator's `legion claims suspend --claim <token>` and then `legion claims resume --claim <token>` instead.
Each refusal says what the claim is doing when it is given, and which operation reaches each state `legion claims list` shows: it names no report, turn, hold or relaunch to come, and ends by telling the caller to ask again later and read the claim's state in that list.
The compaction refuses three more: a claim that is suspended, failed or retired, which runs no session to ask and whose refusal names what starts it again, the fresh session for a workflow role and the daemon's controller keeper for the project's own controller claim (the operator's `legion claims retry --claim <token>` for a controller held for `cyber_policy`, which its keeper retries no more), a claim whose agent has registered and is not ready yet, which has no session to ask either and which the fresh session reaches, and a claim whose role runs on the Claude Code harness, which has no Oh My Pi session to compact at all.
The project's controller holds both as tools of its own, `compact (issue, role)` and `fresh_session (issue, role)`, which name the claim by its issue and role rather than by a token the controller never sees: the effect, the refusals and the answer are the operator's own and only the authentication differs, and a `provider-errors on <KEY>` notice is where the controller reaches for them, the compaction first for a claim whose session the provider keeps refusing and a fresh session when the claim is still refused after it, and the fresh session alone for a claim no process stands behind, which the compaction refuses by name (`skills/legion-controller`).
The controller's own claim is the one asymmetry: a fresh session of it is refused whatever state it is in, because the daemon's controller keeper is what starts the controller — it launches a queued one, resumes one the daemon suspended (its resume is the rule's, which an operator's suspension holds against, so a controller an operator suspended stands until that operator resumes it) and retries one that failed or retired — where a compaction of it is not refused, since the session, its process and everything the controller holds stay and only the transcript gets shorter.
A controller that failed under `cyber_policy` (OpenAI refused its session's content) is the exception: the keeper retries it no more, so the operator's `legion claims retry --claim <token>`, with `--fresh-session` or without, launches its agent again, always in a new session.
The controller cannot name itself through its own door either way, since `controller` is no role a claim token is built from, so the operator's `--claim` is the one way onto that claim.

Use `legion claims forget-session` for a session that is gone rather than refused: a stopped claim's session lost with its volume, or a file session imported before its volume can be reaped.
Read the claim's recorded session from `legion claims list`, then run:

```sh
legion claims forget-session --claim <token> --session <recorded session id> --operator-token-file <file>
```

`--session` is required and must equal the session the claim currently records.
The claim must have no live process: suspend it first, or use a queued, failed, or retired claim.
The daemon clears and persists only `session` and `session_file`, logs the forgotten session and file, and returns them in the answer.
It does not read or change the session database, so the old session row remains there.

Retrying a failed architect then spawns a fresh agent, the daemon's controller keeper does the same for its failed controller claim, and a retired claim starts fresh at its next workflow start or re-admission.
Resuming a suspended claim starts a fresh session with its pending task.

### Copying file sessions before turning it on

This runbook copies only from the release before issue pods, `legion-v10.0.0`, whose every role runs in a Sandbox of its own and keeps its session on its tree's volume.
A deployment on `legion-v10.1.0` to `legion-v10.2.x`, which runs one pod per issue, has no copy path: its switch to `postgres` is a drain at a pushed boundary, every tree closed, and the sessions on those volumes are lost.
There is no way back either, and nothing to go back to: this release has no second store, and nothing copies a row out to a file.

Before it reaps a Sandbox-owned volume, including a disk-shape replacement, an issue or tree cleanup, an orphan cleanup, or a controller cleanup, the daemon reads the retiring Sandbox's pod template.
Under `postgres`, the providers volume's `OMP_SESSION_SQL_DSN` item proves the Sandbox stored sessions in a database; under `cloudsql-iam`, the launcher command's `--session-instance`, `--session-database`, and `--session-user` flags do.
Either marker permits the reap.
Without a database marker, the daemon refuses when a matching claim records a session; it has no providers-Secret read permission or session-store connection, so it cannot inspect the session database.
Its refusal names the claim, session, and volume.
To keep the session's contents, run the import procedure below first, then [clear the stopped claim's recorded session](#starting-fresh-when-a-session-is-lost-or-wedged).
When `issue_close` already cleared its resume path, the importer searches `<tree-volume>/sessions/*/*_<session>.jsonl` by the retained session id; exactly one match imports, no match reports the claim and id, and several matches are refused.
Only clearing that record permits the reap.
The next generation starts fresh, while the imported session row remains in the database.

On `legion-v10.0.0`, a deployment whose sessions are files on its tree volumes copies each one into the table once, while those volumes still exist, after the last write to any of them and before any agent writes the same session under SQL storage.
The order below is what keeps a copy current: nothing checks, at a resume, that a row still matches the file it was copied from, so a session written after its copy would resume from the older row without a word.
Do not drain the deployment by lowering the linger instead: a closed tree's cleanup deletes its volume, and with it any session not yet copied.
Steps 1 to 5 below take the place of steps 1 to 3 of [Upgrading a deployment with running trees](#upgrading-a-deployment-with-running-trees): its steps 1 and 2 drain every tree and so delete its volume, and its step 3 runs before step 1 here (below).
Step 6 here hands back to that section.

**A daemon-launched controller is cleared first.**
Under `controller: daemon` the earlier release resumes a suspended controller at its next look, within a minute (`keep` in `internal/daemon/controller.go` at `legion-v10.0.0`), so the controller cannot be held still for the copy.
Clear its claim before step 1 with step 3 of the upgrade section.
Its Sandbox goes, and its volume and session go with it, so step 5 clears the session its claim still records and the controller this release launches starts a fresh session.

1. **Stop every writer, keeping the linger as it is.**
   Tell every agent to push its work, then suspend every claim (`legion claims suspend`) until each tree is at a pushed boundary: no pod running and no claim recording a locator (`legion claims list --json`, every `locator` absent).

2. **Save the claims and stop the daemon at once.**
   `legion claims list --json --operator-token-file <file> > claims.json` (the daemon of any release prints the list this command reads), then scale the daemon to 0 straight away, so nothing launches, resumes, or cleans up a tree from here on.

3. **Copy every tree.**
   Copy one tree at a time, in the pod of [A shell on an issue's disk](#a-shell-on-an-issues-disk) with that tree's claim: a pod of the worker image, under gVisor, with the tree's volume read-only at `/legion` and nothing else mounted.
   The import reads two more files, and both come from your machine after the pod is `Ready`.
   `claims.json` from step 2 goes to the import's standard input (`--claims -`).
   `<url file>` is a file of mode 0600 on your machine that holds the session database's `postgres://` URL, one that a pod on the Legion pool can reach; under `postgres` it is the value of the providers Secret's `session_dsn_secret` key.
   The URL goes into the pod on standard input, into a file of mode 0600 in a directory of mode 0700, so no command line holds it:

   ```sh
   kubectl -n legion apply -f legion-tree-shell.yaml    # its claimName is this tree's claim
   kubectl -n legion wait --for=condition=Ready pod/legion-tree-shell --timeout=300s
   kubectl -n legion exec -i legion-tree-shell -- sh -c 'umask 077 && mkdir /tmp/import && cat > /tmp/import/dsn' < <url file>
   kubectl -n legion exec -i legion-tree-shell -- sh -c 'legion sessions import --dsn-file /tmp/import/dsn --claims - --tree <ROOT ISSUE> --tree-volume /legion; rc=$?; rm -rf /tmp/import; exit $rc' < claims.json
   kubectl -n legion delete pod legion-tree-shell
   ```

   The second `exec` removes the URL's directory whatever the import's exit, and it exits with the import's own status.
   The pod's own files go when the pod is deleted.

   For each claim with a recorded session file the import reads that file from the volume (its path below the agents' sessions directory, below `<tree-volume>/sessions`; without `--tree-volume` it reads the recorded path itself) and writes it as one row keyed by that recorded path: the whole file as `content`, `byte_len` its size, `mtime_ms` the file's, no title and no parts, which is how Oh My Pi reads a row an older release of it wrote.
   When `issue_close` already cleared a claim's resume path, the importer finds `*_<session>.jsonl` below the volume's sessions directory from the retained session id; exactly one match imports, none names the claim and session as missing, and several are refused by name.
   It creates the two tables with Oh My Pi's statements for them, each table named `public.<table>` as Oh My Pi names it, when the database has none.
   It prints one line per claim of the tree — `copied`, `copied before (identical …)`, `recorded no session`, `failed` (a file or retained session the volume does not hold) or `refused` (several files for one retained session id, or a table row with other content, which it leaves as it is) — then a `missing` line for every claim of the whole list, any tree's, whose recorded session the table does not hold, then a count of each.
   It exits 1 on any `failed` or `refused`, on a `missing` of the claims it was asked to copy (another tree's is reported only), and when `--tree` selects no claim of the list, which is a mistyped key.

   - Every statement it runs, like every statement of the launcher's session lookups and Claude Code saves, runs in a transaction whose first statement is `SET LOCAL search_path = pg_catalog, pg_temp`, which then sets `restrict_nonsystem_relation_kind` to `'view, foreign-table'`, and names each table `public.<table>`; a read-only one also sets `row_security` off.
     So no function, operator or table that another login planted in `public`, or in a schema named for the login, resolves in those statements; a view another login made at a table's own name fails the statement rather than runs in it, and the import refuses a relation at either name that is no table; and a row-security policy on the tables fails a read rather than runs in it.
     The pin covers name lookup and those relations alone: a trigger, a rule, a default or a constraint that the tables' owner attaches still runs as whoever writes.
     It is set in each transaction because a PgBouncer pool in transaction mode refuses `search_path` as a startup parameter.

4. **Copy every tree again.**
   Each run must print only `copied before` or `recorded no session` for its tree's claims, and its `missing` lines may name only claims step 5 is to clear: one whose volume was gone before step 3 (the cleared controller's, or a claim of a tree closed earlier), or a `failed` you cannot fix.
   A `refused` here means a writer was still running: the session grew on its volume after step 3 copied it, and the import never overwrites a row it already holds, so it refuses the file it now finds.
   Going on would resume the agent from the older row and lose every turn after it.
   Go back to step 1 instead: scale the earlier daemon back up, suspend whatever runs, save the list again, and scale it to 0 at once (step 2); then delete that row and its parts in one transaction pinned as the import's own are, `BEGIN; SET LOCAL search_path = pg_catalog, pg_temp; SET LOCAL restrict_nonsystem_relation_kind = 'view, foreign-table'; DELETE FROM public.omp_session_files_parts WHERE path = '<path>'; DELETE FROM public.omp_session_files WHERE path = '<path>'; COMMIT;`, and copy again.
   Nothing writes a row under SQL storage before the switch, so in this runbook a `refused` has no other cause.

5. **Roll out the new daemon, then clear only sessions the import reported missing.**
   For every `missing` line from step 4, take that claim's recorded session from `claims.json` and run:

   ```sh
   legion claims forget-session --config legion.yaml --operator-token-file <file> --claim <token> --session <recorded session id>
   ```

   The command does not read the session database.
   It clears only the matching session record from the claim, and an old row in the session database stays there.
   A refusal naming a different recorded session means the saved list is stale: suspend writers, save the list again, and copy again before deciding whether to clear it.
   A live or launch-uncertain claim is refused; suspend it, or wait for it to reach queued, failed, or retired before running the command.

   Retry each failed architect with `legion claims retry --claim <token> --operator-token-file <file>`.
   A daemon-launched controller is retried by its keeper; a retired workflow claim starts fresh when the workflow starts it.
   Each fresh launch provisions its workspace from the issue's branch.

6. **Only then delete the old Sandboxes and their volumes, then finish the post-rollout checks and dump in [Upgrading a deployment with running trees](#upgrading-a-deployment-with-running-trees).**

### The image guard

An Oh My Pi built before the `session.storage` setting ignores the two variables and keeps sessions on files without a word
— the one silent fallback this setting must never allow.
The check lives inside the image: `legion probe-image`, which the image build runs before it publishes, starts the image's own Oh My Pi with a nonsense `OMP_SESSION_STORAGE` value and passes only if it refuses, then prints `session-storage=probed` on its OK line.
The daemon's image probe passes only an OK line that carries its daemon API contract, which a `legion probe-image` of this release prints only after that probe passed, under every store.
The daemon never probes a host Oh My Pi for this: pods run the image's build, not the host's.

## Kubernetes runtime: the Go daemon on Agent Sandbox

Under the Go coordinator, `runtime: kubernetes` runs every issue as one Agent Sandbox:
an `agents.x-k8s.io` `Sandbox` (kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox, LEGION-206) named for the issue, `legion-<project>-<issue>`, whose one pod runs under gVisor on the Legion pool, or in a GKE Sandbox microVM where `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox` puts the issue there ([Pods in microVMs](#pods-in-microvms)).
The pod holds two init containers and one container, `roles`, whose PID 1 is one `legion launcher`, a supervisor with no workflow policy that runs every workflow role
— `architect`, `planner`, `implementer`, `tester`, `reviewer`, `merger`:
it holds one connection to the daemon's worker stream per role, each authenticated with that role's own token, and starts or stops that role's `legion worker-shim` and Oh My Pi when the daemon tells it to, each role's generation in Linux namespaces of its own.
Every role of the issue shares the issue's checkout, the pod's own disk it sits on, the temporary directory every role's agent is told (`TMPDIR=/legion/scratch/tmp`, one directory of the issue's scratch, below) and the pod's network, and every one of their sessions is a row in the session database rather than a file any of them holds;
each role keeps its own home, config home, `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, `/run/lock` and `/dev/shm` mounts, state directory, agent-secrets key, GitHub App credential and launch credentials.
A role's Secret holds its launcher token, projected under that role's own directory of the container and bound to the pod's uid, which no role's process sees, and the two gh files its `gh` and `git` read the role's App token from ([Anatomy of a Sandbox pod](#anatomy-of-a-sandbox-pod));
the daemon accepts a launcher connection only for that role, that pod and that token.
Each generation's boot token and launch credentials (the Envoy and Dispatch bearers, a spec's secrets) travel in the authenticated start command, and the launcher writes them owner-only and exclusively into a fresh `g<generation>` directory of its role's memory-backed private directory, removing anything already there without following it, and removes that directory when the generation ends:
a role started in a running pod never waits on the kubelet to refresh a Secret, and no credential is in an argv, an environment value, a log or an error.
The role's own agent sees only its own private directory, inside its namespaces, so it can read its own generation's credentials, as a pane can; it cannot read another role's.
The generation's system prompt travels the same way: the daemon composes it (the role's prompt parts, its addressing, the deployment's `instructions` and each arm's) and sends it in that start command, the launcher writes it as `system-prompt.md` into the same `g<generation>` directory, and the agent's one `--append-system-prompt` (Claude Code's `--append-system-prompt-file`) names that file.
No argument grows with the prompt, so a prompt longer than the 131,072 bytes Linux allows one argument (`MAX_ARG_STRLEN`) launches, and no other role's process can read or change the file, since it is in this role's private directory alone.
A prompt whose start command would pass the 1 MiB a launcher reads in one frame is refused before anything starts: the claim fails at once with cause `launch_refused`, charged no launch failure, and its `lastStartFailure` and `failure.detail` name the role, the prompt's size and the limit.
The daemon sets no bound of its own on a model's context, which it cannot read; Oh My Pi answers a request too large for its model.
What the container mounts for the pod rather than for a role is every role's alike:
the operator's providers Secret (`provider_keys`) and, under `runtime.kubernetes.agent_secrets`, the projected broker token.
A role process is addressed by the pod's uid, its role and its generation (the incarnation `<pod uid>/<generation>`):
in a healthy running pod, starting, suspending or recovering one role never restarts the pod or touches another role.
A new generation of a role in a running pod is a new child of its launcher.
A pod is replaced after it dies, when it was not made by this runtime, or when a closed issue is re-admitted after suspension (`packages/daemon/internal/runtime/sandbox`).

Releasing a role ends only its process.
The issue owns its Sandbox, its role Secrets and its `-boot` Secret, and nothing else:
its disk belongs to its pod, as a generic ephemeral volume the pod's own template declares, so the Sandbox owns no `volumeClaimTemplates` entry and the disk is created and deleted with the pod ([The disk dies with its pod](#the-disk-dies-with-its-pod)).
The one exception is a microVM pod under `keep_volume`: its Sandbox owns one `issue` claim template, and the claim made from it outlives the pod ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)).
Each Sandbox carries the tree's `legion.dev/tree` label, which is how the tree's cleanup finds them.
Each tree also has one durable lifecycle record (`tree_lifecycles`, keyed by the normalized project token and the tree):
an epoch that is open, cleanup-reserved, or cleanup-confirmed, and the authority that opened it.
Workflow admission opens a root's epoch in the fact that gives it its slot; the authenticated operator spawn of a root architect opens an operator tree's.
Every claim binds the open epoch in the same short transaction that first writes it, and every spawn, resume or retry binds again before it launches, all under the fact path's one global serializer.
A reserved epoch refuses those writes with a named wait that keeps the start's outbox row and charges no launch failure;
a confirmed epoch admits nothing until a fresh root admission opens the next one.
A workflow root whose key names an open operator tree waits for its slot behind that tree's epoch, and when it leaves the workflow while it waits (a person parks it, or someone moves it to a running tree's status) its record goes to `done` and nothing more:
the operator's claims and pod carry the root's tokens and names, so the workflow queues no stop, no `issue_suspend` and no linger close for them (`leaveUnderOperator`, `internal/workflow/linger.go`).
`todo` with the label queues it again.

A workflow close or withdrawal queues a separate `issue_suspend` effect for each affected issue, after its per-role stops.
The effect checks both workflow generations, later starts, unfinished stop effects and every stored role, including a launch not yet present in the runtime's watch.
A held turn, unfinished or uncertain launch, or Kubernetes error keeps the effect pending; a superseded close finishes without acting.
Once the roles have stopped, the daemon sets that issue's Sandbox to `Suspended` and waits for its pod to disappear, which takes the disk that pod owns.
Then it deletes the Sandbox, whatever the close was:
a child set `done`, one set `backlog`, `icebox` or `triage`, and a root leaving the workflow with its tree are one case now, since a Sandbox kept behind would hold nothing (`SuspendIssue`, `internal/runtime/sandbox/issue_suspend.go`), logging `sandbox runtime: deleted the closed issue's
Sandbox and the role Secrets it owned` — the six role Secrets go with it by owner reference.
Where the Sandbox owns a kept volume, the foreground delete deletes that volume too ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)).
An `issue_close` retires the claim and keeps its whole session, the id (the volume reaping's evidence) and the resume path, so a later admission resumes each role in the session it recorded, or in a new one once supervise's `forgetSession` has dropped it (a session no store holds any more is dropped and reported, R8).
The parent's Sandbox is another issue's and is never touched.
A daemon restart retries the stored effect.
Re-admission during linger makes the Sandbox, the pod and its disk afresh and resumes the recorded sessions, and a claim whose session supervise's `forgetSession` has dropped starts a new one;
the issue pod's launch turn orders a concurrent resume after any suspension already in flight.

Linger expiry reserves its tree only while the root still lingers at the close's generation, so a re-admission that committed first fences it;
an operator close reserves after it authenticated the root close.
Either reservation comes before the census, which then reads every stored claim of the tree, including one that persisted before the reservation but has not launched yet, and deletes nothing until all of them retired.
A reservation that is not confirmed resumes on the next attempt, even after a re-admission, and stays the new start's wait until API confirmation:
every close row of the tree, however stale its generation or the linger it closed, still retires its claim and drives that cleanup before the checks that finish a stale close apply.
A launch checks its tree's epoch again just before it records `launching` and calls the runtime, so a reservation committed after the claim bound refuses it there, with the same uncharged wait.
Every lifecycle step takes the global serializer before it reads the lifecycle row.

Once every claim of the tree has retired, the runtime deletes the tree's Sandboxes, found by listing them from the API by the tree's label, in any order (`CleanupTree`, `internal/runtime/sandbox/cleanup.go`):
each delete carries the listed object's UID and resourceVersion plus `foreground` propagation and is awaited until the API no longer has it, the listing is read again until it holds none, and a delete the API refuses because the Sandbox changed since the listing lists again after a short wait.
Nothing is handed over any more: the cleanup deletes every Sandbox the listing names, a carried child's included, because a child carried into a tree of its own has nothing left to be handed
— the work was on its pod's disk, which went with the pod, or on a kept volume, which goes with the Sandbox — and that child's own tree creates a Sandbox for it at its first launch (`ensureSandbox`).
A Sandbox the new tree's launch relabelled before the cleanup reached it fails the cleanup's fence and is no longer in the next listing, so it is left to that tree.
The orphan sweep still keeps a Sandbox whose home is another tree (`Store.IssueSandboxHome`:
a child whose hand-over is pending, or one carried into a tree of its own that it is in or can still be admitted into), which is how a carried child's Sandbox survives a sweep between its launch and its old tree's cleanup.
Agent Sandbox v1.0.3 creates each Sandbox's PVC with that Sandbox as its controller owner and `blockOwnerDeletion: true`;
foreground deletion keeps the owner visible until Kubernetes garbage collection deletes every blocking dependent
— an issue Sandbox's six role Secrets, and the claim a controller's or a cache's Sandbox owns.
The restricted daemon has no PVC API verb, so a Sandbox's absence after its foreground delete is the API's confirmation that what it owned is gone; it does not read or delete a PVC.
An issue's ephemeral disk is not among those dependents: it is its pod's own, and it goes when the delete takes the pod.
A kept volume is among them: its claim is the issue Sandbox's, so the delete waits until the garbage collector deletes it ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)).

An operator-created tree has no workflow record:
its stored operator authority, not a zero or sentinel generation, selects the operator cleanup entry point, which then applies the same cleanup without manufacturing a workflow issue.
A tree closed before any of its Sandboxes was created lists none and confirms its reservation without deleting anything.
A root that left admission's waiting line before a slot opened its tree (labelled `todo`, then set to `backlog`, `icebox` or `done`) lingers as any root does, but its tree never had a lifecycle and holds nothing a cleanup releases, so its linger's close rows reserve nothing and finish.

A child of a closed tree re-admitted as a root of its own keeps its key, so its claims and its Sandbox's name.
Its old tree's cleanup does not wait on a claim of it that runs nothing;
each of its claims is re-pointed to its new tree before its first start there, and binds that tree's epoch;
and its root launch takes over the Sandbox its old tree left, if the cleanup has not reached it yet:
the Sandbox is relabelled for the new tree (`ensureSandbox`, `internal/runtime/sandbox/relaunch.go`), and whether it is that Sandbox or one made afresh, the launch brings a new pod, with a disk of its own or on the kept volume of a relabelled Sandbox, and the roles resume from the session table.
A role still in a turn when the old tree closed holds that close's suspension until the turn ends, and the carry's new generation can reach the issue before the close's suspend row of a role has run at all, after a stop of the old tree finished without acting (a production check's look start supersedes the linger's suspend), or before that look's start, already past its fences, brings its claim up in the old tree.
So the move itself, a hand-over, an orphan carry or an adoption, queues a suspend of the old tree for every role of the issue (`Engine.StopLeftTree`, `internal/workflow/adopt.go`).
Every row of the old tree serves an earlier generation, but such a suspend or tree close still stops a claim that stands in the old tree, waiting while its claim's machine is still to come (a rolling restart).
The cleanup waits on every claim still running in its tree, so a claim that no stop reached would hold it, and the old root's next run with it, until the new tree started the issue, which a carried child held on a blocker or behind the admission cap does not do.
When the stop completes as the row runs, it makes the old tree's close rows due at once (`stopInLeftTree`, `internal/daemon/outbox.go`); a suspension held for a turn is instead picked up at the close row's next retry, at most 64 seconds on.
Such a row releases nothing of the old tree itself: the deletes of the old tree's Sandboxes run on the close rows of the issues still in that tree, so the carried issue's lane, and its new tree's start on it, do not wait behind them.
Nor does a start of the new tree launch anything while a claim of the issue still runs a process in another tree:
the start suspends that claim itself, as the daemon and keeping its session, and waits on its backoff, charging nothing, until the claim has stopped (`stopElsewhere`).
When that call stops a claim and no other claim of the issue still runs, it makes the close rows of the tree it stood in due at once.
If another claim still runs, `stopElsewhere` returns its wait before that wake; when it later finds the first claim already stopped, that tree's close rows retry at most 64 seconds on.
Either stop is bounded where the old tree's close would have ended the turn, at the old root's linger expiry (`linger_hours`):
a turn that ends within the linger ends on its own, and one still running at the expiry is stopped there.
Once the old root no longer lingers (it was reopened, say), there is no close left to wait for, and the stop falls back to the stop timeout (`worker_stop_timeout_seconds`) from then (`carriedStopDeadline`):
a role still in a turn is stopped that long after, losing only the tool call in flight.
Either way the claim keeps the issue's branch and its session, which the new tree's start resumes: a phase worker's with its phase's resume task, and the issue's own architect's, now its root's, with the task the start of a carried root gives it;
the workspace is provisioned again from that branch in the new pod.
A turn that hangs inside the linger is the operator's to stop sooner:
`legion claims suspend` stops it at the stop timeout (`worker_stop_timeout_seconds`) from then and makes the hold the operator's, so the new tree's start of that role waits for the operator, with the claim already re-pointed to the new tree, and `legion claims resume` relaunches its session there.
A Sandbox the old tree left `Running`, none of whose claims runs any more, is relabelled and suspended in one patch fenced to the uid and resourceVersion it read, so the launch waits its pod out;
while a claim of the old tree still runs, the launch is refused, naming it.
That holds whether the new tree's start or the old tree's cleanup comes first:
a cleanup that reaches the issue first deletes its Sandbox, and the new tree's first launch makes one (above), while the orphan sweep keeps a Sandbox whose home is the tree it is labelled with.
A Sandbox's home ends when its issue can no longer be admitted into that tree.
For a tree admission has not opened, a child set to `backlog`, `icebox` or `done`, or to a status only a running tree has (`in_progress`, `testing`, `needs_review`, `retro`), leaves the waiting line and lingers like any root, so its Sandbox stays until its linger expires;
one whose label is taken off leaves the line with no linger, so its Sandbox goes at the next sweep.
Taken out by its label, once it is `todo` with the label again it waits in the line and is admitted into the phase it stood in, continuing its run in a pod of its own from the issue's branch:
its roles' sessions continue from the session table, and whatever the pod it had was working on went with that pod's disk ([The disk dies with its pod](#the-disk-dies-with-its-pod)), or with the kept volume of the Sandbox that the sweep deleted.
Taken out by a status, it comes back as any root does after its linger:
a new generation at `admitted`, its design gate and handoffs cleared (`ClearTreeGeneration`), its architect starting over from the issue's branch.
A hand-over fence counts only while the child's record still names the tree the fence was written for, and a hand-over Dispatch refuses permanently drops its fence with its row (`finishRefused`, `internal/daemon/outbox.go`).
Past that the Sandbox is an orphan, which the sweep deletes, fenced and logged, taking its pod, the disk that pod owns and a kept volume that the Sandbox owns.
A child re-admitted after its old tree's cleanup took its Sandbox, one that had left the workflow before the close (a parked child the close does not hand over), finds no Sandbox and makes one at its next launch;
its re-pointed claim still names its session (`Retree`, `internal/supervise/lifecycle.go`, keeps it:
the supervisor knows nothing of Sandboxes, and a check there would race the cleanup), which the session table holds and the role resumes.
That launch creates the issue's pod on a new disk, so it provisions its workspace from the issue's branch, as every new pod on a new disk does ([The disk dies with its pod](#the-disk-dies-with-its-pod)), and nothing is reported lost
— the same path a root re-admitted after its own tree's close takes.

Before the daemon opens its store, so before any schema write, image probe or reconcile, it checks that Agent Sandbox is installed and refuses a namespace that holds a Sandbox of its project whose pod template is neither of the containers its labels allow
— for an issue's (`legion.dev/issue`), the one `roles` container or, from the layout before contract 39, exactly the six role containers;
for the project controller's (`legion.dev/role=controller` with no tree), the one `controller` container
— or that does not own exactly the volumes a Sandbox of that kind owns.
That rule is the kind's, not one rule for both:
an issue's Sandbox owns at most the one claim template named `issue`: none where its pod's disk is the pod's own, and that one where a microVM pod keeps its volume ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)).
The project controller's owns exactly the one named `issue`, so a controller Sandbox owning none and any Sandbox owning a template named something else, `tree` above all, are refused (`treeVolumeLayout` in `internal/runtime/sandbox/install.go`).
The refusal names every such Sandbox, each with its reason, and how many there are.
That catches every per-claim Sandbox of the layout before issue pods, running or suspended, the controller Sandbox a `controller: daemon` daemon made before the controller ran in a launcher pod (`role=controller`, one `worker` container), and the tree-volume layout's own Sandboxes that own a `tree` template
— the tree root's and that layout's controller.
The census accepts one kind of issue Sandbox rather than refuse it: one whose disk shape is not the one its issue's launch renders (`diskShapeChange`, `internal/runtime/sandbox/relaunch.go`).
That is a Sandbox that still owns the `issue` template the release before the pod-owned disk gave it, or one that a change of `keep_volume`, of the issue's sandbox, or of the volume's class, size or access modes left behind.
`spec.volumeClaimTemplates` is immutable in the CRD, so the only way to the launch's shape is the delete-and-create of the issue's next launch that starts a pod, and a refusal would stop the daemon until an operator had deleted one Sandbox per open issue by hand.
So the census logs the Sandbox instead, and the launch replaces it ([Cutting over to the pod-owned disk](#cutting-over-to-the-pod-owned-disk), [A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)):
`sandbox runtime: the issue Sandbox does not have the disk shape its launch renders, so the issue's next launch that starts a pod replaces it`, with the Sandbox in its `sandbox` attribute and the reason in its `reason` attribute:
`a Sandbox of the release before the pod-owned disk`, `the launch now keeps a volume`, `the launch now keeps no volume` or `the volume's class, size or access modes changed`.
The census logs nothing for a Sandbox that has its launch's shape.
A repository cache's Sandbox (`legion.dev/cache`) is judged by its own shape alone (`cacheSandboxShape`), never as a pod of a kind.
Once the store opens and before it migrates, the daemon refuses a claim that still records a Sandbox locator of the layout before issue pods (no pod uid, container or generation), that earlier controller's claim included.
A deployment of an earlier layout clears all of it before it upgrades ([Upgrading a deployment with running trees](#upgrading-a-deployment-with-running-trees)).
The daemon runs on a host its pods can reach and serves the worker stream they dial.
The controller is `legion controller start` on the operator's machine, or, under `controller: daemon`, a pod of its own with one launcher that the daemon launches ([The controller](#the-controller)).

### Daemon migration identifiers and release order

A migration's version is the leading digits of its file name (`internal/store/migrations`).
The numbered migrations are the sequence the daemon grew up with, 1 to the number its series closed at (`0067_phase_assignment.up.sql`, recorded once in `migrationid`), each taken once;
every migration added since takes the UTC moment its author created it, 14 digits `YYYYMMDDHHMMSS`, so two branches open at the same time cannot both claim one version.
A timestamp sorts after every number, so a fresh database applies the numbered migrations in their old order and the timestamped ones in the order they were written.

`schemaVersion` is the highest version applied, not proof that every version below it is applied:
`Migrate` applies every version `schema_version` lacks, in version order, so a migration that merges below one a database already has still runs there, once.
A deployed database applies each migration as the release carrying it deploys, so it can apply two migrations written on branches open at the same time in the other order than a fresh database does;
a migration must not depend on that order, and one that needs another's effect is written after that one has merged.

The release that reads the version cast to `bigint` goes out before any release that carries a timestamped migration:
the release before it reads `max(version)` uncast, so a deployment that skips it costs the daemon it replaces one failed state read on each connection that prepared the uncast read, which pgx then drops.

A daemon of a release before migration `0058_catch_up_cursor` that runs on a database a later release has migrated applies Dispatch's events without moving any issue's catch-up cursor (`issues.caught_up_seq`).
Before a later release starts on that database again, set every cursor to null (`update issues set caught_up_seq = null`), or its boot catch-up replays the events the earlier daemon already applied;
a catch-up from a null cursor replays nothing and sets the cursor to the issue's latest event on Dispatch (the comment of `0058_catch_up_cursor.up.sql` says why).

### Upgrading a deployment with running trees

This section is for a deployment that runs the release before issue pods (`legion-v10.0.0`), whose every role runs in a Sandbox of its own.
Issue pods (LEGION-462, sjawhar/legion#1752) and per-issue volumes (LEGION-632) land in this one release, so one drained cutover takes a deployment from per-claim Sandboxes to independent issue pods;
a deployment that ran an issue-pod build on one tree volume (a build of #1752's branch before this release) drains the same way, and its Sandboxes are refused the same way.
A daemon at this release refuses to boot while either layout's work is still in place:

- **A per-claim Sandbox** in its namespace, running or suspended, is refused by the census before the store opens (`rejectLegacyIssueSandboxes` in `internal/runtime/sandbox/sandbox.go`, run by `run` in `internal/daemon/daemon.go` before `store.Open`).

- **A Sandbox of the tree-volume layout that owns a volume**
  — one whose claim template is named `tree`, not `issue` (the tree root's own Sandbox, or that layout's controller Sandbox), or a controller Sandbox of that layout owning no template at all
  — is refused by the same census (`treeVolumeLayout` in `install.go`), each named with its reason: `Sandbox <name> owns no volume;
  it is of the tree-volume layout before per-issue volumes, so drain and remove it as
  docs/kubernetes.md's "Upgrading a deployment with running trees" says`, or `Sandbox <name> owns a
  volume claim template named "tree", not "issue"; it is of the tree-volume layout …`.
  Such a Sandbox is never adopted: a root's volume holds every clone and workspace of its tree, which only this drain may take apart.
  That layout's *issue* Sandboxes own no template, which is this release's own shape, so the census passes over them by their volumes;
  the root's Sandbox is refused all the same, so no daemon of this release boots on that layout, and the drain below deletes every Sandbox of a tree, children first.

- **A per-claim locator** on any claim is refused once the store has connected and before it migrates (`HasLegacySandboxClaims` in `internal/store/claims.go`).

Nothing is written before either refusal: `store.Open` only connects and pings, and the first write is `Migrate`, after both checks.
So a refused boot leaves the database as the earlier release left it, and re-pinning the earlier release's image recovers.
In the cluster a refused boot is a crash-looping Deployment: the earlier release's pods keep running, but nothing supervises them.

**Every rollout of this release turns on a store that keeps sessions in a database**, since the loader accepts no other ([Selecting the store](#selecting-the-store)), so the copy is part of this upgrade rather than an option beside it:
steps 1 to 3 below are replaced by steps 1 to 5 of [Copying file sessions before turning it on](#copying-file-sessions-before-turning-it-on), which keep every tree's volume until its sessions are in the table.
When `controller: daemon` ran, step 3 below runs before copy step 1:
the earlier release resumes a suspended controller within a minute, so it cannot be held still for the copy, and copy step 5 accounts for its claim.
Copy step 6 deletes the per-claim Sandboxes and hands back to steps 4, 5 and 6 below:
the two checks, the dump, and the rollout, whose `legion.yaml` names the store and that store's own key:
`session_dsn_secret` under `postgres`, and `session_database` under `cloudsql-iam`.
The copy itself runs the same way under either, since `legion sessions import` takes the database as a `--dsn-file` URL the machine running it can reach, which under `cloudsql-iam` is the operator's to supply: no pod holds one.

No migration turns a per-claim Sandbox or locator into an issue pod's, and nothing on a tree volume of either earlier layout carries over (below), so the upgrade drains the deployment while it still runs the earlier release:

1. **Drain every tree.**
   Move each tree's root issue out of the workflow on Dispatch (`done`, `backlog`, `icebox` or `triage`) and let its linger expire, which closes the tree.
   A tree no workflow issue backs, one an operator spawned, is closed with `legion claims close` on its root claim;
   the earlier release refuses that for a workflow issue's tree, which the workflow closes.
   Each claim of a closed tree is released and retires, and a retired claim records no locator.

2. **Let the cleanup finish.**
   On the earlier release, releasing a claim deletes its Sandbox by name, and the root's Sandbox takes the tree volume with it (`Release` in `internal/runtime/sandbox/sandbox.go` at `legion-v10.0.0`;
   on an issue-pod build on a tree volume, the tree's close deletes each child's Sandbox and then the root's, the volume with it).
   Wait until every Sandbox is gone, or delete one left behind once no claim of it runs.

3. **Clear the controller's claim, if `controller: daemon` ran.**
   Set `controller: operator` and boot the build that ran it once.
   It stops the controller its earlier boot launched, logging `controller: stopping the controller an earlier boot under controller: daemon launched; this
   daemon leaves the controller to its operator`:
   the stop deletes the claim's Sandbox, and with it the controller's volume and session, and retires the claim, so `legion claims list` shows `legion-<project>-controller` `retired`.
   That removes the controller Sandbox of either earlier layout, the per-claim one and the one owning a `tree` template, both of which the census refuses.
   In the cluster each of these boots is a configuration change of its own through the deploy path.

4. **Check that nothing is left.**
   `<project>` below is `legion.yaml`'s `project` lowercased with every non-alphanumeric removed (`claim.ProjectToken`), the value of every Sandbox's `legion.dev/project` label and of the `claims.project` column.
   Both of these must come back empty:

   ```sh
   kubectl -n <namespace> get sandboxes -l 'legion.dev/project=<project>,!legion.dev/probe'
   ```

   ```sql
   -- connected as the daemon is, with its postgres_dsn
   select token, state from claims where project = '<project>' and locator->>'runtime' = 'sandbox';
   ```

   The query lists every claim that records a Sandbox locator at all, which is stricter than the boot check:
   on the earlier release every such locator is a per-claim one.

5. **Dump the database**, `pg_dump -Fc -T omp_session_files -T omp_session_files_parts -f <dump
   file> '<postgres_dsn>'` with the daemon's `postgres_dsn`.
   It is the only way back ([Rolling back](#rolling-back-the-upgrade)).
   The two `-T` options leave out Oh My Pi's session tables:
   where they share the daemon's database under a login of their own, the daemon's login cannot read them and a `pg_dump` that names them exits 1 with `permission denied for table
   omp_session_files`.
   A rollback restores the dump into a new database, so the session tables in this one are left as they stand.

6. **Roll this release out in one step:**

   - the daemon at this release, with its `legion.yaml` at this release's shape:
     `runtime.kubernetes.issue_volume` where the file set `tree_volume`, one `resources.issue` entry where it set a `resources.<role>` entry per workflow role, and `resources.controller` as `{cpu, memory}` (with `cpu_request` and `memory_request` below them where the requests were lower) where it set that entry's `requests` and `limits`, and a store that keeps sessions in a database with that store's key, both required
     — for a deployment today `session_store:
     postgres` with the `session_dsn_secret` key the providers Secret holds the database's URL under ([Configuration](#configuration) and [Selecting the store](#selecting-the-store) name each refusal);
     keep a copy of the whole file as it was, since the earlier release refuses this release's shape key by key and a rollback puts that copy back ([Rolling back](#rolling-back-the-upgrade) names every refused key);

   - `runtime.kubernetes.image` pinned to a worker image built from it, since the image probe refuses a worker image whose `pi-legion` declares another daemon API contract (`ProbeImage` in `internal/runtime/sandbox/probe.go`); and

   - for an operator-launched controller, every operator's `legion` and `pi-legion` at this release's daemon API contract, the number on the first line of `legion version --contracts` of this release's `legion`.
     `legion controller start` refuses a `pi-legion` speaking another contract (`probeAndMint` in `cmd/legion/controller.go`), and the daemon refuses a `legion` or `pi-legion` of another contract with 409 (`internal/api/controller.go`).
     That `pi-legion` release must be published before the rollout.
     Contract 20 adds the controller's credential route (`POST /legion/v1/controller/github-credential`) and the controller pod's `GH_*` environment variables (LEGION-668).

**Why deleting a live tree's Sandboxes loses its work.**
On the earlier release the tree volume is the root Sandbox's `volumeClaimTemplates` entry, so Agent Sandbox creates the volume's claim with that Sandbox as its owner, and deleting the root Sandbox deletes the volume (`sandboxManifest` in `internal/runtime/sandbox/manifest.go` and `Release` in `sandbox.go`, both at `legion-v10.0.0`).
That loses every change in its working copies that was not pushed and, where that release kept sessions as files on the volume (its own `session_store: pvc`, a value this release's loader refuses), every session recorded on it.
Where it kept them in the table (`postgres`), a session copied there first ([Copying file sessions before turning it on](#copying-file-sessions-before-turning-it-on)) is kept, and its agent resumes it in a workspace provisioned from its issue's pushed branch.
A volume kept anyway is never mounted again:
the earlier release names a tree's claim `tree-legion-<project>-<root issue>-architect`, from the root architect's own Sandbox (`SandboxName` and `TreeClaimName` in `names.go` at `legion-v10.0.0`), and an issue-pod build on a tree volume `tree-legion-<project>-<root issue>`, from the root issue's Sandbox, where this release gives an issue no claim of either name:
its pod's disk is the pod's own ephemeral volume, named `<pod>-issue` and created with the pod ([The disk dies with its pod](#the-disk-dies-with-its-pod)), or, for a microVM pod under `keep_volume`, the claim `issue-legion-<project>-<issue>` of the issue's own Sandbox ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)), a name that `IssueClaimName` (`internal/runtime/sandbox/names.go`) gives the project controller's claim too.
So no pod of this release ever mounts a claim of either earlier layout.
Suspending the tree's claims on the earlier release instead (`legion claims suspend`) keeps their Sandboxes, `Suspended`, and the census refuses a suspended per-claim or tree-volume Sandbox all the same.

#### Rolling back the upgrade

Roll back by restoring the dump from step 5 and re-pinning the earlier release; work done under this release since the upgrade is not in the dump.
Re-pinning without the restore does not work.
Once this release has booted it has applied migrations 0033 to 0054 (`internal/store/migrations`), and the earlier release cannot read what they and this release write:

- it refuses an `issue_suspend` outbox row as an unknown kind (`decodeOutboxJSON` in `internal/record/outbox.go` at `legion-v10.0.0`);

- it refuses an issue pod's locator, whose Sandbox name carries no role (`checkLocator` in `internal/runtime/sandbox/sandbox.go` at `legion-v10.0.0`);

- nothing stops it booting on the newer schema:
  `Migrate` applies the migrations it has not recorded and compares nothing against the version the database is at (`internal/store/store.go`, the same at `legion-v10.0.0`), so it would boot and then fail row by row.

**Nothing of an issue's disk survives the rollback; push first.**
An issue's disk is its pod's own and goes when the pod ends ([The disk dies with its pod](#the-disk-dies-with-its-pod)), a kept volume goes with its Sandbox ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)), and the earlier release ends every one of them:
the dump was taken after the drain, so every claim in it is retired, and at boot the earlier release sweeps orphans with a grace of 0 (`reconcileBootOrphans` in `internal/daemon/daemon.go` at `legion-v10.0.0`), deleting every Sandbox labelled `legion.dev/project=<project>`, but the image probe's, whose name is not that of a claim it has not retired (`ReconcileOrphans` in `internal/runtime/sandbox/sandbox.go` at `legion-v10.0.0`).
That is every Sandbox this release made:
each issue's `legion-<project>-<issue key lowercased>`, the controller's and each repository cache's, each pod with it, each issue pod's disk with that pod and each kept volume with its Sandbox.
No step keeps a disk the earlier release can use: deleting a Sandbox with `--cascade=orphan`, which kept a Sandbox-owned volume before the pod-owned disk, keeps no ephemeral disk, since that disk belongs to the pod and not to the Sandbox;
and the earlier release could not use one anyway, since it never mounts a claim of this release's (below).
