The boot makes at most ten attempts of at most 10 s each, waiting 1 s doubling to 16 s between them, 3 min 15 s in all at worst (`storeOpenRetry`, `packages/daemon/internal/daemon/daemon.go`), and logs each wait as `boot probe failed transiently; waiting to run it again` with `probe` `Postgres store`, `attempt` (`<n>/10`), `retryIn` and `detail`.
After the tenth attempt it exits naming the last error, with the host and never the password.
Every other error refuses the boot at once, as before: a refused password (28P01), a connection `pg_hba.conf` does not admit (28000), a database that does not exist (3D000), a TLS failure, and a DSN the driver cannot parse.
A stop during the attempts ends the boot at once.

The boot prepares none of the repositories its records name: the refresher prepares them once the API serves, beside the boot, so GitHub's rate limit on a repository never holds the boot there.
The boot's only reads of a repository are the fill of a record that lacks its repository columns and the one-time rename pass's reads of a configured pair's names, each read bounded at 15 s (both below).
A GitHub rate limit on the boot's App logins read, or on its proof of each App's key (the App's `GET /app/installations` under its JWT), is waited out.
The boot waits until the time GitHub names, its `Retry-After`, else the limit's reset, at most one hour each, and one minute where GitHub names no time, doubling for each further such refusal of the same call, and then makes the call again.
It logs each wait at warn as `boot probe waits out GitHub's rate limit; it runs again at the time GitHub names` with `probe` (the call: `GitHub App logins read` or `GitHub App key proof`), `until`, `wait`, `waited` (the time the boot has waited for rate limits so far), `limit` and `detail`, and such a wait counts against no attempt.
All of one boot's rate-limit waits end 70 minutes after the first of them; then a logins read or a key proof that GitHub still refuses ends the boot, naming the call, GitHub's last answer and the time waited, and, for the key proof, the App.
A key proof GitHub refuses for anything but its rate limit or its own trouble, such as a 401 or a 403 that names no rate limit, still stops the boot at once, naming the App.
The fill of a record that lacks its repository columns does not wait out GitHub's rate limit: a read the limit refuses leaves the record for the refresher, as any failed read does.
A stop during a wait ends the boot at once.

A malformed seed refuses the boot immediately at startup, before any network connection is attempted.
A NATS authorization violation at connect time is the same: the server said no synchronously, and the boot refuses it at once.
An EOF during the NATS handshake also refuses at once
— the connection simply closed, and nats.go returns that synchronously too
— though no crash in the audited journal took this shape, so refusing rather than waiting here is a judgment call.

A NATS permission violation on a JetStream call (a refused consumer or stream grant) is reported asynchronously:
the server tells the connection of it well before the blocked call's own attempt bound runs out, but the blocked call itself does not return early on that report
— it waits out its own bound exactly as a call that will never get an answer does.
Only once that bound runs out, at 30 seconds, does the boot learn of the violation at all, by folding the connection's own last-reported error into the one the blocked call returns, so it recognizes the refusal by name and refuses outright.
A clustered JetStream that is itself unavailable
— every server reachable, none of them answering the API request
— surfaces the exact same way at the exact same 30-second bound: a bare request timeout, nothing in its own text to say why, nothing to fold in.
The boot cannot tell that shape from a permission violation whose report never arrived
— the two take the same 30 seconds either way, so timing offers no way to distinguish them — and refuses both rather than waiting on either.

A Postgres failure while reconciling admission is not covered by either wait:
an error Postgres itself returns exits as soon as it comes back, and only Postgres accepting a connection and then never answering waits out the same 30-second bound before the boot gives up.

Several shapes an operator should know wait forever rather than exit, none of them obviously "network trouble" on their face:
a Dispatch 401 or 403 (a bad or revoked bearer token);
a NATS or Dispatch host that does not resolve (a typo in `nats_urls` or `dispatch_url`'s hostname);
a non-Dispatch 4xx, such as an HTML 404 from a `dispatch_url` whose path is wrong but whose host answers;
and a TLS handshake that stalls, or a `nats_urls` entry on a port that never speaks first, such as an HTTP or TLS port (no answer within the attempt), while every TLS refusal named above stops the boot at once.
Each of these waits silently: no line is logged beyond the generic `boot probe failed
transiently` warn above, though its own `detail` carries the error's own text (`UNAUTHORIZED:
...`, `no such host`), not a separate line calling out the credential or configuration problem by name.

A Dispatch 401 or 403 is the one with an operational consequence worth naming plainly:
the daemon does not exit on one, so nothing re-reads `dispatch_token_file` until an operator restarts it by hand to pick up a corrected or renewed token.

With several `nats_urls`, or a clustered NATS whose advertised addresses this daemon cannot reach, an authorization violation on one server can surface as a dial failure, or the generic "nats:
no servers available for connection" answer, from a different server nats.go tries next, so the boot waits and the logged `detail` may never name the authorization error at all (LEGION-580).

While the readiness gate waits, callers outside the daemon see it as still booting, not as down:
the API port is already bound by this point (the same as during the image probe, both before this gate), so it accepts a connection but serves nothing until the gate passes, and `legion status` reports the daemon's PID alive but not yet answering.
The key proof under the App's JWT mints no token for an owner;
every other step of the boot that reads GitHub or writes a cache's credential mints the token that step needs.
One such step fills a record that lacks its repository columns, one read per such record, each bounded at 15 s, and a read that fails leaves the record for the refresher.
The one-time rename pass, before the consumers open, reads GitHub for a `repository_renames` pair only while a stored row still names the pair's `from`: then it reads both role Apps' installations on each of the pair's names that the daemon holds no answer for (at boot, both) and, where the daemon holds no spelling of the `to`, GitHub's spelling of it, each read bounded at 15 s;
once no row names a pair's `from`, the pass reads nothing of GitHub for that pair.
Under `keep_volume`, an issue whose Sandbox keeps its volume keeps its old name until the end of its last pod, or until a later boot finds no kept volume ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)).
Until then, the pass's `left` count can stay above 0.
The refresher's reads of each repository's installations, name and default branch run beside the boot, once the API serves, and hold neither the boot nor the port.
A pane's `legion` tool calls (`read_record` and `handoff_complete`, the latter minting its grant in-process first) and `controller start` all wait on that same API, so none of them succeeds until the daemon actually serves;
a pane's plain `gh` and `git` do not, since they read the role's credential from its gh files and call the daemon for nothing.

Rollout order for the server's `legion-daemon` user:
the server admits `legion-daemon` (its public key applied) with the daemon's grants first;
then its seed is stored, every daemon gets it and restarts, and its `legion daemon connects to NATS` line must read `paneUser=false` (#1494).
Only then is the `legion-pane` seed written.
A clean boot line proves the user, not every grant:
the check before the pane seed is written also has each daemon consume a Dispatch and a GitHub event with no error line, and searches each daemon's log for `NATS refused the daemon`, since a missing grant on the exceptions lane (`notifications.envoy.exceptions.notifications.role.>`) still boots healthy and consumes both events, and that error line is its only sign.
`legion-pane` is never granted the daemon's subjects above.
Reversed, a daemon holding only the `legion-pane` seed connects as `legion-pane`, and each refused subject logs the error line above (a refused consumer or subscription never delivers).

### The deployment's private-name rules

The leak guard runs up to two checks before a role writes ([Worker image](#worker-image)):
the shared public leak check, where one is named for the role (the deployment's `leak_check` setting in a pod, or on a pane's machine the check its operator installed), and the deployment's own private-name rules, where the deployment names a rule file (`packages/daemon/internal/leakguard`).
The `legion` binary carries no private-name rule.
A deployment names its own rule file, in gitleaks' rule format.
Each is the operator's to name, so a write gets one of four guards:

- a shared check and a rule file named: the check runs, then the visibility read, then the rules over a public destination;

- a rule file and no shared check: the visibility read, then the rules over a public destination;

- a shared check and no rule file: the check alone, with no visibility read;

- neither: no leak guard at all, and every write is cleared with nothing read; the daemon says so in two boot lines, one that no leak check is configured and one that no rule file is named.

The key and the variable below work the same way under `runtime: tmux` (`docs/deployment.md`, "What a pane's Dispatch credential is").

**Where the file is named.**
`private_name_rules_file` in `legion.yaml` names the file:

```yaml
private_name_rules_file: private-name-rules.toml   # relative to legion.yaml's directory
```

A relative path resolves against `legion.yaml`'s directory, and an empty value is refused (`private_name_rules_file must not be empty`).
Where the file sets no such key, `LEGION_PRIVATE_NAME_RULES_FILE` in the daemon's environment names the file.
An empty value of the variable names no file, as an unset variable does.
Where both name a file, the key wins.
A daemon of an earlier release refuses `private_name_rules_file`.
So a deployment that may roll back across this release sets the variable instead of the key.

**What the daemon does with it.**
The daemon reads the file once, at boot, and compiles it with the guard's own loader (`readBoot`, `packages/daemon/internal/daemon/bootreads.go`, and `compilePrivateNameRules`, `privatenamerules.go`).
A file it cannot read or compile refuses the boot, and `legion config check` refuses it in the same words before any boot.
The refusal names the key or the variable, and the file.
The daemon's own branch create runs the rules boot compiled.
Every launch carries the file's bytes as the launch secret `LEGION_PRIVATE_NAME_RULES` (`launchSecrets`, `packages/daemon/internal/daemon/launchsecrets.go`):
each worker under either runtime, and the controller under `controller: daemon`.
The runtime writes the secret to a file of the launch's own and points `LEGION_PRIVATE_NAME_RULES_FILE` at that file:
`/var/run/legion/private/g<generation>/LEGION_PRIVATE_NAME_RULES` in a pod ([Anatomy of a Sandbox pod](#anatomy-of-a-sandbox-pod)), and a 0600 file under `<state_dir>/secrets` in a tmux pane.
A role keeps the copy its launch was handed.
So a changed file reaches a role only after the daemon restarts and that role launches again.
`runtime.tmux.pane_env` may not set `LEGION_PRIVATE_NAME_RULES_FILE`.
While the deployment names a file, `runtime.kubernetes.pod.env` may not set that variable either, and no `provider_keys` entry may be named `LEGION_PRIVATE_NAME_RULES`.

**The bound.**
The guard reads at most 256 KiB of a rule file (`MaxRulesFile`, `packages/daemon/internal/leakguard/rules.go`), and the daemon refuses a longer file at boot.
A deployment's file is a few kilobytes of regular expressions.
The bound is there because the file rides every launch's start command.
Under `runtime: kubernetes` that command is one frame, and a launcher reads no frame longer than 1 MiB, so the daemon refuses a start whose frame is longer before it sends it (`checkStartFrame`, `packages/daemon/internal/runtime/sandbox/launcher.go`).
The same frame carries the role's system prompt and the launch's other files, all of it JSON-encoded, and JSON doubles each backslash of a regular expression.
A file near 1 MiB would therefore fail every launch.
The bound also refuses a pointer to a log or an image, named by mistake, rather than reading that file into memory whole.

**What the file may hold.**
What the file holds is the whole of what the guard's private-name step detects (`LoadRules`, `rules.go`).
The guard refuses a file in each of these cases, and so does the daemon at boot:

- The file is longer than 256 KiB.

- The file is no TOML.

- The file holds a key that gitleaks' rule format does not have, and the refusal names the key.
  gitleaks itself ignores an unknown key, so a misspelt `[[rule]]` would compile to no rule at all.

- The file holds an `[extend]` section.
  Write the extended rules into the file itself.

- The file holds two rules of one `id`, and gitleaks would run only the last of them.

- The file holds no rule.

- A pattern of the file does not compile.

The guard ignores `gitleaks:allow`.
A line that carries those words is scanned like any other line, so no writer can exempt a line from the deployment's rules.

**What the rules read.**
The private-name step runs only for a destination GitHub reports public, and for one the caller cannot name.
It scans each record of the write on its own, so a rule that needs two words matches only where one record holds both.
A report names a record by its label: as it was written where that is printable text of at most 200 bytes with no `\`, and otherwise as **The report** below says.
A push has these records:

- The ref name, labelled `the ref name`.

- Each commit's author, committer and message, labelled `commit <sha7> author`, `commit <sha7> committer` and `commit <sha7> message`.

- Each added or renamed path, labelled by the path.

- Each added line, labelled by its file's path.
  The report's `on line <n>` is the line in that file.

A gh call has these records:

- Each argument, labelled `the gh call's argument <i>`.
  A field given to `-f`, `--raw-field`, `-F` or `--field` of `gh api` or `gh workflow run` is two records: its value, labelled `the gh call's field <name>`, and its name, labelled `the gh call's field <name> (name)`.
  Only those two commands have field options: in every other command `-f` and `-F` mean other things (`-F` is `--body-file` in `gh pr create`), so there every argument is one record, read whole.
  An option's value is read as that option's value and never as an option of its own, so `gh api -t '-f…'` is a template, read whole.
  A `gh api` call's endpoint is also read decoded, because GitHub decodes the percent-escapes of an endpoint's path and query: it decodes a REST path, and stores a release asset's `name` and `label` query values decoded.
  Its path with its percent-escapes decoded is a record, labelled `the gh call's argument <i>, path`, and so is each value of its query, decoded as a URL query is, labelled `the gh call's argument <i>, query <key>`, and each key of its query, decoded the same way, labelled `the gh call's argument <i>, query <key> (name)`; each is a record only where decoding changes the text.
  A key is read because GitHub may store it as a name: a server that merges a query into a request's parameters, as a Rails parser does, reads `inputs%5Bnotes%5D=1` as an input named `notes`; that is not measured, since measuring it takes a write, and the read costs one record.
  A `;` inside a query value stays in the value, as GitHub keeps it (measured on `api.github.com` on 2026-11-25: `?per_page=1&x=a%62c;d` came back as the pair `x=abc%3Bd`), so such a pair is read decoded with its `;`.
  A path whose escapes do not decode is read only as written, and so is a pair of a query whose key or value does not decode.

- The call's standard input, labelled `the gh call's standard input`, and each file the call sends, labelled by its path.
  A call that only prints, such as gh's help of a command (`--help`, or a `-h` that no option of the command takes), sends nothing beside its arguments, so the guard opens no file its options name: `legion gh pr comment 1 --body-file <file> --help` passes where no file is at `<file>`, and its arguments are read as any call's are.
  A `-h` counts as help only after the command's name, where no option of the command takes it; before the command's name, a `-h` passes only as the whole argv, `gh -h`; any other `-h` there is refused, such as `gh pr -h`, `gh -R acme/widgets -h` or one with words after it, since gh can take the next word as its value and run another command (`gh -h status config set -h github.com editor x` runs `gh config set`, whose own `-h` is `--host`).

- Each JSON string of a request body (`gh api --input <file>`, `gh api --input -`, or the standard input of `gh workflow run --json`) that is exactly one JSON document, labelled `<record>, JSON <path>`, where `<record>` is the body's own label.
  An object's name is a record too, labelled `<record>, JSON <path> (name)`.
  A path of more than 8 steps is shown as its first 2 steps, `…` and its last 5, and a step longer than 64 bytes is cut there, with `…`, so a deep body's labels stay short.
  An empty string is no record, since no rule can match it.
  A body that is not exactly one JSON document is read as one record.
  A body sent to a whole URL on another host than `api.github.com`, such as a release asset uploaded to `uploads.github.com`, is read as one record, because GitHub stores it as sent.
  Where such a body is exactly one JSON document, its JSON strings are read beside that record too, because whoever parses the stored document reads each string decoded, `\u0074` as `t`.
  A call to such a URL that gives fields, no `--input` and a method other than `GET` is refused, because gh would send its fields as one JSON document that GitHub stores as sent; send the asset's bytes with `--input <file>` or `--input -`.
  With `--input`, or with the method `GET` (`-X GET` or `--method GET`, in any case), gh puts the fields in the URL's query string instead, and they are read as any field of the call is.
  A file or standard input longer than 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes) is refused, because the guard reads no more than that of what a call sends, so a release asset past that size is refused too.

- Each string literal of a GraphQL query, labelled `<record>, GraphQL string <k>`, where `<record>` is the label of the record that holds the query.
  A `gh api` call's query is read so whatever spelling of GitHub's GraphQL endpoint the call names (`graphql`, `/graphql`, the API's full URL), and wherever the query comes from: a field, a file, a JSON body's `query`, or standard input named by `-F query=@-`.
  A query that does not lex is read as written.

Each text that a write to a public repository sends and GitHub stores and shows is read as GitHub stores it, but a release asset's file and a label gh takes from the name of a file a glob pattern matched, which are handled as on `main` (the last row).
The table lists each of them, what GitHub does to it before it stores it, and the records the guard reads of it; `TestEveryTextGitHubStoresIsReadAsItIsStored` (`packages/daemon/internal/leakguard/gh_fields_test.go`) holds a row for each record the table names:

| What the call sends | What GitHub stores | What the guard reads |
| --- | --- | --- |
| An argument, such as a title, a body or a tag | the text as written | `the gh call's argument <i>`, as written |
| A field of `gh api` or `gh workflow run` (`-f`, `--raw-field`, `-F`, `--field`) | the name and the value as written: gh JSON-escapes them, and GitHub stores the strings | `the gh call's field <name>` and `the gh call's field <name> (name)`, as written |
| A JSON request body sent to GitHub's REST API (`gh api --input <file>` or `--input -`) | each JSON string, its escapes decoded | `<record>, JSON <path>` and `<record>, JSON <path> (name)`, decoded |
| A body sent to a whole URL on another host than `api.github.com`, such as a release asset uploaded to `uploads.github.com` | the bytes as sent | `<record>`, as sent, and where the body is exactly one JSON document `<record>, JSON <path>` too, decoded |
| The file of a file option (`--body-file`, `--notes-file`, `--from-file`, and the `-F` that is one of them), and the file of a field's `@<path>` (`-F <name>=@<path>`, `--field <name>=@<path>`) but a GraphQL query's, which its own row covers | the text as written | the file's path, labelling its text as written |
| A `gh api` endpoint's path | the path, its percent-escapes decoded | `the gh call's argument <i>, path`, decoded, beside the argument as written |
| Each pair of a `gh api` endpoint's query | the value, its percent-escapes decoded and a `;` in it kept | `the gh call's argument <i>, query <key>`, decoded with its `;`; a pair whose key or value does not decode is read only as written, in the argument |
| Each key of a `gh api` endpoint's query | the key, its percent-escapes decoded, where GitHub merges the query into the request's parameters (not measured) | `the gh call's argument <i>, query <key> (name)`, decoded; a pair whose key or value does not decode is read only as written, in the argument |
| A GraphQL query (a `query` field, a file, a JSON body's `query`, or `-F query=@-`) | each string literal, its escapes decoded | `<record>, GraphQL string <k>`, decoded |
| The inputs of `gh workflow run --json`, on standard input | each input's JSON string, its escapes decoded | `the gh call's standard input, JSON <path>`, decoded |
| A release asset of `gh release upload` or `gh release create` | the file's bytes, its name and its label | as on `main`: each argument as written, so an asset's path or `#label` written in an argument is read and refused as any argument is; the rule pass opens no asset's file, and a label gh takes from the name of a file a glob pattern matched is in no argument and goes unread; the shared check reads the call's arguments too |

A text that `legion leak-check text` checks has two records, `the title` (its first line) and `the body` (the rest).
A path rule reads only a record's path, and only a pushed file's records carry one: its added or renamed path and each of its added lines.
A file that a gh call sends carries no path, because GitHub never sees the name the file has where the call runs.
So no label, JSON path or line number is read as a path.

**The report.**
A refusal by the private-name rules starts `LEAK CHECK: refusing <the write>: the deployment's private-name rules match it`.
Under that line it shows one line for each distinct finding among the 40 shown; a line the report already shows, such as a path rule's finding on every added line of a file, is not written again.
Each line is indented two spaces:

```text
<record>: <description>: matched "<match>" on line <n>: "<line>"
```

`<record>` is the record's label.
A character that does not print, and `\`, stands in it as Go writes it in a quoted string, so a newline in a field's name or a path cannot break the report apart either.
A label longer than 200 bytes is shown as its first 60 bytes, `…` and its last 140.
`<description>` is the description the deployment's rule gives.
`<match>` and `<line>` are Go-quoted, so a newline or a control character cannot break the report apart.
The match is cut at 200 bytes.
The line is a window of at most 120 bytes on each side of the match shown.
`…` marks each cut.
A path rule's finding stands on no line, and reads `<record>: <description>: matched the path`.
A report shows at most 40 lines, and then `… and <k> more matches not shown`.
The report masks nothing it shows.
It shows the text because the agent that would make the write wrote it, so nothing in it is hidden from that agent.
This repository's public CI never prints the guard's report.

**What the boot and a role say.**
With no file named, boot logs this line before anything that can stop the boot:

```text
daemon: the deployment names no private-name rule file (private_name_rules_file in legion.yaml, or LEGION_PRIVATE_NAME_RULES_FILE in the daemon's environment): every role's guard runs no private-name rule
```

With a file named, boot logs this line once it has read and compiled the file:

```text
daemon: the deployment's private-name rules are <path> (sha256 <hex>, <n> rules), handed to every launch
```

The sha256 is of the bytes every launch carries, so an operator can tell one version of the file from another.
`GET /legion/v1/state` shows the path, and never the rules, as `settings.private_name_rules_file`, and leaves the key out while no file is named.

Where its launch names no rule file, a role's guard runs the shared check alone, reads no visibility and builds no record; where the deployment names no shared check either (the `leak_check` setting above), it runs nothing and clears every write.
`legion leak-check pre-push`, `legion leak-check text` and `legion gh` print nothing of it, on any command, since a line on each would break a script that reads what they print.
The boot's line above says it once, in the daemon's log.
`legion gh` logs such a call with the visibility source `no-rules` (`packages/daemon/cmd/legion/gh_reads.go`).
Where `LEGION_PRIVATE_NAME_RULES_FILE` names a file the guard cannot use (missing, unreadable, longer than 256 KiB, or refused above), the guard refuses the write as a setup failure:
`LEAK CHECK SETUP ERROR: <the write>: the private-name rule file <path>, which LEGION_PRIVATE_NAME_RULES_FILE names, <why>`.
`<path>` is shown as the report shows a label, and so is every path, repository and option a setup failure of the guard names.
A deployment that named rules meant them to run, and a guard that ran none in their place would pass what they refuse.

**The operator-launched controller.**
Under `controller: operator` the daemon launches no controller, so no launch hands that controller the rules.
`legion controller start` runs Oh My Pi on top of the operator's own environment ([Operator-launched controller](#operator-launched-controller)).
So an operator who wants that controller's guard to run the rules exports `LEGION_PRIVATE_NAME_RULES_FILE` there.
That controller's gh tokens are the review App's read-only tokens, so no write of its gh reaches GitHub, with the rules or without them.

**Deploy order.**
A pod's guard runs the rules its daemon hands it at launch.
So each project moves its daemon to this release before its pods' image, or with it.
A rollback goes in the reverse order: the pods' image first, then the daemon.
A pod of an older image runs the rules its own `legion` binary embeds, whatever its daemon hands it.
A pod of the new image under an older daemon runs no private-name rule, and nothing says so: an older daemon logs no line about the rules, and the pod's commands print nothing of it.
A deployment that may roll back across this release names its file in `LEGION_PRIVATE_NAME_RULES_FILE`, since an older daemon refuses `private_name_rules_file`.

<a id="issue-pods-in-microvms"></a>
### Pods in microVMs

A project's issue pods and its controller's pod run under gVisor unless `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox` names the other sandbox for them.
The other sandbox is a GKE Sandbox microVM: the pod runs under the `microvm` RuntimeClass, on the nodes of a ComputeClass the operator names.
The block can put every issue pod of the project in a microVM, or only the pods of a list of its issues, for a canary.
The controller's pod (`controller: daemon`) follows `type` alone: it runs in a microVM where `type` is `microvm`, and in gVisor otherwise, since `canary_issues` names issues and the controller has none.
One daemon serves one project, so the block is that project's (`readSandbox`, `packages/daemon/internal/config/kubernetes.go`).
`deploy/kubernetes/daemon/legion.yaml.example` carries it, commented out:

```yaml
runtime:
  kubernetes:
    sandbox:                                # optional
      type: gvisor                          # gvisor (the default) or microvm
      canary_issues: [WIDGETS-12]           # issues whose pods run in the sandbox type does not name; default []
      microvm:                              # where a microVM pod runs
        compute_class: example-microvm      # required while type is microvm or canary_issues names an issue
        storage_class: example-microvm-disk # default: runtime.kubernetes.storage_class
        keep_volume: false                  # true keeps a microVM pod's volume past the pod (below)
        metadata:                           # optional: the pod-local metadata endpoint (below)
          workload_pool: example-project.svc.id.goog
          identity_provider: https://container.googleapis.com/v1/projects/example-project/locations/us-central1/clusters/example-cluster
```

- `type` is the sandbox of every issue pod of the project and of its controller's pod: `gvisor`, the default, or `microvm`.

- `canary_issues` lists the issues whose pods run in the sandbox `type` does not name: in a microVM on a gVisor project, and in gVisor on a microVM project.
  Each entry is one exact issue key, named once.
  It never moves the controller's pod.

- `microvm.compute_class` is the ComputeClass whose nodes run the microVM pods.
  It is required while `type` is `microvm` or `canary_issues` names an issue.

- `microvm.storage_class` is the StorageClass of a microVM issue pod's workspace volume.
  Left out, it is `runtime.kubernetes.storage_class`.
  The controller's disk stays on `runtime.kubernetes.storage_class` in either sandbox ("The disk", below).

- `microvm.keep_volume` makes a microVM issue pod's workspace volume a claim that the issue's Sandbox owns, which outlives the pod ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)).
  It is `false` by default, and a gVisor pod's volume ends with its pod whatever it says.

- `microvm.metadata` turns on the pod-local metadata endpoint ([The pod-local metadata endpoint](#the-pod-local-metadata-endpoint)).

An issue's sandbox is `type`, or the other one when `canary_issues` names the issue's exact key (`SandboxConfig.Of`, `packages/daemon/internal/runtime/sandbox/types.go`).
The daemon decides it each time a launch builds the issue's pod, from the issue the launch is for (`prepare`, `packages/daemon/internal/runtime/sandbox/manifest.go`).
The controller's sandbox is `type` (`SandboxConfig.Controller`, `types.go`), which `prepare` reads each time a launch builds the controller's pod.
A `microvm` block does nothing while no issue pod runs in a microVM.
The loader still checks its keys, but it requires no `compute_class` then and refuses none of the `scheduling`, `pod.env` and `agent_secrets` keys below, so a revert that empties `canary_issues` can leave the block in place.
`legion state --json` shows the block as the loader settled it, under `settings.runtime.kubernetes.sandbox`:
`canary_issues` is `[]` when the file names none, `microvm` is absent when the file names no such block, and its `storage_class` is the class the microVM issue pods' disks use.
The block's `keep_volume` is `false` where the file names none.

The loader refuses each of these, naming the key, and `legion config check` shows each before anything starts:

- a `sandbox`, `microvm` or `metadata` that is not a mapping: `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox must be a mapping`, and likewise `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.microvm` and `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.microvm.metadata`.

- a key the block does not know: `unknown key runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.<key>`, and likewise under `microvm` and `metadata`.

- a `type` that is neither word: `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.type must be 'gvisor' or 'microvm'`.

- a `canary_issues` that is not a list of non-empty strings: `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.canary_issues must be an array of non-empty strings`.

- a `canary_issues` entry that is not an issue key: `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.canary_issues entry "<entry>" is not an issue key, such as LEGION-208`.

- a `canary_issues` entry named twice: `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.canary_issues names <KEY> twice`.

- no `microvm.compute_class` while an issue pod runs in a microVM: `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.microvm.compute_class is required while runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.type is microvm or runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.canary_issues names an issue: the ComputeClass whose nodes run the microVM pods`.

- a blank `compute_class` or `storage_class`: `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.microvm.<key> must not be empty`.

- a `keep_volume` that is not `true` or `false`: `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.microvm.keep_volume must be true or false`.

- a `metadata` block without `workload_pool`: `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.microvm.metadata.workload_pool is required: the cluster's Workload Identity pool, <PROJECT_ID>.svc.id.goog`.

- a `metadata` block without `identity_provider`: `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.microvm.metadata.identity_provider is required: the cluster's identity provider, https://container.googleapis.com/v1/projects/<PROJECT_ID>/locations/<LOCATION>/clusters/<CLUSTER>`.

- a `workload_pool` in another form: `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.microvm.metadata.workload_pool "<value>" must be the cluster's Workload Identity pool, <PROJECT_ID>.svc.id.goog`.

- an `identity_provider` in another form: `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.microvm.metadata.identity_provider "<value>" must be the cluster's identity provider, https://container.googleapis.com/v1/projects/<PROJECT_ID>/locations/<LOCATION>/clusters/<CLUSTER>`.

- a `scheduling.node_selector` key `sandbox.gke.io/runtime` while an issue pod runs in a microVM: `runtime.kubernetes.scheduling.node_selector must not set sandbox.gke.io/runtime while an issue pod runs in a microVM (runtime.kubernetes.sandbox): the RuntimeClass places the pod`.

- a `scheduling.tolerations` key `sandbox.gke.io/runtime` while an issue pod runs in a microVM: `runtime.kubernetes.scheduling.tolerations[<n>].key must not be sandbox.gke.io/runtime while an issue pod runs in a microVM (runtime.kubernetes.sandbox): the RuntimeClass places the pod`.

- a `pod.env` entry `GCE_METADATA_HOST` or `GCE_METADATA_IP` while `metadata` is set and an issue pod runs in a microVM: `runtime.kubernetes.pod.env must not set GCE_METADATA_HOST while runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.microvm.metadata is set and an issue pod runs in a microVM: that pod's launcher sets it to the metadata endpoint it serves`.

- an `agent_secrets.audience` or `agent_secrets.exchange_audience` equal to `workload_pool` while `metadata` is set and an issue pod runs in a microVM: `runtime.kubernetes.agent_secrets.audience must differ from runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.microvm.metadata.workload_pool (both <pool>) while an issue pod runs in a microVM: the cluster projects one volume per audience, so the two tokens would be one`, and likewise `runtime.kubernetes.agent_secrets.exchange_audience`.

**Where a microVM pod runs.**
The daemon renders the placement of a microVM pod, an issue pod or the controller's, from the block (`placement`, `manifest.go`):

- `runtimeClassName: microvm`, in place of `gvisor`.

- The node selector is a gVisor pod's, `legion.dev/pool: legion` and then the operator's `scheduling.node_selector`, with `cloud.google.com/compute-class` set to `microvm.compute_class`.
  That entry replaces any class the operator's selector names, and every other entry stays.

- The tolerations are a gVisor pod's, the pool's `legion.dev/pool=legion:NoSchedule` and then the operator's, less any operator toleration whose key is `cloud.google.com/compute-class`, which tolerates the class being replaced.
  One toleration follows them: `cloud.google.com/compute-class=<compute_class>:NoSchedule`, operator `Equal`, the taint GKE puts on the nodes of a custom ComputeClass.

- The priority class is `scheduling.priority_class`, as on every pod.

- The pod names nothing of `sandbox.gke.io/runtime`.
  GKE's `microvm` RuntimeClass adds that node affinity and its toleration to the pod at admission, which is why the loader refuses an operator selector or toleration on that key (above).

The daemon never changes the operator's `scheduling` itself: every gVisor pod of the project keeps the selector and tolerations as the file writes them.

**The label.**
A microVM pod, an issue pod or the controller's, carries the label `legion.dev/sandbox: microvm`, and no gVisor pod carries it (`labelSandbox`, `names.go`).
It is the label a NetworkPolicy selects the microVM pods by: `podSelector: {matchLabels: {legion.dev/sandbox: microvm}}`.
It is on the pod template alone, so on the pod, and never on the Sandbox or its Secrets, which carry the labels they carry in gVisor.
A Sandbox is kept across its pods, and each of them can run in either sandbox, while the daemon builds the template again for each pod.

**The disk.**
A microVM issue pod's workspace volume, its generic ephemeral volume, is of `microvm.storage_class`, else of `storage_class`, at `issue_volume` (`claimSpec`, `manifest.go`).
`claimSpec` is the one place an issue disk's claim takes its class from, for a launch (`diskSpec`) and for the boot census, so a source of the issue disk added later takes its class from the same place.
The kept volume is such a source: with `microvm.keep_volume: true`, the volume is a claim that the issue's Sandbox owns and that outlives the pod, of the class and size that `claimSpec` gives ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)).
The controller's disk is always of `storage_class`.
That disk is the claim template the controller's Sandbox owns, and `spec.volumeClaimTemplates` is immutable in the CRD, so a class that followed the controller's sandbox would need a new Sandbox at each change of `type`, and the delete of the old Sandbox takes the controller's volume with it.
So a microVM controller pod mounts a disk of `storage_class` on a node of `microvm.compute_class`, and the nodes of that ComputeClass must attach disks of `storage_class` (dispatch://INFRA-3728).

**What stays in gVisor.**
Each repository cache pod and the image probe's pod run under gVisor whatever the block says, with the operator's `scheduling` as the file writes it (`probe.go`, `repocache.go`).
So the boot's image probe runs the image under gVisor, and never in a microVM.

**The stop-eviction annotations.**
A microVM pod carries the annotations its kind carries in gVisor, an issue pod's and the controller's alike: `karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt: "true"`, `cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "false"` and `legion.dev/pod-shape`.
On the nodes of a custom ComputeClass the two stop-eviction annotations hold no node upgrade off, as GKE Autopilot's extended duration does ([Anatomy of a Sandbox pod](#anatomy-of-a-sandbox-pod)).
The cluster's maintenance window decides when such a node is upgraded, and a pod the upgrade evicts ends as a pod whose node goes does ([The disk dies with its pod](#the-disk-dies-with-its-pod)).
A kept volume stays through that end, and the issue's next pod mounts it ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)).

**Drift.**
A microVM pod's recorded shape (`legion.dev/pod-shape`, [The disk dies with its pod](#the-disk-dies-with-its-pod)) holds a `sandbox` member: its RuntimeClass, its ComputeClass and its metadata endpoint, and an issue pod's disk's StorageClass and `keep_volume` where it is `true` (`sandboxShape`, `drift.go`).
A microVM controller pod's member holds no StorageClass, since its disk stays on `storage_class` ("The disk", above), and no `keep_volume`, which changes nothing for the controller's pod.
A gVisor pod's shape holds no `sandbox` member, so it reads byte for byte as a shape recorded before the block existed, and adding the block opens no update round on a gVisor pod.
The sweep compares each issue pod with the shape of the sandbox the configuration now gives the pod's issue (`storedShapeKey`, `drift.go`).
So a change of an issue's sandbox, through `canary_issues` or `type`, opens an update round on each pod it moves, and on no other pod.
The round names the drift `sandbox null, now {…}` for a pod that moves into a microVM, and `sandbox {…}, now null` for one that moves back.
A change of `microvm.compute_class`, `microvm.storage_class`, `microvm.keep_volume` or `microvm.metadata` opens a round on each microVM issue pod alone.
A shape with `keep_volume` off reads byte for byte as one recorded before the key existed, so the release that adds the key opens no round.
With `microvm.storage_class` left out, the microVM issue pods take `storage_class`, so a change of `storage_class` opens a round on each microVM issue pod, and still on no gVisor pod.
The controller's pod is in no round: its launch compares the pod's recorded shape with the shape that launch would build (`launch.shapeKey`, `drift.go`, and `relaunch`, `relaunch.go`).
A daemon boot re-adopts a running controller pod and replaces nothing, whatever its shape.
A launch that installs nothing replaces a live controller pod whose shape differs, so the controller moves into a microVM, or back into gVisor, at its first such launch after a change of `type`: when its process ends, or when the operator suspends and resumes its claim (below).
A launch that installs a stale-plugin pair replaces it only where its image differs (`podImageDrift`, [Pinning a release that drops what a running pod still uses](#pinning-a-release-that-drops-what-a-running-pod-still-uses)), and the fresh pod is built in the sandbox `type` names.
A change of `microvm.compute_class` or `microvm.metadata` moves a microVM controller pod at its next launch that installs nothing, and a change of `microvm.storage_class` or `microvm.keep_volume` alone moves no controller pod.
Neither `canary_issues` nor a `microvm` block on a gVisor project moves it.
To move the controller at once, suspend its claim and resume it: `legion claims suspend --operator-token-file <file> --claim legion-<project>-controller`, then `legion claims resume --operator-token-file <file> --claim legion-<project>-controller`.
`legion claims suspend` ends only the controller's process and never suspends its Sandbox (`Runtime.Suspend`, `sandbox.go`), so the launch at the resume finds the pod live.
Where that launch installs nothing, the pod's recorded shape differs from the shape the launch would build, so it builds a new pod in the sandbox the configuration gives the controller, and it keeps the controller's Sandbox and its disk.
Where the launch at the resume installs a stale-plugin pair into a pod already on the configured image, it keeps the pod in its old sandbox, since such a launch replaces the pod only where the image differs (`podImageDrift`).
The controller then moves at its next launch that installs nothing.
A role launched into a pod that its round keeps starts as that pod was built:
the launcher's `--microvm` and metadata flags and the projected token are fixed when the pod is created, and nothing the daemon sends a generation depends on the sandbox.
So a role of a gVisor pod whose issue joins `canary_issues` starts in gVisor until the round replaces that pod.

**Upgrading.**
The release that adds the block, daemon API contract 151, refuses one volume name that the release before it took: `workload-identity-token` as a `runtime.kubernetes.pod.volumes[].name`.
The name is now the daemon's own, for the projected token volume of the metadata endpoint ([The pod-local metadata endpoint](#the-pod-local-metadata-endpoint)).
The loader refuses it in every deployment, one that runs only gVisor pods and sets no `sandbox` block included:
`runtime.kubernetes.pod.volumes[<i>].name workload-identity-token is a volume Legion puts in every pod`, where `<i>` is the volume's place in the list, from 0 (`CheckPod`, `packages/daemon/internal/runtime/sandbox/operatorpod.go`).
A daemon of that release does not start on a file it refuses, so run that release's `legion config check` on the file before the rollout (`legion start --check-config` on a release from before that command).
Where the check refuses the name, give that volume another name, in `volumes` and in each `volume_mounts` entry whose `volume` names it.
The release that runs the controller's pod in the project's sandbox, the one with the entry for `dispatch://INFRA-4567` ("Rolling back", below), refuses one mount path that the release before it took: a `runtime.kubernetes.pod.volume_mounts[].mount_path` at or under `/var/run/legion/workload-identity`.
The path is now the daemon's own, where a microVM controller pod mounts the metadata endpoint's token (`ControllerWorkloadIdentityDir`, `names.go`).
The loader reserves it in every deployment, one that runs only gVisor pods included (`legionMountPaths`, `manifest.go`), and refuses such a mount at boot:
`runtime.kubernetes.pod.volume_mounts[<i>].mount_path <path> overlaps /var/run/legion/workload-identity, which Legion mounts in every pod: a mount may be neither at, under, nor above one of Legion's`, where `<i>` is the mount's place in the list, from 0, and `<path>` is its `mount_path` (`CheckPod`, `operatorpod.go`).
`legion config check` of that release shows the refusal, so run it on the file before the rollout.
Where the check refuses the path, mount that volume at another path.

**Rolling back.**
The release that adds the block is daemon API contract 151, whose entry in `packages/daemon/internal/api/version.go` is for `dispatch://INFRA-3729`.
A daemon below contract 151 refuses the key at boot (`unknown key runtime.kubernetes.sandbox`), so a rollback below that contract removes the `sandbox` block from `legion.yaml` before it pins the earlier release.
`legion start --check-config` of that release shows the refusal first.
An earlier daemon reads no `sandbox` member in a pod's recorded shape, so it replaces a microVM pod only for another drift.
The earlier image is such a drift, so each microVM pod's update round brings its issue back to a gVisor pod.
Where a microVM pod's launcher connects to such a daemon before that round replaces the pod, the daemon's answer carries no `kernelKills`.
The launcher then drops each report of a process the pod's kernel stopped, with a line, and tells no role; the `ended` line stays in the container's log ([Memory in a microVM pod](#memory-in-a-microvm-pod)).
A daemon of a release before `microvm.keep_volume` refuses that key at load, and it replaces the Sandbox of each kept volume at the issue's next launch, which deletes the volume ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)).
The release that runs the controller's pod in the project's sandbox is the one whose `packages/daemon/internal/api/version.go` carries the entry for `dispatch://INFRA-4567`.
Its daemon API contract is 217.
A daemon below it builds the controller's pod in gVisor whatever `type` says, and one of contract 151 or later reads the same `sandbox` block.
It re-adopts a running microVM controller pod at its boot, and its answer to that pod's launcher carries no `kernelKills`.
The launcher then drops each report of a process the pod's kernel stopped, with a line, and the controller is told nothing; the `ended` line stays in the `controller` container's log.
That daemon compares the controller's pod with its gVisor shape alone, so the controller returns to gVisor at the first launch that replaces its pod.
That is the daemon's next launch that installs nothing.
Under a daemon of the release that guards the controller's pod's memory, the launch that installs its plugin pair replaces the pod too where it runs another image, and a rollback that pins the earlier image has such a launch: the relaunch onto that daemon's plugins after its boot ([Contract discipline](#contract-discipline)).
Suspending and resuming the controller's claim returns it to gVisor at once where the launch at the resume installs nothing ("Drift", above).

#### The pod-local metadata endpoint

Under Workload Identity a pod gets its Google credential from GKE's metadata server on its node.
Set `microvm.metadata` when a microVM pod does not reach that server.
Each microVM pod's launcher then serves, inside the pod, the paths of that server a Google client reads for the pod's own account (`packages/daemon/internal/launcher/metadata.go`): each microVM issue pod's, and the controller's pod's where `type` is `microvm`.
It gets the access token it hands out the way GKE's server does: it exchanges a projected Kubernetes ServiceAccount token at Google's Security Token Service.
A gVisor pod, and a microVM pod without the block, get none of it.

The block has two keys, and both are required:

- `workload_pool` is the cluster's Workload Identity pool, `<PROJECT_ID>.svc.id.goog`.

- `identity_provider` is the cluster's identity provider, `https://container.googleapis.com/v1/projects/<PROJECT_ID>/locations/<LOCATION>/clusters/<CLUSTER>`.

With the block the daemon adds two things to each microVM pod, an issue pod or the controller's (`workloadIdentityVolumes`, `manifest.go`, and the `launcherContainer` of `issuePod` and of `controllerPod`, `podkind.go`):

- a projected ServiceAccount token volume, `workload-identity-token`, for the audience `workload_pool`, with `expirationSeconds: 3600` and mode 0440, mounted read-only in a directory where the token is the file `token`.
  An issue pod mounts it at `/var/run/legion/roles/workload-identity` (`WorkloadIdentityDir`, `names.go`).
  That directory is under `/var/run/legion/roles`, which every role's namespace covers, so no role's process reads the token.
  The controller's pod mounts it at `/var/run/legion/workload-identity` (`ControllerWorkloadIdentityDir`, `names.go`), and its launcher reads the token at `/var/run/legion/workload-identity/token`.
  That pod has no role namespaces, so the controller's agent can read the token too.
  That gives the agent no identity it lacks: the endpoint its launcher serves hands it access tokens of the same Workload Identity principal, the pool's own (below).
  The kubelet writes a fresh token before the old one expires, and the launcher reads the file again at each exchange.

- the launcher flags `--metadata-workload-pool <workload_pool> --metadata-identity-provider <identity_provider>`, beside `--microvm`.

Before it starts any role's generation, the controller's included, the launcher listens at `127.0.0.1:8169`.
That is the pod's loopback, which every role of an issue pod shares, since a role has no network namespace of its own.
Once it listens, it sets `GCE_METADATA_HOST` and `GCE_METADATA_IP` to that address in its own environment, so its own Google clients read the endpoint, the session database's proxy under `cloudsql-iam` among them ([Selecting the store](#selecting-the-store)).
It also sets both on every role generation it starts, over any value the generation's start command carried, so a role is told only the address its own launcher serves.
Go's `cloud.google.com/go/compute/metadata` and Python's `google-auth` read `GCE_METADATA_HOST`, and Node's `gcp-metadata` reads `GCE_METADATA_IP` before it.
So `runtime.kubernetes.pod.env` must not set either variable while the endpoint is on (the refusal above).
A launcher that serves no endpoint leaves each generation's environment as it is.

The endpoint answers each path below as GKE's server answered it from a Legion issue pod: the status, the `Metadata-Flavor: Google` header where GKE's carries it, the `Content-Type` (`application/text`, or `application/json` for a JSON body), the `Location` of a 301, and the body.
`packages/daemon/internal/launcher/testdata/gke-metadata.json` holds that recording, and the endpoint's tests compare its answers with it.
`<pool>` is `workload_pool`, `<account>` is `default` or `<pool>`, and each path below that does not start with `/` is under `/computeMetadata/v1/`:

- `/` answers `computeMetadata/`, and `/computeMetadata/` answers `v1/`, to any request.

- `/computeMetadata/v1/` itself lists `instance/`, `project/` and `universe/`.

- `project/` lists `project-id`, and `project/project-id` answers `<pool>` without `.svc.id.goog`.

- `instance` answers 301 to `instance/`, which lists `service-accounts/` alone, the one entry of GKE's list that the endpoint serves.

- `instance/service-accounts` answers 301 to `instance/service-accounts/`, which lists `default/` and `<pool>/`.

- `instance/service-accounts/<account>` answers 301 to the same path with a final `/`, which lists `aliases`, `email`, `scopes` and `token`.
  With `?recursive=true` that directory answers the JSON `{"aliases":["default"],"email":"<pool>","scopes":[…]}`.

- `instance/service-accounts/<account>/email` answers `<pool>`, `aliases` answers `default`, and `scopes` lists `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform` and `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/userinfo.email`.

- `instance/service-accounts/<account>/token` answers `{"access_token":"…","expires_in":<n>,"token_type":"Bearer"}`, where `<n>` is the whole seconds the token has left.
  `?scopes=<a>,<b>` names the token's scopes, and a request that names none gets `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform`.

- `universe/` lists `universe-domain` and `universe_domain`, and each of the two answers `googleapis.com`.

A request's `alt` query value chooses the form of three kinds of answer, as it does on GKE's server (`metadataAnswer.serve`, `metadata.go`).
The three are a value, such as `email`, a list value, which is `aliases` or `scopes`, and a directory's listing:

- Where the first `alt` value of the request is `json`, in any letter case, the endpoint answers JSON with `Content-Type: application/json`.
  A value is a JSON string: `email` answers `"<pool>"`.
  A list value and a listing are a JSON array of the lines of the text form: `aliases` answers `["default"]`, and `/computeMetadata/v1/` answers `["instance/","project/","universe/"]`.
  The JSON is on one line with no line break after it.
  A listing names only the entries that the endpoint serves, in either form.

- A request with any other `alt` value, such as `text` or `xml`, or with no `alt`, gets the text form with `Content-Type: application/text`.

- The token and an account's `?recursive=true` answer JSON whatever `alt` says.
  `?recursive=true` on any other directory answers 404 whatever `alt` says (below).

The recording holds GKE's answers to `?alt=json`, `?alt=JSON`, `?alt=text` and `?alt=xml`, read from the same pod on 2026-11-16.

The token is the one Google's Security Token Service gives for the projected token: the launcher sends it to `https://sts.googleapis.com/v1/token` with the audience `identitynamespace:<workload_pool>:<identity_provider>` and the subject token type `urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:jwt`.
The launcher keeps one token for each set of scopes, for at most 16 sets, and exchanges again at the first request after that token has less than 5 minutes left.
One exchange waits at most 30 seconds.
The endpoint impersonates no Google service account.
The account it names and the token it hands out are the pool's own, which is what GKE's server answers for a Kubernetes ServiceAccount bound to no Google service account.
So a pod whose ServiceAccount is bound to a Google service account gets the pool's token from the endpoint, not that service account's.

The endpoint serves no other path.
Among those are `project/numeric-project-id`, `instance/zone`, `instance/hostname`, `instance/id`, every `attributes/` path, and `instance/service-accounts/<account>/identity`, which GKE's server answers 404 for an account bound to no Google service account.
It answers each of them 404 `Not Found`, as GKE's server answers a path it does not know, and answers `?recursive=true` on any directory but an account's the same way.
The first time it answers a path so, it logs `launcher: metadata: not served path=<path>` in the `roles` container's log, or in the `controller` container's log in the controller's pod, with no role prefix, so the log names each path a tool asked for and did not get.
It remembers at most 256 such paths, and logs no path past them.

Every path under `/computeMetadata/v1/` refuses a request without `Metadata-Flavor: Google` with 403 `Missing required header "Metadata-Flavor": "Google"`, as GKE's server does.
It refuses a request with an `X-Forwarded-For` header with 403 `Request cannot contain header: X-Forwarded-For`, also as GKE's server does, so a request a proxy forwards gets no token.
Both refusals come before anything else is read.

A failed exchange answers 500 `token exchange failed`.
It logs `launcher: metadata: token exchange failed scopes="<scopes>" reason="<the service's error>"`, at most one such line a minute, with the reason cut to 256 bytes and never a token in it.

The endpoint bounds how long a client may hold a connection open, so that no process in the pod holds one open without end (`httpServer`, `metadata.go`):

- A client has 10 s to send a request: its request line, its headers and any body it names.
  The 10 s start when the connection opens.
  On a connection that the client keeps open after an answer, they start again when the first bytes of the next request arrive.
  At the bound the endpoint closes the connection.
  A client that sent nothing, or a request line and part of its headers, sees the connection close with no answer.
  A client that sent part of a request line sees `400 Bad Request` and then the close.
  The endpoint reads no body.
  So a client that names a body and does not send it sees its answer at the bound, with `Connection: close`, and then the close.

- The 10 s do not bound the answer.
  They end once the request is read, so the endpoint answers a request with no body however long its token's exchange takes, 30 s at most (above).

- A connection that the client keeps open after an answer has 60 s to start its next request.
  At that bound the endpoint closes the connection, and a later request needs a new connection.

A listen that fails, as when another process of the container holds the address, logs `launcher: metadata: off reason=<error>` and sets neither variable, in the launcher's own environment or on any generation.
The pod and its roles then run without the endpoint, and the container does not fail.

The endpoint was proven on 2026-11-15 against a fake Security Token Service, with the launcher's server at `127.0.0.1:8169` and each client told its address through `GCE_METADATA_HOST` and `GCE_METADATA_IP`:
Go's `cloud.google.com/go/compute/metadata` (`OnGCE`, the project id and the email) and `golang.org/x/oauth2/google` (`FindDefaultCredentials`), Python's `google-auth` 2.62.2 (`google.auth.default`), Node's `gcp-metadata` 9.2.3, and a `curl` of `instance/service-accounts/default/token`.
Each library read the project `example-project` and the fake service's token, the `curl` read that token, and the launcher logged no `not served` line.

#### Memory in a microVM pod

A microVM's kernel is the pod's own, and its out-of-memory killer stops one process of the container rather than the whole pod.
So the launcher of a microVM pod, an issue pod or the controller's, runs no memory guard ([The memory guard in an issue pod](#the-memory-guard-in-an-issue-pod), [The memory guard in the controller's pod](#the-memory-guard-in-the-controllers-pod)), and writes one line that says so:

```text
launcher: memory guard: off reason=the pod runs in a microVM, whose own kernel stops one process
```

It runs the guest watch in the guard's place (`memoryguard.Guest`, `packages/daemon/internal/memoryguard/guest.go`, started by `serveMemoryGuard`, `packages/daemon/internal/launcher/memoryguard.go`).
The guest watch ends no process itself.
It steers the pod's kernel to stop a command before an agent, names each process the kernel stopped, tells that process's role, and logs the pod's memory each hour.
As the guard does, it runs only where the launcher is the container's first process: a launcher started any other way writes the guard's `off reason=the launcher is pid <n>, …` line and runs neither.
The launcher knows that its pod runs in a microVM from its own `--microvm` flag, which is fixed when the pod is built, and never from the daemon's answer.
`runtime.kubernetes.memory_guard` configures the gVisor guard alone, `issue_pods` the gVisor issue pods' and `controller_pod` the gVisor controller pod's:
the guest watch runs whatever that block says, `enabled: false` included, and a microVM pod's launcher applies no `memoryGuard` settings from any answer.

**In the controller's pod.**
Where `type` is `microvm`, the controller's launcher runs the guest watch by the rules of this section over the controller pod's classifier (`controllerClassifier`, "What it spares, and what it may end" in [The memory guard in the controller's pod](#the-memory-guard-in-the-controllers-pod)).
The processes that classifier protects are the ones that section's guard spares, and the session processes it marks are the shim and every direct child of the shim.
Every process of the container is the controller's, so each process the watch names is reported to the controller, and its `ended` line names `role=controller`.
That pod has no `role-init`: once the shim has exited, the launcher, PID 1, drains the exited generation itself, sending SIGTERM over the container's processes, waiting up to its stop grace for them to go, and sending SIGKILL to each one left (`cleanExitedGeneration`, `packages/daemon/internal/launcher/process.go`).
That drain's SIGKILL takes the place of `role-init`'s in "The kills" and "What the sign does not show" below, so the watch's `SessionDrain` there is the stop grace and a second more, where an issue pod's is 3 s (`controllerSessionDrain`, `packages/daemon/internal/launcher/memoryguard.go`).
The watch's lines are in the `controller` container's log, with no role prefix, and the daemon tells the controller of each kill as "Whom it tells" in [The memory guard in the controller's pod](#the-memory-guard-in-the-controllers-pod) says.

**The score.**
The watch lists the container's processes every 100 ms, the guard's default interval, which `interval_milliseconds` does not change.
It asks the guard's classifier which processes are protected and whose role each one is (`podClassifier`, "What it protects, and why" in [The memory guard in an issue pod](#the-memory-guard-in-an-issue-pod)).
At each scan it raises to `oom_score_adj` 1000 every process of a role that the classifier does not protect, where that process reads lower:
an external program a command runs, a language server, the eval kernel, and a process that an Oh My Pi restart left under the role's `role-init`.
It reads the process's start time again before each write, so a pid that another process took is not raised.

The processes the classifier protects keep the starting score, which is the launcher's own `oom_score_adj` at its start:
the launcher and the steps it runs itself, each `role-init` and shim, each agent, Oh My Pi's `__omp_worker_*` helpers, the Claude bridge's processes and the test database.
The watch sets one of them that reads above the starting score back to it, so an agent that raises its own score in its in-process shell does not stay raised.
A process of no role that the classifier does not protect, such as a shell that `kubectl exec` started, keeps the score it reads.

The kernel's out-of-memory killer stops the process with the highest badness.
A process's badness is its resident pages plus `oom_score_adj × limit / 1000`, where `limit` is the pod's memory limit in pages.
So a raise from the starting score to 1000 adds `(1000 − starting score) / 1000` of the limit to a command's badness.
The kernel therefore stops a raised command first, unless a protected process is larger than that command by more than that share of the limit.
The kubelet sets a container's starting score by its pod's QoS class, so the share differs by class:

- A `Guaranteed` container starts at `-997`.
  The raise then adds 199.7% of the limit, which is more than any process can hold.
  So a raised command outranks a protected process of any size, Oh My Pi included.

- A `Burstable` container starts at `1000 − 1000 × memory request / node memory`, which read 992 for a 1Gi request.
  The raise then adds `memory request / node memory` of the limit, 0.8% at 992.
  The kernel then stops a protected process before a command where that process is larger than the command by more than that share.
  Such a process can be an agent.

The tester measured both starting scores, `-997` and 992, on runc nodes, where a container runs on the node's own kernel, and not in a microVM (the result at `aae5e969`, dispatch://INFRA-3729).
A microVM pod's own starting score is the `score=` of its watch's `start` line ("The lines", below).

An issue pod is `Guaranteed` while each `cpu` and `memory` request of `runtime.kubernetes.resources.issue` equals its limit.
That holds unless the file sets `cpu_request` or `memory_request` below its limit.
A request that the file leaves out takes the file's limit where the file sets one.
Else it takes the default's request, which equals the default's limit ([Configuration](#configuration)).
Keep each request equal to its limit where issue pods run in microVMs, so that the score protects Oh My Pi.
The controller's pod is `Guaranteed` by the same rule over `runtime.kubernetes.resources.controller`, so keep those requests equal to their limits where the controller runs in a microVM.

The watch can only raise a score.
The `roles` container drops every capability, and without `CAP_SYS_RESOURCE` no process can set a score below a process's starting value, so no agent can be set below the starting score.
An agent set lower would also shield its commands, since a process starts at its parent's score.
A process can raise the score of another process of the same user with no capability, and it can set a raised process back to the starting score with none either.
A write that fails, as a write to a process that is not dumpable does, is logged once (`score failed`, below), counted in the hour's `unraised`, and not tried again while that process lives.

**What the score does not do.**

- It does not cover an external program's first moments.
  A program starts at its parent's score, which is the starting score when the agent's shell ran it, and keeps that score until the next scan raises it, 100 ms at most.
  In that time the kernel ranks it with the agents by its size alone.

- It does not separate the memory of Oh My Pi's shell from Oh My Pi's own.
  Oh My Pi's bash tool runs its shell inside the Oh My Pi process, so a builtin of that shell, such as `cat`, `grep`, `sed`, `head` or `tail`, uses the agent's own memory at the agent's score.
  Only an external program that the shell starts is a process of its own, which the watch can raise.

**The kills.**
The kernel counts each process it stops in the cgroup's `oom_kill`: the `oom_kill` line of `memory.events` on cgroup v2, and of `memory.oom_control` on cgroup v1.
Nothing else tells the launcher which process it stopped, since a stopped command's exit goes to its parent, the shell that ran it, and not to the launcher.
So at each scan the watch keeps every process it read, by its pid and its start time, with its role, whether it runs its role's session, and its resident size (the `rss` field of its `stat`), and it reads the counter after the scan.
The watch reads a process's role and size again at each scan until a pass sees SIGKILL pending in it (below), and then keeps what the last scan whose snapshot came before that pass read: a scan keeps what it read, its snapshot, only after its own pass.

The watch names a process as stopped only on the sign that the kernel's stop leaves on it: the process is still in `/proc`, running or a zombie, and its `status` has SIGKILL pending for its whole thread group, the `0x100` bit of its `ShdPnd` mask.
The kernel raises the counter and then sends SIGKILL to the process it stops (`__oom_kill_process` in the kernel's `mm/oom_kill.c`), and that SIGKILL stays pending until the process's parent reaps it.
A process's `SigPnd` mask, the signals pending for one of its threads, is no sign.
The kernel adds SIGKILL to that mask in each thread of a process that any fatal signal is ending (`complete_signal` in the kernel's `kernel/signal.c`), such as the SIGTERM that `role-init`'s drain sends to every process of a role whose agent has ended.
So while kills are pending, at each scan the watch makes a pass over the processes it holds, a process that has just become a zombie among them, which the scan itself leaves out, and reads the `status` of each one that has not shown SIGKILL pending yet.
It then reads that process's start time again, so that a pid back with another start time, which is another process, is not taken for it.
A process that shows SIGKILL pending is not read again, and each pass weighs it until one names it or sets it aside; after that it is never weighed for a later kill while the watch holds it, so a process the kernel stopped is named once.
Every pass follows one rule: it names a process only on the sign that process shows, so a delay can leave a kill unnamed, and it names a wrong process only within the rule's one limit ("What the sign does not show", below).
Of the processes that a pass weighs, it first sets aside those of a role whose session has ended (below).
The pass counts the rest with each process that a scan first read with SIGKILL already pending during the same wait (`size`, below), which no pass names.
Where they are no more than the kills left to name, each of the rest is named for one kill, with the role and the size that the last scan whose snapshot came before that pass read of it.
Where they are more, the watch reads the counter again.
Where the counter rose, the kernel has stopped another process since the last read: the pass names none of the rest and sets none of them aside, and it leaves them, with what the watch read of them, to the next pass, which weighs them against the larger count.
That is the one case where a pass leaves a process to the next, and it comes after the pass has set aside the processes of a role whose session ended, which the next pass would set aside too: a role's session that has ended stays ended for the rest of the wait.
Where the counter did not rise, the sign does not say which one the kernel stopped, and the watch sets the rest all aside and names none of them.
Each of those processes goes on counting until the wait ends, or until the first scan after it has left `/proc`, as a process first read with SIGKILL pending during the wait does.
So while they count, and while the counter does not rise again in the wait, a process that another sender SIGKILLs later in the wait meets the same count rather than a name.
No later wait names or counts them, a zombie that stays in `/proc` among them.

A role's session ends with a SIGKILL of its own `role-init`'s.
Once the role's shim has exited, `role-init` sends SIGTERM to every process of the role's namespace, waits up to 2 s (`roleNamespaceDrain`) for them to go, and then sends SIGKILL to each one left (`kill(-1)`, `runRoleShim` in `packages/daemon/internal/launcher/roleinit_linux.go`), which shows in `ShdPnd` as the kernel's does.
On a stop, `role-init` sends that `kill(-1)` as soon as it has reaped the shim.
So the watch keeps, for each role, the time that it last saw one of the role's session processes leave `/proc`: the role's `role-init`, its shim, or a direct child of its shim.
Such a process has left where its `stat` is gone or its pid is back with another start time, and a zombie has not left.
Every such SIGKILL comes after a session process of its role has left, so each pass looks for those processes once, after its last `status` read.
Such a SIGKILL that one of the pass's `status` reads saw came after the departure, so that look finds the departure, and that same pass sets the role's processes aside (below).
Each such SIGKILL reaches the processes of its own role alone, so the pass weighs every other role's processes as ever.
A scan lets go of a session process that it no longer holds only once that process has left, and it keeps a zombie.
A role whose session process left at most 3 s before the first rise of the wait, or at any time since, has no process named for the rest of the wait.
Its processes that a pass sees show SIGKILL pending are set aside, and no pass counts them against the kills left to name, so that the set-aside does not block another role's real victim.
The kills stay pending, to end on the `killed unnamed` line, unless a pass names another process in the victim's place within the rule's one limit ("What the sign does not show", below).
A process of that role that the watch counts already is not set aside: it goes on counting, and can leave another role's kill unnamed, within the same limit.
The 3 s are `roleNamespaceDrain` and a second more, which the launcher passes the watch (`SessionDrain`): `role-init` sends its `kill(-1)` within one 10 ms poll of the drain's end, and the rest of the second covers a `role-init` that the memory pressure behind the rise runs late.
A session process that shows the sign before it leaves, as an agent that the kernel stopped does while it is a zombie its shim has not reaped, is named as any process is.
Where a session process of its role, that process itself among them, has left by the time the pass that would name it looks for those processes, it is set aside instead, and its kill ends on the `killed unnamed` line, unless a pass names another process in its place within the rule's one limit, as above.

The classifier counts every direct child of the shim as a session process, by its place in the tree: the agent, and the shim's other direct children, the secrets renewer, the working copy's adoption and the CodeGraph warm-up, alike.
Where one of those ends by itself, the watch names no process of its role for the rest of that wait either.
That costs kills left unnamed, and a wrong name only within the rule's one limit ("What the sign does not show", below).

The kernel shows that sign only until the process's parent reaps it.
For a 1.5 GiB process whose parent reaps it at once, the sign showed for 51 to 85 ms, and the 100 ms scan alone named such a process 3 times of 5.
So on cgroup v2 the watch also wakes on the file-modified event of `memory.events`, which the kernel raises whenever one of the file's counters changes.
At that event the watch reads the counter at once, and where the counter did not rise and no kill is pending, as when the cgroup only reached its limit, it reads nothing more.
While kills are pending, it then makes a pass at once over the processes that the last scan left it, the scan's own pass with the same rule, and again after pauses of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 ms, about 30 ms in all, until no kill is left to name, because the kernel raises the counter just before it sends SIGKILL.
It does that once for each rise of the counter: at the event whose read rose, or at the first event after a scan that read the rise, since the rise's own event can come just after that scan's read.
Any other event while kills are pending costs the read of the counter alone, so a stream of `max` and `high` events from a pod under pressure does not read statuses for the whole wait, and the scans go on reading.
The wake does not scan `/proc` or set any score.
The 100 ms scan stays as the fallback.
It is the only path on cgroup v1, whose `memory.oom_control` raises no such event, and where the watch of the event cannot start or ends (`wake off`, "The lines", below).

The watch never names a process because it left `/proc`, or because it had the highest `oom_score` before the rise.
A command that exits by itself in the same moment leaves `/proc` too, and in a burst of kills the kernel's next victim is often the process that grew after the first kill.
So a command that exits by itself is never named, and its role is never told.

Where the counter rises again during a wait, the new kills join the ones that wait.
The wait ends 2 s after the counter's last rise, the time the kernel's `oom_reaper` gives a stopped process to exit, or as soon as a process is named for each of its kills.
When the wait ends, the kills that the watch named no process for have one `killed unnamed` line ("The lines", below), which names no process and tells no role.

**What the sign does not show.**

- The rule that every pass follows has one limit, and this item and the next one are the one statement of it.
  The rest of this page and the comments of `packages/daemon/internal/memoryguard/guest.go` and `packages/daemon/internal/launcher/memoryguard.go` refer to these two items and do not repeat their cases.
  A pass weighs against the kills left to name only the processes that it holds and that show SIGKILL pending: the ones it may name, and the ones it counts but never names.
  Where the kernel's victim is not among them at a pass, a held process that something other than the kernel, or than `role-init`'s drain, has sent SIGKILL can be named in the victim's place.
  That process can be of any role, or of no role.
  Where no such process is held, the victim's kill can be left unnamed.
  A kill can also be left unnamed, with no wrong name, where a pass counts a process that no kill of the wait reached (the next item).
  The known cases of this limit are these, and any other order of events in which the victim is not among them at a pass is a case of the same limit:

  - It has left `/proc`.
    Its parent reaped it before a pass read its `status`.
    Or the watch counted it, and it has left since: a counted process counts until the first scan after it has left `/proc`.

  - It started after the last scan, and no scan has read it yet.
    A wake reads no new process, and a scan's pass runs before that scan's snapshot, so the passes of the wakes before that scan, and that scan's own pass, do not hold it.
    Where kills are still pending at that scan, it counts from the next pass on.

  - It is a process of a role whose session process left at most 3 s before the first rise of the wait, or at any time since.
    That session process is the role's `role-init`, its shim, or a direct child of its shim, one that ended by itself among them.
    The pass sets the victim aside and counts it against no kill, so that the set-aside does not block another role's real victim.

  - It was first read with SIGKILL pending while no kill was pending.
    It counts in no wait.
    But the kernel can raise the counter just after a scan reads it, and the rise of its own kill is then read at the next read of the counter, at the wake or the next scan.

  - The kernel has not sent its SIGKILL yet when a pass reads its `status`.
    The kernel raises the counter just before it sends SIGKILL, so a wake's first pass can read the victim before the signal, and so can the pass of a scan that read the counter between the rise and the signal.
    The victim then shows nothing.
    Where that pass names another process for the last kill left to name, no kill is pending after it, and no pass reads the victim again.
