of these twelve names its agent carries no `LEGION_WORKSPACE`, because it is told no tree, issue or checkout (`controllerPod.agentEnv`, `podkind.go`), and its `GH_CONFIG_DIR` is its bundle's first owner's directory, because its launch names no repository: the default is then the bundle's first directory, sorted, which is usually an owner the review App is installed on whose lease the mint answered for, though a configured rename also puts the pair's `from` owner in the bundle as an alias directory, and such a name can sort first and be taken, and the bundle is one read-only directory per owner that App is installed on, with none for a repository (`appauth.ControllerCredential` and `bundleDefault`, `credential.go`);
[Daemon-launched controller](#daemon-launched-controller) has the rest of it.

The token behind `DISPATCH_TOKEN_FILE` is the daemon's own, not the role's.
The daemon reads it once at boot from `dispatch_token_file` (`readBoot`, `packages/daemon/internal/daemon/bootreads.go`) and puts it in every launch's secrets as `DISPATCH_TOKEN` (`secrets[dispatchTokenKey]`, `packages/daemon/internal/runtime/sandbox/manifest.go`, the key from `names.go`), and the role's launcher writes it into the generation's `g<generation>` directory beside the generation's other launch credentials.
The daemon-launched controller takes the same path, because `prepare` adds that secret to every launch it builds, whichever kind of pod the role names.
So every role of every issue of the project, and that controller, present the same bytes.
Under `dispatch_token_broker: true` this holds only for a launch into a live pod built before the setting, whose `DISPATCH_TOKEN_FILE` holds the shared token `dispatch_token_transition_file` names.
Every other launch carries no Dispatch token, and its role trades its pod's exchange identity for a token of its own session ([The daemon's own Dispatch credential](#the-daemons-own-dispatch-credential-dispatch_token_broker)).

When `dispatch_token_file` holds one of the deployment's shared agent tokens (`DISPATCH_AGENT_TOKEN`), Dispatch matches the bytes against them (`MatchesSharedAgentToken`, `packages/envoy/internal/dispatch/auth/agent_token.go`) and reads no person, no service and no project from them.
Whatever the bearer, the acting session is the one the request body names (`bearerSessionActor`, `packages/envoy/internal/dispatch/api/server.go`), which for the daemon's own writes is `legion-daemon:<PROJECT>` (`DaemonSession`, `packages/daemon/internal/dispatch/client.go`), so a shared agent token names nobody.
Dispatch takes any other bearer as a service token or a personal token (`optionalActor`, `server.go`), and every role's session then carries that token's service or owner as well.
`dispatch whoami` in a role tells the two apart:
for a shared agent token it answers `Session <id> runs under the shared token: no owner, …` (`packages/envoy-client/src/dispatch-commands/session.ts`).

The Kubernetes service-account tokens this runtime projects for a role are the broker's, under `runtime.kubernetes.agent_secrets` (`agentSecretsVolumes`, `manifest.go`): `agent-secrets-token` for its `audience`, and `agent-secrets-exchange` for its `exchange_audience` where that key is set (`exchangeTokenProjection`).
Each reaches the secrets broker and nothing else.
A microVM pod whose deployment sets `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.microvm.metadata`, an issue pod or the controller's, carries another projected token, `workload-identity-token`, for the Workload Identity pool's audience.
The pod's launcher exchanges it at Google's Security Token Service for the token its metadata endpoint hands out ([The pod-local metadata endpoint](#the-pod-local-metadata-endpoint)).
In an issue pod no role's namespace shows it, nor in the controller's pod where its launcher runs the roles-dir form under a `writer_audience`.
In the controller's single-role form the controller's agent can read it, which gives the agent no identity that the endpoint does not already serve it.
A pod whose `session_database` names a `writer_audience` carries another projected token, `session-writer-token`, for that audience.
No role's namespace shows it, and the launcher's session proxy exchanges it at Google's Security Token Service to impersonate the session database's service account ([What `cloudsql-iam` puts in a pod](#what-cloudsql-iam-puts-in-a-pod)).
Dispatch can verify a projected token minted for its own audience (`DISPATCH_OIDC_AUDIENCE` in `packages/envoy/cmd/dispatch/settings.go`, checked by `serviceTokenActor` in `packages/envoy/internal/dispatch/api/server.go`), and the runtime projects none.
The operator's own pod volumes are outside this statement: the operator controls them.
An operator-launched controller can differ:
`legion controller start` points `DISPATCH_TOKEN_FILE` at the controller file's own `dispatch_token_file` (`controllerEnvironment`, `packages/daemon/cmd/legion/controller.go`), so it presents the token that file holds, which need not be the daemon's; under `dispatch_token_broker: true` in its place, the session is handed no bearer at all and trades this machine's identity at the broker for a DPoP-bound token of its own, and the start drops an inherited `DISPATCH_TOKEN` and `DISPATCH_TOKEN_FILE`, which it would otherwise present instead.
Under either setting the start also sets `PERSON_SIGNIN_TRADE=off` in the controller's environment (`controllerPersonTradeVar`).
The TypeScript client (`packages/cipher-client`, which pi-envoy, pi-legion, claude-envoy and the `dispatch` command use) then trades this machine's identity for the controller's own Dispatch credential under `dispatch_token_broker`, and for its Envoy credential where no bearer names one, even where the operator ran `agent-secrets login` on the machine, so no credential the controller trades at the broker acts in its operator's name.
A bearer the controller is given is presented as it is at main: the token `dispatch_token_file` names, and an Envoy bearer from the operator's environment (`ENVOY_TOKEN`, `ENVOY_TOKEN_FILE`) or from the `envoy.json` under the HOME the controller keeps (`envoy.token`), each of which resolves before the broker route.
That client alone reads the setting, and its name lies outside `AGENT_SECRETS_*` because `agent-secrets NAME -- <cmd>` strips that prefix's variables from its child but for a few (`sessionIdentityVars`, `packages/envoy/cmd/cipher/main.go`), so a `dispatch` command the controller runs under `agent-secrets NAME --` keeps it.
The setting does not change the controller's own `agent-secrets` secret reads: they are signed exactly as they would be without it.
What the broker can already issue is [The Dispatch identity the broker can issue](#the-dispatch-identity-the-broker-can-issue).
`dispatch://INFRA-267` is where Legion's pods and its daemon get tokens of their own, and Dispatch already accepts one, as that section says.

Every role is told `LEGION_GH_OWNERS_DIR=/var/run/legion/gh`, the bundle's root (its own, bound there in its namespaces), `GH_CONFIG_DIR` at the issue's repository's owner's directory under it (the table above), and `LEGION_GH_PATH=/usr/local/bin/gh`, the image's real gh.
The root holds one directory per owner account the role's App is installed on and one file of its own, `renames.txt`, the configured renames the project's pairs resolve to, which both wrappers route a moved repository by and read from there and from nowhere else (`ghconfig.PairsFile`; the role Secret's `github-renames` key, projected like the gh files).
The `gh` first on its PATH is `/opt/legion/bin/gh`, which runs `legion gh`:
it runs the real gh with `GH_CONFIG_DIR` at the one directory every repository the command targets is routed to, read as gh reads it from the real gh's own help (see docs/deployment.md, "What a pane's gh, git and jj are"): the owner's, or the directory of the owner a configured rename moved a repository to where a pair names it, each repository routed on its own; and at the issue owner's when the command names no repository at all;
a command it cannot read for certain, one whose repositories route to two directories (two owners' repositories, or a repository a pair moved beside another of the owner it moved from), one naming an owner the bundle holds no directory for, and one naming a repository a pair moved to an owner the bundle holds no directory for are refused with exit 2 and send nothing;
a read `legion gh` reads for certain that names only owners the bundle holds no directory for, names no repository a configured rename moves, and has no `github.com` remote of the working directory read for it runs with `GH_CONFIG_DIR`'s token instead (docs/deployment.md, "What a pane's gh, git and jj are", says which calls are such reads).
In a checkout whose one gh-resolved line is `remote.origin.gh-resolved base`, on an `origin` whose one fetch URL gh keeps as a `github.com` URL that is not ssh, a command of the groups gh resolves through that marker (`repo set-default` only with `--view` or `--unset`) counts origin's repository alone (docs/deployment.md, "What a pane's gh, git and jj are").
`git` reads the same files through `!legion git-credential` (`workspace.GitHubCredentialHelper`) with `credential.useHttpPath` on, so the helper answers from the `hosts.yml` of the owner of the repository in the path git asks about — of the owner that repository moved to where a pair names it — and from nothing else, but for a repository of an owner the bundle holds no directory for.
The helper reads such a repository from GitHub once (`GET /repos/<owner>/<name>` through `/usr/bin/curl`, within 10 s), with the token of the directory `GH_CONFIG_DIR` names where that is a directory of the bundle, and answers a fork with the token it would answer for the fork's `parent`, or else for its `source`, where the bundle holds that owner's directory, and every other repository of such an owner with nothing.
That is how a role pushes a commit to the branch of an outside contributor's pull request from a fork in a personal account: the helper answers the token of the repository the fork was made from, which is usually the base of its pull requests, and GitHub decides which branch of the fork that token may update.
The shared clone names it as its `credential.helper`: `workspace-init provision` is passed it as `--credential-helper '!legion git-credential'`.
Every role is also told it outside any clone, among nine git configuration entries git reads after every configuration file, the clone's own `.git/config` among them (`gitConfigPairs`, `manifest.go`):
`GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=9`, `credential.https://github.com.helper` reset to empty and then set to `!legion git-credential`, `credential.https://github.com.useHttpPath=true`, `core.fsmonitor` set to empty, `core.hooksPath=/dev/null`, and the four pack settings `core.packedGitWindowSize=32m`, `core.packedGitLimit=256m`, `pack.windowMemory=64m` and `core.deltaBaseCacheLimit=64m` (`packWindowConfig`, `internal/workspace/config.go`).
The pack settings bound the pack data one git maps, 32 MiB at a time and 256 MiB at most; the last two bound the `pack-objects` a push runs, which the first two do not.
git's defaults map 1 GiB windows up to 32 TiB, and gVisor counts every window a process has touched whole as the pod's memory: with the defaults, a `git log`, `git status`, push or fetch on one pack of 5.94 GB or 12.3 GB reached 5.2 GiB to 8.8 GB, and pods were killed at their 8 GiB limit.
The same four are in the worker image's `/etc/gitconfig`, for provisioning's git, which reads none of these entries; in the shared clone's own `.git/config`, written at every provisioning, for the shared public leak check's git, which reads no other configuration; and on the command line of the feed's fetch and of the repository cache's own git, whose repack keeps its own larger settings (`repackMemory`).
Every shared clone takes them in its `.git/config`, a host clone of the tmux runtime too, which the daemon provisions the same way, where they only bound git's pack windows.
A role's own `-c` still overrides one of them for its command, and the entries win over a deployment image's own `/etc/gitconfig`.
A role that runs when the release lands keeps its five pairs until its next generation: the entries travel in the role's start command, and a role the daemon adopts again is not relaunched for a change of them.
The issue's roles share the clone and each can write its `.git/config` and hooks, so `core.fsmonitor` and `core.hooksPath` keep a role's `git status` or `git commit` from running an fsmonitor program or a hook another role planted, with the credentials of the role that runs git.
Of the settings that run a program, the entries pin those two and no others, and they do not make the roles of one issue a boundary against each other.
Every role can write the whole issue volume, and the roles share the pod's network namespace, so code one role plants runs in a sibling, with the sibling's credentials, through any of these:

- the checkout, which the roles share by design: a test the tester runs, a script or build step the reviewer runs;

- the clone's other git settings that run a program or route a request:
  a filter driver (`filter.<name>.clean` with `.git/info/attributes`), `diff.external`, a `textconv`, `core.pager`, `gpg.program`, an `ext::` transport, and `http.proxy`, which sends the sibling's GitHub token through a proxy the planting role runs, with no program of its own run in the sibling at all;

- the clone's `.jj/repo/config.toml`, which a sibling's jj moves into its own config home and obeys (`ui.pager`, an alias);

- the workspace's `.omp/` directory, whose extensions a sibling's Oh My Pi loads when it starts;

- a role's installed plugins: an installing launch loads the plugin pair from `/legion/scratch/state/<role>/legion-plugins/g<generation>` on the issue volume, which every role of the issue can write;

- the caches every role shares on the issue volume, which `go run`, `uvx` and `bunx` run code from:
  `GOMODCACHE` and `GOCACHE` (`/legion/go`), uv's cache and Pythons (`/legion/uv`), bun's install cache, and `XDG_CACHE_HOME` and `XDG_DATA_HOME` (`/legion/scratch`);

- the one temporary directory every role's agent is told, `TMPDIR=/legion/scratch/tmp` (below):
  a script, an archive or a patch a role writes there to run or read a moment later is a file every sibling can replace first, and a tool that names a file in it by a fixed name reads whatever is there;

- the session transcripts: under `postgres` they are rows, and the database's URL is in the providers mount the container holds for the pod rather than for a role, so every role of the issue reaches them there.
  Under `cloudsql-iam` each generation's connection is private to its role (the socket is in that role's private directory), but every role signs in as the pod's one IAM login, whose rights reach every session row, so any role that opens a connection of its own reads and writes a sibling's transcript as well ([Session store](#session-store)).
  With `impersonate_service_account`, that login is the service account's.
  The pod's identity can impersonate that account, so every role can sign in as it, and can use every other role that the account holds ([Selecting the store](#selecting-the-store)).
  With `writer_audience`, the proxy impersonates the account with the session writer token, and no role reads that token: it is under `/var/run/legion/roles`, which role-init covers in each role's namespaces.
  The socket admits only the launcher and the generation's Oh My Pi process, so no other process of a role opens a connection of its own ([What `cloudsql-iam` puts in a pod](#what-cloudsql-iam-puts-in-a-pod)).
  Two routes stay open, and each reaches the database through Oh My Pi, the admitted process.
  The first is code inside Oh My Pi: code that a tool call writes into `.omp/tools` or into an installed plugin, which Oh My Pi loads at its next start (the `.omp/` directory and the installed plugins above).
  The second is Oh My Pi's RPC stdin: a child of Oh My Pi can open `/proc/<omp pid>/fd/0`, the pipe the shim writes Oh My Pi's RPC frames to (`spawnOnce`, `internal/shim/shim.go`), and write RPC commands there, which Oh My Pi then acts on.
  Also, `writer_audience` alone does not stop a tool call from getting the pod's own credentials from the metadata server, or from the pod-local metadata endpoint in a microVM pod.
  Those credentials impersonate the account until the deployment removes the account's grant to the pod's own principal ([Selecting the store](#selecting-the-store)).

The issue's roles trust one another's writes to the volume as they did when each ran in a container of its own.
The namespaces keep a role's tokens and private files out of a sibling's own reads, and no further.
One credential is the pod's and not a role's: the exchange token of `runtime.kubernetes.agent_secrets.exchange_audience` ([Operator configuration](#operator-configuration)), which every role of the pod reads at the same path, and every role's session is registered for that one pod.
Each role's session is registered bound to that role's own key: the thumbprint of the key the role's shim names at its hello, which the daemon sends with every write of the registration.
The broker refuses a trade for a session proved with any other key, so a sibling role that holds the pod's exchange token and its own key is refused another role's session.
Set `exchange_audience` only as [Operator configuration](#operator-configuration) says under that key: once your daemon, its worker image and its broker run a release that holds plan E's t-e-53, t-e-39 and t-e-41, as this release does, and once the broker's `BROKER_POD_REGISTRARS` lists the daemon as a registrar of its pods.
The worker image's Oh My Pi must also take `--session-id`, as the Oh My Pi that this release's `.omp-pin` names does.
The daemon already holds each session id to the claim of its project that first recorded it (t-e-54) and registers no session another of its claims holds.
That closes a direct mint only: the roles of one issue are no boundary against code a sibling plants in another role's process, which then runs with that role's key as it runs with that role's tokens ([Trust model](#trust-model-the-provisioning-token) lists what a plant reaches).
Through the helper, every git a role runs, the setup command's ([Configuration](#configuration)) and an agent's own clone of another repository included, answers `https://github.com/<owner>/…` from the role's own files when `<owner>` is an owner the role's gh files hold a directory for (in an issue pod, an owner both role Apps are installed on) and the role's App is installed on that repository;
git in the shared clone asks the same helper it asked before, and every other host is left to the configuration files.
The `legion` in the helper resolves on the PATH of whichever process runs git.
`GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN` and `GH_HOST` are set to the empty string, which gh ignores, so no value the image or an operator's rc file leaves in the environment outranks the files.
No container is told `LEGION_GIT_PATH` or `LEGION_JJ_PATH` (for the credential helper and the grant file, see the table above), and nothing is installed under the issue's volume for a pod to run:
a pod's `git` and `jj` are the image's, resolved on its PATH.
The daemon renders the gh keys when it writes the role Secret at the pod's start, logging `sandbox runtime: github credential
written` with the sandbox, role, App, `expiresAt` and directories, and a refresher walks every live role each minute, re-rendering its bundle for the pod's own repository, which its `workspace-fetch` argument names (for the controller, which works none, the owner its `github-default` records), from the daemon's cached leases and updating the Secret only for the directories whose `hosts.yml` changed (`sandbox runtime:
github credential refreshed`, the same fields); the kubelet rewrites the projection in place, so the next `gh` runs with the new token.
The `appauth` lease re-mints 20 minutes before its token expires, so a new token lands at least 15 minutes before the old one lapses, and GitHub keeps the old token valid until its own expiry.
`gh config set`, `gh alias set` and `gh auth login` cannot write the read-only directory, and `gh auth status` reports the account as `x-access-token`.
A `task` subagent inherits the container's environment, so its `gh` acts as the same App.

Every role is told where to put what it writes without being told where, and every one of those values names a path on the issue's volume.
Four of them are the issue's, one directory each that every role of it is told the same, under the issue's scratch `/legion/scratch` (`scratchRoot`, `manifest.go`):
`TMPDIR=/legion/scratch/tmp`, `XDG_CACHE_HOME=/legion/scratch/cache`, `XDG_DATA_HOME=/legion/scratch/data` and `BUN_INSTALL_CACHE_DIR=/legion/scratch/bun/install/cache` (`roleEnvironment`, `manifest.go`).
A directory per role is what those four replace, by the human's decision of 2026-10-20 (specification version 20):
the issue's roles already share the pod, the pod's disk whole, the one workspace they all work in, uv's Pythons and cache and the two Go caches, and each can read and write what the others write, so a cache per role bought an isolation the pod does not have and cost a copy of every cache per role.
`XDG_STATE_HOME=/legion/scratch/state/<role>` is the one directory of the scratch named for a role (the state home above), and a sibling can write it too.
The two Go caches are the issue's as they already were, one pair every role of the issue is told:
`GOCACHE=/legion/go/build` and `GOMODCACHE=/legion/go/mod` (`goBuildCache` and `goModCache`, `manifest.go`), beside the workspaces rather than under the scratch, on the same volume beside uv's cache.
Both are empty on a new disk, which every fresh pod gets unless its volume is kept ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)), and the module cache fills from the image rather than from `proxy.golang.org`:
`/opt/go/go.env` names the image's own copy of this repository's modules first in `GOPROXY` ([Worker image](#worker-image)).
Both hold content addressed by its hash, and the roles of one issue may fill them at once:
of the build cache `go help cache` says "The cache is safe for concurrent invocations of the go command", and what reaches the module cache is a module zip or `go.mod` the go command has verified against a known hash (`go help module-auth`) into a directory it then makes read-only, which only `go build -modcacherw` leaves writable.
A pair is 751 MiB of build cache and 375 MiB of module cache for this repository, so six roles with a pair each would hold five redundant copies, about 5.5 GiB of a 50 GiB volume spent on nothing.
It was proven live in an issue pod: two `go build ./...` at once against one empty shared pair both exited 0 in 227 s, filling 751 MiB of build cache and 375 MiB of module cache
— two concurrent builds of one module leave one build's worth of content in the shared pair, which is why sharing is both safe and cheap
— and the cache that race left rebuilt and tested clean.
What those figures measure is one build:
a cold `cd packages/daemon && go build ./...` into an empty pair
— `packages/daemon` alone, one of the two modules `go.work` names, with nothing of `packages/envoy` built and no test run.
A second, separate run of it measured 752 MiB and 375 MiB in 114 s, exit 0.
A role that runs tests leaves more: after `go test -count=1 ./...` over that same one module the pair holds 1.3 GiB of build cache and 931 MiB of module cache, measured in this issue's own container, and that after-tests pair is the one the sizing above does its arithmetic with, because roles run tests.
Bun's install cache is one of the four the issue's roles share, and sharing it is what bun's own behaviour asks for:
bun hardlinks out of its install cache into whatever it installs for, and the issue's roles share one checkout (`workspace.Location`, `packages/daemon/internal/workspace/provision.go`, names the repository and the issue, never a role), so a file edited in place inside `node_modules` is already in the packages every role runs from, whatever we do about caches;
what a cache per role confined was afterwards
— only that role's later installs would put the changed copy back (LEGION-198, where bun's hardlinking was first met).
The state home is the one that stays the role's, and for a mechanism rather than caution:
Oh My Pi names its browser broker's lock from the state root, the name is an abstract unix socket, and an abstract socket name is one name across every process that shares a network namespace, which every role of a pod does, so one state home would block every role's browser broker but the first (above).

Sharing the cache home gives the issue's roles one Playwright browser registry, since playwright-core resolves it to `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/ms-playwright`, and `Registry.install()` takes an exclusive lock on that directory with about ten minutes of back-off, so a second role installing at the same time waits rather than races.
Two things follow and are worth knowing before meeting them:
an install still waiting when the back-off is spent fails with a lock error, and `playwright install --force`, which removes a current installation before writing the new one, can remove a browser tree another role of the issue is running from.

Sharing `BUN_INSTALL_CACHE_DIR` gives them one bun install cache, which no lock of bun's own guards:
filling a cold entry of it from several roles at once races.
Six concurrent `bun add --backend=copyfile --exact chalk@5.3.0 lodash@4.17.21` into six separate directories against one empty cache left one exit 0 and five exit 1 with `ENOENT: failed copying files from cache to destination`, measured twice in this issue's own container on bun 1.3.14, where the same six against the cache they had just filled all exited 0
— the race is the cold fill of an entry, not the install out of it, and `--backend=copyfile` governs only how files leave the cache.
The install Legion renders for an installing launch takes `/usr/bin/flock` on the cache directory, after a `mkdir -p` of it so the lock's inode exists before anything fills the cache, and retries the install once (`installBlock`, `packages/daemon/internal/runtime/sandbox/plugins.go`), so a plugin-version bump, which makes the pair cold for every role of a kept pod at once, does not fail their launches.
That wait is bounded (`installLockWait`), since `flock` otherwise waits forever and one stalled install would be charged to every role of the pod:
the bound is a third of the registration deadline that configuration gives
— `worker_boot_timeout_seconds` times `worker_boot_registration_deadline_intervals`, so 120 seconds at the defaults
— floored at one second, since a wait that rounded down to zero would render `-w 0`, which is `-n`: no wait at all, and the cold-fill race back.
A proportion rather than a fixed number because it has to hold at whatever the operator sets:
the script runs the install twice, so two waits take two thirds of the deadline and the remaining third is left for the install and the agent's start, where a constant sized for the defaults would be two waits of 240 seconds against the 180 second deadline of a halved boot timeout and could never fire before the deadline retired the role.
That remainder holds at every configuration but the smallest, where the floor takes over:
under a three-second deadline two floored waits of a second consume it, deliberately, since being serialised and then retired is no worse than racing
— an unserialised cold fill fails the launch anyway.
Above that floor the bound is also long enough for the last of six roles to queue behind five serialised installs of the pair, 24 seconds each at the defaults
— the half of the bound a smaller divisor would break, which `TestTheInstallLockWaitIsABoundInProportionToTheRegistrationDeadline` holds against the installs rather than against the derivation.
A wait that times out exits 1, so it takes the retry and then the script's named failure
— that one bump's launch fails the way it did before the lock existed, rather than hanging.
`flock` is advisory and per-inode, which holds exactly where this needs it
— every role of one pod shares a kernel and that inode on the issue's volume — and nowhere wider, so two pods would not be covered.
Two agents of one issue running `bun install` at once against a cold shared cache can fail the same way, nothing Legion renders wraps those, and the failure is a failed install with a clear error rather than a corrupted one
— bun stops, it does not half-write the workspace — so a second run succeeds against the cache the first filled.
That is why an agent's own install is a documented consequence and the install Legion renders was a blocker: nothing is there to retry that one.

`XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is the one XDG home not on the volume:
every role is told `/home/legion/.config`, where its namespace binds its own config home, the copy on `role-homes` of the pod's shared in-memory one that holds the jj configuration `workspace-init` writes (above), and `workspace-init` keeps every value it had.
The other paths are all under the issue volume's own whole-volume mount at `/legion`:
the scratch adds no volume and no mount, and no directory of it is a `sub_path` mount of its own.
The roles of an issue share one scratch, the state homes under its `state` directory the only part of it named for a role, and the role's shim makes six directories
— the four the issue's roles share, plus the shared Go pair
— before Oh My Pi starts (`podsafety.EnsureScratch`), since a role told a temporary directory nothing created cannot run;
`podsafety.EnsureStateHome` makes Oh My Pi's profile directory under the state home.
What puts them off the container's own filesystem is the ephemeral-storage bound:
on GKE Autopilot an issue pod is admitted with at most 10Gi for all six roles together (Warden caps a pod's main containers' summed ephemeral-storage requests at 10Gi and clamps each container's limit to its request;
[Issue sizing](#issue-sizing-one-reservation-per-pod)), while ordinary work measurably needs more:
this repository's Go build cache 751 MiB and its Go module cache 375 MiB (the measurement above), a Playwright Chromium about 400 MB, a Postgres with a data directory about 300 MB, and a cold bun install cache 1.4 GB.
A pod past its ephemeral-storage limit is evicted whole by the kubelet, and all six roles of an issue run in its one container, so one role's overrun takes every role of that issue down with it
— which is what those caches did on GKE Autopilot.
The disk is the pod's alone and dies with it, so what a pod downloads and builds serves that pod's roles and no later one, except on a kept volume, where it serves each later pod of the issue ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)).
The role's `$HOME` stays off the disk: it is an overlay of the image's own content (`~/.omp`, its profile's plugins, natives and agent directory), which every pod must keep reading, with the role's writes on the pod's `role-homes` disk `emptyDir`, so a recipe that writes somewhere else under the home directory is still bounded by the pod's ephemeral-storage limit.

Every role is told `UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR=/legion/uv/python/<issue>` (the issue key as a DNS label), `UV_CACHE_DIR=/legion/uv/cache` and `UV_LINK_MODE=copy`.
uv keeps the Pythons it installs and its cache on the pod's own disk beside the workspace, so a project's `.venv`, which links to its interpreter there, runs as it is for every role of the pod that made it;
a later pod of the issue installs its own, unless the volume is kept.
The disk is that pod's alone, so no other issue's pod ever installs into either directory, at the cost of one download per issue.
uv copies each package from the cache into a `.venv`:
with the cache and the `.venv` on one filesystem it would otherwise hardlink them, and an edit made in place inside the `.venv` would change the cache and every later install from it.
So each `.venv` is a full copy of its packages on the pod's disk, beside the cache, and a deployment sizes `issue_volume` for the clone, the workspace, the issue's Python and one copy of its packages, and for the workspace's CodeGraph index (`.codegraph/`, 185 MB for this repository).
`uv cache clean` and `uv cache prune` remove cache entries under a lock that stops at the pod;
the disk is the pod's own, or a kept volume that one pod mounts at a time, and no other pod uses uv on it, so either may run whenever the issue's roles are idle.

Each role's shim is started with `--warm-codegraph`:
once its Oh My Pi has written its first frame
— its extensions loaded, its RPC loop serving
— the shim builds the workspace's CodeGraph index in the background (`codegraph init`, or `codegraph index` to repair one an earlier build left partial, as `codegraph status --json` decides).
Nothing waits on it: not the launch, not the role's registration, not a prompt.
Six role shims share one workspace, so the warm-up holds a lease at `.codegraph/legion-warm.lock` for its run
— an exclusive create whose holder refreshes its mtime every 10 s, taken over once it is 60 s stale, the takeover itself under a second exclusive create beside it so two shims that both read one stale lease never both build
— and a shim that finds the lease held leaves the build to its holder.
When a build finishes, the shim's warm-up logs one line in the `roles` container's log, prefixed `<role>: `, `codegraph warm-up for <workspace> built the index: codegraph init took
<duration>, done <duration> after launch` — the build's own duration and the time since the role's launch (`codegraph index` in place of `init` for a repair)
— which stage 4b's `repository-tools` checkpoint reads (`kubectl logs <pod> --all-containers`).
A stop mid-build — the launcher's one SIGTERM to the role's process group
— ends Oh My Pi and the `codegraph` child together, and the shim exits only once the warm-up has released its lease:
it waits for that release at least 3 s and at most what the pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (`worker_stop_timeout_seconds`, which the launcher passes the shim as `--stop-grace`) leaves once the agent's 5 s grace and the 1 s stdout drain are spent (4 s with the default 10 s).
The whole stop fits inside the grace from 9 s up, so the daemon refuses a smaller `worker_stop_timeout_seconds` under `runtime: kubernetes` at configuration load (`legion config check` says so, quoting the key and the floor), and the relaunch is never told a live build holds the workspace;
it runs the warm-up again, and `status` on the index that stop left on the pod's disk answers complete, so nothing runs, or reports it partial, which `codegraph index` repairs.
A relaunch in a new pod finds no index and builds one, as the issue's first pod did, except on [a kept volume](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod), where it finds the index that the earlier pod left.
The tester's `affected` and the reviewer's `impact`/`callers` queries answer once `codegraph status --json` reports `index.state: "complete"`;
before that a role falls back to grep, as its prompt says.
The init containers never call `codegraph`.

Every pod runs:

- with `runtimeClassName: gvisor`, except an issue pod whose sandbox is a microVM and the project controller's pod where `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.type` is `microvm`, each of which runs with `runtimeClassName: microvm` ([Pods in microVMs](#pods-in-microvms));

- with `serviceAccountName` set to the operator's `pod.service_account` (the namespace's default when it names none) and `automountServiceAccountToken: false`;

- under Pod Security "restricted": non-root user 1000 on the pod, and on each container no privilege escalation, ALL capabilities dropped and the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile;

- on the Legion pool, with its node selector and toleration (and, for a microVM pod, an issue pod or the controller's, the `cloud.google.com/compute-class` selector and toleration of its ComputeClass), and nothing else of its placement that Legion itself sets:
  no affinity (GKE Autopilot adds its own to an annotated pod, below);

- `Guaranteed` at the default reservations:
  every container's cpu and memory request equal to its limit (the two quantities the kubelet's QoS class reads);
  `Burstable` when its `resources` key (`issue` or `controller`) sets a lower `cpu_request` or `memory_request`;
  and its ephemeral storage a request under a larger limit ([Issue sizing](#issue-sizing-one-reservation-per-pod), "The node-disk bound");

- annotated against autoscaler eviction:

  - `karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt: "true"`, Karpenter's own, which GKE's cluster-autoscaler ignores;

  - the issue pod and the project controller's additionally carry `cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "false"`, the upstream Cluster Autoscaler's own annotation, which GKE Autopilot honours as a request for up to seven days of extended-duration protection from its own scale-down and node-upgrade eviction
    — not indefinitely, and not from node pressure or an OOM, a higher-priority Pod, Compute Engine maintenance or node repair, or an operator-initiated drain;

  - on GKE Autopilot this second annotation also adds a required node affinity (`cloud.google.com/extended-duration-pods`) and gives the pod a node of its own whenever possible, which usually costs each pod it creates (an issue's first launch, or a relaunch that replaces the pod) a fresh node and a cold image pull ([Image size and pull time](#image-size-and-pull-time));

  - a pod carrying it is refused outright under the `cloud.google.com/gke-spot` node selector or toleration (GKE offers no extended duration to a Spot Pod requested any other way, such as the `autopilot-spot` compute class);
    the boot probe (below) carries only Karpenter's, so it does not catch a `gke-spot` scheduling config before every issue and controller launch is refused;

  - the image probe pod (below) carries only the first:
    a dedicated node per boot would cost more than the eviction window buys a probe that is already short-lived and retried on failure.

The project controller's Sandbox under `controller: daemon`, `legion-<project>-controller`, is the same pod with a one-role list:
it carries `legion.dev/project` and `legion.dev/role=controller` and no tree or issue label, runs no init container and one launcher container, `controller`, carrying the controller's reservation, and owns a volume of its own the same way, `issue-legion-<project>-controller` ([Daemon-launched controller](#daemon-launched-controller)).
Where `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.type` is `microvm` it runs in a microVM, placed and labelled as a microVM issue pod is ([Pods in microVMs](#pods-in-microvms)).
Its launcher's command then adds `--microvm`, and, where the deployment sets `runtime.kubernetes.sandbox.microvm.metadata`, `--metadata-workload-pool <pool> --metadata-identity-provider <provider>` after it, all before `--stop-grace`, and its container mounts the projected token volume `workload-identity-token`, read-only, at `/var/run/legion/workload-identity` ([The pod-local metadata endpoint](#the-pod-local-metadata-endpoint)).

The image probe runs as a Sandbox of its own, `legion-probe-<project>-<digest12>`, with `shutdownPolicy: Delete`, its one container carrying the probe's own fixed reservation
— 500m and 1Gi, over a 5Gi disk bound and a 1Gi disk request (`probeReservation`, `internal/daemon/kubernetes.go`), none of an issue pod's, since `legion probe-image` starts one Oh My Pi at a time and runs no lane, and a probe sized as an issue pod could keep the daemon from booting on a full pool ([The image is probed before it publishes](#the-image-is-probed-before-it-publishes), [Issue sizing](#issue-sizing-one-reservation-per-pod)).

### The repository cache

Each repository a live record of the project names has a cache of its own, and so does a repository a launch works:
one Sandbox, `legion-<project>-cache-<owner>-<repo>-<8 hex>` (`CacheSandboxName`, `names.go`;
the hex is of the repository's name, so two repositories whose names slug alike get two caches), labelled `legion.dev/project` and `legion.dev/cache=true` and annotated `legion.dev/cache-repo: <owner>/<repo>`, which is the one place its repository is read from (`kubectl -n legion get sandbox -l legion.dev/cache`).
It is no issue's and no claim's: no tree's cleanup lists it, and nothing of it registers on the worker stream (`internal/runtime/sandbox/repocache.go`).
Its pod runs one container, `cache`, the image's `legion workspace-init cache --repo <owner>/<repo> --root /legion/cache --listen :8418 --refresh
10m0s` (`refresh_minutes`, as a duration), on the Legion pool under gVisor with the operator's ServiceAccount, and nothing of an agent's:
no model route, provider key or Dispatch variable.
It owns one volume, `cache-<sandbox>`, of `runtime.kubernetes.repository_cache.volume` (20Gi by default), holding a bare clone of the repository at `/legion/cache/<owner>/<repo>.git`, and a headless Service of its own name, whose DNS name resolves to the pod only while it is Ready.
Its Secret, `<sandbox>-token`, holds the implement App's reading lease on the repository's owner, the same lease an issue pod's `workspace-fetch` clones with ("Trust model: the provisioning token"), read again as every transfer from GitHub starts and brought to the current lease on the gh refresher's minute, and the cache's own bearer token, 32 random bytes made with the Secret and kept while it stands;
the issue pods of that repository are given the same bearer token in their provisioning Secret, and no other pod has it.

The process clones the repository once, through the same one-shot credential as an issue pod's fetch but, the first time, within `workspace.CacheFetchTimeout` (2 hours) rather than an issue pod's 30 minutes
— its first clone is the repository's one full download, and on 2026-10-26 one deployment's cache with one CPU under gVisor was killed at 30 minutes 289 times running, never ready
— then fetches every branch from GitHub every `refresh_minutes` (10 by default), pruning the branches GitHub deleted and keeping what each fetch brings as a pack.
Once a day, after a fetch, it repacks the clone (`git repack -a -d`, within 2 hours, `repackTimeout`, and with git's memory bounded, `repackMemory`:
a full repack of a 3.2 GB clone peaked at 4.35 GiB unbounded, past the cache's 4Gi limit, and at 1.78 GiB bounded), holding no lock a tar takes:
a tar is served throughout and is taken again if the repack swaps the packs under it, and only the next fetch waits.
A repack that fails is logged and tried again a day later, and the partial files it left in `objects/pack` (every `tmp_*` — a pack, its index, reverse index, bitmap, mtimes
— and `.tmp-*`) are removed at once, each logged, as they are after a fetch that fails;
a process starting on a volume where a killed one left any removes them before its first fetch.
A repack that fails for lack of space ("Room on the cache's volume", below) is recorded, and `/healthz` carries the time of that failure as `repackOutOfSpaceAt`.
The cache also keeps that time in `.legion-repack-out-of-space` on its volume, so a pod that replaces it reports the failure too.
The next repack that succeeds clears the failure and removes the file.
A fetch into the clone keeps an issue pod's 30-minute bound, since every tar waits for it;
git's transfer sets no stall limit, so a stalled fetch holds every tar for up to those 30 minutes.
Restarted after a fetch was killed, it also removes the git lock files that fetch left before it fetches again.
As its container's PID 1 it reaps, after each refresh, the processes git's helpers leave it when a git dies (`git remote-https`, `git index-pack`).
It serves, on port 8418:

- `GET /readyz`: 503 until the first clone is whole, then 200, with nothing else; the pod's readiness probe, which carries no token.

- `GET /healthz`: `503 {"ready":false,…}` until the first clone is whole, then `200 {"ready":true,
  "repo":"<owner>/<repo>","head":"<default branch's commit>","lastFetchAt":"…","bytes":<n>,
  "streams":<s>,"volumeBytes":<v>,"availableBytes":<a>,"fetchOutOfSpaceAt":"…","repackOutOfSpaceAt":"…"}`, `streams` being the `/tar` requests it is sending or holding in its queue at the answer;
  it waits on no fetch, and answers any request, since it holds nothing secret and nothing of the repository's content.
  `volumeBytes` is the volume's size and `availableBytes` the bytes available to the cache, from a `statfs` of `/legion/cache` at each answer.
  Where that `statfs` fails, `volumeError` carries its error, and the two figures are absent.
  `fetchOutOfSpaceAt` and `repackOutOfSpaceAt` are each the time of that step's last failure for lack of space since the step last succeeded, and each is absent while there is none.
  The 503 answer carries these room fields too, since the volume is there before the first clone.

- `GET /tar`: the clone's refs and packs as a tar stream
  — `HEAD`, `packed-refs`, `refs/`, `objects/pack/pack-<id>.pack` and the `objects/pack/pack-<id>.idx` git reads each pack through, no loose object or configuration
  — which waits for a fetch under way to finish, so it never streams a half-written ref or pack, and waits for no repack.
  At most 32 streams are sent at once (`maxStreams`, `internal/repocache/server.go`);
  a request past them waits, first come first served, for one to end, within its own deadline.
  Streams share the cache pod's sending rate evenly, so without the bound a large launch slows every stream at once until none finishes:
  on 2026-10-26 one cache sent a 4.0 GB clone (51 packs) at about 400 MB/s in all over 290 streams, about 48 minutes before any reached its last byte, past the fetch's 30-minute `FetchTimeout`, and every fetch failed and started over.
  Bounded, each stream takes its share among 32 and the queue drains at the same total rate.

`/tar` answers only a request whose `Authorization: Bearer` is the cache's own token; any other is 401 and names nothing.
`/healthz` and `/tar` name their repository in a `Legion-Repository` header on every answer.
Each fetch also points the clone's `HEAD` at the branch GitHub names as the default now, once the fetch has brought that branch, so a default branch renamed on GitHub is the one the cache publishes and its tar's `HEAD` names from the next tick.
A fetch that fails is logged and tried at the next tick, and the cache stays ready on what it last fetched;
a restarted cache whose volume holds its clone fetches into it, and serves it as it is when GitHub cannot be reached;
a first clone that fails ends the process, and the kubelet restarts it.
A fetch into the clone that fails for lack of space is recorded too, and `/healthz` carries the time of that failure as `fetchOutOfSpaceAt` until the next fetch succeeds.
The cache keeps a fetch's failure in memory alone, since the next fetch reports it again.
A first clone that fails is not recorded: that cache never turns Ready, and `legion state` shows it `failing` under `repositories`.

An issue pod's `workspace-fetch` fills a fresh feed from its repository's cache alone ([Anatomy of a Sandbox pod](#anatomy-of-a-sandbox-pod)).
It asks the cache's health with no credential, takes nothing from a cache whose answer names another repository, so a cache pod replaced and its address reused by another repository's cache can put nothing into the feed, and presents the cache's token with its request for the tar alone.
It holds every pack and index it received to the checksums git wrote into them
— each file's own trailing hash over its bytes, and the pack hash the index records, which must be that pack's
— and checks every object the refs reach is there (`git fsck --connectivity-only`) before the feed is used, and a damaged or incomplete history fails the fetch.
A pack that arrived without its index is indexed here instead (`git index-pack`).
Re-indexing every pack the cache wrote is what the feed no longer does: it inflates and rehashes every object, 8 to 12 minutes per issue pod on a 3.2 GB cache.
The feed takes the index's names on the cache's word instead, which trusts every writer of the cache's indexes:
`git index-pack`, which named every object by its content when `git fetch` received the pack from GitHub;
the daily `git repack -a -d`, whose `pack-objects` writes new indexes from names it already holds without hashing the objects again;
the cache pod's volume; and whoever answers at the cache's address, since the bearer token proves the pod to the cache and nothing proves the cache to the pod.
An index whose checksums hold but which maps an object's name to another object passes the fetch's checks, and a checkout of a blob it misnames writes the other blob's content without an error, which jj in the issue's workspace does not record as a change in a repository of realistic size.
The daemon checks that the cache's Service is the cache's own once, before it tells a pod the address (below).

From GitHub the fetch then takes, by exact name, the default branch GitHub names now and the default branch the daemon recorded for the issue while GitHub has it (`LEGION_DEFAULT_BRANCH` on the fetch container), and `refs/heads/legion/*`, pruned within those.
Before that delta it reads every branch GitHub has with its tip (one `git ls-remote --symref <url> HEAD refs/heads/*`) and deletes every other branch of the feed that is not exactly GitHub's tip, on a fresh feed and on one a retry of the init container finds on the pod's disk alike, logging each with its reason (`removed <branch> from the feed: GitHub no longer has
it`, or `…: GitHub has moved it, and this fetch brings only the default branch and the issue
branches`).
So after a fetch every branch of the feed is GitHub's as it stood then, or absent:
the issue's clone is made from the recorded default branch and the issue's own branch, both current, an issue branch GitHub deleted is gone, and an agent that wants another branch as GitHub has it now fetches it from GitHub through its clone's `origin`.
A fresh feed streamed from a cache that is behind loses, at that point, every branch outside the delta that moved since the cache's last refresh;
nothing provisioning reads is among them.
A large branch pushed between the cache's refresh and a wave of launches is never pulled into every issue pod at once.
A recorded default GitHub no longer has leaves the feed too, and provisioning refuses an issue with no branch whose recorded default is gone rather than starting it from an old tip.

A cache that is not ready is waited for, and one that never becomes ready fails the fetch, naming its last answer;
the issue pod's failure then names the cache's state (`the repository cache of <owner>/<repo>, which a fresh feed
comes from alone, is failing: container cache CrashLoopBackOff: …`).

The issue pods reach the cache on port 8418 at its Service's name, `<cache>.<namespace>.svc`, the headless Service the Agent Sandbox controller makes for the cache's Sandbox.
Since the fetch presents the cache's token to whatever that name reaches, the daemon hands an issue pod the cache's address and token only once the Service of that name is the cache's own:
controlled by the cache's Sandbox, by uid, selecting exactly the pods the controller stamps with the hash of the Sandbox's name (`agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-name-hash`), and headless (`clusterIP: None`) with no `externalName`, the shape the controller makes.
Anyone who may create a Service in the namespace could make one of the cache's name first, or write a controller reference into one itself, which the API server accepts.
The controller refuses to adopt one without its tracking label, or one with a cluster IP, and leaves it standing;
one with the label and no cluster IP, an `ExternalName` Service among them, it adopts, writing its own controller reference and the exact selector but keeping the planted `type` and `externalName`, so it would send the token to its maker's host.
Either way the launch waits, logging `the repository cache's Service is not the cache's` with the Service and why, and fails at the boot timeout naming them, with no pod made and no token written, and `legion state` shows the cache `refused` with the same reason.
The controller never resets a Service's type: delete such a Service, and the controller makes the cache's own.
While the daemon's Services list or watch is failing, its store may hold a Service that has since changed, so it trusts none:
launches wait the same way, and the cache shows `refused` with `its Service …
cannot be checked: the Service store may be stale: …`.
The daemon reads each Ready cache's `/healthz` every minute at its pod's address, as the store holds it, with no credential, so a daemon outside the cluster that reaches pod addresses but resolves no cluster name reads it too;
an answer from a pod that took the address once the cache's pod was gone names another repository, and is that read's failure.
A NetworkPolicy that isolates the namespace's pods must admit both, or every fresh feed waits on a cache it cannot reach and `legion state` shows the read's failure.

`legion state --json | jq .repositories` shows them:
each `live[]` repository carries `cache` (`repo`, `sandbox`, `state` — `starting`, `cloning`, `ready`, `failing` with the kubelet's `reason`, or `refused` with the Service's
— `ready`, `address`, the cache's Service, while Ready behind its own Service, and from the last health read of the pod it runs now `head`, `lastFetchAt` and `bytes`, or `healthError`) once the cache exists, and `caches` lists the caches of repositories no live record names any more, each with `retainedUntil`.

An issue pod's launch makes its repository's cache when there is none yet, and the daemon makes the cache of each repository a live record names at boot and on every orphan sweep after it, once a minute:
a missing cache is created (its Sandbox `Suspended`, then its Secret owned by that Sandbox, then its pod template and `Running`), and a cache whose pod runs another image than the daemon's, runs as a ServiceAccount other than `runtime.kubernetes.pod.service_account`, has ended, or was left `Suspended`, or whose Sandbox's pod template reserves other than `runtime.kubernetes.repository_cache.resources` now says, gets a new pod while its Sandbox and volume stay, so a new release, a new account or a new reservation costs a pod, not a clone.
The reservation is read from the Sandbox's pod template, never from the pod, since GKE Autopilot rewrites a pod's requirements at admission; the account is read from the pod, where the API server keeps a named account as written and writes `default` for a pod that names none.
A pod still running is replaced only once it serves no stream:
the daemon asks its `/healthz` first, whose `streams` counts the tars it is sending or holding in its queue, and while that is above 0 it logs `repository cache pod is replaced once it serves no
stream` and leaves the pod to a later sweep, because the replacement would end every one of those tars, failing each fetch reading one and making its issue pod again.
A cache of an earlier release answers no `streams`, and one whose `/healthz` cannot be read is replaced at once, as before.
A launch whose cache cannot be made fails, naming why.
The cache of a repository no live record names, and no launch worked since the last read of the live records, is annotated `legion.dev/cache-unused-at` at the sweep that finds it so, kept for `runtime.kubernetes.repository_cache.retain_hours` (168 by default), and then deleted with its volume and Secret;
named by a live record again before that, it loses the annotation and stays.
A cache that an earlier release marked under the annotation's old name keeps the time of its first mark, the earlier of its marks that is a time:
at the first sweep after the upgrade, one whose first mark is less than one retention old has that time written under `legion.dev/cache-unused-at` and the old annotation removed, so it retires one retention after its first mark, and one whose first mark is one retention old or more is deleted at that sweep;
one none of whose marks is a time is annotated with that sweep's time and loses the old annotation, so it is kept one retention, and the sweep logs a warning naming the cache and each value (`repository cache carries no mark that is a time`).
A cache that a live record names loses the old annotation at that sweep.
Each cache that loses the old annotation is logged once, at info, with its repository, the old value and what the sweep did.
A cache the sweep cannot make or repair — its owner's token cannot be minted, say — is a warning naming it, tried again at the next sweep.
The boot census refuses a Sandbox labelled `legion.dev/cache` that is not one this runtime builds (no repository annotation, or another container or claim template), by name.

**Room on the cache's volume.**
A fetch or a repack fails for lack of space when git's error holds `No space left on device` or `Out of diskspace`, matched case-sensitively.
It also fails for lack of space when the volume has less than 1 GiB available as the step fails, because git reports a ref it could not write for lack of space with neither phrase (`cannot lock ref '<ref>': unable to create directory for <path>`).
The cache reads the volume for that test before it removes the partial files, because the removal frees space.
Where that read fails, git's words alone decide.
A repack needs free space of about its clone's reachable objects: `git repack -a -d` writes them all into one new pack before it deletes the packs that pack replaces.
On 2026-11-19 one deployment's cache logged `Out of diskspace` for its repack, and then `No space left on device` for every fetch.

The cache keeps a repack's failure in `.legion-repack-out-of-space` at the volume's root (`/legion/cache`), beside `.legion-last-repack`, as one RFC 3339 UTC time and a line feed.
The file is outside the clone, so `/tar` never streams it.
The cache writes the file after it removes the failed repack's partial files, so the write has room.
It logs a write that fails, and keeps the failure in memory all the same.
A new cache process reads the file before it serves, so its first `/healthz` answer, the 503 one included, carries the failure.
It logs and ignores a file it cannot read or whose text is not an RFC 3339 time.
A recorded failure does not change when the cache fetches or repacks.

Kubernetes reports the bytes available on each claim through the kubelet's `kubelet_volume_stats_available_bytes` metric ([Kubernetes metrics reference](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/metrics/)).
The kube-prometheus alert on that metric is `KubePersistentVolumeFillingUp` ([its runbook](https://runbooks.prometheus-operator.dev/runbooks/kubernetes/kubepersistentvolumefillingup/)).
These standard signals see the cache's claim as they see any other claim.
Legion's own signal is the `repository-cache-room` row of [The deployment's capability report](#the-deployments-capability-report).
While the row is open, the controller's `tick` notice names it in `openCapabilities`, and the project's controller names it in the day's report.
`legion state` shows the room in that row alone: a cache under `repositories` carries no room field.

The remedy is to grow the cache's claim in place ([Expanding Persistent Volumes Claims](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes/#expanding-persistent-volumes-claims)).
The claim is `cache-<sandbox>`, which the row's detail names, and its StorageClass must set `allowVolumeExpansion: true`.
Raise the claim's `spec.resources.requests.storage`, for example `kubectl -n legion patch pvc cache-<sandbox> -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"40Gi"}}}}'`.
Then raise `runtime.kubernetes.repository_cache.volume` in `legion.yaml`.
That key sizes only the caches the daemon makes later: a cache that exists keeps its claim.
The daemon does not grow a claim itself, since it has no PVC verb ([RBAC the Go daemon needs](#rbac-the-go-daemon-needs)).

After the claim grows, the next fetch that succeeds clears the fetch's failure, and a fetch runs every `refresh_minutes`.
A kept repack failure stays for up to 24 hours after the claim grows, until the next repack runs and succeeds.
Until then the row stays open, unless `capabilities.decided.repository-cache-room` names a reason.

### A pod whose address moved

A role process's addresses are fixed when it is launched, and nothing changes a running process's argv or environment.
The daemon hands every role process, the daemon-launched controller's included, six from its configuration.
The worker stream listener, `tcp://<advertise_host, or bind with none set>:<worker_stream_port>`, is in every launcher container's command (item 3 of the anatomy list above), so it is fixed for the pod's life:
a launcher dials it and never redials elsewhere.
The other five reach a generation's Oh My Pi in the start command its launcher receives, never in the pod spec, so they are fixed for that generation's life:
`LEGION_DAEMON_URL` (`daemon_url`), `ENVOY_NATS_URL` (`nats_urls`), `ENVOY_URL` (`envoy_url`), `DISPATCH_URL` (`dispatch_url`) and, when the runtime enrolls pods, `AGENT_SECRETS_URL` (`runtime.kubernetes.agent_secrets.url`);
the daemon-launched controller's generation also carries `LEGION_SLACK_CHANNELS` (the project's `slack_channels`), recorded and compared like these.
Each moves when the daemon restarts with its key changed, and with no `advertise_host` set the stream also moves when the daemon restarts on another host.
A daemon that restarts re-adopts each live claim by its recorded locator (the boot orphan sweep), and re-adoption alone would leave the role holding the old addresses:
a launcher dialling a stale stream never reaches the new daemon, and a stale `LEGION_DAEMON_URL` fails every call the agent makes to the daemon's API (its phase completion, its record read) while its stream still works.

So the runtime compares a role's addresses with what it hands now on every evaluation of the role (each watch event, the probe-interval sweep, each probe):

- **The stream** is read from the `roles` container's launcher command in the pod spec, before the launcher's own state, since a launcher on a stale stream would only ever read as disconnected.

- **The secrets broker's enrollment**, for a role that enrolls, is read from the pod spec at the same point:
  the `agent-secrets-token` volume's projection of the broker's token (its audience, expiry and path) and the role's own key directory, which a generation of the role started now runs against.
  Like the stream, both are fixed for the pod's life, so turning `runtime.kubernetes.agent_secrets` on, or changing its `audience` or `token_expiry_seconds`, leaves every running workflow role holding a pod that lacks them.
  Where the block names an `exchange_audience`, the `agent-secrets-exchange` volume's projection of the exchange token (its audience, expiry and path) is read the same way, and a pod that lacks it, or projects another audience, has drifted for its update round as an enrollment that lacks its token has.

- **The other five** are read from a record on the issue Sandbox (`addresses.go`).
  Before it sends a generation's start command, the daemon merge-patches the role's own annotation, `legion.dev/addresses-<role>`, with the generation and, for each of the five, its variable, its name and the sha256 of its whole value.
  The patch carries the Sandbox's uid, so a Sandbox deleted and recreated meanwhile is never written, and it leaves every other role's annotation as it was.
  A later daemon reads the record from its informer cache, with no API read of its own, and compares the digests once the role's launcher reports it runs that generation.
  A role with no record, or a record of another generation, is never stale, so a generation started before records existed is not relaunched for want of one;
  a record that cannot be read is reported stale, and the relaunch writes a fresh one.
  The record holds no raw value: a URL's credentials travel only in the start command, never into a cluster object.

A role holding any other value is reported `stale_address` rather than `alive` (`ObservationKind`, `internal/runtime/runtime.go`), and the observation's detail names each address that moved, with the name it holds and the one a generation started now is handed (`--connect
tcp://192.0.2.5:13371, now tcp://192.0.2.7:13371`, `ENVOY_URL https://envoy.internal.example, now
https://ENVOY.INTERNAL.EXAMPLE`, or `agent-secrets-token audience=agent-secrets expiry=3600s
path=token, now audience=agent-secrets-next expiry=3600s path=token`).
The supervisor logs that detail, so every printed endpoint is constructed from its scheme, host and port alone, adding `xxxxx@` when userinfo is present.
Path, query and fragment never appear, which also protects a value an earlier daemon accepted before the current endpoint grammar refused queries and fragments, and a value that yields no scheme and host is named only `xxxxx`.
`ENVOY_NATS_URL` is named entry by entry from the URLs the loader accepted, never by splitting the joined value, since raw commas are valid in userinfo.
A role this daemon started always compares equal, so only the roles a daemon under another configuration started are ever reported, from the boot that re-adopts them; nobody runs a command for it.
The operator's own variables (`runtime.kubernetes.pod.env`) are not compared: a change there reaches the pods created after it.

The supervisor relaunches each reported claim at once, through the launch path a death uses:
a `Resume` of its recorded session, or a `Spawn` when it has not registered yet.
What the relaunch replaces follows from what moved.
An issue pod whose launcher dials a stale stream, or which runs the layout before one container, cannot run its roles as a pod created now would, and no worker of it can be asked to push first:
such a launcher never redials, so it never reaches this daemon to be tasked, and that layout's workers predate the contract that added the op (`movedInPod`, `packages/daemon/internal/runtime/sandbox/addresses.go`).
Every role of such a pod is reported at once, from the boot that re-adopts them:
the first of them relaunched replaces the pod, under the pod's launch turn, and the others, whose relaunches wait on that turn, resume into the new pod, whose launcher dials the current stream for every role.
None of them is charged, and none is found gone when the pod is replaced under it.
What an issue pod lacks that its workers can be asked about first — the broker enrollment its roles are started against now, the operator mount holding a file `role_config_files` names for any of its roles, and the session store it was created under — is drift rather than a moved address (`driftedInPod`):
the relaunch keeps that pod, the role runs in it as the pod was built, and the update round is what replaces it, once every role the round asks has answered, no turn runs and each role's report since its last turn names no running background work, or at the round's bound ([The disk dies with its pod](#the-disk-dies-with-its-pod)).
The controller's pod holds every one of those facets as a moved address, since no round covers it (`roundCovers`):
it is replaced at its relaunch when its one launcher dials a stale stream, when it lacks the broker enrollment under `runtime.kubernetes.agent_secrets`, and when it lacks the mount of one of its own `role_config_files`.
A role whose environment alone moved, the broker's URL, `LEGION_SLACK_CHANNELS` for the controller and the other addresses its agent is told among them, starts its next generation in the same pod, handed the current values, and the pod and its other roles are left as they are.
The stale observation is never charged, since the process did nothing wrong; a relaunch the runtime refuses is charged as any launch failure is.
A turn the stale process was in used the addresses it holds and ends with the relaunch, so the turn is lost:
its task goes back to waiting and is sent again once the relaunched agent is ready, the recovery a death in a turn gets.
A claim whose suspension was held for that turn's end is suspended instead, as it is when its process dies.

The record costs one API write per generation started, the annotation's patch (844 bytes in the runtime's tests, with Dispatch and the broker unset), where a start in a running issue pod made none before.
Stage 4b drives both cases with real agents on the cluster:
`address-moved-env-same-pod` respells `envoy_url`'s host, and `address-moved-stream-new-pod` swaps the daemon's API and worker-stream ports ([`scripts/e2e/README.md`](../scripts/e2e/README.md#stage4b-sandbox-treesh)).

### A shell on an issue's disk

Some of provisioning's refusals name `jj` commands against the issue's clone, the repository its workspace is a `jj workspace` of, `-R /legion/repos/github.com/<owner>/<repo>` (`packages/daemon/internal/workspace/bookmark.go`):

- a local bookmark deleted and never pushed: restore it, cancel the deletion, or start from the repository's default branch;

- a conflicted local bookmark: keep an added commit, or start from the repository's default branch.

The refusals for an origin row that racing fetches conflicted or moved name no command, because provisioning again settles them.

Each refusal is in the failing pod's `workspace-init` log (`kubectl -n legion logs <pod> -c workspace-init`), and the daemon's log quotes its tail.
Nothing is registered before a refusal, so the pod's next attempt refuses again.
The clone is only on the issue's disk, and a pod whose `workspace-init` refuses runs no `roles` container to exec into, so those commands are run nowhere:
the remedy is the replacement pod (below).
A shell reaches a running pod's disk from the operator's context only: the daemon's identity creates no pod and has no exec ([RBAC](#rbac-the-go-daemon-needs)).

**The issue's pod is running.**
Its `roles` container mounts the disk at `/legion`:

```sh
kubectl -n legion get pods -l legion.dev/issue=<KEY> --field-selector=status.phase=Running
kubectl -n legion exec -it <pod> -c roles -- sh
ls /legion/workspaces/<owner>/<repo>/<issue key lowercased>   # read files; start nothing
```

The shell runs as the issue's agents do, user 1000 under gVisor, but it carries the container's environment, not any agent's:
the `roles` container's spec holds only what the kubelet resolves, which is `POD_UID` from the downward API, and every other variable the agent is told
— the operator's `runtime.kubernetes.pod.env` included, and among them `XDG_STATE_HOME=/legion/scratch/state/<role>`, the role's state home
— arrives in its launcher's start command (`launchEnvironment`, `manifest.go`);
`/proc/<agent pid>/environ`, the process whose `argv[0]` is `omp` under the role's `legion worker-shim`, holds the agent's whole environment.
The shell starts in the issue's workspace, the container's working directory.
The clone is at `/legion/repos/github.com/<owner>/<repo>` and the issue's workspace at `/legion/workspaces/<owner>/<repo>/<issue key lowercased>` (`workspace.Location`, `internal/workspace/provision.go`);
no other issue's workspace is on this volume.
Every role writes that clone and workspace, so a role can plant configuration there that starts a program
— for jj a legacy `config.toml` without its `config-id` or a workspace's `.jj/repo` file pointing at a repository of the role's own, for git a filter, fsmonitor or promisor remote, for `omp` an extension under the workspace's `.omp/` — and a `jj`, `git` or `omp` run in this shell obeys it, as user 1000 outside every role's namespaces, with every role's credentials in reach.
No flag makes a jj read safe: `--ignore-working-copy --no-pager` still verifies a signature through a planted `signing.backends.gpg.program`, and the migration of a planted legacy file writes the pod's shared config home.
So run no `jj`, `git` or `omp` here; read files, and take work out of the pod as [Carrying unpushed work out of an issue's pod](#carrying-unpushed-work-out-of-an-issues-pod) says.
A refusal's `jj` commands are not run in this shell either:
a pod whose `workspace-init` refuses has no running `roles` container, and its remedy is the replacement pod below.

**No pod of the issue is running.**
Then there is nothing to reach.
The issue's disk was its pod's own and went with the pod ([The disk dies with its pod](#the-disk-dies-with-its-pod)), so no claim is left to mount, and the clone, the workspace and everything the issue's roles wrote are gone with it.
A kept volume is the exception: its claim stays with the issue's Sandbox, and the issue's next pod mounts it with everything on it ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)).
A refusal above is worked in the pod that raised it or not at all:
a pod whose `workspace-init` is failing has no running `roles` container to exec into, and the remedy there is to let the pod be replaced.
The runtime reads a failed init container as the end of every role of that pod (`InitFailed`, `internal/runtime/sandbox/observe.go`) and the next launch replaces the pod outright instead of waiting on its launchers (`relaunch.go`);
the replacement provisions a fresh clone and workspace from the issue's pushed branch, on a disk of its own.
On a kept volume, the launch first resets the volume for a failure local to it, so the replacement provisions on a new, empty volume too (the reset in [A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)).
Nothing is saved first, because a shell on the old disk could carry nothing over.

**The one stopped disk still worth mounting: a tree volume of the release before issue pods.**
That release's tree volume is its root Sandbox's, not a pod's, so it outlives every pod of the tree, and copying the sessions off it is the one procedure that still needs a stopped disk reachable:
step 3 of [Copying file sessions before turning it on](#copying-file-sessions-before-turning-it-on).
The pod below is the one that step starts for each tree, and the step gives the commands that bring the database URL and the claims list into it and run the import there.
The tree's claim is the one its labels name (`kubectl -n legion get pvc -l
legion.dev/project=<project>,legion.dev/tree=<ROOT ISSUE>`).
By that step of the runbook the tree's root Sandbox is `Suspended` with no pod of its own and the earlier release's daemon is stopped, so nothing launches a pod that would want the volume while yours holds it;
the claim is `ReadWriteOnce` and this pod mounts it read-only, which the import is:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: legion-tree-shell, namespace: legion }   # no legion.dev/* labels
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  nodeSelector: { legion.dev/pool: legion }
  tolerations: [{ key: legion.dev/pool, operator: Equal, value: legion, effect: NoSchedule }]
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
    runAsGroup: 1000
    fsGroup: 1000             # the tree's own pods ran as it: its files are group 1000
    seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }
  containers:
    - name: shell
      image: <runtime.kubernetes.image>      # the daemon's worker image, by digest
      command: [sleep, "3600"]
      securityContext: { allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, capabilities: { drop: [ALL] } }
      volumeMounts: [{ name: tree, mountPath: /legion, readOnly: true }]
  volumes: [{ name: tree, persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: <the tree's claim above> } }]
```

```sh
kubectl -n legion apply -f legion-tree-shell.yaml
kubectl -n legion wait --for=condition=Ready pod/legion-tree-shell --timeout=300s
kubectl -n legion exec -it legion-tree-shell -- sh
kubectl -n legion delete pod legion-tree-shell
```

The pod carries no credential of its own.
An agent of that tree could plant git and jj configuration in a clone on the volume ([Trust model](#trust-model-the-provisioning-token)), which a `jj` run in this shell would obey, and the pod gives that configuration nothing to take.
The session copy brings one credential in, the database URL, for the one command it runs there: `legion sessions import`, which reads the volume's session files as data, starts no `git`, `jj` or `omp`, and runs in the `exec` that removes the URL when it ends.
Run no other command in the pod while the URL is in it, and no command that holds a token at any other time.

### Carrying unpushed work out of an issue's pod

A running issue pod's workspace can hold work its branch on GitHub lacks: commits no role pushed, and edits not yet in a commit.
To keep that work when the pod must go (step 2 of [Rolling back the upgrade](#rolling-back-the-upgrade)), copy the clone's objects and the workspace's files out of the pod with `tar`, rebuild the work in a throwaway container, and push the resulting bundle from a clone of your own.
Run no `git` or `jj` in the pod, and bring no credential into it, for two reasons.

- **The shell can read every role's credentials.**
  `kubectl exec -c roles` runs as user 1000, the launcher's own user, outside every role's namespaces, so it can read everything under `/var/run/legion/roles/`.
  The pod's `fsGroup` opens the mode-0440 mounts to it:
  each role's gh files (`<role>/gh`) and launcher token (`<role>/launcher`), the providers Secret at `/var/run/legion/providers` (the provider keys, the `legion-pane` NATS nkey seed when the daemon has one and, under `postgres`, the session database's URL, the login to every conversation of the deployment), the projected ServiceAccount token at `/var/run/legion/agent-secrets-token` when the pod is enrolled with the secrets broker, the broker's exchange token at `/var/run/legion/agent-secrets-exchange/token` where `agent_secrets.exchange_audience` is set, the Workload Identity pool's projected token at `/var/run/legion/roles/workload-identity/token` in a microVM pod with the metadata endpoint, and the session writer token at `/var/run/legion/roles/session-writer/token` where `session_database.writer_audience` is set.
  It reads the rest as their owner: each running generation's `<role>/private/g<generation>/` files, which the launcher writes owner-only (the boot token, the Envoy and Dispatch bearers, a spec's secrets and, under `cloudsql-iam`, the session database's URL file and socket), each role's `<role>/agent-secrets/` key directory and each role's home under `.homes/`, whose files a role writes as user 1000 outside its namespaces.
  It reads each agent's environment through `/proc/<pid>/environ` too, and whatever the operator's `runtime.kubernetes.pod.volume_mounts` mount.
  Where the pods' ServiceAccount is federated to a cloud identity, it can act as that identity, as every role can.
  Under `cloudsql-iam` with `impersonate_service_account`, that identity can also impersonate the service account, so the shell and every role can act as that account: they can sign in to the session database as it, and use every other role that it holds.
  Under `writer_audience`, the shell reads the session writer token, because the token is in the container's namespaces, outside every role's.
  With it, the shell can impersonate the account and write the project's session database.
  So whoever may exec into a Legion pod may write its project's session database.
  A deployment that sets the member must therefore grant `pods/exec` on Legion pods to no agent identity.
