  No role reads the token: role-init covers `/var/run/legion/roles/` in each role's namespaces.

- **The clone's configuration is every role's to write.**
  The clone's `.git/config`, its hooks, a legacy jj configuration file and the workspace's `.jj/repo` pointer are on the issue's disk, which every role writes ([Trust model](#trust-model-the-provisioning-token)), and the shell's git is given none of the overrides a role's git is.
  That configuration can name programs git and jj start
  — a working-copy filter, a signing program, a promisor remote's `uploadpack`, a pager — and they run as user 1000 with every role's credentials in reach.
  Disabling hooks and fsmonitor is not enough, and the daemon's own guards (`sharedRepository`, `internal/workspace/config.go`) do not cover a command run by hand.
  `tar` reads no configuration.

So the pod runs only `tar`, and every `git` that touches the pod's bytes runs in a throwaway container on your machine with no network and no credential, inside the container's own filesystem.
It reads the two archives from your directory and writes only a git bundle back, and fetching a bundle runs nothing.
Run the steps from an empty directory, run no git on anything but the bundle outside the container, and delete the directory once the push is done:

```sh
pod=<pod> K=<KEY> image=<runtime.kubernetes.image>   # the daemon's worker image, by digest
clone=/legion/repos/github.com/<owner>/<repo>
ws=/legion/workspaces/<owner>/<repo>/<issue key lowercased>
# 1. In the pod, tar alone: the clone's refs, worktree records and objects, and the workspace's
#    files. Each refuses a directory reached through a symlink; the tree drops every .git and .jj.
#    An exit of 1 after "file changed as we read it" (the agents still write) is not a failure.
kubectl -n legion exec "$pod" -c roles -- sh -c 'set -e; cd -P "$1/.git"
  test "$(pwd -P)" = "$1/.git"
  tar --hard-dereference -cf - refs worktrees $(test -f packed-refs && echo packed-refs) objects
  ' sh "$clone" > "$K-git.tar"
kubectl -n legion exec "$pod" -c roles -- sh -c 'set -e; cd -P "$1"; test "$(pwd -P)" = "$1"
  tar --hard-dereference --ignore-case --exclude=.git --exclude=.jj --exclude=./.codegraph \
  -cf - .' sh "$ws" > "$K-tree.tar"
# 2. In a throwaway container: rebuild the work under configurations git init wrote, and bundle
#    what origin lacks.
docker run --rm -i --network none --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e HOME=/tmp -v "$PWD:/w" --entrypoint sh "$image" \
  -s "$K" "$ws" <<'EOF'
set -eu
K=$1 ws=$2 git=/w/$K-git.tar tree=/w/$K-tree.tar
refuse() { echo "refused: $*" >&2; exit 1; }
bad=$(tar -tvf "$git" | awk '$1 !~ /^[-d]/'); test -z "$bad" || refuse "$git holds $bad"
bad=$(tar -tvf "$tree" | awk '$1 !~ /^[-dl]/'); test -z "$bad" || refuse "$tree holds $bad"
cd "$(mktemp -d)" && git init -q --bare pod.git
tar -C pod.git --exclude=objects/info -xf "$git" objects refs \
  $(tar -tf "$git" | grep -x packed-refs || true)
id=
for g in $(tar -tf "$git" | grep '^worktrees/[^/]*/gitdir$'); do
  case $(tar -xOf "$git" "$g") in "$ws/.git" | */"${ws#/legion/}/.git") id=${g%/gitdir} ;; esac
done
test -n "$id" || refuse "no worktree record names $ws"
base=$(tar -xOf "$git" "$id/HEAD")
echo "$base" | grep -Eqx '[0-9a-f]{40}' || refuse "$id/HEAD is not a commit id"
git -C pod.git update-ref refs/rescue-base "$base"
git init -q work && cd work
git fetch -q ../pod.git 'refs/jj/*:refs/jj/*' 'refs/heads/*:refs/rescue/*' \
  'refs/remotes/origin/*:refs/remotes/origin/*' refs/rescue-base:refs/rescue-base
git symbolic-ref HEAD "refs/heads/rescue-$K" && git reset -q "$base"
tar -xf "$tree"
git -c core.excludesFile=/dev/null add -A
git status --short
git diff --cached --quiet ||
  git -c user.name=rescue -c user.email=rescue@invalid commit -q -m "Edits left in $K's workspace"
echo "unpushed commits of other branches, not in the bundle:"
git log --oneline --glob=refs/rescue/ --not --remotes=origin "rescue-$K"
git bundle create "/w/$K.bundle" "rescue-$K" --not --remotes=origin
EOF
# 3. In a clone of your own, fetched from GitHub first: read what the bundle adds, then push it.
git fetch origin
git fetch "<dir>/$K.bundle" "rescue-$K:refs/remotes/rescue/$K"
git log --stat --oneline "origin/legion/$K..rescue/$K"
git push origin "refs/remotes/rescue/$K:refs/heads/legion/$K"
```

The workspace's git worktree record (`<clone>/.git/worktrees/<id>/HEAD`, the entry whose `gitdir` names the workspace's `.git`, absolute or relative) names the parent of jj's working-copy commit as of jj's last command there, or a commit a role made with `git commit` since;
the files carry everything after it, snapshotted or not.
Step 2 names that commit with a ref of its own in the bare repository, so the fetch reaches it and every unpushed commit below it, bookmarked or not.
The rebuild resets the index to that commit and lays the files over it, so a file the repository tracks stays as the tree holds it even when a `.gitignore` names it, a submodule's gitlink stays, and every new file the tree holds is added, those over jj's `snapshot.max-new-file-size` included.
`objects/info` stays out of the bare repository, so no alternates file borrows objects from elsewhere.
`git status --short` prints the edits left out of a commit, and the next log the unpushed commits on other branches, which the bundle leaves out; none of either and `Refusing to
create empty bundle` together mean nothing below the working copy was left unpushed.
The bundle is as trustworthy as a push of the role's own:
read the log's `--stat` before pushing, and refuse a change under `.github/workflows/` unless the implement App holds `workflows: write`, since your own credential may push a workflow the App could not.
The log fails when the issue never pushed `legion/<KEY>`; read `git log --stat --oneline rescue/<KEY>` then, and the push creates the branch.
`git fetch` refuses the bundle when your clone lacks a commit it builds on, such as one since force-pushed away on GitHub;
drop `--not --remotes=origin` and run step 2 again.
`git push` refuses anything but a fast-forward of GitHub's branch; when it does, push to a branch of another name and merge from there.
The pod's agents run while you copy, so finish steps 1 and 2 while it is still there, and repeat step 1 when step 2 refuses an archive;
step 2 starts in a fresh directory of the container each run.

### Running a workload in the cluster from a role

A role sometimes needs something *running* rather than installed — a database for a test, a broker, a second copy of an application under test.
Its own pod holds a server only as a test harness's own rootless install at the pod's fixed reservation, which is how the Dispatch browser suite's Postgres runs today ([The tools a role's own work needs](#the-tools-a-roles-own-work-needs));
a server image, or more processors than the pod reserves, it cannot hold, and the worker image cannot carry a running server, so a role starts one in the cluster as a Job and reaches it by a Service name.
What makes that possible is the deployment's, not Legion's:
the ingress rule that admits connections from the namespace Legion's pods run in, the grant on Services and the admission rule that holds them, and the quota that counts them are declared in the deployment's own repository and applied by a person (dispatch://INFRA-206).
This section is what a role does where they exist.
Every rule below is that issue's and this issue's specification (dispatch://INFRA-71), each one stated as the condition the namespace's admission enforces;
a workload that breaks one is refused at submission with a message naming the rule it broke, so nothing here has to be taken on trust
— with the one exception this section marks where it arises, the reachability label, which admission does not check and whose absence is a workload that starts, costs its quota and answers nothing.

**A role has this only where its deployment gives it.**
Every Legion pod sets `automountServiceAccountToken: false` (`AutomountServiceAccountToken`, `internal/runtime/sandbox/manifest.go`), so a role holds a Kubernetes credential only where its operator projects one through `runtime.kubernetes.pod.volumes` ([Configuration](#configuration));
the image carries the client and no credential for it ([Worker image](#worker-image)).
Three answers tell a role which deployment it is in, and they are the gate for everything below:

```sh
kubectl -n <namespace> auth can-i create jobs      # may this role start a workload at all
kubectl -n <namespace> auth can-i create services  # may it give one a name on the network
kubectl -n <namespace> auth can-i get services     # `kubectl apply` reads the live object before it creates one
```

The third is not a duplicate of the second.
The sequence writes its Service with `kubectl apply`, which is client-side by default and reads the object it is about to create before it creates it, so a role that may create a Service but not read one gets `Error from server (Forbidden): error
when retrieving current configuration of: … cannot get resource "services"` and never reaches the create.
Both verbs are needed for the sequence as written, which is why the gate asks for both.
A deployment that granted the create without the read would still admit a `kubectl create` of the same file;
this section publishes no second form for that case, and no deployment answering that way has been measured
— in this one, before dispatch://INFRA-206's declarations were applied, both Service answers were `no`.

None of the three is the answer a role with no credential gets.
The image ships no kubeconfig and sets no `KUBECONFIG`, so without a projected token `kubectl` builds no in-cluster configuration at all:
it falls back to `localhost:8080` and **exits 1**, its last line `The
connection to the server localhost:8080 was refused - did you specify the right host or port?` (measured from a role container with the in-cluster environment removed).
That is as conclusive as `no` — nothing in this section applies, and a tool the work needs on the issue's own files arrives the way it already does, below.
A `yes` to the first and a `no` to either of the others is a deployment where the sequence as written does not run:
a workload can be started there, and the sequence cannot give it a name to be reached by.

**Unless all three commands answer a bare `yes`, submit nothing.**
The sequence submits its Job before its Service, and the Service step is refused `Forbidden` wherever either Service answer is `no`, so a refusal there finds a Job already submitted, and the sequence's own trap deletes it.
Measured on 2026-10-25 with a Service step the namespace's admission refused
— a refusal of another kind that ends the step the same way, with `kubectl apply` failing
— the trap deleted the Job within six seconds of its submission, while its pod was still `Pending`, and nothing of it was left.
A role whose shell went away before the trap ran removes it with the recovery line under the sequence.

`<namespace>` is the namespace the workload runs in, and each command names it because a pod's `kubectl` has no kubeconfig and takes its default namespace from the pod instead:
`POD_NAMESPACE` when that is set, else the `namespace` file the projected credential carries (`/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/namespace`), else `default`.
Without `-n`, the gate answers for whatever namespace the pod's projection names, which a role cannot see from this page and cannot assume is the workload's.
In a pod projected as this deployment projects one, that file names the workload's namespace, so the form without `-n` answers as `-n <namespace>` does, which is why it reads as working;
the same account asked with `-n` the namespace Legion's own pods run in answers `no` to all three (measured from a role container on 2026-10-25).
The sequence below passes no `-n` and runs in that default namespace, so the gate's answers hold for it only where the default is `<namespace>`.

The sequence has two sources for its namespace, and they agree only where `POD_NAMESPACE` does not say otherwise.
Its `kubectl` commands, the recovery line's included, take that default, `POD_NAMESPACE` first;
its reachability address is built from the `namespace` file alone.
Where a pod set `POD_NAMESPACE` to another namespace, the Job and its Service would be made in one and the check would dial a name in the other, with no Service behind it.
That gap is latent, recorded here rather than closed:
Legion's runtime sets no `POD_NAMESPACE` (nothing in `packages/daemon` names it), an operator's `runtime.kubernetes.pod.env` could, and it was unset in the role container the runs of 2026-10-25 below came from.

The rules the workload must satisfy.
Every one but the last is enforced by the namespace's admission rather than by anyone's good behaviour;
the last is enforced by nothing, which is why it is marked where it stands:

- it runs under gVisor (`runtimeClassName: gvisor`) on the compute class the deployment's declaration names, selected by `nodeSelector`;
  that class creates a machine rather than falling back to a general one, so a small workload waits about eighty seconds to start;

- its largest container requests at least four processors — a smaller job belongs in the role's own pod;

- it bounds itself **twice**: `activeDeadlineSeconds` on the Job *and* on its pod template, each at most twelve hours, with `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` on the Job at most twenty-four, so the Job and its pod go on their own and nobody may orphan one.
  Each of the three is a refusal of its own: a manifest that sets the deadline on the template alone is refused as plainly as one that sets neither;

- it carries no identity: `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, and no service account of its own;

- it mounts only an empty directory, the downward API, or an ephemeral filesystem volume of the scratch storage class the deployment's declaration names, whose claim template carries no labels, annotations, data source, volume or selector.
  **No disk outlives the workload**, which is what a database a test fills and discards needs;

- it carries the pod label the deployment's declaration names for a workload that asks to be reachable.
  **This is the one rule admission does not enforce**:
  a workload without that label is admitted, started, charged against the shared quota, and reachable by nothing, because the ingress rule selects the label rather than the namespace.
  Nothing refuses it and nothing says so; the symptom is the reachability check below ending at its deadline with `TimeoutError` every try — a timeout, not a refusal.
  A refusal is a workload the packets do reach:
  still starting in the first seconds, nothing listening on the port if it lasts the whole wait, as the readings under the sequence set out.
  It is why the check is the step after the wait rather than the last.
  A role that sees it compares the labels on **the workload's** pod, which the sequence's trap prints before it deletes anything (`--show-labels`;
  a pod of this namespace — a role may not read its own, in the namespace Legion's pods run in), with the deployment's declaration
  — not the Service's endpoints, which this identity may not read (`kubectl auth
  can-i get endpoints` answers `no`).
  The label's name is in that declaration, with the compute class, the storage class and the namespace; a role reads it there rather than here.

Name the workload for the issue **and for the run**, as everything else on this cluster is named for what owns it (`issue-legion-<project>-<issue key lowercased>`, `legion-<project>-<issue key lowercased>` above).
The issue is the name's prefix, `<issue key lowercased>-<what it is>-`, which the Job's manifest carries as `metadata.generateName`;
the run is the API server's part, five random characters it appends at each create, answering with the whole name
— for instance `infra-71-postgres-` followed by five such characters — which the sequence reads from that answer and writes into its Service.
The issue key carries its project, so the name cannot collide with another project's.
The rest is the server's for a reason: a name a role picks itself can be one that something else in the namespace already holds or will declare, and a Service takes its Job's name, so the Job's name is taken among the Services too, and the first anyone knows of it is another stack's apply failing `AlreadyExists`.
A name the API server generates is not one any declaration chose: it exists from the create that made it.
`kubectl apply` refuses `generateName` before it sends anything (`error: from <prefix>: cannot use generate name with apply`), which is why the sequence creates its Job with `kubectl create` and applies only its Service.

A name a role reuses is a name something else is using, as was measured here before the server named the run.
A bare `postgres`, or even `infra-71-postgres`, is shared by six roles of one issue under one identity, and every step after the Job's acts on whatever holds that name:
both waits select its pod, the reachability check reaches its database, and the trap's `kubectl delete job` takes it and its Service away mid-test.
And a role that re-ran the sequence after any failure met a worse version of the same thing, because a pod keeps its `job-name` label while it terminates:
measured here, the second run's `--for=create` returned 0 in **1 s on the previous run's dying pod**, and the Ready wait reported `condition met` for one pod and `NotFound` for the other while the workload that would actually serve was still `Pending`.
A reader who took that Ready at its word would run the reachability check against a workload that is not up and be sent, by the bullet above, to the one failure this section says announces nothing.
A suffix new at each create, which the server makes, is what removes the whole class: the selector cannot match a corpse that never carried it.

The Job's manifest is the first of the two the sequence below writes, under the name the API server gives it.
The name on the network is the second, a Service, held to a cluster-internal address: no node port, no load balancer, no external address and no external name.
It is admitted only while the Job it fronts owns it, so removing the Job removes it too and leaves nothing for a person to sweep
— which is why its `ownerReferences` carries the Job's own uid, read from the create's own answer.
It selects its pods by that same uid and by nothing else:
the namespace's admission requires a Service's selector to be exactly `batch.kubernetes.io/controller-uid` at the uid of the Job that owns it, because a rule checking a submission sees only the object submitted and cannot look a Job up, so a selector by name would let a Service owned by one Job front another's pods.
A `job-name` selector, though the Job puts that label on its pods too, is refused at submission, naming that rule.

The whole sequence, from a role holding nothing but its checkout and that credential.
It writes both manifests outside the checkout, into a directory `mktemp` makes under `$TMPDIR` (or `/tmp`), never the issue's workspace:
the workspace is a jj working copy of this public repository, so a manifest left there is snapshotted into the role's working-copy commit and the password in it can reach the branch.
It runs as a `bash` of its own, from a file, and detached from the command that starts it, because its clean-up is a trap and a role's bash tool ends a command that runs past its timeout by killing that command and every process under it, too fast for any trap to run (below).
Detached, the sequence is outside what the tool kills; the last line holds the call until the sequence has ended and then prints what it printed.
The three lines in angle brackets are the only ones a role fills in: the issue key, and the two lines it reads from the deployment's declaration.

```sh
sequence=$(mktemp "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/sequence.XXXXXX")              # not the checkout: see above
cat > "$sequence" <<'SEQUENCE'
set -euo pipefail
echo "sequence: process $$; a deliberate stop is: kill -TERM -- -$$"
workload=""                                    # the Job's create sets it; the trap reads it
run=$(python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(4))')
echo "run: sequence-run=$run"                  # the Job's label, which exists before its name
dir=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/workload.XXXXXX")
password=$(python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(16))')

cleanup() {
  status=$?
  trap - EXIT INT TERM HUP
  trap '' INT TERM HUP                         # this shell ignores any further stop
  # Each kubectl below runs under setsid -w, in a session of its own, out of the stopped group:
  # kubectl dies of a SIGTERM it inherited ignored, and its waits catch SIGINT and SIGHUP too.
  set +e
  if [ -z "$workload" ]; then                  # no name read: find this run's Job by its label
    echo "cleanup: no Job name was read; deleting by label sequence-run=$run"
    setsid -w kubectl delete job -l sequence-run="$run" --cascade=foreground --ignore-not-found \
      || { echo "cleanup: the Job's delete failed"; [ "$status" -ne 0 ] || status=1; }
    setsid -w kubectl get jobs -l sequence-run="$run"   # empty is no proof none is left: see below
    rm -rf "$dir"
    echo "sequence: exit $status"
    exit "$status"
  fi
  if [ "$status" -ne 0 ]; then                 # what the readings below send a role to look at
    setsid -w kubectl get pods -l job-name="$workload" --show-labels
    setsid -w kubectl logs -l job-name="$workload" --tail=20
    setsid -w kubectl get pods -l job-name="$workload" \
      -o jsonpath='{range .items[*].status.containerStatuses[*]}{.name}: {.state}{"\n"}{end}'
    setsid -w kubectl get service "$workload" --ignore-not-found \
      -o jsonpath='{range .spec.ports[*]}port {.port} -> targetPort {.targetPort}{"\n"}{end}'
  fi
  setsid -w kubectl delete job "$workload" --cascade=foreground --ignore-not-found \
    || { echo "cleanup: the Job's delete failed"; [ "$status" -ne 0 ] || status=1; }
  setsid -w kubectl wait --for=delete service/"$workload" --timeout=60s \
    || { echo "cleanup: the Service is still there"; [ "$status" -ne 0 ] || status=1; }
  setsid -w kubectl get job,service "$workload" --ignore-not-found   # nothing once both are gone
  setsid -w kubectl get pods -l job-name="$workload"                 # "No resources found"
  rm -rf "$dir"
  echo "sequence: exit $status"
  exit "$status"
}
trap cleanup EXIT
trap 'exit 130' INT
trap 'exit 143' TERM
trap 'exit 129' HUP

cat > "$dir/job.yaml" <<YAML
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  generateName: <issue key lowercased>-postgres-   # the API server adds five characters
  labels: { sequence-run: "$run" }      # on the Job alone, not its pods: how the trap finds it unnamed
spec:
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 3600           # on the Job, at most 43200
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600         # at most 86400
  backoffLimit: 0
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        <the pod label the deployment's declaration names for a workload that asks to be reachable>
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      activeDeadlineSeconds: 3600         # on the pod template, at most 43200
      automountServiceAccountToken: false
      runtimeClassName: gvisor
      nodeSelector:
        <the compute-class selector the deployment's declaration names>
      containers:
        - name: db
          image: mirror.gcr.io/library/postgres@sha256:979bccfde35445db618c65107d27d08c6c21339d8dc3ad4c830c6633947be0e4   # Google's mirror: the cluster pulls this image itself, and this example is outside CI's reach
          terminationMessagePolicy: FallbackToLogsOnError   # an exited server's last lines stay in its status
          env:
            - { name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD, value: "$password" }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "4", memory: 8Gi }      # the largest container asks at least 4 CPU
          volumeMounts: [{ name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql }]
      volumes:
        - name: data
          emptyDir: {}                    # dies with the pod, by design
YAML
created=$(kubectl create -o jsonpath='{.metadata.name} {.metadata.uid}' -f "$dir/job.yaml")
workload=${created% *} uid=${created#* }       # the name it was given, and what the Service must name
echo "workload: $workload"                     # the name the recovery line below needs

cat > "$dir/service.yaml" <<YAML
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: $workload
  ownerReferences:
    - { apiVersion: batch/v1, kind: Job, name: $workload, uid: $uid }
spec:
  type: ClusterIP                         # the only kind this namespace admits
  selector: { batch.kubernetes.io/controller-uid: $uid }   # its owner's pods, no one else's
  ports: [{ port: 5432, targetPort: 5432 }]
YAML
kubectl apply -f "$dir/service.yaml"

kubectl wait --for=create pod -l job-name="$workload" --timeout=120s   # it does not exist yet
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l job-name="$workload" --timeout=300s
ns=$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/namespace)
address="$workload.$ns.svc.cluster.local"
python3 - "$address" 5432 <<'PY'                                  # does it answer yet?
import socket, sys, time
host, port = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])
readings = {
    "ConnectionRefusedError": "reachable, and nothing listens on that port: read the pod's status, log and ports printed below",
    "TimeoutError": "packets dropped: compare the pod's labels printed below with the reachability label",
    "gaierror": "the name does not resolve: no Service of that name in the namespace the address names",
}
deadline = time.monotonic() + 60
while True:
    try:
        with socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=5):
            print("answered")
            break
    except OSError as error:
        if time.monotonic() >= deadline:
            kind = type(error).__name__
            print(f"never answered: {kind}: {error}")
            print(f"reading: {readings.get(kind, 'not one this section reads')}")
            sys.exit(1)
        time.sleep(2)
PY
kubectl logs -l job-name="$workload" --tail=5                    # and what it says it is doing

# The work itself goes here, inside this script: "$address" port 5432, user postgres, password
# "$password". The trap above tries to remove the workload on every exit it runs on, and prints
# `sequence: exit <status>` last. It can leave the workload: on a SIGKILL or the role's pod going
# away, or on another signal the trap neither catches nor ignores, which can end the sequence or
# its trap part-way with no `sequence: exit` line; on a clean-up step that fails, which it prints;
# and on a create the API server stores after its label delete has listed the Jobs (see below).
SEQUENCE
echo "sequence: $sequence, its output in $sequence.log"
flock "$sequence" setsid -f bash "$sequence" > "$sequence.log" 2>&1 < /dev/null   # out of the tool's reach
flock "$sequence" cat "$sequence.log"          # waits for the sequence to end, then prints its output
```

On every exit of that `bash` — the work's end, a failed step, or `SIGINT`, `SIGTERM` or `SIGHUP` — the trap runs.
When the status is not 0 it first prints what the readings below send a role to look at:
the workload pod's line with its labels, the last twenty lines of its log, its container's state, and the Service's port and target port.
The state is there because a log read from a pod whose server has exited can fail
— the read goes to the machine the pod ran on, and on 2026-10-25 it timed out in two of eight runs of a server that had stopped
— while the state comes from the cluster's own record, and `FallbackToLogsOnError` in the Job puts the last lines of the server's log into it when the server exits with an error.
Then the trap deletes the Job with `--cascade=foreground`, which returns once the Job's pod is gone, since the Job controller's owner reference on the pod holds the Job's deletion back (6 s for a running `postgres:16`, 31 s for one still initialising, measured 2026-10-25);
waits for the Service, whose owner reference, written without `blockOwnerDeletion`, holds nothing back, so the foreground delete does not wait for it;
lists the Job, the Service and the pods by this run's name, which prints nothing and `No resources
found`; and exits with the status it began with, or 1 when a clean-up step failed after a run that had succeeded, printing it last as `sequence: exit <status>`, since the call that waits for a detached sequence prints its output and not its status.
A trap that runs before the sequence has read its Job's name from the create's answer
— the create refused, or a stop that landed first — looks for the Job by this run's label instead.
The sequence draws eight random hexadecimal characters before the create, prints them as `run: sequence-run=<value>`, and writes them as a label on the Job's own metadata, not its pod template, so the label is never one a pod carries and cannot be read as the reachability label.
That trap prints `cleanup: no Job name was read; deleting
by label sequence-run=<value>`, deletes every Job the server lists with that label, with `--cascade=foreground`, lists the Jobs carrying it, and exits with its status.
After a refused create, or a stop before the create's request left, there is no Job, and the delete finds nothing.
Otherwise the delete finds the Job only if the API server has stored it by the time the delete lists the Jobs.
In every run measured on 2026-10-25 for dispatch://INFRA-232 whose label delete found a Job
— the stop placed between the create's answer and the line that reads it, and two of the twenty-six stops in the bullet below, sent 0.33 s and 0.35 s after the first line (that issue's tester measured two more, at 0.318 s and 0.320 s, sjawhar/legion#2195)
— the delete removed it, and none of the twenty-six left a Job.
Nothing the 0.33 s and 0.35 s runs printed shows whether their stop landed while the create was in flight or after its answer.
A create the server finishes only after that listing
— its request still in flight when a stop or a failed connection ended `kubectl create` — leaves a Job the delete never saw.
No run measured that case, and none rules it out.
The trap's own listing shows such a Job only if the server stored it before that listing, and prints `No resources found` if later, so an empty listing there does not show that no such Job exists;
the block's closing comment names this case among those the trap can miss.
Such a Job would run until the 3600 s deadline it and its pod carry, holding the four processors it requested.
So after every run whose trap printed `cleanup: no Job name was read`, list `kubectl get jobs -l sequence-run=<the printed value>` once more after the sequence has ended, and remove any Job it lists with `kubectl delete job -l sequence-run=<the printed value> --cascade=foreground`, the recovery that removed a Job a `SIGKILL` left before its name was printed, measured on 2026-10-25.
No wait was measured either: how long after its client is gone the server can still store a create is not known, so an empty listing shows only that no such Job was stored by the time the listing ran.
Another run's Job carries a value drawn for that run, so neither command touches it.
No Service exists on that path: the sequence applies its Service only once it has read the name.

**A timeout of the role's own bash tool is what the detaching is for.**
The tool ends a call that runs past its timeout by signalling the command and every process under it and killing them almost at once:
on 2026-10-25 a probe logging every 20 ms after a `SIGTERM` logged for 70 ms in one run and not at all in two others, and the sequence as this page published it before it detached, run in a call's foreground with a 40 s timeout, was gone with its Job, its Service and its running pod left behind, in two runs.
That is the `SIGKILL` case below, and nothing in the call's output says so.
A process in a session of its own is still killed while it descends from the call (`setsid --wait` was, measured the same day);
`setsid -f` hands it to the system's init, which is what takes it out of the tool's reach.
Run as published here, with the same 40 s timeout, the call ended at its timeout and the sequence ran on, answered, ran its trap and left nothing.
A call that timed out has printed the sequence's file and its log before anything else, so a later call re-attaches with `flock <the sequence's file> cat <its log>`, which waits for the sequence to end and prints everything it printed;
`cat` of the log alone shows how far it has got.

A stop signal sent to the sequence's process group
— `kill -TERM -- -<process>`, which its first line prints, is the deliberate stop
— runs the trap at once; one sent to its `bash` alone runs it only when the step in progress returns, which each step's own timeout bounds.
Measured on 2026-10-25: that `kill -TERM` during the work ran the trap and the sequence exited 143 with nothing left;
`SIGHUP` and `SIGINT` sent to the group during the Ready wait, and `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM` sent to it during the check, each ran the trap within a second;
`SIGTERM` sent to the `bash` alone during the Ready wait ran it 76 s later, when the wait returned, and `SIGINT` sent to it alone during a check that was being refused ran it 58 s later, when the check gave up.
Once the trap runs, its shell ignores further `SIGINT`, `SIGTERM` and `SIGHUP`, and it runs each of its `kubectl` commands under `setsid -w`, in a session of its own, so a stop sent to the sequence's group while the trap runs
— a second stop, or one sent after a failed step or the work's end started the trap
— reaches neither the shell nor its `kubectl`, and the clean-up runs to its end.
The sessions are needed because `kubectl`, a Go program, dies of a `SIGTERM` it inherited ignored, and while it waits it catches `SIGINT` and `SIGHUP` too:
on 2026-10-25, `kubectl wait --for=delete` started with all three ignored, against an API server whose watch never answered, ended on each of them, and kubectl's source shows its `delete` waiting through the same code.
Of the stop signals, only a `SIGKILL` ends a clean-up in progress, and it ends the shell alone:
the `kubectl` then running finishes in its own session, and `flock … cat` waits for it.
A signal the trap neither catches nor ignores can end the clean-up too.
Measured on 2026-10-25 on this block, filled in, with one fixture line for the work, each stop sent to the group:
`SIGTERM` once it had answered and then a second `SIGTERM` 0.5 s later, a `SIGINT` 0.3 s later or a `SIGHUP` 0.3 s later, each printed `sequence: exit 143` and left nothing;
with failing work, one `SIGINT` or one `SIGTERM` sent as the trap began its readings printed `sequence: exit 1` and left nothing.
The block without these lines failed those runs:
a `SIGTERM` during the readings ended the trap there, and with the ignore but no sessions a second `SIGTERM` killed the trap's `kubectl delete` (it printed `cleanup: the Job's
delete failed`); each left the Job, its Service and its pod.
A `SIGKILL` before the trap runs, or the role's pod going away, ends the sequence with no trap and no `sequence: exit` line:
a `kill -KILL -- -<process>` once it had answered left the Job, its Service and its pod, and the two lines below removed them in 1 s.
The Job's two deadlines bound what such a run leaves, and a role that stopped that way
— or that ran the sequence in its tool's foreground and saw the call time out — removes it with the name the sequence printed once its Job was created:

```sh
kubectl delete job <the printed workload name> --cascade=foreground
kubectl wait --for=delete service/<the printed workload name> --timeout=60s
```

A role that lost the name lists the Jobs with `kubectl get jobs`.
Its issue's start with its issue key, and so do its sibling roles', so it deletes only the one it started.
A run can leave a Job with no name printed:
a `SIGKILL` or the role's pod going away before the name printed;
a label delete that failed, printing `cleanup: the Job's delete failed`;
and a stop or failed connection whose create the server stored only after the trap's label delete had listed the Jobs (above).
Each printed its label first, and `kubectl delete job -l sequence-run=<the printed value> --cascade=foreground` removes that Job once the server has stored it, as it removed the one a `SIGKILL` left on 2026-10-25; it had no Service yet.

That check is `python3`, which the image carries, because **the role container had no client for any of these servers** when it was written ([Worker image](#worker-image)), a role may not `exec` into the workload's pod, and installing one in its own pod is the withheld `operator-setup` capability.
The first of those three reasons has since changed, and only the first:
the image this repository builds carries `psql`, `redis-cli`, `sqlite3`, `nc` and `dig` from dispatch://INFRA-221's merge on 2026-10-25 onward, and a role has them once its deployment pins a digest built from that merge or a later commit of `main` ([Pin by digest, never by tag](#pin-by-digest-never-by-tag))
— a role on an older digest still has none of them, and `python3` runs on both.
The role container the runs of 2026-10-25 below came from was one of those: `command -v psql redis-cli sqlite3 nc dig` found none of the five.
What the check proves is what a role needs first, that the address resolves and the port answers, and when it does not, it names the class of the failure, which is what the readings below key on.

It loops because `kubectl wait` cannot tell a role the server is listening.
The pod carries no readiness probe, so `condition=Ready` means the container started, and a database spends its first seconds initialising with its listener closed
— `postgres:18`'s entrypoint does exactly that.
A connection *refused* in those first seconds is the workload reachable and not listening yet: the loop retries and it answers.
When the minute runs out, the check prints the class of its last attempt alone, with a reading for it, and each reading is the next thing to check rather than a proof:

- `ConnectionRefusedError` — the packets reach the workload and nothing listens on the port its Service sends them to.
  The pod's line, which the trap prints with the rest before it deletes anything, says which way to look.
  `Running` is a server listening somewhere other than the Service's `port -> targetPort`, or one still starting a minute after Ready, and its log tells the two apart;
  any other status is a server that stopped, whose reason is in its log or, when the log cannot be read, in its container's state.
  The cluster refuses rather than drops in both cases, whether the pod runs with nothing on that port or has already exited.
  A server that stops by itself shows here and not at the Ready wait:
  a `postgres:16` given an invalid setting ran its initialisation, was Ready long enough for the wait to return and exited about a second later, and a container that exited the moment it started was reported Ready all the same, so in both the check was refused every try.

- `TimeoutError` — the packets are dropped rather than refused, which is what the missing reachability label above produces:
  compare the pod's labels, which the trap prints, with the deployment's declaration first.

- `gaierror` — the name does not resolve:
  there is no Service of that name in the namespace the address names, because the address was mistyped or because of the namespace gap above.
  The sequence stops at a refused Service step before it reaches the check, so a refusal there never shows as this.

Speaking the protocol is a client library onto the issue's own disk, the way every other tool that works from the checkout arrives (below), run from the checkout against that same address, or, on a digest that carries them, one of the image's five clients
— never a binary a role installs into its pod itself.
The trap's listing asks for the Service by name as well as the Job and its pod, because the grant that admits a Service also lets this identity get, list and watch one, so the listing is what shows the Service went with its Job.
The Service's endpoints are still out of reach (`kubectl auth can-i get endpoints` answers `no`, and so does the same question of `endpointslices`), which is why the bullet above compares the workload pod's labels rather than the Service's endpoints.

What a workload there cannot do, so nobody plans around it:
it cannot mount the issue's disk, which belongs to another namespace, to one node at a time and to one pod, and a role may not run a command inside its pod
— the grant is create, read, follow and delete, never `exec`.
A formatter started that way would never see the file it would format, so **a tool that works on the checkout does not belong here**:
those are the image's own clients, or arrive through its package runners onto the pod's own disk, which every role of the issue shares for as long as that pod runs.
That is also why the two notes recording `kubectl auth can-i` answering `no` are not contradicted here (`a-pod-rehearses-a-checkpoints-own-readers-…-LEGION-578.md` in `docs/solutions/legion/`, and `prove-a-published-worker-image-from-a-pod-…-LEGION-764.md` in `docs/solutions/testing/`):
each answers for a different verb — creating a Sandbox, creating a pod, `exec` into one
— in the namespace Legion's own pods run in, which this changes nothing about.

Two costs are shared and are the reason a role cleans up after itself rather than waiting for a deadline.
One quota covers that whole namespace and is shared with the team's builds, so a workload left running is charged against both:
measured on 2026-10-25, the namespace's quota for Jobs counted `requests.cpu` 4 for each of these workloads while it existed, 48 with twelve at once, and was back at 0 once the last of them was deleted.
And every project's pods run as the account that project's configuration names (`service_account`), so the agents of every project that names the same account hold one identity: a password written into a Job is readable by every other agent of that identity, and any of them may delete any workload there.
The other half is reach: the ingress rule admits the namespace Legion's pods run in rather than an identity, naming no pod and no port, so every pod there
— every project's agents, with a Kubernetes credential or without one
— reaches a labelled workload at its Service name, and the password in the Job, which every holder of the identity can read, is the only lock on it.
Narrowing the identity to a per-project one is dispatch://INFRA-153's work, not something to design around here.

### Issue sizing: one reservation per pod

Every container of a Legion pod carries a cpu and memory limit with a request no greater than it (`requirements`, `internal/daemon/kubernetes.go`), and an ephemeral-storage limit over a smaller ephemeral-storage request (the node-disk bound, below):
an issue pod's `roles` container and both its init containers the issue pod's one reservation (`runtime.kubernetes.resources.issue`, the daemon's default where the file sets none
— [Configuration](#configuration)), the controller's launcher the controller's (`runtime.kubernetes.resources.controller`), and the image probe's one container the probe's own fixed 500m / 1Gi, request equal to limit (`probeReservation`, [Configuration](#configuration)).
At the default an issue pod reserves 2 CPU and 8 GiB, the init containers adding nothing:
a pod's effective request is the larger of its containers' sum and its largest init container, and they carry the same reservation.
Every pod reserved is what the `resource-limits` row of [The deployment's capability report](#the-deployments-capability-report) measures, so on a Kubernetes deployment it is `present` with or without a `resources` block;
its detail names the pods, if any, that are `Burstable`.

One number frees nothing at run time.
Under gVisor every process of a pod already used whatever the pod had free (below), so the pod's peak must fit its reservation:
an issue pod on the production cluster that still ran its own builds, measured at 1-minute resolution, used its whole 19Gi for minutes while its reviewer ran a review (2026-10-21).

**Guaranteed or Burstable.**
The kubelet's QoS class reads cpu and memory alone (the disk bound's request under its limit changes no pod's class).
A deployment that sets no `cpu_request` or `memory_request` below its limit runs only `Guaranteed` pods:
each reserves its peak for its whole life and bursts past nothing, and it is never the class the kubelet evicts first under node memory pressure.
An issue pod given a lower request — `issue: {memory: 32Gi, memory_request: 8Gi}`, for issues whose `lean` processes each map a few GiB at import and can pass 20 GiB on a large proof, but which use little between builds
— is `Burstable`, as is the controller's pod given a lower `controller` request; the image probe pod stays `Guaranteed`.
The init containers carry the same reservation, so they never raise the pod's effective request above its container's.
The scheduler and the pool's limits count the requests, so more pods fit a node and a request-billed cluster bills less.
The cost is that the burst is not reserved:
a node whose pods together use more memory than it has is under memory pressure, and the kubelet evicts `Burstable` pods using more than their request before any `Guaranteed` pod, or the kernel OOM-kills the container.
Either stalls the tree as an OOM kill of a `Guaranteed` pod does — the pod is relaunched and its roles resume their sessions, but the turn in flight is lost.
Request at least what the issue's roles need to boot and to idle together, and set a `Burstable` pod only where losing a turn under pressure is cheaper than reserving the peak.

On GKE Autopilot, which bills a pod by its requests, a pod on the default general-purpose platform or the `Balanced` or `Scale-Out` class is honoured a request below its limit only in a cluster that supports bursting:
GKE 1.30.2-gke.1394000 or later on cgroup v2, with the GKE-managed `efficiency-daemon` DaemonSet running (`kubectl get daemonset -n kube-system efficiency-daemon`);
a cluster that does not support it sets each limit to the request, so the issue pod above would run `Guaranteed` at an 8Gi limit ([Resource requests in Autopilot](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/autopilot-resource-requests#resource-limits), "Setting resource limits in Autopilot").
A pod that requests an accelerator or a specific machine series (the `Performance` class) can burst on any GKE version that supports that hardware.
Where it can burst, a general-purpose, `Balanced` or `Scale-Out` pod bursts only into the node's burstable capacity
— the sum of the requests of the pods on that node, plus a small buffer Autopilot adds for its system pods
— and GKE terminates containers in lower-QoS pods first when memory use passes it;
a `Performance`-class or accelerator pod bursts into the node's allocatable instead ([Configure Pod bursting in GKE](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/pod-bursting-gke#burstable-capacity), "Bursting availability in GKE" and "Burstable capacity in GKE").
That node is itself sized from the requests:
GKE adds up the cpu, memory and ephemeral-storage requests of the pods and DaemonSets that will run on the new node and rounds them up to the nearest machine type in the series that holds them, and Autopilot bills that VM ([Optimize Autopilot Pod performance by choosing a machine series](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/performance-pods#how-gke-selects-machine-type), "How GKE selects a machine type" and "Pricing"; all three pages read 2026-10-18).
So on Autopilot every class sets the burst ceiling from the requests.
Legion's issue and controller pods carry `cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "false"`, which on Autopilot gives each a node of its own whenever possible ([Anatomy of a Sandbox pod](#anatomy-of-a-sandbox-pod)), so on the general-purpose platform an issue pod's ceiling is about its own requests, whatever its limits say:
with `issue: {memory: 32Gi, memory_request: 8Gi}` the pod requests 8Gi and never reaches its 32Gi limit.
On a `Performance` node the ceiling is those requests rounded up to a machine type, and a lower request still picks a smaller, cheaper VM.
To give an issue real headroom on Autopilot, raise its request rather than its limit alone.

The `issue` default is the size INFRA's issue pods have run at since dispatch://INFRA-3504's roll (read 2026-11-25), with heavy builds and whole test suites run outside the pod ([Configuration](#configuration)).
An issue pod on the production cluster that still ran its own builds was measured on 2026-10-09, under `GOMAXPROCS=3`:
`go test ./...` of `packages/daemon` peaked at about 1.45 GiB of summed RSS, a cold `go build ./...` at about 0.97 GiB, `bun test` of a plugin package at about 1.2 GiB, Biome and `bun install` at about 0.8 GiB each and `tsc` at about 0.75 GiB.
A role's Oh My Pi process was about 1 GiB after half an hour of work, and a headless Chromium's largest process about 0.45 GiB.
A role's Go test lane, its agent and a browser summed to about 3.9 GiB, and a `Guaranteed` pod OOM-killed mid-turn stalls its tree.
A deployment whose roles still run heavy builds and whole test suites in the pod sizes `issue` from those readings, not from the default.

Legion sets no affinity itself (GKE Autopilot adds its own to an annotated pod, [Anatomy of a Sandbox pod](#anatomy-of-a-sandbox-pod)):
each pod owns its volume and shares nothing with another pod, so the scheduler bin-packs it wherever the `legion` pool has room for its reservation, and Karpenter adds a node under the pool's limits when none has, of the smallest type the pool's requirements allow.
In production (read 2026-10-08) those are `instance-cpu Gt 3` and `instance-memory Gt 65535`, so the floor is an 8-vCPU, 64 GiB type whose allocatable is about 7.9 CPU and 60.8 GiB:
a 2 CPU / 8 GiB issue pod fits, three per node (7.9 / 2 by cpu, where 60.8 / 8 would place seven), cpu the binding dimension.
On GKE Autopilot each issue and controller pod tends to get a node of its own instead ([Anatomy of a Sandbox pod](#anatomy-of-a-sandbox-pod)), so node count there tracks pod count rather than this three-per-node packing.
The scheduler puts a pod with a kept volume only in the zones of the first pod that mounted its claim, one zone for a zonal disk and two for a regional disk, wherever else the pool has room ([A kept volume on a microVM pod](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod)).
The **controller's** pod, whose Sandbox owns its claim, and an issue pod with a kept volume are the pods that wait on a volume when they are relaunched onto another node:
each one's `ReadWriteOnce` volume must detach from the old node first, which shows as transient `FailedAttachVolume` or `Multi-Attach` events until the old pod is gone; then it runs on.
Every other **issue** pod waits on neither: its disk is the pod's own generic ephemeral volume, so a replacement takes no predecessor's claim and nothing detaches (INFRA-80).
What it may wait on instead is the predecessor's claim being *reaped*
— the kubelet and the garbage collector removing it with its pod
— which is a different mechanism with different events, and which [The disk dies with its pod](#the-disk-dies-with-its-pod) covers.

Under gVisor the container cgroup changes nothing inside the sandbox:
`runsc` sizes the sandbox from the pod's cgroup, so inside a pod `nproc` is max(2, ⌈Σ cpu limits⌉)
— except on GKE Autopilot's container-optimized compute platform, where a sandboxed pod reads `nproc` 2 whatever it reserves and whatever its host holds (measured 2026-11-05 at 2, 2.5, 3, 4 and 6 CPU, each on an 8-vCPU node, dispatch://INFRA-928/artifact/measurements-2026-11-05-md):
there the pod's own cgroup cpu quota (`cpu.cfs_quota_us`/`cpu.cfs_period_us`) read Σ cpu limits exactly at each of those sizes, which is why that quota, not `nproc`, is what [the live proof](../scripts/e2e/README.md) asserts there,
while a pod of the same cluster placed on a node of a named machine series (`cloud.google.com/machine-family`) read 3 at a 3-CPU limit, its whole reservation, where the rule above holds
— and `/proc/meminfo`'s `MemTotal` is about Σ memory limits of the pod's containers, and an active role may use the pod's whole reservation while its siblings idle.
The reservation is the pod's working set, and its request is what the scheduler counts.
Measured on INFRA's pool on 2026-11-05, a pod's own processes on that platform reached about 1.3 to 1.9 cores whether the pod reserved 2, 2.5 or 3 CPU (1.321, 1.367 and 1.392 cores over 300-second runs on one node, and 1.8227 cores in a running issue pod at a 3-CPU limit), so reserving more cpu there bought that workload little more work ([kubernetes/kubernetes#91665](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/91665), "Actual CPU capacity is lower than assigned CPU capacity when gVisor sandbox is enabled").

**The bound.**
Concurrently running issue pods are bounded by the nodes the pool's `limits.cpu` and `limits.memory` let Karpenter make: Karpenter counts each node's whole capacity against those limits, not the pods' requests, and stops making nodes once a limit is reached ([NodePools](https://karpenter.sh/docs/concepts/nodepools/), `spec.limits`).
Karpenter checks the limits eventually consistently, because it provisions in parallel, so a rapid scale-out can make nodes past a limit (the same page).
At the defaults three pods fit a floor node, so `limits.cpu: 256` makes about 32 floor nodes and places about 96 two-CPU pods (less what the nodes' daemonsets hold), and a larger instance type places more, up to the 128 two-CPU pods that 256 CPU holds; `limits.memory` divided by 64 GiB, a floor node's memory, bounds the nodes too when that is the smaller, three pods to each (a `Burstable` issue pod's lower request places more on each node)
— where the tree-volume layout ran one tree per node, each pinned to a node of its own.
`admission_cap` counts the issues the daemon has started, not the pods: an issue holds no admission slot in `accepting`, `retro` or `merging`, and, save three roots that keep theirs, none while it waits on another issue in a phase that keeps one (`docs/site/src/content/docs/legion/concepts.md`, "Admission and the `legion` label"), and its pod can stand where it holds no slot — through its acceptance, its retro and its merge; while it waits on another issue, from the release of its slot for that wait until it takes a slot again; while it owes its worker a start and waits in the line for a slot, as after a merge sends it back to work; and, past the close, during each look of its production check.
So the issue pods a deployment runs at once are at most `admission_cap`, plus the issues standing in `accepting`, `retro` or `merging`, plus the issues that released their slot to wait on another issue, plus the issues owed a start that wait in the line for a slot, plus the production-check looks open at that moment.
Fewer run than that bound, for two reasons.
Under the default idle release a pod with no turn in progress and no turn due for ten minutes is released with its disk (a [kept volume](#a-kept-volume-on-a-microvm-pod) stays) while its slot stands, and the daemon makes the pod again at that issue's next turn; `idle_minutes: 0` turns the release off, and a pod then stands from its issue's first role start to its close, and again for each look of a production check after it.
And an open issue of a live tree is not a running pod by itself: a child the daemon has not started yet has no slot and no pod, and neither has any issue of a tree whose root still waits in the line.
A pod the pool cannot place stays `Pending`, unscheduled;
once it has been for longer than `worker_boot_timeout_seconds` the boot watchdog reads it dead ([Liveness rules](#liveness-rules)), one launch failure, its relaunch meets the same pool, and the claim fails once its launch failures run out
— no later than its registration deadline.
Two pods beside the issue pods count against the same limits:
the image probe pod, its own 500m / 1Gi, present at every boot and daemon restart for as long as the probe runs;
and, under `controller: daemon`, the controller's pod, 1 CPU / 4Gi at the default, for as long as the daemon runs.
Size the pool's limits for the nodes that bound needs, three default issue pods to a floor node, plus room for those two pods, since `admission_cap` counts the issues the daemon has started rather than the pods kept by an issue in `accepting`, `retro` or `merging`, by an issue that released its slot to wait on another issue and by a production check.

A pool with no room for the probe pod itself does not refuse the boot.
The probe pod stays `Pending` with `PodScheduled=False Unschedulable`;
once it has been so for longer than `worker_boot_timeout_seconds` — the same bound the liveness rules give an issue pod, long enough for Karpenter to add a node when the pool's limits allow one, so a cold pool scaling up is not read as full
— the attempt ends waiting on capacity (`stuck`, `internal/runtime/sandbox/probe.go`).
That stop can always fire within the attempt:
the attempt's own budget is derived from `worker_boot_timeout_seconds` whenever `slow_command_timeout_seconds` would otherwise leave it less room (`ProbeBudget`, "Image size and pull time" above), so the attempt outlives the boot timeout by construction.
Ending the attempt, its Sandbox deleted, the daemon logs `boot probe is waiting on capacity; running it again` with `probe=worker image`, the pod's name and the scheduler's own reason in `detail` (`probe pod
legion-probe-<project>-<digest12> is Unschedulable: 0/83 nodes are available: 25 Insufficient cpu …`) and `retryIn`, the probe's longest interval, 5 min.
It then creates the probe Sandbox again, as many times as it takes:
such a wait is counted against none of the probe's six attempts (`bootprobe.Run`, `Outcome.Waiting`), since a full pool says nothing about the image and a daemon that exited would not make room.
The daemon stays up through it, but serves nothing yet:
the probe runs before the API is served (`plan.probe` precedes `serve` in `internal/daemon/daemon.go`), so `legion state` answers nothing while the probe waits, and the log is where the wait shows.
Once a probe pod is placed and passes, the `pool-capacity` row of [The deployment's capability report](#the-deployments-capability-report) records how many attempts waited and the scheduler's last reason, open until `capabilities.decided.pool-capacity` names a reason;
a boot whose probe pod scheduled at its first attempt reads it `present`.

**The node-disk bound.**
Pods of unrelated trees share a node, and what an issue pod writes outside every volume
— the `roles` container's root filesystem (the image's own content and whatever a recipe writes outside the told directories) and the `role-homes` disk `emptyDir`, which holds each role's home overlay and its `/tmp` and `/var/tmp` (the issue's temporary directory, its cache and data homes and bun's install cache are one set its roles share on the issue's volume, each role's state home is a separate directory there, and the two Go caches are one pair on that volume shared by the issue's roles)
— is the node's disk, the node's allocatable ephemeral storage (its root volume; read it with `kubectl get node <n> -o
jsonpath='{.status.allocatable.ephemeral-storage}'`).
That disk must hold the sum of the pods' actual disk use, which Σ of their `ephemeral_storage` limits bounds above:
an issue pod's limit is 80Gi at the default, its request 6Gi.
A pod past its limit is evicted — the offending issue's pod alone
— rather than the node reaching `DiskPressure`, where the kubelet evicts by its own ranking and another tree's pod can go.
The request is what the scheduler counts against the node's allocatable ephemeral storage;
at the default 6Gi it binds little, so a node's disk can be oversubscribed by the pods' limits.
In production (read 2026-10-09) the Legion node class carries one 700Gi gp3 root device, and a node's allocatable ephemeral storage is about 629 GiB of it;
with CPU and memory placing about three issue pods per node at the defaults, their limits sum to about 240Gi of those 629 GiB, so the bound has room before any request is raised.
An operator with a known root volume raises `ephemeral_storage_request` toward the issue's expected use so the scheduler reserves disk and places no pod a full node could not hold.

**GKE Autopilot's bound is per pod, not per node.**
The node-disk framing above is AWS/self-managed EKS's:
ephemeral storage there is the shared node's own root volume, and raising `ephemeral_storage_request` toward an issue's real use is an operator's own call, bounded only by what the node has.
GKE Autopilot has no such headroom: Warden, its admission webhook, caps ephemeral storage at 10Gi for the sum of a pod's main containers and 10Gi for each init container (server dry runs on the production cluster, 2026-10-24:
two init containers at 10Gi beside a 10Gi main container are admitted; a main container at 11Gi is refused, `Total ephemeral-storage
requested by containers … higher than the Autopilot maximum of '10Gi'`;
an init container at 11Gi is refused, `Max ephemeral-storage requested by init containers …`), and it clamps a container's limit to its request.
The init containers carrying the pod's reservation add nothing against that cap, so a GKE deployment sets `issue: {ephemeral_storage: 10Gi, ephemeral_storage_request: 10Gi}`:
the issue pod's whole 10Gi, shared by its six roles.

### The memory guard in an issue pod

An issue pod's six roles share one memory limit, and under gVisor the host kernel sees the pod's sandbox and not the processes in it:
a container that passes its limit is stopped whole, `OOMKilled`, and every role's turn ends with it ([Liveness rules](#liveness-rules)).
The memory guard in the pod's launcher, where the deployment runs it (it is on by default), acts before that point.
When the pod's anonymous memory reaches a share of the limit, the guard ends with `SIGKILL`, of the processes that are neither Legion's own nor an agent's own, the process that grew the most over its last few reads, else the largest one it has read at most once in its last two readings near the limit, else the one that grew the most since the guard's first kill while the reading stays near the limit, else the largest, a fork that still runs its parent's program counted by what it holds over its parent, and, from halfway between that share and the limit, every process that grew over its last few reads and, where one it may end is not new to its stay near the limit, every one that grew since the guard's first kill in that stay, every one that started during that stay and is no fork with memory of its own, and every one new to that stay with memory of its own, each a kill of its own, and the daemon tells the role of each process it ends why, on the role's own topic.
The rest of the pod goes on: the guard never ends a role's agent, its shim or its `role-init`, so no role's turn ends for the kill, and the command that was ended fails in the turn that ran it.
The guard is `packages/daemon/internal/memoryguard`, and the launcher runs it with the issue pod's rules (`serveMemoryGuard` and `podClassifier`, `packages/daemon/internal/launcher/memoryguard.go`).

Measured on 2026-11-14 in gVisor test pods with memory limits of 4, 8 and 19 GiB, in the tester's `wc-gvisor` result at `bebc420b` (dispatch://INFRA-3557, from the Jobs of dispatch://INFRA-3557/artifact/wc-gvisor-jobs-md):
with the guard off, the kernel stopped the sandbox when `AnonPages` was 95.5% to 99.4% of the limit;
with the guard on at the defaults, each growing process — 64 MiB every 0.25 s, 256 MiB every 0.25 s, shared anonymous memory, a memfd written and never mapped, and a grower beside an unwritten 16 GiB memfd or with about 1 MiB of arguments — was ended when the reading was 85.0% to 90.0% of the limit, 8.8 to 14.7 ms after the guard's first reading at the mark, and the pod went on.
The earlier runs of those Jobs, recorded in the same issue's `wc-gvisor` results, put the kernel's lowest kill point at 95.4% (the tester's run at `bde5a751`) and took up to 36.9 ms to decide (the implementer's 8 GiB run of shared anonymous memory at `d6f81bbf`).

**Where it runs.**
Only a launcher that is its container's first process, PID 1, runs the guard: the `legion launcher` of an issue pod's `roles` container ([Anatomy of a Sandbox pod](#anatomy-of-a-sandbox-pod)).
Only that process sees every process of the container, and every process that no `role-init` holds is its own; the rules below rest on both.
A launcher started any other way writes one `off` line and runs no guard.
The launcher of the controller's pod runs a guard with rules of its own ([The memory guard in the controller's pod](#the-memory-guard-in-the-controllers-pod)).
Where `session_database.writer_audience` is set, the controller's launcher runs the roles-dir form as its container's first process, and the guard it runs there is this one, over the controller's `role-init`, at the settings the daemon hands the controller's pod (`serveMemoryGuard`).
A microVM issue pod's launcher runs no guard: the pod's own kernel stops one process rather than the whole pod, and the launcher runs the guest watch in the guard's place ([Memory in a microVM pod](#memory-in-a-microvm-pod)).

**What it reads.**
Each interval, `interval_milliseconds` (100 ms by default), the guard reads two files: `AnonPages` of `/proc/meminfo`, the pod's anonymous memory, which is its reading, and the cgroup's `memory.limit_in_bytes`, the container's limit.
Each of the two reads took 0.025 to 0.044 ms at the median in the read-cost Job of dispatch://INFRA-3557/artifact/wc-gvisor-jobs-md (`infra-3557-19g-readcost-fbf6z`, 2026-11-14).
The guard never acts on the cgroup's counter, `memory.usage_in_bytes`, because the counter also counts the pages of the files a process maps, which the kernel can take back:
in the tester's `wc-gvisor` result at `bebc420b` a file mapped and read raised the counter to 97.2% to 105.4% of the limit, and an LMDB map larger than the limit raised it to 107.4% to 134.9%, while `AnonPages` stayed under 11% and the guard ended neither process.
One read of the counter took about 18 ms at the median in a running INFRA issue pod of six roles, measured on 2026-11-14, and 0.04 ms in that read-cost Job, so the guard reads it every 5 seconds for its hourly line and once at each kill, never between a reading and the kill it sends at that reading, and never each interval.
In the band below the mark, at or above the mark and after a kill it also lists the container's processes and reads the sizes of those it may end, by which it chooses what to end ("What it ends", below);
at the first reading at or above the mark, where the band read sizes, it reads before its kill at most the `smaps` of the processes the band found, with the `exe` link and arguments of those the band read running their parent's program, and, where those show no growth or the reading is at or above the urgent share, one listing of the processes and, within half an interval, the files of the newest of those started since the band's last reading, and it reads every size only after its kill.
At or above the urgent share, where the processes it may end at that reading hold one that is not new to the stay, it reads on after its kills, up to one interval from the reading at the mark, the files and `smaps` of the processes new to the stay that those reads did not reach ("What it ends", below).
At or above the urgent share after a kill, once the processes it killed have exited or the wait has passed, it reads the `smaps` of the processes it read at the reading before first, and lists the processes and reads the rest only after the kills those reads send ("After a kill: the rise rule", below).
Where `AnonPages` or the limit cannot be read, where the limit reads as no limit (2^62 bytes or more), where the system has no `pidfd_open`, through which the guard ends a process, or where the guard cannot list the processes of `/proc`, the guard writes one `off` line and does nothing more while the launcher runs.

**What it ends.**
The mark is `act_percent` of the limit (85 by default), and the band is the 10% of the limit below the mark, from 75% to 85% of the limit at the default.
At each reading in the band or above it, before a kill and after one, the guard lists every process of the container, finds the ones it may end (below) and reads their sizes.
It reads no size below the band, none while it is off, and none after it has given a rise up until the reading goes below the mark: a pod below its band pays for its readings alone.
The list leaves out a zombie or a dead process, state `Z` or `X` in its `stat`, whose `status` counts one thread or none:
it holds no memory, and under gVisor its `exe` link answers `EACCES`, which would otherwise count it unread.
A process in either state whose other threads still run is one whose main thread alone has exited: the guard keeps it in the list as a live process, and counts it unread, since its `exe` does not read ("What it does not do", below).
It measures each process it may end from its `/proc/<pid>/smaps`: the sum of its `Anonymous:` lines, plus the resident size (`Rss:`) of each of its shared maps of memory-backed files, which are `/dev/zero (deleted)` (shared anonymous memory), `/memfd:…`, `/dev/shm/…` and `/SYSV…` (`smapsSize`, `proc.go`).
Shared anonymous memory and a memfd raise `AnonPages` while their pages read 0 in `Anonymous:`, so without the second term a process that grows that way would not be seen.
It also adds each memfd the process holds open by a file descriptor and has not mapped shared, at its size as `stat` reads it through that descriptor or the pod's `Shmem` reading at the decision, whichever is less (`heldMemfdBytes`, `proc.go`):
ending the process frees that memfd's pages too, and no line of its smaps shows them.
`Shmem`, the pages of the pod's memory filesystems and memfds, bounds those pages where the size does not: an unwritten memfd made large with `ftruncate` has its size and no pages, and under gVisor neither its size nor its block count shows its pages, so in an 8 GiB gVisor pod on 2026-11-14 the holder of an unwritten 16 GiB memfd, counted at that size, was ended first and freed nothing, and the kernel stopped the sandbox.
A memfd counts once: one that a process the guard measures maps shared counts through that map's `Rss:` alone, and one that several of them hold by a descriptor counts for the largest of them by its smaps.
A map of a file on disk adds nothing, which is why a process that maps a database is not ended for its map.
A region that several processes map counts in each of them, since gVisor gives no `Pss` that would divide it.
The guard keeps the sizes it reads of each process for 300 ms, by the process's pid and start time, so a process that takes the pid of one that ended has no earlier read.
It ends the most grown process first.
A process's growth over the window is its size at this reading less its size at its oldest read in the last 300 ms, and a growth under 1 MiB is none.
A process with no earlier read in that window, a fresh fork among them, has not grown.
Of the processes that did not grow over the window, the ones new to this stay in the band that hold memory of their own come next, the largest first.
A stay in the band is the guard's readings in a row in the band, at the mark and after a kill, since it last read no size (below the band, while it was off or after it gave a rise up), and a process is new to it where the two readings before the one the guard decides at did not both read it: the guard has read it at most once since the band's second-to-last reading.
Such a process has no earlier read to grow from, or one alone, and can be a runaway that began between two readings or just before the band's last one.
Where the stay holds fewer than two readings before the one decided at, every process is new to it, which leaves the order by size; at the first reading at or above the mark, a process counts as new only where a read at that reading reached it (below).
A process new to the stay that ranks at nothing, a fork whose parent's size covers its own (below), is not in this tier: it has told the guard nothing of its own, and the tiers below rank it.
Of the rest, the ones that grew by 1 MiB or more since the first kill of this stay in the band come next, the most grown first; before the stay's first kill no process has grown since one.
A process's growth since that kill is its size at this reading less its size at the reading the first kill was sent at.
For a process the guard first read only after that kill, it is its size less 0 where that first read is not a fork's read (below), and less that first read where it is one, so a fork has not grown at that first read.
A process the guard read before that kill has its size as of it by the same test, each read with its own flag ("After a kill: the rise rule", below).
By INFRA-3368's architect's decision of 2026-11-20T08:13Z on INFRA-3531 R1 of spec version 43, such a process holds memory of its own, and this tier is there so that a grower comes before a process that never grew:
at `28732f65`, in `8g-latepool-r2`, the guard first read five of six growers after the stay's first kill, took those first reads as their sizes as of that kill, saw none grown since, and its third kill ended the probe's 4.8 GB parent by `rule=largest` while four of them lived.
Whether the guard goes on after a kill (below) still takes such a first read as the process's size as of the kill.
It is measured from the stay's first kill, not the previous one, because growers that step every 250 ms in step with each other show no step in the 100 ms after the previous kill:
at `d22d8da3`, in `4g-latepool-kxv5k` and `4g-latepool-zxhnw`, the two kills after a fall went by `rule=largest` to the probe's parent and a sleeping fork while the growers rose from 90.6% to 95.9% of the limit, 7.3 MiB and 40.9 MiB below that wave's kill point (dispatch://INFRA-3531/artifact/t17k-2026-11-18-tar-gz).
A reading below the mark that is still in the band ends a rise and not the stay, so a rise that follows such a dip measures from the stay's first kill, which a rise before it sent; the stay ends, and with it those sizes, only below the band, while the guard is off or where it gives a rise up.
It counts across such a dip because at `15bdbd3c`, which let those sizes go at any reading below the mark, in `8g-latepool-r2`, `8g-latepool-r3` and `8g-latefork2-r1` one grower was left, the reading sat about 2 MB below the mark and came back, and the first kill of that second rise, seeing no growth since the dip, ended the probe's 4.8 GB parent by `rule=largest sizes=reread new_read=0:0` (dispatch://INFRA-3531/artifact/tester-evidence-15bdbd3c-2026-11-18-tar-gz).
At `43213c99`, which keeps them across such a dip, `8g-latepool-spqk2`'s reading dipped 1.9 MiB below the mark and stayed in the band, and the first kill of its second rise ended the grower by `rule=grew sizes=reread`, as three more second rises of that wave ended growers (dispatch://INFRA-3531/artifact/t17p-2026-11-18-tar-gz).
A reading that cannot read a process the pod still runs, its `smaps` or its `exe` unreadable at that reading, takes none of these from it: the process keeps its sizes as of the kills, its reads in the stay and its reads in the window, and its growth is measured from them when the guard reads it again, though it counts as new to the stay until two readings in a row have read it.
Only a process that has ended, or whose pid now names another process, loses them, since otherwise a grower whose one read failed would count as not grown, behind a larger process that never grew.
The processes that fit none of these come last, largest first, so where none grew and none is new to the stay with memory of its own the guard ends the largest.
Where the tier of the processes new to the stay, or the last tier, ranks by size, a process that runs its parent's executable with its parent's arguments, read whole, where the guard has read that parent in this stay, is a fork that has not run a program of its own:
it ranks by its size less its parent's size at the guard's latest read of the parent, and by nothing where its parent's size is the larger.
Under gVisor such a fork reports the pages it shares with its parent as its own, so a sleeping fork ranks near nothing, and a fork that grows ranks by what it holds over its parent.
A fork that ranks at nothing is not in the tier of the processes new to the stay, however new it is (above).
A fork whose parent the guard has not read in this stay (a protected parent, or one no reading of this stay could read), and one that runs another executable or the same one with other arguments, rank at their whole size.
The guard compares the arguments whole: where the first 4 KiB it reads of the two lists are equal and either was cut there, a list of exactly 4 KiB included, it reads both `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` files whole at that decision, once for each parent however many forks it has, and a file it cannot read is no match.
At the first reading at or above the mark, with each `smaps` it reads again of a process the band found running its parent's program, its parent among the band's processes, the guard reads that process's `exe` link and arguments again before the discount applies, within the same half interval and one interval as those reads (below).
A process that has run another program since the band read it ranks at its whole size, and one whose `exe` link cannot be read is left out of that decision, as one whose `smaps` cannot be read is; the listing after the kill reads it.
A process the band found whose `smaps` the reading at the mark does not read again keeps the program the band read, and where one of them grew by the band's sizes below the urgent share (below) the guard reads nothing before the kill: growth puts the first one first there, and the discount orders only processes of equal growth.
It reads the program again because the band can read a process between its fork and its exec, while it still runs its parent's program and reports its parent's pages:
at `18c3c5bb`, `4g-latepool-djcvt` ended a grower the band had read so with its whole size taken off (`rule=grew sizes=reread less_parent=31051776`), and `4g-latepool-rjm8m`'s first kill ended the probe's 2.4 GB parent by `rule=largest sizes=reread` 115.1 ms after the reading at the mark, while the growers the band had read so ranked at nothing (dispatch://INFRA-3531/artifact/t17n-2026-11-18-tar-gz).
The parent itself ranks at its whole size, so where nothing grew and no process new to the stay holds memory of its own, a pool's parent can be ended before its forks by `largest`, and its end frees nothing while the forks hold the pages, as a fork's end did before.
Growth over the window and since a kill, the floor and the `ended` line's `size` count each process's own size whole: the discount only orders.
