— `runtime.kubernetes.resources.controller` where the file sets a field, the daemon's default of 1 CPU and 4Gi otherwise
— as request and limit alike unless the file sets a lower `cpu_request` or `memory_request`, so at the default the pod is `Guaranteed`, never the class the kubelet evicts first under node memory pressure (a lower request makes it `Burstable`, [Issue sizing](#issue-sizing-one-reservation-per-pod), "Guaranteed or Burstable");
the image probe pod carries its own, smaller reservation, not the controller's, so a controller reservation the pool cannot place leaves the probe, and the boot, unaffected ([Issue sizing](#issue-sizing-one-reservation-per-pod)).
Its launcher, as PID 1 of that container, runs in a gVisor pod the memory guard, which near the limit ends, of the processes that are neither Legion's own nor the agent's own, the process that grew the most over its last few reads, else the largest one it has read at most once in its last two readings near the limit, else the one that grew the most since the guard's first kill while the reading stays near the limit, else the largest, a fork that still runs its parent's program counted by what it holds over its parent, and, from halfway between the mark and the limit, every process that grew over its last few reads and, where one it may end is not new to its stay near the limit, every one that grew since the guard's first kill in that stay, every one that started during that stay and is no fork with memory of its own, and every one new to that stay with memory of its own ([The memory guard in the controller's pod](#the-memory-guard-in-the-controllers-pod)).
In a microVM it runs the guest watch in the guard's place ([Memory in a microVM pod](#memory-in-a-microvm-pod)).

**The pod under `writer_audience`.**
Where `runtime.kubernetes.session_database.writer_audience` is set ([Selecting the store](#selecting-the-store)), the `controller` container runs the launcher's roles-dir form for its one role: `legion launcher --roles-dir /var/run/legion/roles --role controller` (`controllerPod.rolesDirContainer`, `podkind.go`).
The launcher refuses the writer audience in the single-role form, whose agent runs in the container's own namespaces, where the writer token would be in its view.
The container lays out its volumes as an issue pod lays out one of its roles (`rolesDirLayout`).
The launcher token, the gh files and the private, state and agent-secrets key directories are under `/var/run/legion/roles/controller`, and the role homes volume is at `/var/run/legion/roles/.homes`.
Every mount at or under `/home/legion` is under `/var/run/legion/home` instead (`homeMountsView`).
The container mounts the writer token at `/var/run/legion/roles/session-writer`, and the broker's tokens once for the pod where it enrolls (`podTokenMounts`).
It mounts nothing at the fixed paths of the single-role form: `/var/run/legion/launcher`, `/var/run/legion/private`, `/var/run/legion/state`, `/var/run/legion/gh` and `/var/run/legion/agent-secrets`.
role-init starts the controller's generation in namespaces of its own and binds the controller's own gh, private, state and agent-secrets key directories back at those paths, but not its launcher token.
So the controller's agent finds each directory where it always has, and it reads neither the writer token nor the launcher token.
The roles-dir form changes five things for the controller:

- The memory guard knows the controller's processes by the `role-init` above them, as an issue pod's guard knows each role's (`podClassifier`), in place of `controllerClassifier`, and it spares what an issue pod's guard spares in a role.
  Before the daemon's first answer it runs at an issue pod's defaults, and that answer hands it `runtime.kubernetes.memory_guard.controller_pod`'s settings, as in the single-role form (`launcherHelloAck`).
  In a microVM the launcher is told `--microvm` and the metadata endpoint's flags, with the endpoint's token at `/var/run/legion/roles/workload-identity`, and runs the guest watch over the same classifier, with role-init's drain (`controllerPod.rolesDirContainer`, `serveMemoryGuard`).

- The git lock sweep finds no clone, because the container's working directory is `/legion`, which is no jj workspace, and no start of the controller names a workspace.
  It writes one line, `launcher: the git lock sweep's working directory "/legion" is no jj workspace it can sweep (…); it takes its workspace from the first role start`, and then sweeps nothing (`newGitLockSweep`, `internal/launcher/gitlocks.go`).

- The launcher's lines for the role, and the lines of the controller's shim and Oh My Pi, carry the prefix `controller: ` in the container's log, as each role's lines do in an issue pod.

- A process that the controller's generation leaves running after its shim exits gets role-init's drain: SIGTERM over the role's namespace, two seconds (`roleNamespaceDrain`), then SIGKILL (`runRoleShim`, `internal/launcher/roleinit_linux.go`).
  In the single-role form, the launcher as PID 1 gives such a process up to `--stop-grace` (`cleanExitedGeneration`).

- The controller's home overlay, its `/tmp` and `/var/tmp` and its own config home are on the role homes volume, a disk `emptyDir` that counts against the controller pod's ephemeral storage ([Issue sizing](#issue-sizing-one-reservation-per-pod)).

Without the member, the controller's pod is the pod this section describes above.
A writer audience added, dropped or changed is a moved session store (`movedSessionStore`), so the next launch into the controller's pod replaces it.

The Sandbox is the claim's alone, where an issue's is its tree's.
A release of the claim (a switch back, or `legion claims stop`) deletes it, and its role Secret and volume with it.
The orphan sweep keeps it while the controller's claim is not retired, running or suspended, so a suspended controller's session survives, and deletes it once the claim is retired.
The sweep reads the claim from the store again under the pod's launch turn, so a controller launched after the sweep read the daemon's claims keeps its Sandbox.
Either delete runs under the pod's launch turn and only at the version of the Sandbox it was decided on:
a controller relaunched into the Sandbox since has written it, so the delete is refused, the daemon logs `sandbox runtime: kept a sandbox written since its
delete was decided; the orphan sweep decides it again` naming it, and the next sweep decides again.
The controller Sandbox a daemon made before the controller ran in a launcher pod (`role=controller`, one `worker` container), and the one a daemon of the tree-volume layout made (a claim template named `tree`), are refused at boot like every Sandbox of a layout before this one, each named:
remove it before enabling issue pods ([Upgrading a deployment with running trees](#upgrading-a-deployment-with-running-trees), step 3).

**Reaching it.**
Nobody types into the pod.
A person reaches the controller through Dispatch (a message to its session on the Agents page, a reply to its ask, a mention) or Envoy, and reads its session with `kubectl -n <namespace> logs legion-<project>-controller -c controller` (its launcher's log, which carries the shim's and Oh My Pi's) or its session in the session database, where every session is a row rather than a file on any volume.
A Send from the Agents page is answered in the conversation that page shows.
Wakes reach it as they reach the operator's controller: it subscribes to `notifications.legion.<project>.controller` once it holds the role.

**Switching back.**
To hand the controller back to a person, set `controller: operator` (or drop the key), drop `runtime.kubernetes.resources.controller`, which the daemon refuses at boot unless `controller: daemon`, and restart the daemon.
At boot, before it re-adopts or relaunches anything, that daemon stops the controller's claim the earlier boot left, unless it is retired already:
its Sandbox is released and the claim retires (`legion claims list` shows it `retired`), logged as `controller: stopping the controller an earlier boot under controller: daemon launched; this daemon
leaves the controller to its operator`.
Then, whether it stopped the claim at this boot or found it retired, it ends the controller record's registration while the record still names that claim's session, minting it a capability nobody holds, logged as `controller: ending the registration of the
controller an earlier boot under controller: daemon launched; this daemon leaves the controller to
its operator`; a record naming another session, the operator's controller's once it has registered, or none, is left as it is.
The file store left a residual here — a controller whose session died with its volume, switched back before its fresh launch registered, left the record naming a dead session the switch back would not end
— and the table closes it: a session outlives the pod and the volume it ran on, so the claim this daemon stops still records the session the record names.
A daemon that cannot stop the claim refuses to boot, naming it (`stop legion-<project>-controller, …`), with the record untouched;
one that stopped it but cannot end its registration refuses naming it too (`end the registration of
legion-<project>-controller, …`), and the next boot, finding the claim retired, ends it.
The claim route refuses a launch of that claim on such a daemon (409, `legion-<project>-controller is a
launch of the daemon's own controller, and this daemon leaves the controller to its operator
(controller: operator)`), and the token of an earlier launch is an invalid boot token, so no pod of the daemon's can replace the operator's registration.
Then start the controller with `legion
controller start` ([Operator-launched controller](#operator-launched-controller)).
Releasing the Sandbox deletes the controller's volume with it, and with the volume the working root its pods shared, but not its session, which is a row in the session database.
So switching to `controller: daemon` again relaunches the claim after the keeper's first one-minute wait, on fresh budgets, and the controller comes back on the conversation it recorded, in a pod whose `/legion` is empty.
A `legion claims stop` of the controller under `controller: daemon` releases it the same way, so the keeper's retry after it brings the same session back on the same empty root.

**Rolling back the image.**
A daemon built before LEGION-592 cannot run against a database a `controller: daemon` daemon used:
it lists the controller's claim as an issue keyed `""`, which every agent's plugin refuses.
Nothing deletes a claim row, and a switch back only retires this one, while that release lists every claim of its project whatever its state or role.
With the row present, every agent's `read_record` fails, and the operator's controller cannot claim, since its boot check reads the project from `GET /healthz` before it registers and that release answers that route without a `project` (`packages/pi-legion/src/controller-session.ts`).
So the fallback from `controller: daemon` is `controller: operator` on this release, never the previous image.
A revert that cannot be avoided goes in this order:

1. Remove `controller` and `runtime.kubernetes.resources.controller` from `legion.yaml`:
   the earlier release refuses both as unknown keys, and without them this release runs `controller: operator`.
   Restart this release with that file and let it boot once.
   Do not skip this boot: only this release ends the stopped controller's registration.
   It also releases the controller's Sandbox and volume itself, which the earlier release's orphan sweep would otherwise do at its first boot:
   that sweep counts no retired claim as known, so it takes a retired claim's Sandbox as readily as one whose row is gone.
   The boot is done when `legion claims list` shows `legion-<project>-controller` `retired`.
   If the boot is refused, stop here and follow the refusal's entry in troubleshooting.

2. Stop that daemon: the earlier release must not run beside it for the same project, and while it runs it still holds the claim in memory, so any write of that claim would put the row back.

3. Read the row, then delete it.
   `<project>` is the project's token: `project` in `legion.yaml` lowercased, with every character outside `a-z0-9` dropped, so `project: LEGION` gives `legion-legion-controller`; `legion claims list` shows it.
   Run `select token, state from claims where token = 'legion-<project>-controller';` and check it returns exactly one row, in state `retired`.
   Then run `delete from claims where token = 'legion-<project>-controller';` and check it answers `DELETE 1`;
   its pending delivery, if any, goes with it (`on delete cascade`).
   Delete by token, never by role: several projects' daemons can share the database.
   If either check shows anything else, do not start the earlier release.

4. Start the earlier release.

### Operator-launched controller

Under `controller: operator` the daemon launches no controller, under either runtime:
it has no process of the controller to start or resume, and it stops at boot the claim of one an earlier boot under `controller: daemon` launched ([Switching back](#daemon-launched-controller)).
It holds the controller's record and reads the session's liveness from the Envoy role registry, and says when no controller is registered ([Controller liveness](#controller-liveness)).

**The operator token.**
`operator_token_file` in `legion.yaml` names a file holding one long random string (`openssl rand -hex 32`).
The Go daemon requires it under every runtime, because the operator routes that spawn and drive claims authenticate against it as well as the controller's (`operator_token_file is required: the operator routes that spawn and drive claims authenticate
against the bearer it names`).
It is read once at boot, and is never an environment variable or a flag.

**The operator-side file.**
`legion controller start` reads a small file of its own, never the daemon's `legion.yaml`, whose loader would run both GitHub Apps' `private_key_command` on your machine and demand keys the controller never uses.
`deploy/kubernetes/daemon/controller.yaml.example` is the complete shape:
the same key names as `legion.yaml`, only the fourteen the controller needs (`project`, `daemon_url`, `operator_token_file`, `envoy_url`, `envoy_token_file`, `nats_urls`, `nats_nkey_seed_file`, `dispatch_url`, `dispatch_token_file`, `dispatch_token_broker`, `instructions`, `omp_invocation`, `omp_launch_prefix`, `state_dir`;
`nats_nkey_seed_file` is the Go CLI's alone, which the TypeScript CLI refuses as unknown).
Any other key is refused naming it and the example (`unknown key "runtime" in the
controller configuration; legion controller start reads only … — see
deploy/kubernetes/daemon/controller.yaml.example`);
`nats_urls` is required;
`dispatch_url` goes with exactly one Dispatch credential — `dispatch_token_file`, the bearer a file holds, or `dispatch_token_broker: true`, this machine's own identity traded at the secrets broker — and the load refuses the two together and either with no `dispatch_url`, while a `dispatch_url` naming neither is the start's refusal, since the loader reads no environment and only a trade proves the broker route (`dispatch_url is configured with no Dispatch credential: …`);
and relative paths resolve against the file's own directory, with no `~`.
The operator token and the NATS nkey seed each sit in a file only you can read (mode 0600):
a group- or world-readable one is refused naming the path and mode (`… is readable by its group or
others (mode 0640); chmod 0600 it`).
The daemon's read of either of its seeds holds a file it owns to the same rule, and lets the group read only a root-owned file, as a pod's kubelet-mounted Secret is ([Configuration](#configuration)).

**Starting it.**
Run `legion controller start --config controller.yaml`, where `daemon_url` (or `--daemon-url <url>`, which replaces it) is the daemon's API as your machine reaches it.
In order, and keeping nothing until the daemon has answered, the command:

1. reads the file and refuses as above, the operator token file others can read included;
   then refuses a stdin that is not a terminal (``stdin is not a terminal: Oh My Pi would run headless
   print mode, …; run `legion controller start` at a terminal``), since given step 6's positional word with no terminal Oh My Pi runs headless print mode, which would run the start command only after step 3's mint had revoked the running controller;
   then a `dispatch_url` whose file names neither Dispatch credential, a blank or unreadable Envoy or Dispatch token file, a secrets broker that refuses this machine under `dispatch_token_broker` (which also refuses a machine proving no identity and a deployment naming no broker), a `nats_nkey_seed_file` that is blank, unreadable, readable by its group or others, or holds no nkey user seed, a missing or blank instructions file, and an Oh My Pi invocation that does not resolve;

2. reads the `repositories` block of the daemon's unauthenticated `GET /legion/v1/state`, and refuses a daemon that does not answer, a body with no `repositories` object, and a `live` entry that is not `owner/name`;
   an empty `live` list, or one whose every repository a role App is missing from, launches the controller all the same, its addressing naming the owners the review App is installed on, or saying it is installed on no owner, so the controller has no GitHub owner, while `legion state` names each repository a role App cannot work and why.
   Then it probes that Oh My Pi as the controller will run it, with `omp models`, which starts no session, and refuses a pi-legion it does not load, or one speaking another daemon API contract, loaded without pi-envoy or with a pi-envoy at another plugin interface version, or loaded beside the pre-split package;

3. asks `POST /legion/v1/controller/secret` with the operator token as `Authorization: Bearer` and the contract step 2 held the plugin to (`{"pluginContract": <N>}`).
   The daemon compares the token in constant time, then refuses a contract that is not its own with 409, naming both, before it mints anything, so a `legion` and a daemon from different releases never cut the running controller off.
   Otherwise it mints a fresh controller capability, which replaces the previous one and its registration and ends every controller grant: the last start wins.
   The answer also carries the daemon's `gates.design` as the list of steps it gates (`designGateSteps`, empty for a deployment that gates none), and an answer that names no list, or one naming a step that is not `decisions`, `criteria` or `spec`, is refused with a request to upgrade the daemon;

4. writes the secret 0600 under the local state directory (`state_dir`, by default `$XDG_STATE_HOME/legion/<project>-controller`), beside the `legion` launcher and the deployment instructions;

5. asks `POST /legion/v1/controller/github-credential` with the capability step 3 minted (`{"secret": <capability>}`).
   The daemon compares the capability's hash in constant time under its controller lock and answers the review App's read-only token for every owner that App is installed on, each reaching every repository that owner's installation holds and rendered as gh's two files (`owners`, each owner's `hosts` and `config`, `default`, the first owner, `app`, `expiresAt`, the soonest expiry, `renames`, the configured pairs the bundle routes a moved repository by, each `<owner>/<name>` as GitHub spells it, which a project configuring none answers without, and `installed`, the owner accounts the review App is installed on, lowercased and sorted, read with the bundle, which the first fetch names in the controller's addressing because `owners` cannot say it: a bundle also holds a directory for an owner a configured rename moved a repository away from, and none for an installed owner whose lease GitHub refused), which the command writes as a gh bundle under `<state_dir>/gh`, one 0700 directory per owner and the pairs in the root's `renames.txt` (`hosts.yml` 0600 through a temp file and rename), printing `[legion] the controller's gh acts as the review App for owners
   <owners> (read-only) from <dir>; this process refreshes the tokens before they expire
   (<expiresAt>)`.
   While Oh My Pi runs, a goroutine re-fetches every minute, asking for the default the first answer named (`"default"` in the request), and rewrites only the owners whose `hosts.yml` changed, logging each change, failure and stop to `<state_dir>/github-credential.log` (never to the terminal, never a token);
   a 403 `INVALID_CONTROLLER_CAPABILITY` (a later start replaced the capability) or 409 `CONTROLLER_LAUNCHED` ends the loop, and the files last until the tokens' expiry
   — the loop's lifetime is Oh My Pi's, not the command's signal context.
   Against a daemon with no GitHub App (500 `GITHUB_TOKEN_SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE`) or whose review App is installed on no account (500 `GITHUB_OWNER_UNCONFIGURED`, `the review App is installed on no account, so the controller has no GitHub owner`; the code keeps its name for the clients already deployed), the command empties the 0700 `gh` directory, prints the line of that code, and runs no loop:
   `[legion] the daemon has no GitHub App to act as; the controller's gh acts as nobody` for the first, and `[legion] the review App is installed on no account, so the controller has no GitHub owner; the controller's gh acts as nobody` for the second, where the App exists.
   Any other failure of this fetch (unreachable, 403, 409, 502) exits 1 naming the route and the daemon's sentence, and Oh My Pi never starts:
   the mint in step 3 has already replaced the incumbent, as every post-mint failure does.
   Before step 3 the command finds the real gh its session's `gh` wrapper runs:
   the operator's `LEGION_GH_PATH`, or the first `gh` on its PATH that is not the state directory's own wrapper, and refuses to start with neither (`gh is not on PATH`) or when that first `gh` is a script, a `gh` wrapper of the operator's machine that would answer in place of the review App;

6. runs Oh My Pi interactive in the foreground (`omp_launch_prefix` and `omp_invocation`, one `--append-system-prompt` naming the file `<state_dir>/secrets/<controller claim>-<run>-system-prompt.md`, this run's own, which the command writes first and removes when Oh My Pi exits, and which holds the controller prompt, the daemon's `Design gate steps:` line, the project's repositories sentence and the deployment instructions, then the one positional word `/legion-controller-start`, no `--resume`, no `--mode rpc`) with the controller's environment (`LEGION_CONTROLLER=1`, `LEGION_ROLE=controller`, `LEGION_DAEMON_URL`, `LEGION_PROJECT`, `LEGION_STATE_DIR`, `LEGION_CONTROLLER_START_MESSAGE` (Oh My Pi runs the positional word once its startup is over and its TUI listens, and pi-legion's command of that name claims the controller and sends the message as the session's first turn, which the operator sees, can type during and can interrupt with Esc;
   it sends it once the controller is registered, right before the role claim and the live wake subscription, so the controller's first turn runs its start procedure deterministically, with nothing typed, rather than racing a card or a wake for the session's one first-turn slot
   — LEGION-392), its grant and secret files, `LEGION_GH_OWNERS_DIR` naming `<state_dir>/gh` (the bundle step 5 wrote), `GH_CONFIG_DIR` its default owner's directory (the bundle's root, empty, when the daemon has no GitHub App), `LEGION_GH_PATH` the real gh, with `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN` and `GH_HOST` emptied, so nothing inherited outranks the files, the Envoy and Dispatch endpoints, `PERSON_SIGNIN_TRADE=off` (the controller's own broker credentials trade this machine, never its operator's sign-in), and `NATS_NKEY_SEED_FILE` naming `nats_nkey_seed_file` when the file sets it) on top of the operator's own environment, less `NATS_DAEMON_NKEY_SEED` and `NATS_DAEMON_NKEY_SEED_FILE` (the controller is pane-side, and never gets the daemon's seed) and less `LEGION_BOOT_TOKEN` and `LEGION_BOOT_TOKEN_FILE` (a start from inside a Legion pane inherits that pane's, and the plugin takes a controller carrying one for a daemon-launched controller), and exits with Oh My Pi's exit code.

A refusal before the secret is written removes the directories made for the probe, so the state directory is as it was.

**How the daemon sees it.**
The session's pi-legion extension registers on `POST /legion/v1/claims/register` with the capability and takes the controller role.
The daemon records `controllerLocator: {runtime, external: true, sessionId, registeredAt}` (`legion state
--json`, `GET /legion/v1/state`), `runtime` being the daemon's own.
On every orphan sweep it reads `GET /v1/roles/legion-<project>-controller` from the Envoy listener with its bearer.
The controller is alive while the listener names the recorded session as the role's holder, which it does only for a session inside its own live window (`ENVOY_SESSION_LIVE_WINDOW`, 5 minutes by default); the daemon keeps no staleness window of its own to drift from it.
It is gone when the listener answers 404 for a role nobody claimed or for a holder it reports `gone`, when another session holds the role, and when a listener of an earlier release answers 404 naming no `holder_state` at all.
It is unknown, never gone, when the listener reports the holder `unresponsive` — past the live window but inside the gone horizon, its claim kept, which a session stalled under load reads as — and when the listener is unreachable, refuses with anything but a 404, or answers a body the probe cannot read.

**Re-running and failing.**
Running the command again mints a new capability and takes the role.
Closing the terminal leaves the project without a controller until you run it again.
Failures name what to fix:

- a wrong token: `<daemon_url>/legion/v1/controller/secret: the daemon answered 403 Forbidden: Invalid
  operator token — the operator token does not match the daemon's operator_token_file`;

- an unreachable daemon: `could not reach the Legion daemon at <daemon_url>: …; is the port-forward
  running? (never falls back to another address)`.
